skill.approach.paed.rapport.title: Establishing paediatric rapport and communication
skill.approach.paed.rapport.oneLine: Engage the parent and child through play, calm pacing, and eye-level dialogue before physical touch
skill.approach.paed.rapport.why: A frightened, crying child cannot be examined reliably: tachycardia, tachypnoea, abdominal guarding, and vocalisation mask real pathology. Establishing mutual trust with both the caregiver and the infant or toddler before initiating examination is essential for accurate clinical evaluation.

steps.text: Greet the accompanying caregiver warmly and acknowledge the child by name without invading personal space immediately.
Position yourself at eye level with the child rather than towering over them.
Allow the child to observe you conversing calmly with the parent before making direct physical contact.
Use a familiar toy, torchlight, or warm stethoscope bell as a playful bridge to demystify instruments.
Perform non-threatening visual observation from a comfortable distance before laying hands on the patient.

skill.approach.paed.rapport.practice: Role-play entering a consultation room with a toddler seated on a caregiver lap. Practise engaging the parent first, descending to eye level, and introducing a stethoscope playfully without triggering distress.
pitfalls: Approaching the child abruptly with cold instruments or unwashed hands before establishing rapport.
Ignoring the child completely and directing all conversation exclusively to the accompanying adult.
Towering over a small child on an adult examination couch while wearing intimidating formal clothing.
Attempting invasive manoeuvres such as throat examination early in the consultation.

probes.q: Why should you observe an infant from a distance before touching them?
probes.a: Direct touch or disturbing the child can induce crying, which artificially alters respiratory rate, heart rate, and abdominal softness.

probes.q: How does engaging the caregiver first help put a fearful young child at ease?
probes.a: Young children take emotional cues from their primary caregiver; seeing their parent interact calmly with the doctor signals safety and reduces fear.

probes.q: A 2-year-old child screams every time the stethoscope approaches their chest. What techniques can you use to complete auscultation?
probes.a: Allow the child to hold or touch the stethoscope bell, demonstrate it on the parent or a toy first, warm the diaphragm, and auscultate while the child is held on the mother lap or during quiet pauses.

rubric.text: Greets caregiver and addresses child warmly by name
Lowers posture to child eye level
Observes child breathing and interaction before touching
Introduces instruments playfully and warms stethoscope bell

sources.locator: diseases_of_infancy_and_childhood: Clinical pearls and evaluation
The Field of Pediatrics: Clinical Evaluation of the Child

teach.heading: The triangle of paediatric communication
teach.body:
Paediatric assessment is never a two-way dialogue: it is a triangular relationship between clinician, caregiver, and child.

Infants and toddlers look to the parent for cues of safety. Winning the parent confidence relaxes the child, whereas a clinician who ignores the child fosters anxiety and active refusal.

teach.heading: Order of inspection and examination
teach.body:
Unlike adult practice, paediatric examination does not proceed strictly from head to toe.

Always inspect undisturbed vitals first from a distance while the child is calm. Perform chest auscultation and gentle abdominal palpation early, and leave distressing procedures such as throat inspection and otoscopy for the very end.

skill.approach.paed.consent_assent.title: Parental consent and paediatric assent
skill.approach.paed.consent_assent.oneLine: Obtain informed parental permission and developmentally appropriate child assent before examination
skill.approach.paed.consent_assent.why: Children lack legal capacity to grant independent informed consent; ethical and legal standards mandate that parents or guardians grant proxy consent. However, failing to explain procedures to older children and ignoring their assent breeds medical distrust and physical resistance.

steps.text: Introduce yourself and explain the purpose, scope, and sequence of the clinical examination to the parent or guardian.
Ensure the legal guardian is present in the cubicle throughout the entire encounter.
Explain each step to the child using age-appropriate, non-frightening vocabulary.
Seek verbal or affirmative behavioural assent from children aged seven years and older.
Pause or modify the examination if the child shows severe distress, unless immediate emergency life-support is required.

skill.approach.paed.consent_assent.practice: Rehearse explaining an abdominal and chest examination to the mother of an 8-year-old child, followed by explaining the same manoeuvres directly to the child to secure their assent.
pitfalls: Assuming parental consent allows rough or forced physical examination of a terrified older child.
Failing to explain to the parent what manoeuvres will be performed, causing maternal alarm.
Examining an adolescent without clarifying privacy, chaperone availability, and confidentiality boundaries.

probes.q: What is the distinction between informed consent and assent in paediatric clinical practice?
probes.a: Informed consent is the legally binding permission provided by the parent or legal guardian, whereas assent is the affirmative agreement of the developmentally capable child.

probes.q: At what approximate developmental age should a clinician routinely seek assent from a paediatric patient?
probes.a: Children around seven years of age and older generally have sufficient cognitive maturity to understand simple procedures and participate in assent.

probes.q: During an elective clinical examination, an alert 9-year-old child adamantly refuses to allow abdominal palpation despite maternal consent. How do you proceed?
probes.a: Do not restrain the child. Pause, address the child specific fears, demonstrate the manoeuvre on the parent hand or your own, and gently negotiate agreement before touching.

rubric.text: Secures explicit parental permission with clear explanation of procedures
Explains steps to the child in simple language to seek assent
Ensures chaperone or parent presence throughout the physical examination
Respects child modesty and avoids unnecessary exposure

sources.locator: diseases_of_infancy_and_childhood: Clinical pearls and evaluation
Paediatrics: Doctor-Patient-Parent Communication and Ethics

teach.heading: Dual consent framework in paediatrics
teach.body:
In paediatric ethics, autonomy is shared and evolving.

The parent or guardian holds legal authority to give proxy informed consent. Meanwhile, the child has moral personhood: seeking assent honours their dignity and fosters a lifelong therapeutic partnership with healthcare.

teach.heading: Age-adapted explanations
teach.body:
Children under seven require comfort, simple sensory previews, and parental proximity rather than formal assent discussions.

For school-age children and adolescents, explain what will happen, why it helps them feel better, and what sensations to expect. Never tell a child a procedure will not hurt if it will produce discomfort.

skill.approach.paed.positioning.title: Age-appropriate positioning for child examination
skill.approach.paed.positioning.oneLine: Adapt physical positioning across infants, toddlers, and older children to optimise comfort and clinical signs
skill.approach.paed.positioning.why: Placing an infant or toddler supine on a cold adult examination table triggers distress, vigorous crying, and voluntary guarding of the abdominal wall. Adapting the position to the child developmental stage preserves calm and ensures accurate physical findings.

steps.text: Assess the child developmental age and emotional state before deciding on the examination location.
Examine neonates and young infants on an examination cot under a radiant warmer or on the parent lap with warm hands.
Position infants aged six to twenty-four months seated on the mother lap facing forward or hugging the mother chest.
Conduct heart and lung auscultation from behind or over the mother shoulder while the child remains relaxed.
Transition older cooperative children to a reclined or supine position on the couch with a parent standing immediately beside them.

skill.approach.paed.positioning.practice: Demonstrate three distinct positioning setups: auscultating an infant over the mother shoulder, palpating a toddler abdomen on the parent lap, and inspecting an adolescent chest on a couch.
pitfalls: Insisting on forcing an unwilling toddler flat onto a high examination table.
Exposing the entire body of a newborn simultaneously, precipitating hypothermia.
Attempting abdominal palpation while a child hips and knees are fully extended and rigid.

probes.q: What is the optimal position to examine an unsettled 10-month-old infant?
probes.a: Seated or reclining comfortably on the parent lap, often hugging the parent chest or facing outward.

probes.q: Why should an infant knees and hips be slightly flexed during abdominal palpation?
probes.a: Flexing the hips and knees relaxes the rectus abdominis and anterior abdominal muscles, facilitating deep palpation.

probes.q: How does examination position differ between an infant undergoing respiratory assessment and an adolescent?
probes.a: An infant is best examined on the parent lap or over the shoulder to avoid crying, whereas an adolescent is examined sitting upright and then reclined at 45 degrees with appropriate draping.

rubric.text: Positions infant or toddler securely on caregiver lap
Maintains environmental warmth and exposes only the region being examined
Flexes lower limbs gently during abdominal palpation
Reassures child continuously throughout positional adjustments

sources.locator: diseases_of_infancy_and_childhood: Clinical pearls and evaluation
The Field of Pediatrics: Physical Examination of the Infant and Child

teach.heading: Developmental staging of the examination setting
teach.body:
Physical positioning must follow developmental psychology.

Young infants under six months tolerate a warm flat cot if comforted by a soother or maternal voice. Toddlers between six months and two years exhibit intense stranger anxiety and must remain on the parent lap.

teach.heading: Specific positions for specific organs
teach.body:
Chest auscultation is easiest with the toddler facing the mother chest while you listen from behind.

Abdominal palpation can be conducted with the child semi-reclined in the mother arms, using the mother hand resting gently under yours to dissipate apprehension and voluntary muscle guarding.

skill.hx.paed.presenting_complaint.title: Paediatric presenting complaints and illness history
skill.hx.paed.presenting_complaint.oneLine: Elicit chronological complaints from the caregiver and assess systemic functional impact
skill.hx.paed.presenting_complaint.why: Children cannot provide a structured medical history themselves; relying on unstructured caregiver narrative risks missing critical timeline clues and red-flag symptoms. Eliciting complaints chronologically alongside feeding, activity, and elimination changes establishes the disease severity.

asks.text: Note who the primary informant is, their relationship to the child, and assess their reliability.
What main problems caused you to bring the child to hospital? Elicit symptoms in the caregiver own words.
How long has each symptom been present? List complaints in chronological order of onset with precise durations.
Explore each symptom: onset, progression, aggravating or relieving factors, and diurnal or postural variations.
How has this illness affected the child feeding, fluid intake, activity, and alertness?
Ask about bowel frequency, stool consistency, and urine output frequency over the past 24 hours.

skill.hx.paed.presenting_complaint.practice: Practise taking presenting complaints from a caregiver for a child with fever and cough, organizing them into a strict chronological list with durations and documenting functional feeding impact.
pitfalls: Writing medical diagnoses such as bronchopneumonia instead of caregiver-reported symptoms such as cough and fast breathing.
Failing to ask about urine output and fluid intake in an infant with acute fever or vomiting.
Recording complaints in the haphazard sequence they were narrated rather than true chronological order of onset.

probes.q: What are the essential elements required when recording a paediatric chief complaint?
probes.a: The symptom reported by the informant and its exact chronological duration, arranged in order of appearance.

probes.q: Why is urine output frequency a mandatory inquiry in any acutely unwell infant?
probes.a: Urine output is the most sensitive bedside functional marker of systemic hydration, renal perfusion, and fluid balance in children.

probes.q: A mother states her child has been having asthma attacks for two weeks. How should this complaint be formulated in the case record?
probes.a: Document the primary caregiver symptoms with durations, such as recurrent episodes of breathlessness and wheezing for two weeks, rather than accepting the diagnostic label.

rubric.text: Identifies informant relationship and assesses reliability
Lists complaints chronologically with individual durations
Elicits impact on feeding, activity level, and urine output
Inquires about diurnal, postural, or seasonal variations

sources.locator: diseases_of_infancy_and_childhood: Clinical pearls and evaluation
The Field of Pediatrics: Pediatric History Taking

teach.heading: The anatomy of paediatric chief complaints
teach.body:
The chief complaint is the chronological framework of the paediatric encounter.

Always record the informant identity and credibility. List symptoms in chronological order with exact durations. Never write a diagnosis as a complaint: write fever for 3 days and rapid breathing for 1 day, never pneumonia.

teach.heading: Functional red flags in childhood illness
teach.body:
Children manifest acute illness through physiological decompensation of baseline routines.

Always interrogate three vital functional pillars: feeding volume (has intake dropped below half?), alertness (is the child lethargic or irritable?), and urine output (at least 4 to 6 wet nappies or normal urination in 24 hours).

skill.hx.paed.birth_antenatal.title: Antenatal and maternal history
skill.hx.paed.birth_antenatal.oneLine: Screen maternal health, infections, drug exposures, and fetal growth across three trimesters
skill.hx.paed.birth_antenatal.why: Adverse intrauterine events directly determine neonatal viability and long-term neurodevelopment. Identifying maternal TORCH infections, gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, teratogenic drugs, or fetal growth restriction provides the diagnostic key for congenital anomalies and developmental delays.

asks.text: Was the pregnancy planned, confirmed early, and registered with an antenatal clinic?
Did the mother experience fever with rash, lymphadenopathy, or joint pains in the first trimester?
Were there any drug exposures, herbal remedies, radiation, or unprescribed medications taken during organogenesis?
When was quickening first felt, and were routine antenatal ultrasound anomaly scans reported normal?
Did the mother develop hypertension, proteinuria, swelling, or elevated blood glucose during the second or third trimester?
Were tetanus toxoid (or Td) immunisations and iron-folic acid supplementation received as per national guidelines?

skill.hx.paed.birth_antenatal.practice: Take an antenatal history from the mother of a child presenting with microcephaly and developmental delay, systematically exploring first-trimester fevers, rash, and scan results.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about first-trimester fever with rash in a child presenting with congenital heart defects or cataracts.
Overlooking maternal gestational diabetes in a neonate presenting with macrosomia, jitteriness, or hypoglycaemia.
Assuming antenatal history is irrelevant in an older child presenting with short stature or intellectual disability.

probes.q: Why is the first trimester especially vulnerable to maternal teratogenic insults?
probes.a: The first trimester encompasses embryonic organogenesis, when major organ systems form and are vulnerable to malformations.

probes.q: What fetal and neonatal risks are linked to maternal pregnancy-induced hypertension and pre-eclampsia?
probes.a: Uteroplacental insufficiency causing intrauterine growth restriction, oligohydramnios, preterm birth, and neonatal respiratory distress.

probes.q: A child presents with sensorineural deafness, cataract, and patent ductus arteriosus. What specific maternal history should be interrogated?
probes.a: First-trimester maternal febrile illness with maculopapular rash and retroauricular or suboccipital lymphadenopathy, indicative of congenital rubella syndrome.

rubric.text: Inquires about antenatal care registration and routine ultrasound scans
Screens systematically for first-trimester fevers, rash, and drug exposures
Checks for gestational diabetes, hypertension, and anaemia
Documents maternal tetanus toxoid vaccination and iron-folate intake

sources.locator: neonatal_sepsis_congenital_long_case: Maternal risk factors and neonatal presentation
The Fetus and the Neonatal Infant: The High-Risk Pregnancy

teach.heading: Trimester-by-trimester inquiry
teach.body:
Structure maternal inquiry chronologically across gestation.

First trimester focuses on teratogens: fevers with rash (rubella, CMV), radiation, and abortifacient drugs. Second trimester reviews quickening (typically 16 to 20 weeks) and anomaly scans. Third trimester screens for pre-eclampsia, bleeding, and fetal growth restriction.

teach.heading: Maternal metabolic and nutritional health
teach.body:
Maternal systemic conditions alter fetal metabolic programming.

Gestational diabetes leads to fetal hyperinsulinaemia, macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycaemia. Maternal severe anaemia, hypertension, or poor weight gain impairs placental transfer, producing symmetrical or asymmetrical fetal growth restriction.

skill.hx.paed.birth_natal_neonatal.title: Natal and neonatal transition history
skill.hx.paed.birth_natal_neonatal.oneLine: Detail delivery events, immediate birth cry, resuscitation, and nursery transition milestones
skill.hx.paed.birth_natal_neonatal.why: Perinatal asphyxia, birth trauma, prematurity, and neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia are leading causes of cerebral palsy, developmental delay, and sensory deficits. A detailed natal and neonatal history pinpoints the timing and severity of hypoxic or metabolic brain injury.

asks.text: What was the gestational maturity at delivery (preterm, term, or post-term in completed weeks)?
Where was the delivery conducted (home, primary centre, hospital) and what was the mode of delivery?
Did the baby cry immediately at birth, or was there delayed crying, bag-and-mask ventilation, or chest compressions?
What was the birth weight, and was it appropriate for gestational age?
Within how many hours was breastfeeding initiated, and did the baby feed vigorously?
Did the neonate experience jaundice, seizures, cyanosis, fever, or require admission to a neonatal nursery?

skill.hx.paed.birth_natal_neonatal.practice: Practise eliciting a natal history from a mother whose child has spastic diplegia, clarifying gestational maturity, birth cry delay, and NICU phototherapy or ventilator support.
pitfalls: Failing to ask specifically whether the infant cried immediately after delivery versus requiring active resuscitation.
Not recording neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion or phototherapy in a child with choreoathetosis.
Confusing term low birth weight with prematurity by omitting completed weeks of gestation.

probes.q: Why is the immediate birth cry a critical milestone in neonatal transition?
probes.a: An immediate vigorous cry indicates successful pulmonary expansion, clearance of lung fluid, and effective independent respiration.

probes.q: What is the clinical definition of low birth weight, and how is it distinguished from prematurity?
probes.a: Low birth weight is a birth weight under 2500 grams regardless of gestational age, whereas prematurity refers to birth before 37 completed weeks of gestation.

probes.q: A child with cerebral palsy had severe neonatal jaundice with lethargy and arched back posturing. What mechanism accounts for this outcome?
probes.a: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia crossed the blood-brain barrier and deposited in the basal ganglia, leading to acute bilirubin encephalopathy and kernicterus.

rubric.text: Ascertains gestational age in completed weeks and birth weight
Documents immediate birth cry or details of neonatal resuscitation
Inquires about timing of breastfeeding initiation
Screens for neonatal jaundice, seizures, or special care admission

sources.locator: neonatal_seizures_asphyxia_long_case: Perinatal events and neonatal reflexes
The Fetus and the Neonatal Infant: Delivery Room Emergencies

teach.heading: The natal transition audit
teach.body:
Natal history reconstructs the critical minutes of transition from intrauterine to extrauterine life.

Elicit place of delivery, skilled attendance, amniotic fluid character (meconium staining), and duration of rupture of membranes. An immediate vigorous cry demonstrates adequate respiratory drive and cardiac output.

teach.heading: Neonatal nursery vulnerabilities
teach.body:
Events in the first four weeks of life leave permanent neurological footprints.

Screen for neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia requiring phototherapy or exchange transfusion. Inquire whether delayed feeding, jitteriness, hypothermia, or convulsions required nursery admission or intravenous dextrose therapy.

skill.hx.paed.development.title: Developmental history across four domains
skill.hx.paed.development.oneLine: Evaluate developmental milestones across gross motor, fine motor, personal-social, and language domains
skill.hx.paed.development.why: Developmental delay is often insidious and missed during routine visits until significant disability sets in. Systematic domain-specific assessment distinguishes isolated motor, speech, or social deficits from global developmental delay and detects neurodevelopmental regression.

asks.text: Assess gross motor milestones: neck holding (3 mo), sitting without support (8 mo), standing without support (12 mo), walking (15 mo).
Assess fine motor and adaptive skills: bidextrous grasp (4 mo), transfer of objects (6 mo), pincer grasp (9-12 mo), scribbling (15-18 mo).
Assess personal-social milestones: social smile (2 mo), recognises mother (3 mo), stranger anxiety (6 mo), waves bye-bye (9 mo).
Assess language and communication: cooing (3 mo), monosyllables (6 mo), bisyllables (9 mo), words with meaning (12 mo), short sentences (2-3 yr).
Has the child ever lost previously acquired milestones, suggesting neurodegenerative regression?
Inquire about vision and hearing responses: turns to voice, tracks light, startled by sound.

skill.hx.paed.development.practice: Take a complete developmental history from a mother of an 18-month-old child, eliciting key milestones in each of the four domains and calculating developmental age.
pitfalls: Assuming developmental delay without correcting for prematurity in an infant born before 37 weeks.
Asking vague questions like 'is the child doing well?' instead of querying specific verifiable milestones.
Missing milestone regression, which points to inborn errors of metabolism or neurodegenerative disease rather than static encephalopathy.

probes.q: What are the four primary domains assessed in a paediatric developmental history?
probes.a: Gross motor, fine motor and adaptive, personal-social, and language.

probes.q: At what age should an infant sit steadily without support, and why is this milestone pivotal?
probes.a: Sitting without support occurs at 8 months; it indicates maturation of trunk balance and anti-gravity postural stability.

probes.q: A child who was walking and speaking in short sentences at two years stops speaking and loses walking ability by age three. What does this indicate?
probes.a: Milestone regression, indicating a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, subacute encephalopathy, or metabolic storage disorder rather than a static cerebral palsy.

rubric.text: Evaluates all four developmental domains systematically
Applies corrected age for prematurity up to two years of life
Asks specifically about loss of previously attained skills
Verifies basic vision and hearing responses

sources.locator: growth_short_stature_long_case: WHO velocity and developmental assessment
Growth, Development, and Behavior: Developmental Assessment

teach.heading: The four pillars of development
teach.body:
Development reflects central nervous system maturation and must be charted across four separate streams.

Gross motor tracks head control, sitting, and locomotion. Fine motor charts visual-motor and pincer coordination. Personal-social traces emotional interaction and autonomy. Language captures receptive and expressive communication.

teach.heading: Red-flag milestones and regression
teach.body:
Developmental red flags demand urgent formal evaluation.

Key red flags include absent neck holding by 4 to 5 months, unable to sit unsupported by 9 to 10 months, not walking by 18 months, or absent single words by 18 months. Any loss of previously established milestones is a red flag for metabolic or degenerative disorders.

skill.hx.paed.diet_infant.title: Infant feeding and breastfeeding history
skill.hx.paed.diet_infant.oneLine: Assess breastfeeding initiation, exclusivity, latching technique, and complementary feeding transitions
skill.hx.paed.diet_infant.why: Suboptimal infant feeding is the single greatest contributor to under-five malnutrition, recurrent diarrhoeal illness, and stunting. Eliciting breastfeeding exclusivity, bottle use, and complementary food hygiene reveals the root causes of failure to thrive.

asks.text: When was breastfeeding started after birth, and were any prelacteal feeds (honey, sugar water, animal milk) given?
Was the infant exclusively breastfed for the first six completed months of life without water or teas?
What was the frequency of day and night feeds, and did the mother feel her breasts softened after feeding?
Was bottle feeding or artificial teat feeding introduced, and how were bottles cleaned and sterilised?
At what exact age were complementary semi-solid foods introduced, and what food items were offered?
How thick was the complementary food, how frequently was it fed daily, and who prepared and fed it?

skill.hx.paed.diet_infant.practice: Interview a mother of an 8-month-old infant with poor weight gain, systematically assessing breastfeeding adequacy, latching symptoms, and the consistency and frequency of complementary feeds.
pitfalls: Equating exclusive breastfeeding with giving water or herbal teas alongside breast milk.
Failing to ask about bottle feeding, which carries a severe risk of bacterial contamination in low-resource settings.
Prescribing vitamin supplements without identifying watery, nutrient-dilute complementary feeds as the cause of malnutrition.

probes.q: What constitutes exclusive breastfeeding according to national and international guidelines?
probes.a: Giving only breast milk from the mother or wet nurse, with no other liquids, water, or solids, except vitamins, minerals, or medicines, for the first six months.

probes.q: Why are prelacteal feeds strongly discouraged in newborn care?
probes.a: Prelacteal feeds introduce enteric pathogens, delay colostrum intake, blunt the infant suckling reflex, and interfere with lactogenesis.

probes.q: A 9-month-old infant is fed only thin dal water and watery rice gruel twice a day. Why does this lead to severe acute malnutrition?
probes.a: Clear dal water and watery gruel have very low caloric and protein density, providing excessive bulk with negligible energy and nutrients.

rubric.text: Screens for prelacteal feeds and colostrum administration
Verifies exclusive breastfeeding duration up to six completed months
Checks for use of feeding bottles or artificial nipples
Details age of onset, consistency, and daily frequency of complementary feeds

teach.heading: The golden standards of early infant feeding
teach.body:
Optimal infant feeding hinges on three non-negotiable milestones.

First, initiate breastfeeding within one hour of birth and ensure early colostrum is consumed. Second, practice exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months. Third, introduce energy-dense complementary foods at six completed months while continuing breastfeeding up to two years.

teach.heading: Complementary feeding pitfalls in India
teach.body:
In Indian households, the commonest nutritional error is giving watery liquids rather than thick mashed feeds.

Dilute dal water or thin rice water provides negligible energy (under 10 to 15 kcal per 100 ml) while distending the small infant stomach. Complementary feeds must be thick enough to stay on a spoon without running off.

skill.hx.paed.diet_calorie_protein.title: Dietary recall and calorie-protein deficit calculation
skill.hx.paed.diet_calorie_protein.oneLine: Conduct a 24-hour dietary recall and calculate energy and protein deficits against expected age norms
skill.hx.paed.diet_calorie_protein.why: Clinical impressions of diet are subjective; only a quantitative 24-hour recall with conversion into kilocalories and grams of protein objectively reveals nutritional failure. Comparing actual intake against expected requirements guides dietary counselling and rehabilitation.

asks.text: Record a step-by-step 24-hour recall of everything the child ate and drank from morning waking to night.
Quantify food portions using standard domestic containers: cup or katori (150 ml), glass (250 ml), teaspoon (5 ml), tablespoon (15 ml).
Determine quantities of raw ingredients: uncooked cereals, pulses, milk volume, oil or ghee, sugar, and animal proteins.
Calculate total daily energy (kcal) and protein intake (g) from the quantified food portions.
Determine the child expected caloric requirement using 100 kcal/kg up to 1 year, or 1000 + (100 x age in years) for older children.
Compute the caloric and protein deficit as percentages of the expected daily requirement.

skill.hx.paed.diet_calorie_protein.practice: Conduct a 24-hour dietary recall for a 4-year-old child weighing 12 kg, calculate total calories and protein consumed, and compute the percentage caloric deficit against expected requirements.
pitfalls: Recording cooked volumes without converting to raw staple amounts (e.g. cooked rice expands threefold over raw grains).
Omitting added sugar in milk or tea and cooking fat, which represent significant caloric fractions.
Failing to calculate the percentage deficit, leaving the severity of dietary restriction unquantified.

probes.q: What is the expected daily caloric requirement formula for a child older than one year of age?
probes.a: 1000 kcal plus 100 kcal for each year of age over one year, or calculated based on expected weight using the Holliday-Segar formula.

probes.q: How much energy is provided per gram by carbohydrates, proteins, and fats?
probes.a: Carbohydrates provide 4 kcal/g, proteins provide 4 kcal/g, and fats provide 9 kcal/g.

probes.q: A 3-year-old child requires 1200 kcal/day but consumes 720 kcal/day on dietary recall. What is the caloric deficit and its clinical interpretation?
probes.a: The deficit is 480 kcal/day, which is a 40 percent deficit, indicating severe caloric restriction that directly drives protein-energy malnutrition.

rubric.text: Takes complete 24-hour dietary recall using domestic measures
Converts food intake into daily calories and grams of protein
Calculates expected daily energy and protein requirements for age and weight
Computes absolute and percentage deficits for energy and protein

teach.heading: Principles of 24-hour dietary quantification
teach.body:
Dietary history translates household cooking into nutritional science.

Use standard domestic utensils: a katori holds 150 ml, a tea cup holds 150 ml, a glass holds 250 ml, and a teaspoon holds 5 ml. Remember that 100 g of raw cereal (rice, wheat) yields roughly 350 kcal and 7 to 11 g of protein, while 100 g of raw pulses yields 350 kcal and 20 to 22 g of protein.

teach.heading: Bedside requirement rules
teach.body:
Calculate target baseline requirements rapidly at the bedside.

For energy, use 100 kcal/kg/day under 1 year, and 1000 + (100 x age in years) for older children. For protein, aim for 2 g/kg/day under 1 year, 1.5 g/kg/day for 1 to 9 years, and 1.2 g/kg/day for children over 9 years. Subtract actual intake to quantify the percentage deficit.

skill.hx.paed.immunisation.title: Immunisation history and schedule verification
skill.hx.paed.immunisation.oneLine: Verify vaccination status against MCP card, inspect BCG scar, and identify due and optional vaccines
skill.hx.paed.immunisation.why: Unvaccinated or partially vaccinated children face catastrophic risks from measles, pertussis, diphtheria, and tuberculosis. Relying solely on caregiver memory leads to missed booster doses; verifying documented records and checking the BCG scar ensures accurate catch-up immunisation.

asks.text: Request and inspect the written immunisation record (Mother and Child Protection / MCP card).
Physically inspect the left upper arm for the presence, size, and character of a BCG scar.
Verify vaccines received at birth (BCG, zero-dose OPV, hepatitis B birth dose within 24 hours).
Verify primary infant vaccines at 6, 10, and 14 weeks (pentavalent, rotavirus, fIPV/IPV, PCV).
Verify 9-month and second-year vaccines (MR/MMR, JE in endemic districts, vitamin A, DPT booster).
Inquire about optional or additional IAP-recommended vaccines (typhoid conjugate, hepatitis A, varicella, influenza).
Ask about any adverse events following immunisation (AEFI) after previous doses, such as high fever or seizures.

skill.hx.paed.immunisation.practice: Examine an MCP card for an 18-month-old child, cross-check against physical presence of the BCG scar, and formulate a catch-up plan for any missed doses.
pitfalls: Relying on parental verbal assurance that 'all injections were given' without reviewing the card or checking the BCG scar.
Assuming BCG failure if no scar is visible at 2 weeks, when scars take 8 to 12 weeks to mature.
Restarting an entire multi-dose vaccine series from dose one after an interrupted interval instead of continuing.

probes.q: Where on the body is the BCG scar typically located, and when does it normally develop?
probes.a: Over the left shoulder at the insertion of the deltoid; the scar develops 8 to 12 weeks following intradermal vaccination.

probes.q: What is the rule regarding intervals when a child presents late for a scheduled multi-dose vaccine?
probes.a: Never restart the schedule; resume from the next due dose regardless of how long the interval has elapsed.

probes.q: A 10-month-old child has received no vaccines since birth. How should primary immunisation be initiated today?
probes.a: Administer BCG (up to 5 years), Pentavalent-1, bOPV-1, fIPV-1, Rotavirus-1, PCV-1, and MR-1 at separate anatomical injection sites.

rubric.text: Requests and examines written immunisation card or MCP book
Inspects deltoid insertion for BCG scar
Verifies birth, primary series, and booster vaccinations systematically
Records optional and special-circumstance vaccines received
Screens for past adverse events following immunisation

sources.locator: rabies_tetanus_diphtheria_long_case: Immunisation and post-exposure prophylaxis
Advisory Committee on Vaccines and Immunization Practices (ACVIP) Schedule

teach.heading: The three-tier immunisation check
teach.body:
Verify immunisation through three rigorous layers.

First, inspect the physical MCP card for recorded dates and batch entries. Second, examine the left upper arm for the 4 to 8 mm BCG scar. Third, categorise vaccines received into National Immunisation Schedule (NIS) components versus optional private vaccines.

teach.heading: Interrupted schedules and false contraindications
teach.body:
Two cardinal clinical principles govern immunisation practice.

First, an interrupted vaccine series is never restarted: simply continue with the next indicated dose. Second, minor upper respiratory infections, mild fever, diarrhoea, or antibiotic therapy are not contraindications to vaccination.

skill.hx.paed.family_pedigree.title: Family history and three-generation pedigree
skill.hx.paed.family_pedigree.oneLine: Construct a three-generation pedigree, screen for consanguinity, and trace inherited disease patterns
skill.hx.paed.family_pedigree.why: Many paediatric disorders (inborn errors of metabolism, thalassaemias, muscular dystrophies, cystic fibrosis) are monogenic. Consanguineous marriage dramatically increases autosomal recessive risk; a three-generation pedigree is the primary diagnostic tool to uncover familial recurrence.

asks.text: Are the parents related by blood (consanguineous marriage)? If yes, determine degree (first cousins, uncle-niece).
Construct a three-generation pedigree using standard symbols: squares for males, circles for females, shading for affected.
Record all pregnancies of the mother, including spontaneous abortions, stillbirths, and unexplained infant deaths.
Are any siblings or first-degree relatives suffering from similar complaints or chronic illnesses?
Inquire about familial history of asthma, allergies, diabetes, epilepsy, or early childhood neurological deaths.
Note whether transmission occurs from father to son (which excludes classic X-linked recessive inheritance).

skill.hx.paed.family_pedigree.practice: Draw a three-generation pedigree for a child presenting with haemolytic anaemia whose parents are second-degree cousins, calculating degree of relationship and highlighting affected individuals.
pitfalls: Writing 'family history non-contributory' without inquiring about consanguinity or early infant deaths.
Failing to ask about spontaneous abortions, which often represent lethal chromosomal or metabolic anomalies.
Drawing only one generation, obscuring recessive or X-linked skip-generation inheritance patterns.

probes.q: In standard medical pedigree drawing, what do a circle, a square, and a double horizontal line represent?
probes.a: A circle represents a female, a square represents a male, and a double horizontal line represents a consanguineous union.

probes.q: What is the genetic risk for each pregnancy when two healthy carrier parents of an autosomal recessive trait conceive?
probes.a: 25 percent (1 in 4) chance of an affected child, 50 percent chance of an unaffected carrier child, and 25 percent chance of a normal non-carrier child.

probes.q: Why does the presence of father-to-son transmission definitively rule out X-linked recessive inheritance?
probes.a: A father passes his Y chromosome to his son and his X chromosome only to his daughters; therefore, an affected father cannot transmit an X-linked condition to a son.

rubric.text: Asks specifically about consanguinity and identifies degree of relation
Constructs three generations using standard symbols
Records maternal miscarriages, stillbirths, and infant deaths
Screens for similar disorders in siblings and extended relatives

sources.locator: inheritance_syndromes_children_long_case: Pedigree analysis and Mendelian patterns
Genetics: Patterns of Inheritance and Pedigree Analysis

teach.heading: Standard pedigree conventions
teach.body:
Pedigree analysis turns family narratives into genetic geometry.

Use squares for males and circles for females. Connect spouses with a horizontal line and consanguineous partners with a double horizontal line. Descending branches denote offspring, listed chronologically from left to right. Filled symbols represent clinically affected individuals.

teach.heading: Consanguinity and recessive disorders in India
teach.body:
Consanguinity is culturally prevalent in several regions of India.

First-degree relatives share 50 percent of their genes, second-degree relatives (uncle-niece, grandparents) share 25 percent, and third-degree relatives (first cousins) share 12.5 percent. High sharing unmasks rare pathogenic autosomal recessive variants, increasing rates of inborn errors and congenital anomalies.

skill.hx.paed.socioeconomic.title: Socioeconomic and environmental history
skill.hx.paed.socioeconomic.oneLine: Determine socioeconomic class, housing standards, sanitation, and environmental health risks
skill.hx.paed.socioeconomic.why: Paediatric disease burden in India is heavily shaped by social determinants: biomass smoke causes severe pneumonia; unboiled surface water drives diarrhoeal dehydration; overcrowding facilitates tuberculosis transmission. Standardised socioeconomic scoring identifies vulnerable children requiring social and nutritional protection.

asks.text: Inquire about parental education: highest level completed by the head of the household.
Determine the occupation of the primary earning member of the family.
Ascertain total monthly family income from all sources in Indian rupees.
What type of housing does the family occupy (pucca, semi-pucca, or kutcha)?
What is the source of drinking water, and is it boiled, filtered, or consumed untreated?
What cooking fuel is utilised (LPG cylinder versus chulha/biomass/wood/cow dung) and how well ventilated is the kitchen?
What toilet and sanitation facilities are available (private flush latrine, community toilet, open defecation)?

skill.hx.paed.socioeconomic.practice: Collect socioeconomic and domestic environment data for a child presenting with severe pneumonia, classify the family under the Modified Kuppuswamy scale, and identify environmental respiratory triggers.
pitfalls: Omitting cooking fuel inquiries in children presenting with recurrent wheeze or severe pneumonia.
Relying on vague terms like 'middle class' without applying an objective validated scoring scale.
Failing to ask about drinking water purification in a toddler presenting with recurrent diarrhoeal episodes.

probes.q: What three parameters are scored in the Modified Kuppuswamy socioeconomic status scale?
probes.a: Education of the head of household, occupation of the head of household, and total monthly family income.

probes.q: Why is indoor biomass smoke (chulha) a major determinant of child morbidity in India?
probes.a: Incomplete combustion releases high concentrations of particulate matter and carbon monoxide, damaging respiratory ciliary clearance and multiplying the risk of severe pneumonia.

probes.q: A family lives in a single-room home with six members and one relative on treatment for chronic cough. What immediate child health risks must be screened?
probes.a: Overcrowding and close contact with a source case pose severe risk for Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission, requiring Mantoux testing and isoniazid preventive therapy.

rubric.text: Elicits head of family education, occupation, and monthly income
Inquires about drinking water source, treatment, and toilet facilities
Screens for cooking fuel type and indoor biomass smoke exposure
Assesses number of living rooms and total household members

sources.locator: diseases_of_infancy_and_childhood: Clinical pearls and evaluation
Community Medicine and Paediatrics: Social Determinants of Health

teach.heading: The social determinants of child survival
teach.body:
A child health is inextricably tied to the domestic environment.

Water supply, waste disposal, crowding, and air quality directly determine microbial and pollutant exposure. A clinician who treats recurrent pneumonia with antibiotics without addressing unventilated biomass cooking guarantees recurrent admission.

teach.heading: Objective socioeconomic stratification
teach.body:
Stratifying families objectively guides holistic discharge planning and welfare support.

In urban and peri-urban India, the Modified Kuppuswamy scale evaluates education, occupation, and monthly income, grouping households into Upper (I), Upper Middle (II), Middle (III), Lower Middle (IV), and Lower (V) socioeconomic classes.

skill.annex.paed.milestones.title: Normal developmental milestones and red flags reference table
skill.annex.paed.milestones.oneLine: Rapid lookup reference for key developmental milestones across four domains with red-flag thresholds
skill.annex.paed.milestones.why: Accurate developmental evaluation requires comparing a child functional performance against standardised normative milestone ages. This reference table allows clinicians to compute the developmental quotient (DQ) and identify red flags requiring urgent neurological referral.
skill.annex.paed.milestones.practice: Use this lookup table to calculate the developmental quotient (DQ = developmental age / chronological age x 100) for a 12-month-old infant whose motor skills are at a 6-month level.
pitfalls: Failing to calculate developmental quotient (DQ) and missing mild-to-moderate developmental delay.
Ignoring fine motor or social delay when gross motor milestones appear relatively preserved.
Delaying referral when red-flag ages are breached (e.g. not walking independently by 18 months).

probes.q: How is the Developmental Quotient (DQ) calculated?
probes.a: Developmental Quotient equals developmental age (average age of milestone attainment) divided by chronological age, multiplied by 100.

probes.q: What Developmental Quotient threshold is considered a critical red flag indicating significant developmental delay?
probes.a: A Developmental Quotient of less than 70 percent is considered a red flag requiring formal multidisciplinary evaluation.

probes.q: At what age should an infant show mature pincer grasp, and how does it differ from immature pincer grasp?
probes.a: Mature pincer grasp emerges at 12 months using the tips of the index finger and thumb; immature pincer grasp emerges around 9 months using the pads of the digits.

rubric.text: Correctly identifies expected milestone ages across all four domains
Accurately calculates developmental quotient using the standard formula
Identifies clinical red flags that mandate specialist referral

sources.locator: growth_short_stature_long_case: WHO velocity and developmental assessment
Growth, Development, and Behavior: Developmental Milestones

teach.heading: Developmental red flags requiring prompt referral
Developmental quotient calculation
teach.body:
Developmental quotient quantifies the degree of functional developmental progress.

Formula: DQ = (Developmental Age / Chronological Age) x 100. In premature infants (under 37 weeks), calculate chronological age from the expected date of delivery until two years of age. A DQ under 70 percent signifies significant developmental impairment.

skill.annex.paed.immunisation_nis_iap.title: National Immunisation Schedule (NIS) and IAP timetable
skill.annex.paed.immunisation_nis_iap.oneLine: Lookup table comparing India National Immunisation Schedule with the IAP schedule
skill.annex.paed.immunisation_nis_iap.why: Indian healthcare providers operate across public programmes (Universal Immunisation Programme / NIS) and private clinical guidelines (IAP ACVIP). A clear lookup reference prevents omissions when transitioning between government dispensaries and private clinics.
skill.annex.paed.immunisation_nis_iap.practice: Compare the NIS and IAP schedules for a 6-week-old infant to explain why additional vaccines (such as injectable polio or PCV) may be offered in private versus public health settings.
pitfalls: Omitting the birth dose of hepatitis B when delivery occurs outside a health facility.
Confusing fractional intradermal IPV (fIPV 0.1 ml) used in public centres with intramuscular IPV (0.5 ml).
Failing to advise vitamin A supplementation at 9 months alongside measles-rubella vaccine.

probes.q: What three vaccines are administered at birth under the National Immunisation Schedule for institutional deliveries?
probes.a: BCG, oral polio vaccine zero-dose (OPV-0), and hepatitis B birth dose within 24 hours.

probes.q: What is the primary schedule for vitamin A supplementation under the National Programme?
probes.a: Total 9 doses: 100,000 IU (1 lakh IU) at 9 months with MR, then 200,000 IU (2 lakh IU) every 6 months up to 5 years of age.

probes.q: Which additional vaccines are routinely recommended in the IAP schedule that were historically not universal in all NIS districts?
probes.a: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (universalised recently), typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV), hepatitis A, varicella, and mumps (MMR).

rubric.text: Accurately references vaccines due by age on the National Immunisation Schedule
Identifies additional vaccines recommended on the IAP ACVIP schedule
Verifies correct route and anatomical site for each scheduled vaccine

teach.heading: IAP ACVIP additions
teach.body:
The Indian Academy of Pediatrics (IAP) recommends additional protective coverage.

Key additions include: Typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) single dose at 6 to 9 months; Hepatitis A vaccine (live single dose at 12 months or inactivated 2 doses); Varicella vaccine (first dose at 15 months, second at 4 to 5 years); and annual Influenza vaccination from 6 months of age.

skill.annex.paed.vaccine_rules.title: Vaccine classification, storage, and clinical administration rules
skill.annex.paed.vaccine_rules.oneLine: Reference guide for vaccine types, cold chain storage limits, reconstitution, and contraindications
skill.annex.paed.vaccine_rules.why: Improper cold chain storage, freezing freeze-sensitive vaccines, or injecting vaccines into improper sites causes vaccine failure and adverse reactions. This reference provides essential clinical rules for safe vaccine handling and administration.
skill.annex.paed.vaccine_rules.practice: Explain the shake test for suspected frozen DPT vials, review reconstitution diluents, and identify true versus false contraindications.
pitfalls: Freezing aluminum-adsorbed vaccines (DPT, TT, Hepatitis B, Hib), which destroys their immunogenicity.
Administering intramuscular vaccines into the gluteal region, risking sciatic nerve injury and reduced antibody response.
Using reconstituted BCG or measles vaccine beyond 4 hours of preparation.

probes.q: What is the recommended storage temperature range for vaccines in the domestic refrigerator or ILR?
probes.a: Plus 2 degrees Celsius to plus 8 degrees Celsius (+2 to +8 C).

probes.q: Which vaccines must NEVER be frozen because freezing destroys their potency?
probes.a: Adsorbed liquid vaccines: DPT, DT, Td, TT, Hepatitis B, Hib, and Hepatitis A.

probes.q: Why is the anterolateral aspect of the midthigh the preferred intramuscular injection site in infants rather than the gluteal muscle?
probes.a: The anterolateral thigh provides a thick muscle mass (vastus lateralis) free of major blood vessels and avoids the risk of sciatic nerve injury in small gluteal muscles.

rubric.text: Identifies correct cold chain temperature limits (+2 to +8 C)
Distinguishes freeze-sensitive vaccines from freeze-tolerant vaccines
States strict time limits for reconstituted vaccines (discard after 4 hours)
Distinguishes absolute contraindications from false contraindications

teach.heading: Cold chain and handling principles
teach.body:
Cold chain maintenance preserves vaccine viability from factory to child.

Maintain all vaccines between +2 and +8 degrees Celsius. Live viral freeze-dried vaccines (OPV, BCG, MMR) can tolerate freezing, but aluminium-adsorbed vaccines (DPT, Td, Hepatitis B, Hib) must NEVER be frozen. Discard reconstituted BCG and MR within 4 hours.

teach.heading: True versus false contraindications
teach.body:
Distinguishing true contraindications prevents dangerous omissions.

True contraindications: anaphylaxis to a prior dose, progressive neurological disease or encephalopathy for whole-cell pertussis, and symptomatic severe immunodeficiency for live vaccines. False contraindications: mild fever, common cold, simple diarrhoea, malnutrition, premature birth, and concurrent oral antibiotics.

skill.annex.paed.ses_scale.title: Modified Kuppuswamy socioeconomic status scale
skill.annex.paed.ses_scale.oneLine: Lookup table for scoring education, occupation, income, and determining socioeconomic class in urban India
skill.annex.paed.ses_scale.why: Standardised socioeconomic classification ensures objective clinical and epidemiological assessment. The Modified Kuppuswamy scale is the gold standard for urban and peri-urban Indian populations, grading households into five socioeconomic tiers based on composite scores.
skill.annex.paed.ses_scale.practice: Calculate the total Kuppuswamy score for a family where the father is a high school graduate working as a skilled worker, and monthly income is 25,000 rupees, determining their socioeconomic class.
pitfalls: Using outdated income thresholds without adjusting for consumer price index updates.
Applying the Kuppuswamy scale to rural agricultural populations (where BG Prasad or Udai Pareek scales are more appropriate).
Evaluating the mother educational and occupational status instead of the defined head of the household.

probes.q: What are the three composite domains evaluated in the Modified Kuppuswamy scale?
probes.a: Education of the head of household, occupation of the head of household, and total monthly family income in rupees.

probes.q: What total score range corresponds to Upper Class (Class I) on the Modified Kuppuswamy scale?
probes.a: A total score of 26 to 29 points corresponds to Upper Class (Class I).

probes.q: Which socioeconomic class does a family belong to if their total Kuppuswamy composite score is 8 points?
probes.a: Upper Lower (Class IV), which covers the score range of 5 to 10 points.

rubric.text: Accurately scores education, occupation, and family income parameters
Computes total composite score out of 29 points
Assigns correct socioeconomic class tier from Class I to Class V

Community Medicine: Socioeconomic Scales and Classification

teach.heading: Family income brackets and socioeconomic classes
Clinical application and degree of consanguinity
teach.body:
Socioeconomic classification is complemented by pedigree genetics in clinical paediatrics.

First-degree relatives (parents, offspring, full siblings) share 50 percent of genes. Second-degree relatives (grandparents, uncles, aunts, nieces, nephews) share 25 percent. Third-degree relatives (first cousins) share 12.5 percent. Consanguineous unions within lower socioeconomic strata combine genetic and environmental vulnerabilities.

skill.gen.paed.appearance.title: General appearance and sick-child triage
skill.gen.paed.appearance.oneLine: Initial assessment of alertness, activity, respiratory effort, and perfusion
skill.gen.paed.appearance.why: Rapid triage using the paediatric assessment triangle identifies children in respiratory distress, shock, or neurological failure within thirty seconds, before touch or instrumentation causes distress.

steps.text: Observe the child from a distance while held undisturbed in the caregiver lap or arms.
Assess appearance and mental state: alertness, eye contact, spontaneous movements, muscle tone, and consolability.
Evaluate work of breathing: nasal flaring, grunting, head nodding, and chest retractions (subcostal, intercostal, suprasternal).
Inspect skin perfusion: check for pallor, mottled skin, and peripheral or central cyanosis.
Note body habitus, resting posture, facial dysmorphism, abnormal movements, and the tone of the cry.

skill.gen.paed.appearance.normal: Alert, interactive child making good eye contact, with strong normal cry, good muscle tone, pink skin, and quiet unlaboured breathing.
skill.gen.paed.appearance.abnormal: Lethargy, unresponsiveness, floppiness, weak or high-pitched cry, audible grunting, severe chest indrawing, mottling, or pallor.
skill.gen.paed.appearance.significance: Distinguishes a stable child from one requiring immediate emergency resuscitation for respiratory failure, decompensated shock, or central nervous system depression.
skill.gen.paed.appearance.practice: Observe paediatric casualty triage. Spend thirty seconds assessing appearance, work of breathing, and circulation from the foot of the bed before touching the patient.
pitfalls: Approaching the child immediately with a cold stethoscope or torch, inducing crying that masks resting appearance.
Assuming a motionless, silent infant is peacefully sleeping when the infant is severely lethargic or exhausted from respiratory effort.
Failing to undress the chest in a warm room to inspect for subcostal and intercostal retractions.

probes.q: What are the three components of the paediatric assessment triangle?
probes.a: Appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to the skin.

probes.q: What is the pathophysiological significance of expiratory grunting in an infant?
probes.a: Grunting is an expiratory sound generated against a partially closed glottis to create positive end-expiratory pressure, preventing alveolar collapse in severe lung disease.

probes.q: How do you distinguish abnormal irritability due to serious illness from simple fussiness in an infant?
probes.a: A fussy child consolidates and quietens when held or fed by the mother, whereas an infant with serious infection or encephalopathy remains inconsolable or displays paradoxical irritability, crying more when handled.

rubric.text: Observes the child initially from a distance without provoking crying
Systematically assesses appearance, work of breathing, and skin circulation
Evaluates muscle tone, spontaneous movements, and cry quality
Promptly identifies danger signs including lethargy, grunting, or severe retractions

teach.heading: The paediatric assessment triangle at the bedside
teach.body:
The paediatric assessment triangle provides an instant physiological appraisal without using medical instruments.

Appearance reflects central nervous system oxygenation and perfusion. Work of breathing reflects airway resistance and pulmonary mechanics. Circulation to the skin reflects cardiac output and core perfusion.

Disruption in one arm indicates localized distress; disruption across two or three arms indicates respiratory failure, shock, or cardiopulmonary arrest.

teach.heading: General danger signs requiring immediate escalation

points.d: The child is unable to drink or suckle at the breast due to extreme weakness, breathlessness, or altered sensorium.
Persistent vomiting of all ingested fluids and feeds, indicating complete intolerance and high risk of dehydration.
Seizure activity during the current illness, indicating central nervous system infection, severe malaria, or metabolic derangement.
Drowsiness, lack of eye contact, or failure to respond to verbal and painful stimuli.

skill.gen.paed.vitals.title: Paediatric vital signs by age
skill.gen.paed.vitals.oneLine: Age-stratified assessment of heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and temperature
skill.gen.paed.vitals.why: Normal paediatric vital signs vary widely from infancy to adolescence. Applying adult cut-offs causes failure to recognise paediatric tachypnoea, tachycardia, or shock.

steps.text: Count respiratory rate first for a full 60 seconds while the child is calm or sleeping, before touching the chest.
Measure pulse rate for a full minute; auscultate apical heart rate in infants, or palpate the radial or brachial artery in older children.
Palpate peripheral pulses (radial, brachial, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis) and femoral pulses bilaterally, checking for radio-femoral delay.
Select a blood pressure cuff whose bladder width covers at least two-thirds of the upper arm length, with bladder length encircling 80 to 100 percent of arm circumference.
Measure blood pressure by auscultation; record systolic at Korotkoff phase 1 and diastolic at phase 5 (or phase 4 in run-off states).
Measure temperature at an appropriate site: axillary measurement is standard; recognize that rectal is 0.5 degrees C higher than oral, which is 0.3 degrees C higher than axillary.

skill.gen.paed.vitals.normal: Age-appropriate heart rate and respiratory rate; systolic blood pressure between 50th and 90th centiles for age, sex, and height; synchronous radial and femoral pulses.
skill.gen.paed.vitals.abnormal: Tachypnoea above WHO age thresholds; resting tachycardia (newborn >160, infant >140, 1-5 yr >120, >5 yr >100 beats/min); hypotension (systolic < 70 + [2 x age]); radio-femoral delay.
skill.gen.paed.vitals.significance: Rapidly detects sepsis, pneumonia, hypovolaemia, heart failure, coarctation of the aorta, or hypertensive emergencies.
skill.gen.paed.vitals.practice: Select cuffs of three different widths on a paediatric training arm. Practise counting respiratory rate for a full 60 seconds on resting infants.
pitfalls: Using an adult cuff on a small child, which produces falsely low blood pressure readings, or a narrow cuff, which gives falsely high readings.
Counting respirations for only 15 seconds in young infants, which misses periodic breathing and irregular respiratory pauses.
Omitting bilateral femoral pulse palpation in a child with hypertension or heart murmur.

probes.q: What are the WHO respiratory rate thresholds defining fast breathing in an infant aged 4 months and a toddler aged 2 years?
probes.a: At 2 to 12 months, fast breathing is 50 breaths per minute or more; at 1 to 5 years, it is 40 breaths per minute or more.

probes.q: What formula gives the 5th centile lower limit of normal systolic blood pressure in children aged 1 to 10 years?
probes.a: 70 plus two times the child age in years in millimetres of mercury.

probes.q: Why should you check for radio-femoral delay, and what does a positive sign signify?
probes.a: You palpate radial and femoral pulses simultaneously; normally femoral pulses are felt at or before the radial pulse. Delay or diminution of the femoral pulse indicates coarctation of the aorta.

rubric.text: Counts respiratory rate for a full 60 seconds while the child is quiet
Selects a blood pressure cuff bladder covering two-thirds of arm length
Palpates femoral pulses bilaterally to check for radio-femoral delay
Interprets vitals against age-specific normal reference values

teach.heading: Age-stratified vital sign thresholds in children
Blood pressure cuff sizing and Korotkoff rules
teach.body:
Blood pressure cuff bladder width must cover two-thirds of the upper arm length between acromion and olecranon. Bladder length should encircle at least 80 percent of the arm circumference.

An undersized cuff gives a falsely high reading; an oversized cuff gives a falsely low reading.

Phase 1 (tapping sound) indicates systolic pressure. Phase 5 (disappearance) marks diastolic pressure. In aortic regurgitation or high-output states where sounds persist to zero, phase 4 (muffling) is recorded.

skill.gen.paed.pallor.title: Paediatric pallor examination
skill.gen.paed.pallor.oneLine: Inspection of conjunctiva, tongue, palms, and nail beds for childhood anaemia
skill.gen.paed.pallor.why: Nutritional iron deficiency, haemoglobinopathies, and haemolysis are widespread in India. Clinical pallor provides immediate bedside screening for severe anaemia before laboratory results arrive.

steps.text: Examine the child in bright, diffuse natural daylight; avoid coloured lights or tinted windows.
Inspect the lower palpebral conjunctiva by gently pulling down the lower eyelid while the child looks upwards.
Inspect the dorsum of the tongue and buccal mucosal surfaces for mucosal pallor.
Examine the palms with fingers gently extended, comparing the child palmar skin and creases to your own palm.
Inspect the fingernail beds and look for koilonychia or flattened nails (platynychia) in chronic iron deficiency.

skill.gen.paed.pallor.normal: Pink palpebral conjunctiva, pink moist tongue, and dark pink palmar creases that stand out clearly from the surrounding skin.
skill.gen.paed.pallor.abnormal: Pale conjunctiva, pale mucosal lining, pale nail beds, or palmar crease pallor where creases appear bleached or indistinguishable from palmar skin.
skill.gen.paed.pallor.significance: Mucosal pallor indicates anaemia; palmar crease pallor strongly correlates with severe anaemia (haemoglobin below 7 to 8 g/dL), demanding urgent evaluation.
skill.gen.paed.pallor.practice: Examine palms of five healthy subjects and observe how palmar creases stay red even when fingers are gently straightened. Compare with an anaemic patient.
pitfalls: Over-extending the child fingers and palm, which mechanically blanches capillaries and creates false crease pallor.
Relying on nail beds alone in a cold, vasoconstricted infant.
Examining under fluorescent or coloured lighting that distorts subtle mucosal hue.

probes.q: Which clinical site is most reliable for identifying severe anaemia on general examination?
probes.a: The palmar creases (and plantar creases in young infants).

probes.q: What physiological change in haemoglobin occurs around two to three months of age in term infants?
probes.a: Physiological nadir (physiological anaemia of infancy), where haemoglobin falls to 9 to 11 g/dL due to down-regulated erythropoietin production after birth.

probes.q: A 3-year-old child presents with severe pallor, frontal bossing, and prominent maxillae. What is the diagnosis and skeletal mechanism?
probes.a: Beta thalassaemia major; severe ineffective erythropoiesis drives massive marrow hyperplasia, expanding the diploic space and facial bones.

rubric.text: Examines the child in bright natural daylight
Examines the lower palpebral conjunctiva and oral mucosa
Checks palmar creases without hyperextending the fingers
Correlates crease pallor with haemoglobin under 7 to 8 g/dL

teach.heading: Diagnostic value of clinical sites for pallor
teach.body:
The tongue and lower palpebral conjunctiva possess superficial capillary networks with minimal melanin, offering direct visibility of capillary blood colour.

Palmar skin is subject to ambient temperature and vasomotor tone. However, the deep palmar creases retain capillary filling; when palmar creases lose their red hue and appear pale, haemoglobin has typically dropped below 7 to 8 g/dL.

Nail beds are least reliable alone because peripheral vasoconstriction produces false pallor.

skill.gen.paed.icterus.title: Paediatric icterus and jaundice examination
skill.gen.paed.icterus.oneLine: Clinical detection of hyperbilirubinaemia in neonates and older children
skill.gen.paed.icterus.why: Jaundice indicates serum bilirubin above 2 mg/dL in children and above 5 mg/dL in neonates. In neonates, rapid progression risks kernicterus; in older children, it signals haemolysis, hepatitis, or biliary disease.

steps.text: Examine the patient in bright natural daylight, avoiding artificial yellow lighting.
In older children, inspect the upper bulbar conjunctiva by gently elevating the upper eyelid while the child looks downwards.
Inspect the mucosal lining under the tongue, hard palate, and buccal mucosa.
In neonates, blanch the skin over the forehead, sternum, abdomen, thighs, and feet with digital pressure for 2 to 3 seconds to unmask underlying dermal jaundice.
Map the cephalocaudal progression according to Kramer dermal zones.
Inquire about and inspect stool colour (acholic clay-coloured stools) and urine staining (dark yellow-brown staining on diapers).

skill.gen.paed.icterus.normal: Pearly white sclera, pink mucosa, and blanched skin without yellow discoloration.
skill.gen.paed.icterus.abnormal: Yellow sclera, yellow mucous membranes, dermal yellowing extending onto the trunk and extremities; clay-coloured stools or dark staining urine.
skill.gen.paed.icterus.significance: In neonates, jaundice involving abdomen or feet warrants immediate serum bilirubin measurement; dark urine with pale stools suggests cholestatic liver disease or biliary atresia.
skill.gen.paed.icterus.practice: Practise digital blanching over the forehead, chest, and thigh on newborn infants under natural light, verifying findings against transcutaneous bilirubinometry.
pitfalls: Examining under fluorescent or incandescent room lights, which masks mild jaundice or misleads assessment.
Confusing carotenaemia with jaundice; carotenaemia stains palms and soles but strictly spares the sclera.
Dismissing neonatal jaundice in the first 24 hours of life as physiological; jaundice under 24 hours is always pathological.

probes.q: What anatomical site is best for detecting mild icterus in an older child?
probes.a: The superior bulbar conjunctiva (sclera) under the upper eyelid, because scleral elastin has high affinity for bilirubin.

probes.q: Describe the cephalocaudal progression of jaundice in neonates according to Kramer zones.
probes.a: Zone 1 is head and neck; zone 2 is upper trunk to umbilicus; zone 3 is lower abdomen and thighs; zone 4 is arms and lower legs; zone 5 is palms and soles.

probes.q: A 3-week-old infant has persistent jaundice, pale acholic stools, and dark urine. What urgent condition must be investigated?
probes.a: Biliary atresia; conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia requires prompt hepatobiliary scan or cholangiogram and Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of age.

rubric.text: Examines sclera and skin in natural daylight
Performs digital blanching to assess dermal jaundice in neonates
Accurately maps jaundice using Kramer cephalocaudal zones
Inspects or inquires about stool colour and urine staining

teach.heading: Kramer dermal zones and bilirubin levels in neonates
Bedside differentiation: unconjugated versus conjugated jaundice

points.d: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-insoluble and does not appear in urine; conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble, turning urine dark yellow-brown and staining cloth diapers.
Normal stools are yellow-green from stercobilin. Pale, clay-coloured, or white acholic stools indicate biliary obstruction.
Jaundice within 24 hours of birth indicates haemolysis (Rh or ABO incompatibility). Jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in term infants demands fractionation.
Free unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier, depositing in the basal ganglia and auditory pathways; conjugated bilirubin does not cause kernicterus.

skill.gen.paed.cyanosis.title: Paediatric cyanosis and peripheral perfusion
skill.gen.paed.cyanosis.oneLine: Differentiating central from peripheral cyanosis and measuring capillary refill time
skill.gen.paed.cyanosis.why: Cyanosis requires at least 5 g/dL of deoxygenated haemoglobin. Differentiating central cyanosis (cyanotic heart disease or severe lung disease) from benign peripheral acrocyanosis guides urgent oxygen or prostaglandin therapy.

steps.text: Inspect the infant in warm surroundings and good natural lighting.
Inspect the tongue, oral mucous membranes, and inner lips to identify central cyanosis.
Inspect peripheral extremities: nail beds, hands, feet, and earlobes for peripheral cyanosis.
Assess peripheral skin temperature from proximal limb to distal toes using the dorsal surface of your fingers.
Measure capillary refill time by pressing firmly on the centre of the sternum or distal fingertip for 5 seconds, then timing the return of pink colour.

skill.gen.paed.cyanosis.normal: Pink mucous membranes and extremities; warm hands and feet; capillary refill time under 2 to 3 seconds.
skill.gen.paed.cyanosis.abnormal: Bluish discoloration of the tongue and oral mucosa (central cyanosis); bluish hands and feet with warm pink tongue (peripheral cyanosis/acrocyanosis); capillary refill time prolonged >3 seconds.
skill.gen.paed.cyanosis.significance: Central cyanosis indicates right-to-left cardiac shunt, transposition of great arteries, or severe alveolar hypoventilation; prolonged capillary refill indicates shock or hypoperfusion.
skill.gen.paed.cyanosis.practice: Practise timing capillary refill using a stopwatch on the sternum. Practise distinguishing warm pink tongue from bluish lips in a chilly environment.
pitfalls: Diagnosing central cyanosis based on blue lips alone in a cold infant; lips turn blue in cold exposure, but the tongue remains pink.
Failing to recognise that a severely anaemic infant (Hb < 5 g/dL) cannot develop cyanosis even when arterial hypoxaemia is critical.
Testing capillary refill on cold, exposed feet instead of centrally over the warm sternum.

probes.q: Which examination site definitively distinguishes central cyanosis from peripheral cyanosis?
probes.a: The tongue and buccal mucous membranes; central cyanosis involves the warm mucosa, while peripheral cyanosis spares the tongue.

probes.q: Why might a child with severe cyanotic congenital heart disease and haemoglobin of 5 g/dL fail to show visible cyanosis?
probes.a: Visible cyanosis requires at least 5 g/dL of reduced (deoxygenated) haemoglobin; with total haemoglobin of only 5 g/dL, generating 5 g/dL of reduced haemoglobin is fatal before cyanosis can be seen.

probes.q: How does the hyperoxia test differentiate cyanotic heart disease from pulmonary disease in a neonate?
probes.a: Administering 100 percent oxygen for 10 minutes produces a marked rise in arterial PO2 (usually >150 to 200 mm Hg) in parenchymal lung disease, but minimal rise (PO2 remains <100 to 150 mm Hg) in fixed right-to-left cardiac shunts.

rubric.text: Inspects the tongue and oral mucosa to evaluate central cyanosis
Performs capillary refill time by pressing firmly for 5 seconds over the sternum
Assesses peripheral skin temperature from proximal to distal
Explains the confounding effect of severe anaemia on cyanosis visibility

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of cyanosis and the 5 g/dL rule
teach.body:
Cyanosis represents bluish tissue discoloration caused by an absolute concentration of at least 5 g/dL of reduced (deoxy) haemoglobin in capillary blood.

In polycythaemia, cyanosis appears at relatively mild arterial desaturation. Conversely, in severe anaemia, life-threatening arterial hypoxaemia can occur without visible cyanosis because total haemoglobin cannot supply 5 g/dL of reduced pigment.

Peripheral cyanosis reflects increased tissue oxygen extraction in slow-flowing capillary beds, leaving the tongue pink.

skill.gen.paed.clubbing.title: Paediatric digital clubbing
skill.gen.paed.clubbing.oneLine: Inspection and palpation of the nail bed, Lovibond angle, and Schamroth window sign
skill.gen.paed.clubbing.why: Digital clubbing takes weeks to months of chronic pathology to develop and is never normal. Identifying it flags cyanotic congenital heart disease, chronic suppurative lung disease, or liver/bowel disorders.

steps.text: Inspect fingers and toes tangentially at eye level to evaluate the profile angle between nail plate and proximal nail fold (Lovibond angle).
Look for Schamroth window sign: ask the child (or demonstrate) to place dorsal surfaces of terminal phalanges of opposite index fingers together.
Palpate the base of the nail bed with your index fingers while stabilizing the phalanx with thumbs to assess increased fluctuation or sponginess.
Inspect the curvature of the nail plate along both longitudinal and transverse axes (parrot-beak or drumstick deformity).
Palpate the wrists and ankles for bone tenderness and swelling (hypertrophic osteoarthropathy).

skill.gen.paed.clubbing.normal: Preserved diamond-shaped Schamroth window, Lovibond angle under 160 degrees, and firm non-fluctuant nail bed.
skill.gen.paed.clubbing.abnormal: Loss of Schamroth window, obliteration of normal 160-degree Lovibond angle, spongy fluctuation of nail bed, parrot-beak curvature, and drumstick deformity.
skill.gen.paed.clubbing.significance: Signifies chronic hypoxaemia, chronic pulmonary suppuration (bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, empyema), cyanotic heart disease, infective endocarditis, or cirrhosis.
skill.gen.paed.clubbing.practice: Demonstrate Schamroth window test on your own index fingers, noting the diamond aperture. Compare profile views of normal nails with curved nails.
pitfalls: Inspecting the nail bed from above instead of viewing the profile angle tangentially at exact eye level.
Confusing curved nails (normal anatomical variant) with true clubbing; curved nails retain a normal Lovibond angle below 160 degrees.
Omitting examination of the toes; isolated toe clubbing occurs in differential cyanosis from patent ductus arteriosus with pulmonary hypertension.

probes.q: What is the normal angle between the nail plate and the proximal nail fold (Lovibond angle)?
probes.a: Less than 160 degrees (typically around 150 to 160 degrees).

probes.q: What physical finding represents grade 1 clubbing?
probes.a: Increased fluctuation and sponginess or softening of the nail bed.

probes.q: What are the four clinical grades of clubbing, and what defines grade 4?
probes.a: Grade 1 is nail bed fluctuation; grade 2 is loss of Lovibond angle and Schamroth window; grade 3 is drumstick appearance; grade 4 is hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy with wrist or ankle periostitis.

rubric.text: Views the nail fold profile tangentially at exact eye level
Performs or demonstrates Schamroth window sign
Palpates the nail bed to detect increased sponginess or fluctuation
Correctly classifies the clinical grade and recalls paediatric causes

teach.heading: The four clinical grades of digital clubbing

points.d: Tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of great arteries, and uncorrected shunt lesions with Eisenmenger syndrome.
Bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, chronic empyema, lung abscess, and chronic fibrocavitary tuberculosis.
Subacute bacterial endocarditis on congenital valvular or septal defects.
Biliary atresia, cirrhosis, chronic active hepatitis, and Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis.
