skill.gen.paed.lymph_nodes.title: Paediatric lymph node examination
skill.gen.paed.lymph_nodes.oneLine: Systematic palpation of cervical, axillary, epitrochlear, and inguinal nodal stations
skill.gen.paed.lymph_nodes.why: Lymphoid tissue is prominent in growing children due to intense immunological exposure. Differentiating benign reactive hyperplasia from serious infections (tuberculosis, HIV) or malignancy (leukaemia, lymphoma) prevents invasive delays.

steps.text: Palpate cervical nodes with child seated: stand behind child, steady the head, and palpate submental, submandibular, pre-auricular, post-auricular, occipital, jugulodigastric, superficial and deep cervical, and posterior triangle chains.
Palpate the supraclavicular fossae bilaterally while the child flexes the neck slightly forward to relax the sternocleidomastoid muscles.

Palpate axillary nodes: face the child, support the child right arm with your left hand, and palpate the right axilla (pectoral, central, subscapular, lateral, apical) with your right hand; switch hands for the left axilla.
Palpate epitrochlear nodes: support the flexed elbow with one hand, cup the posterior groove above the medial epicondyle, and palpate with fingers.
Palpate inguinal chains with the child supine, covering both horizontal and vertical nodal groups.
Characterize any enlarged node: site, size in centimetres, consistency (soft, firm, rubbery, hard, fluctuant), tenderness, mobility, matting, and overlying skin.

skill.gen.paed.lymph_nodes.normal: Small, discrete, mobile, non-tender shotty lymph nodes under 1 cm in cervical or axillary areas, or under 1.5 cm in inguinal areas.
skill.gen.paed.lymph_nodes.abnormal: Cervical or axillary node >1 cm; inguinal node >1.5 cm; epitrochlear node of any palpable size; supraclavicular node of any size; matted, fixed, or fluctuant nodes.
skill.gen.paed.lymph_nodes.significance: Supraclavicular or generalized firm non-tender adenopathy suggests lymphoma or tuberculosis; tender fluctuant acute nodes suggest bacterial adenitis; generalized lymphadenopathy indicates systemic infection (EBV, CMV, HIV) or leukaemia.
skill.gen.paed.lymph_nodes.practice: Map the nine cervical nodal stations on a colleague. Practise supporting the flexed elbow to palpate the epitrochlear groove behind the medial epicondyle.
pitfalls: Omitting the supraclavicular fossae, where any palpable lymph node is pathological until proven otherwise.
Pressing too hard with fingertips against taut neck muscles, which blunts tactile sensitivity and hurts the child.
Failing to examine the drainage territory (scalp, throat, ears, limbs) of any enlarged regional lymph node.

probes.q: What size cut-offs define abnormal lymphadenopathy in paediatric cervical, inguinal, and epitrochlear regions?
probes.a: Greater than 1 cm in cervical and axillary regions, greater than 1.5 cm in inguinal regions, and any palpable node in the epitrochlear region.

probes.q: What is the diagnostic significance of a palpable left supraclavicular lymph node in a child?
probes.a: It represents Virchow node (Troisier sign), draining the thoracic duct; in paediatrics, any palpable supraclavicular node strongly suggests lymphoma, tuberculosis, or intrathoracic/abdominal malignancy.

probes.q: How does tuberculous lymphadenitis differ from acute pyogenic bacterial lymphadenitis on physical examination?
probes.a: Tuberculous adenitis is chronic, painless or minimally tender, firm and matted together, and may progress to a cold abscess or discharging sinus; pyogenic adenitis is acute, warm, red, exquisitely tender, and fluctuant.

rubric.text: Systematically examines all cervical nodal groups from behind or front
Explicitly examines the supraclavicular fossae bilaterally
Examines axillary, epitrochlear, and inguinal nodal stations
Records size, consistency, tenderness, mobility, and matting

teach.heading: Anatomical stations and pathological size thresholds

points.d: Acute pyogenic bacterial adenitis (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes) with local erythema and rapid fluctuation.
Tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis (scrofula); periadenitis binds adjacent nodes into a conglomerate mass, progressing to cold abscess.
Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma; enlarged, painless, movable, rubbery nodes without heat or tenderness.
Metastatic neuroblastoma or rhabdomyosarcoma; rock-hard nodes anchored to underlying tissue or overlying skin.

skill.gen.paed.edema.title: Paediatric oedema examination
skill.gen.paed.edema.oneLine: Assessing pitting versus non-pitting oedema and mapping dependent, facial, and serosal fluid
skill.gen.paed.edema.why: Oedema in children points to distinct paediatric conditions: kwashiorkor (nutritional oedema), nephrotic syndrome, congestive cardiac failure, or lymphatic dysplasias (Turner syndrome). Accurate recognition directs therapy.

steps.text: Inspect both lower limbs, face, eyelids, presacral region, and external genitalia.
Apply firm, steady pressure with your thumb or index finger over a bony surface (dorsum of foot, behind medial malleolus, or anterior tibia) for a full 5 seconds.
Release pressure and stroke your finger across the area to detect an indentation or persistent pit.
Inspect the face and periorbital tissue for morning puffiness, which is prominent in nephrotic syndrome.
In bedridden infants, check the presacral area, scrotum or labia, and lower abdominal wall for dependent pooling.
Evaluate for serosal fluid accumulation: test for shifting dullness or fluid thrill (ascites) and inspect for respiratory compromise (pleural effusion).

skill.gen.paed.edema.normal: No indentation or pitting on sustained digital pressure; clear facial contours without eyelid puffiness.
skill.gen.paed.edema.abnormal: Pitting depression remaining after 5 seconds of pressure over the feet, shins, or sacrum; marked periorbital oedema; non-pitting brawny induration.
skill.gen.paed.edema.significance: Bilateral pedal pitting oedema is the hallmark of kwashiorkor (severe acute malnutrition); periorbital morning puffiness with heavy proteinuria indicates nephrotic syndrome; non-pitting pedal oedema in newborn females suggests Turner syndrome.
skill.gen.paed.edema.practice: Practise timing 5 seconds of thumb pressure over a bony landmark. Compare the rebound feel between pitting fluid and non-pitting lymphatic induration.
pitfalls: Pressing for only 1 or 2 seconds, which fails to displace viscous interstitial fluid in subtle oedema.
Checking only the shins in non-ambulatory infants, where dependent fluid accumulates in the presacral region and scrotum.
Overlooking nutritional oedema because the child appears plump; kwashiorkor produces false roundness (moon face) and soft tissue turgor.

probes.q: How many seconds of firm digital pressure should be applied over a bony surface to test for pitting oedema?
probes.a: At least 5 seconds.

probes.q: What is the clinical definition and significance of bilateral pedal oedema in severe acute malnutrition?
probes.a: Bilateral pedal pitting oedema defines kwashiorkor (or marasmic kwashiorkor if wasting is also present); its presence automatically classifies the child as having severe acute malnutrition (SAM) regardless of anthropometric centiles.

probes.q: What causes non-pitting oedema of the hands and feet in a female neonate?
probes.a: Congenital lymphoedema due to lymphatic hypoplasia, classically seen in Turner syndrome (karyotype 45,X) or Milroy disease.

rubric.text: Applies firm pressure over bone for a full 5 seconds
Examines dorsum of feet, medial malleolus, and presacral area in infants
Inspects face and periorbital tissues for morning puffiness
Distinguishes nutritional (kwashiorkor), renal, cardiac, and lymphatic oedema

teach.heading: Clinical examination and grading of pitting oedema
teach.body:
Digital pressure must be applied firmly against bone for a full 5 seconds to displace interstitial fluid.

Grade 1+ indicates mild pitting (<2 mm) disappearing rapidly. Grade 2+ indicates moderate depression (2 to 4 mm) resolving in 10 to 15 seconds.

Grade 3+ indicates deep pitting (4 to 6 mm) lasting over a minute with noticeable limb swelling. Grade 4+ indicates very deep pitting (6 to 8 mm) persisting for several minutes with severe generalized anasarca.

skill.gen.paed.hydration.title: Assessment of hydration status
skill.gen.paed.hydration.oneLine: WHO clinical assessment of dehydration: mental state, eyes, tears, thirst, and skin pinch
skill.gen.paed.hydration.why: Dehydration from acute gastroenteritis is a leading cause of preventable childhood death. Rapid classification into no, some, or severe dehydration determines whether management is home fluids (Plan A), oral rehydration therapy (Plan B), or intravenous fluid resuscitation (Plan C).

steps.text: Look at the child general condition: observe whether the child is alert and active, restless and irritable, or lethargic and unconscious.
Look at the eyes: observe whether they appear normal, sunken, or deeply hollowed. Note if tears are present when crying.
Inspect the mouth and tongue: check whether mucous membranes are moist, dry, or parched.
Offer fluid by cup or spoon: observe whether the child drinks normally, drinks eagerly and thirstily, or is unable to drink.
Perform the abdominal skin pinch test: pinch skin and subcutaneous fat midway between umbilicus and flank in a longitudinal or transverse fold; release and time the recoil.
In infants with an open anterior fontanelle, palpate gently to assess whether it is flat, depressed, or sunken.
Check radial and brachial pulses, capillary refill time on the chest, and extremity warmth to assess for hypovolaemic shock.

skill.gen.paed.hydration.normal: Alert, active child with normal non-sunken eyes, tears present, moist tongue and mouth, normal thirst, and abdominal skin pinch flattening immediately (<1 second).
skill.gen.paed.hydration.abnormal: Restless, irritable, or lethargic; sunken eyes; absent tears; dry or parched tongue; drinks eagerly or unable to drink; skin pinch returning slowly (1 to 2 seconds) or very slowly (>2 seconds).
skill.gen.paed.hydration.significance: Two or more signs of some dehydration indicate Plan B (75 mL/kg ORS over 4 hours); two or more signs of severe dehydration indicate emergency Plan C intravenous fluids (100 mL/kg Ringer lactate).
skill.gen.paed.hydration.practice: Practise the abdominal skin pinch on a relaxed abdomen: pick up the fold between thumb and forefinger, hold for one second, release, and judge immediate (<1 s) versus slow (1 to 2 s) versus very slow (>2 s).
pitfalls: Relying on abdominal skin pinch in a child with severe wasting (marasmus) or obesity; wasting produces false slow recoil due to loss of subcutaneous fat, while obesity masks slow recoil.
Mistaking a quiet, limp infant for a sleeping baby; an unresponsive, limp infant is in lethargic hypovolaemic shock.
Offering fluids with a bottle while the child is supine, creating an aspiration hazard; always offer fluid by cup and spoon with child upright.

probes.q: What are the four primary clinical signs evaluated in the WHO dehydration assessment matrix?
probes.a: General mental condition, eye appearance, drinking ability/thirst, and the abdominal skin pinch test.

probes.q: How is the abdominal skin pinch performed, and what duration is classified as very slow?
probes.a: Pinch skin and subcutaneous tissue between umbilicus and flank for one second and release; taking longer than 2 seconds to flatten completely is classified as very slow.

probes.q: A 9-month-old infant with diarrhoea is lethargic, has deeply sunken eyes, parched tongue, skin pinch taking 3 seconds, and weak rapid pulses. What is the category and fluid plan?
probes.a: Severe dehydration with impending hypovolaemic shock; initiate Plan C emergency intravenous fluids with Ringer lactate: 30 mL/kg in the first hour, followed by 70 mL/kg over the next 5 hours in infants under 1 year.

rubric.text: Assesses mental status: alert vs irritable vs lethargic
Examines eyes for sunkenness and assesses tongue moisture
Offers fluid by cup to test drinking ability and thirst
Performs abdominal skin pinch correctly and clocks recoil duration
Accurately classifies hydration status into Plan A, B, or C

teach.heading: Rehydration treatment strategies: Plans A, B, and C

points.d: Give extra home fluids and low-osmolarity ORS after each loose stool (50 to 100 mL for <2 years, 100 to 200 mL for 2 to 10 years), continue normal feeding, and provide oral zinc for 14 days.
Give 75 mL/kg of low-osmolarity ORS over 4 hours under observation at the health facility. Reassess at 4 hours: if signs resolve switch to Plan A, if severe dehydration develops switch to Plan C.

Administer 100 mL/kg Ringer lactate (or normal saline): for infants under 1 year give 30 mL/kg in 1 hour then 70 mL/kg in 5 hours; for children 1 to 5 years give 30 mL/kg in 30 minutes then 70 mL/kg in 2.5 hours.

skill.exam.paed.weight.title: Paediatric weight measurement and expected weight
skill.exam.paed.weight.oneLine: Calibrated weighing technique, growth multiplication milestones, and expected weight formulas
skill.exam.paed.weight.why: Weight is the most sensitive dynamic indicator of acute nutritional change and fluid balance in children. Weighing errors lead to toxic drug overdosing, missed failure to thrive, or undetected severe acute malnutrition.

steps.text: Select an appropriate scale: pan scale or hanging spring scale (Salter) for infants under 10 kg; beam balance or calibrated electronic platform scale for older children.
Zero and calibrate the scale with the clean paper lining or towel on the pan before placing the child.
Undress the child completely (infants) or leave minimal light undergarments (older children), removing shoes, wet diapers, and heavy jewellery.
Place the infant gently in the centre of the pan, or have the older child stand upright still in the centre of the platform with weight distributed equally.
Read the weight at eye level when the indicator stabilizes, recording to the nearest 10 g for infants or 100 g for older children.
Calculate the expected weight using clinical formulas and compare measured weight against expected weight and birth weight milestones.

skill.exam.paed.weight.normal: Weight tracking steadily along standard centiles, doubling birth weight by 5 months, tripling by 1 year, and quadrupling by 2 years.
skill.exam.paed.weight.abnormal: Weight-for-age below -2 standard deviations (underweight) or below -3 standard deviations (severe underweight); weight crossing two major centile lines downwards.
skill.exam.paed.weight.significance: Acute weight drop reflects acute dehydrating diarrhoea or severe wasting; failure of expected weight gain indicates chronic undernutrition, malabsorption, or systemic illness.
skill.exam.paed.weight.practice: Zero an infant beam scale with a cloth lining. Practise calculating expected weights mentally for children aged 6 months, 3 years, and 8 years using standard clinical formulas.
pitfalls: Weighing an infant wearing a wet diaper, which adds significant weight and conceals acute weight loss.
Reading the scale while the infant is actively kicking or holding onto the edge of the pan.
Failing to zero or calibrate the scale between consecutive patient measurements.

probes.q: By what ages does a healthy infant double and triple their birth weight?
probes.a: Birth weight doubles by 5 months of age, triples by 1 year of age, and quadruples by 2 years of age.

probes.q: What clinical formulas estimate expected weight for children aged under 1 year, 1 to 7 years, and 7 to 12 years?
probes.a: Under 1 year: (age in months + 9) / 2; 1 to 7 years: (age in years + 4) * 2; 7 to 12 years: age in years * 3.

probes.q: A 4-year-old child weighs 11 kg. Calculate the expected weight and determine the IAP malnutrition grade.
probes.a: Expected weight is (4 + 4) * 2 = 16 kg. Percentage of expected weight is (11 / 16) * 100 = approximately 69 percent, which falls into IAP Grade 2 malnutrition (61 to 70 percent).

rubric.text: Zeroes the scale with the lining sheet in place before measurement
Removes clothing and diaper to measure unclothed weight
Reads scale at eye level and records to nearest 10 g or 100 g
Calculates expected weight using clinical formula and evaluates deficit

teach.heading: Standard clinical formulas for expected paediatric weight

points.d: Weight becomes 2 times (doubles) the birth weight (e.g. 2.5 kg at birth reaches 5 kg).
Weight becomes 3 times (triples) the birth weight (e.g. 2.5 kg at birth reaches 7.5 kg).
Weight becomes 4 times the birth weight (e.g. 2.5 kg at birth reaches 10 kg).
Weight becomes 5 times the birth weight (e.g. 2.5 kg at birth reaches 12.5 kg).
Weight becomes 6 times the birth weight (e.g. 2.5 kg at birth reaches 15 kg).
Weight becomes 7 times the birth weight (e.g. 2.5 kg at birth reaches 17.5 kg).
Weight becomes 10 times the birth weight (e.g. 2.5 kg at birth reaches 25 kg).

skill.exam.paed.length_height.title: Paediatric length and height measurement
skill.exam.paed.length_height.oneLine: Infantometer recumbent length (<2 years), stadiometer standing height (>2 years), and mid-parental height target
skill.exam.paed.length_height.why: Linear growth reflects long-term skeletal development and chronic nutritional or endocrine wellbeing. Measuring recumbent length versus standing height incorrectly creates an artificial shift, distorting growth velocity and stunting diagnosis.

steps.text: In children under 2 years (or length under 85 cm), measure recumbent length using a rigid infantometer with two examiners.
Place infant supine; assistant holds the head firmly against the fixed headboard in the Frankfurt horizontal plane (line from lower orbit to external auditory meatus perpendicular to board).
Primary examiner flattens the knees by gentle downward pressure and brings the sliding footboard firmly against both heels (feet at 90 degrees); read length to the nearest 0.1 cm.
In children aged 2 years and older who can stand independently, measure standing height using a calibrated vertical stadiometer.
Have the child stand barefoot with feet together, knees straight, and heels, buttocks, upper back, and occiput touching the vertical board, looking straight ahead in the Frankfurt plane.
Lower the horizontal headboard onto the crown of the head, ask the child to inhale deeply and stand tall, and record height to the nearest 0.1 cm.
Calculate mid-parental target height: male = [(father height + mother height + 13 cm) / 2]; female = [(father height + mother height - 13 cm) / 2].

skill.exam.paed.length_height.normal: Linear growth tracking along expected centiles: length 50 cm at birth, 75 cm at 1 year, height 100 cm at 4 years (doubling birth length), and 150 cm at 12 years (tripling birth length).
skill.exam.paed.length_height.abnormal: Height below the 3rd centile or below -2 standard deviations for age and sex (short stature); height crossing percentiles downward; annual growth velocity under 5 cm/year between 4 years and puberty.
skill.exam.paed.length_height.significance: Proportionate short stature suggests constitutional delay, familial short stature, chronic undernutrition, or endocrine deficiency (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency); disproportionate short stature indicates skeletal dysplasias (achondroplasia).
skill.exam.paed.length_height.practice: Practise positioning the head in the Frankfurt horizontal plane. Practise two-examiner length measurement on an infant mannequin to ensure knees are flat and heels touch the board.
pitfalls: Measuring a child under 2 years standing up, which underestimates length by approximately 1 cm.
Measuring standing height without having the child remove shoes, thick socks, or hair buns/clips.
Failing to flatten the knees or failing to ensure both heels contact the footboard during infantometer measurement.

probes.q: At what age threshold do you switch from measuring recumbent length to standing height?
probes.a: At 2 years of age (or at 85 cm length if age is uncertain).

probes.q: What are the expected landmark height and length milestones at birth, 1 year, and 4 years of age?
probes.a: 50 cm at birth, 75 cm at 1 year, and 100 cm at 4 years (doubling birth length).

probes.q: How do you calculate mid-parental target height for boys versus girls?
probes.a: For boys: (father height in cm + mother height in cm + 13 cm) / 2. For girls: (father height in cm + mother height in cm - 13 cm) / 2 (target range MPH +/- 2.5 cm).

rubric.text: Selects infantometer for under 2 years and stadiometer for 2 years and older
Positions the head in the Frankfurt horizontal plane during measurement
Flattens both knees and applies footboard firmly against heels
Calculates mid-parental height using the correct 13 cm adjustment

teach.heading: Standard linear growth milestones and clinical formulas

rows: Gain of 15 cm in first 6 months
Gain of 25 cm in first year
Gain of 10 cm in second year

teach.heading: Mid-parental height and short stature evaluation
teach.body:
Mid-parental height (MPH) determines genetic height potential.

For boys, MPH = [(father height + mother height + 13 cm) / 2]. For girls, MPH = [(father height + mother height - 13 cm) / 2]. The target range spans MPH +/- 2.5 cm.

Short stature is defined as height below the 3rd centile or below -2 standard deviations. Proportionate short stature with bone age matching height age suggests constitutional delay or familial short stature. Bone age lagging behind height age indicates hypothyroidism or growth hormone deficiency.

skill.exam.paed.head_circumference.title: Paediatric head circumference measurement
skill.exam.paed.head_circumference.oneLine: Occipitofrontal head circumference technique, cranial growth milestones, and fontanelle assessment
skill.exam.paed.head_circumference.why: Head circumference directly reflects brain volume during the first two years of life, when 90 percent of postnatal brain growth occurs. Detecting microcephaly, macrocephaly, or cranial bossing flags congenital infections, craniosynostosis, hydrocephalus, or rickets.

steps.text: Use a flexible, non-stretchable plastic or fiberglass measuring tape; avoid stretchable cloth or paper tapes.
Remove any hair clips, pins, or braids that would artificially increase the reading.
Position the tape across the broadest part of the forehead, just above the supraorbital ridges and glabella anteriorly.
Pass the tape around the head just above the ears bilaterally to cross the maximal occipital protuberance posteriorly.
Pull the tape snug to compress hair against the skull and read the measurement where the tape crosses to the nearest 0.1 cm.
Repeat the measurement three times and record the maximum value obtained.
Palpate the anterior fontanelle with the infant held upright and calm: assess size (normally 2.5 cm x 2.5 cm at birth, closing by 9 to 18 months), tension (flat, bulging, depressed), and sutures.

skill.exam.paed.head_circumference.normal: Head circumference 35 cm at birth, 43 cm at 6 months, 46 cm at 1 year, and 49 cm at 2 years; anterior fontanelle soft, pulsatile, and level with adjacent bone.
skill.exam.paed.head_circumference.abnormal: Microcephaly (head circumference < -3 SD or < 3rd centile); macrocephaly (> +2 SD); tense/bulging fontanelle; premature suture fusion (craniosynostosis); delayed fontanelle closure beyond 18 months.
skill.exam.paed.head_circumference.significance: Microcephaly indicates congenital TORCH infections, hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy, or chromosomal syndromes; macrocephaly suggests hydrocephalus or storage disorders; delayed fontanelle closure signals rickets, hypothyroidism, or hydrocephalus.
skill.exam.paed.head_circumference.practice: Practise positioning the tape over the maximal occipitofrontal landmarks three times on an infant mannequin to obtain reproducible values within 0.1 cm.
pitfalls: Using a stretchable cloth or paper tape that elongates under tension, falsely underestimating cranial circumference.
Placing the tape too low over the ears or below the maximal occipital protuberance.
Assessing anterior fontanelle tension while the infant is crying or lying flat; fontanelle must be felt with the infant held quietly upright.

probes.q: What anatomical landmarks define the correct path for measuring maximal occipitofrontal head circumference?
probes.a: Just above the supraorbital ridges anteriorly, above the ears bilaterally, and across the maximal occipital protuberance posteriorly.

probes.q: What are the expected normal head circumferences at birth, 6 months, 1 year, and 2 years of age?
probes.a: 35 cm at birth, 43 cm at 6 months, 46 cm at 1 year, and 49 cm at 2 years of age.

probes.q: By what age does the anterior fontanelle normally close, and name three conditions associated with delayed closure.
probes.a: Normally closes by 9 to 18 months of age; delayed closure occurs in rickets, congenital hypothyroidism, hydrocephalus, and Down syndrome.

rubric.text: Uses a flexible, non-stretchable tape for measurement
Aligns tape above supraorbital ridges and across maximal occipital protuberance
Repeats measurement three times and records the maximum value
Palpates anterior fontanelle for size, tension, and closure timing while child is calm

teach.heading: Cranial growth milestones from birth to two years
Clinical interpretation of fontanelles and skull signs

points.d: Diamond-shaped, normally measures 2.5 cm x 2.5 cm at birth and closes by 9 to 18 months. Delayed closure occurs in rickets, hypothyroidism, malnutrition, hydrocephalus, and trisomies.
Triangular, normally closes by 2 months of age. Persistent patency at birth suggests congenital hypothyroidism.
Softening and parchment-like thinning of skull bones giving a ping-pong ball indentation feel; seen in rickets, osteogenesis imperfecta, and hypervitaminosis A.
Prominence of frontal or parietal eminences due to subperiosteal osteoid accumulation in rickets, or extramedullary haematopoiesis in thalassaemia major.

skill.exam.paed.muac.title: Mid-upper arm circumference measurement
skill.exam.paed.muac.oneLine: Midpoint marking and Shakir tape screening for wasting in children aged 6 to 59 months
skill.exam.paed.muac.why: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is an age-independent proxy for skeletal muscle mass and mortality risk in young children. Between 6 and 59 months, muscle and fat change minimally, making MUAC the standard community triage tool for acute malnutrition.

steps.text: Confirm the child is between 6 and 59 months of age (or 1 to 5 years).
Use the child left arm; completely uncover the shoulder and upper arm.
Flex the child left arm to a 90-degree angle at the elbow, placing the forearm across the stomach.
Locate the tip of the acromion process at the shoulder and the tip of the olecranon process at the elbow.
Place the measuring tape between the two bony points, find the exact midpoint, and mark it with a skin marker on the lateral arm.
Straighten the arm so it hangs relaxed and loosely by the child side.
Wrap the Shakir or colour-coded MUAC tape around the arm at the marked midpoint without pinching or indenting the skin; ensure the tape lies flat.
Read the measurement through the window to the nearest 0.1 cm and note the colour zone.

skill.exam.paed.muac.normal: MUAC greater than 13.5 cm (13.5 to 16.5 cm is normal, green zone on Shakir tape).
skill.exam.paed.muac.abnormal: MUAC less than 12.5 cm (red zone: severe undernutrition / severe wasting); MUAC 12.5 to 13.5 cm (yellow zone: moderate undernutrition / moderate wasting).
skill.exam.paed.muac.significance: MUAC <12.5 cm (Shakir red zone) identifies severe wasting requiring immediate nutritional rehabilitation (facility stabilization or community RUTF).
skill.exam.paed.muac.practice: Practise identifying the acromion and olecranon on a colleague, folding the measuring tape in half to mark the exact midpoint, and applying the tape with correct tension.
pitfalls: Measuring MUAC with the arm held flexed or tense, which contracts the biceps and falsely inflates the circumference reading.
Pulling the tape too tightly so that it indents the skin, creating a falsely low reading.
Using MUAC as a primary nutritional index in infants under 6 months of age, where age-specific weight-for-length is required.

probes.q: For which age bracket is mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) used as a primary screening index for acute malnutrition?
probes.a: Children aged 6 to 59 months (1 to 5 years).

probes.q: How do you determine the exact anatomical level for measuring MUAC?
probes.a: Flex the left arm at 90 degrees, identify the acromion process and olecranon process, measure the distance between them, and mark the exact midpoint.

probes.q: What are the Shakir tape cut-offs for severe undernutrition (red zone), moderate undernutrition (yellow zone), and normal (green zone)?
probes.a: Shakir tape classifies < 12.5 cm as severe (red zone), 12.5 to 13.5 cm as moderate (yellow zone), and 13.5 to 16.5 cm as normal (green zone).

rubric.text: Identifies acromion and olecranon processes on the flexed arm
Measures length between landmarks and marks the exact midpoint
Ensures the arm is straightened and hanging loosely before applying tape
Applies tape flat around the arm without indenting soft tissue
Accurately interprets colour zones and centimetre thresholds for acute malnutrition

teach.heading: Rationale of MUAC in the 6 to 59 month age window
teach.body:
In children between 6 and 59 months of age, total arm muscle and subcutaneous fat remain relatively constant despite rapid linear growth.

A single age-independent threshold can therefore screen for acute wasting and mortality risk across this entire age bracket.

MUAC correlates strongly with muscle wasting and predicts death from malnutrition accurately in community field surveys.

skill.exam.paed.body_proportions.title: Paediatric body proportions and skeletal ratios
skill.exam.paed.body_proportions.oneLine: Upper segment to lower segment ratio, arm span versus height, and head-to-chest circumference ratios
skill.exam.paed.body_proportions.why: Body proportions evolve predictably from infancy to maturity. Measuring skeletal ratios differentiates short-limb dwarfism (achondroplasia) from short-trunk dwarfism (vertebral anomalies) and identifies Marfan syndrome or delayed puberty.

steps.text: Measure total standing height (or recumbent length in infants) using stadiometer.
Measure the lower segment: locate the upper border of the pubic symphysis; measure vertically from the top of the pubic symphysis to the floor with the child standing erect barefoot.
Calculate the upper segment by subtracting the lower segment from total height: Upper segment = Total height - Lower segment.
Calculate the upper segment to lower segment ratio (US:LS ratio).

Measure arm span: have the child stand against a flat wall with arms abducted horizontally at 90 degrees to the trunk, palms facing forward; measure distance between the tips of the middle fingers across the back.
Measure chest circumference: place measuring tape around the thorax at the level of the xiphisternum or just below nipples at mid-inspiration, and compare with head circumference.

skill.exam.paed.body_proportions.normal: US:LS ratio 1.7:1 at birth, 1.5:1 at 2 years, 1.3:1 at 3 years, 1:1 at 9 years, and 0.9:1 in adolescents; arm span equals height around 10 years; head circumference exceeds chest circumference at birth, equals chest circumference at 9 to 12 months, and chest circumference exceeds head circumference after 1 year.
skill.exam.paed.body_proportions.abnormal: Elevated US:LS ratio (infantile ratio: achondroplasia, hypothyroidism, rickets); reduced US:LS ratio (short trunk/long limb: Marfan syndrome, vertebral anomalies); arm span exceeding height by >5 cm in adolescents; head circumference smaller than chest circumference in early infancy.
skill.exam.paed.body_proportions.significance: Elevated US:LS ratio indicates rhizomelic limb shortening (achondroplasia); reduced US:LS ratio with arm span exceeding height indicates Marfan syndrome or hypogonadism.
skill.exam.paed.body_proportions.practice: Measure lower segment from the upper border of the pubic symphysis to the floor on a partner, calculate upper segment, and determine whether arm span equals standing height.
pitfalls: Measuring the lower segment from the anterior superior iliac spine or umbilicus rather than the upper border of the pubic symphysis.
Measuring arm span with elbows flexed or arms sagging below horizontal shoulder level.
Failing to recognize that a 2-year-old child normally has an infantile US:LS ratio of 1.5:1 and misinterpreting it as skeletal dysplasia.

probes.q: At what ages does the upper segment to lower segment (US:LS) ratio normally reach 1.3:1 and 1:1?
probes.a: The US:LS ratio is approximately 1.3:1 at 3 years of age, and reaches 1:1 at 9 years of age.

probes.q: What is the relationship between head circumference and chest circumference in a newborn compared to a child over 1 year of age?
probes.a: In a newborn, head circumference is greater than chest circumference; they become equal between 9 and 12 months; and after 1 year of age, chest circumference exceeds head circumference.

probes.q: A 10-year-old child presents with short stature. The US:LS ratio is 1.5:1 (elevated for age). Does this indicate short-limb or short-trunk short stature, and name two causes.
probes.a: Short-limb (disproportionate) short stature; failure of lower limb growth retains an infantile ratio, seen in achondroplasia, untreated congenital hypothyroidism, or rickets.

rubric.text: Measures lower segment accurately from upper border of pubic symphysis to floor
Subtracts lower segment from height and calculates US:LS ratio correctly
Measures arm span across the back with arms abducted to 90 degrees
Compares chest circumference to head circumference by age norms
Differentiates short-limb from short-trunk disproportionate stature

teach.heading: Chronological evolution of the US:LS ratio
Clinical interpretation of disproportionate body ratios

points.d: Short-limb dwarfism: lower segments fail to elongate, retaining an infantile ratio (>1:1 after 9 years). Classic causes include achondroplasia, untreated congenital hypothyroidism, and rickets.
Short-trunk dwarfism (vertebral caries/Pott spine, severe kyphoscoliosis, mucopolysaccharidosis) or abnormally long limbs (Marfan syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome).
Arm span is shorter than length at birth and equals height around 10 years. Arm span exceeding height by >5 cm suggests Marfan syndrome or hypogonadism.
Head circumference exceeds chest circumference at birth by about 2 cm; they equalize between 9 and 12 months; chest circumference exceeds head circumference after 1 year.

skill.annex.paed.growth_charts.title: Growth chart plotting and nutritional classifications
skill.annex.paed.growth_charts.oneLine: WHO Z-score charts, Waterlow criteria for wasting and stunting, and IAP malnutrition grades
skill.annex.paed.growth_charts.why: Plotting anthropometric measurements on standardized growth charts transforms raw measurements into actionable clinical classifications: underweight, wasting, stunting, severe acute malnutrition, and failure to thrive.
skill.annex.paed.growth_charts.practice: Take three clinical vignettes with age, weight, and height; calculate percentage of expected values and determine IAP grade and Waterlow category for each.
pitfalls: Plotting standing height on a recumbent length chart without applying length conversion correction.
Confusing wasting (weight-for-height, an acute nutritional deficit) with stunting (height-for-age, a chronic deficit).
Failing to use corrected gestational age when plotting preterm infants up to 2 years of chronological age.

probes.q: What clinical indices distinguish wasting from stunting in childhood malnutrition?
probes.a: Wasting is low weight-for-height (indicating acute malnutrition), while stunting is low height-for-age (indicating chronic, long-term malnutrition).

probes.q: What are the four grades of protein-energy malnutrition according to the Indian Academy of Pediatrics (IAP) classification?
probes.a: Grade 1 is 71 to 80% of expected weight; Grade 2 is 61 to 70%; Grade 3 is 51 to 60%; Grade 4 is 50% or less of expected weight (with K appended if oedema is present).

probes.q: According to Waterlow classification, how do you categorize a child with weight-for-height <80% and height-for-age <85%?
probes.a: Wasted and stunted (acute-on-chronic malnutrition).

rubric.text: Selects the appropriate sex-specific WHO growth chart for age
Calculates percent expected weight and assigns correct IAP grade (1 to 4)
Correctly applies Waterlow criteria to classify wasting and stunting
Identifies failure to thrive criteria: weight < 3rd centile or crossing 2 major centiles

teach.heading: Waterlow classification of wasting and stunting
WHO Z-score definitions and severe acute malnutrition

points.d: Between -2 SD and -3 SD indicates moderate undernutrition. Below -3 SD indicates severe undernutrition for weight-for-age, height-for-age, and weight-for-height.
In children aged 6 to 59 months, SAM is diagnosed by: (1) weight-for-height Z-score < -3 SD, or (2) MUAC < 11.5 cm, or (3) presence of bilateral pitting nutritional oedema.
Weight-for-age below the 3rd centile, or a downward deceleration crossing two major centile curves (e.g. from 50th to 10th centile) on standard growth charts.

skill.exam.paed.tanner_female.title: Female sexual maturity rating (Tanner staging)
skill.exam.paed.tanner_female.oneLine: Five-stage assessment of breast development, pubic hair, and pubertal tempo in girls
skill.exam.paed.tanner_female.why: Staging pubertal progression identifies precocious puberty (thelarche <8 years, menarche <10 years) or delayed puberty (no breast development by 13 to 14 years, primary amenorrhoea at 16 years), prompting timely endocrine or genetic evaluation.

steps.text: Ensure absolute privacy, warm surroundings, and the continuous presence of a female chaperone or parent throughout.
Explain the examination sensitively to both the girl and parent, obtaining assent and informed parental consent.
Inspect breast development from the front and profile, gently palpating the subareolar tissue to confirm glandular tissue rather than adipose deposition.
Stage breast development (Tanner B1 to B5): B1 preadolescent, B2 breast bud, B3 enlargement without contour separation, B4 secondary mound formed by areola and papilla, B5 mature adult contour.

Inspect pubic hair distribution (Tanner PH1 to PH5): PH1 none, PH2 sparse straight hair on medial labia, PH3 darker curling hair over mons, PH4 adult-type hair sparing thighs, PH5 adult feminine triangle extending to medial thighs.
Inquire about pubertal milestones: onset of thelarche, pubarche, peak height growth velocity, and menarche.

skill.exam.paed.tanner_female.normal: Pubertal onset between 8 and 13 years of age, following the orderly sequence: thelarche (breast budding), pubarche (pubic hair), peak growth spurt (stages 2-3), and menarche (average 2 to 2.5 years after thelarche, at stage 4).
skill.exam.paed.tanner_female.abnormal: Precocious puberty: thelarche before 8 years or menarche before 10 years; delayed puberty: absence of breast budding by 13 to 14 years or absence of menarche by 16 years.
skill.exam.paed.tanner_female.significance: Precocious puberty can cause early epiphyseal closure with stunted adult height; delayed puberty suggests Turner syndrome (45,X), hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, or constitutional delay.
skill.exam.paed.tanner_female.practice: Review schematic diagrams of Tanner breast stages B1 to B5 to distinguish the subtle difference between stage 3 continuous contour and stage 4 secondary mound elevation.
pitfalls: Mistaking lipomastia (adipose deposition in an overweight girl) for true glandular breast budding; subareolar palpation is required.
Assuming menarche occurs at the onset of puberty; menarche is a late milestone, typically appearing at Tanner stage 4 after the peak growth spurt decelerates.
Conducting the examination without an appropriate chaperone or neglecting patient modesty.

probes.q: What is the usual chronological sequence of secondary sexual characteristic development in girls?
probes.a: Thelarche (breast budding), followed by pubarche (pubic hair), peak linear growth spurt, and menarche (TPM).

probes.q: What anatomical feature distinguishes Tanner stage 4 breast development from stage 3?
probes.a: In stage 4, the areola and papilla (nipple) project above the level of the breast mound to form a distinct secondary mound; in stage 3, there is breast enlargement with a continuous contour.

probes.q: What chronological cut-offs define precocious puberty and delayed puberty in girls?
probes.a: Precocious puberty is breast budding before 8 years or menarche before 10 years; delayed puberty is absence of breast development by 13 to 14 years or absence of menarche by 16 years.

rubric.text: Ensures privacy, sensitive explanation, and presence of a chaperone
Palpates subareolar tissue to verify true glandular breast tissue
Accurately classifies Tanner breast development from stage B1 to B5
Accurately classifies Tanner pubic hair distribution from PH1 to PH5
Identifies chronological cut-offs for precocious and delayed puberty

teach.heading: Tanner breast development stages (B1 to B5)

rows: Further enlargement of breast and areola
Areola and papilla elevate above breast

teach.heading: Tanner pubic hair stages (PH1 to PH5)
Pubertal tempo and milestone timelines in girls

points.d: Thelarche (breast bud) is the first sign in over 85 percent of girls, followed within months by pubarche (pubic hair), peak growth velocity during stages 2 and 3, and menarche at stage 4.

Occurs on average 2.0 to 2.5 years after thelarche, usually around Tanner breast stage 4. Epiphyseal fusion follows within 18 to 24 months after menarche, with limited subsequent linear growth (about 4 to 6 cm).
Breast budding before 8 years or menarche before 10 years warrants central versus peripheral pubertal evaluation, bone age X-ray of the left hand, and pelvic ultrasonography.

Lack of breast development by 13 to 14 years, or lack of menarche by 16 years (or >3 years after thelarche), requires karyotyping (Turner syndrome), gonadotrophin assay, and systemic exclusion of coeliac disease.

skill.exam.paed.tanner_male.title: Male sexual maturity rating (Tanner staging)
skill.exam.paed.tanner_male.oneLine: Prader orchidometer testicular volumetry, genital staging, and pubic hair in boys
skill.exam.paed.tanner_male.why: Testicular enlargement (volume >= 4 mL) is the first physical sign of male puberty. Recognizing abnormal pubertal timing identifies central precocious puberty, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, or Klinefelter syndrome.

steps.text: Ensure complete privacy, warm examination environment, and the presence of a chaperone or parent.
Explain the examination respectfully to the adolescent and parent, obtaining assent and consent.
Inspect the scrotum: assess skin rugosity, thinning, and pigmentation.
Palpate each testis gently between your thumb and index finger, bringing it to the lower part of the scrotal sac.
Use a Prader orchidometer to compare each testis directly against the beads; match the volume of the testis (excluding epididymis and scrotal skin) to the nearest bead (calibrated from 1 to 25 mL).
Inspect the penis: evaluate length and circumference of the penile shaft, development of the glans, and urethral meatus.

Stage pubic hair (Tanner PH1 to PH5): PH1 preadolescent, PH2 scanty slightly pigmented hair at base of penis, PH3 darker coarser curly hair over pubic bone, PH4 adult-type hair sparing thighs, PH5 spread to medial thighs.

skill.exam.paed.tanner_male.normal: Pubertal onset in boys between 9 and 14 years of age; initial sign is testicular enlargement >=4 mL, followed by pubic hair, penile enlargement, peak growth spurt (stages 3-4), and spermarche.
skill.exam.paed.tanner_male.abnormal: Precocious puberty (testicular volume >=4 mL before 9.5 years); delayed puberty (testicular volume <4 mL by 14 years); discordance between testicular size and pubic hair (e.g. pubic hair with small prepubertal testes).
skill.exam.paed.tanner_male.significance: Testicular volume >=4 mL confirms activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis (central puberty); prepubertal testes (<4 mL) in a boy with pubic hair or penile enlargement indicates peripheral precocious puberty (congenital adrenal hyperplasia, adrenal tumour).
skill.exam.paed.tanner_male.practice: Practise using a Prader orchidometer to calibrate tactile size appreciation: distinguish 1 to 3 mL (prepubertal) from 4 mL (early puberty), 10 to 12 mL (mid-puberty), and 20 to 25 mL (adult).
pitfalls: Including the scrotal skin or epididymis in the orchidometer measurement, which overestimates testicular volume.
Examining with cold hands, which triggers a brisk cremasteric reflex and retracts testes into the inguinal canal.
Assuming penile enlargement or pubic hair is the first sign of puberty; testicular enlargement is the true initial sign.

probes.q: What testicular volume measured by a Prader orchidometer marks the onset of puberty in boys?
probes.a: 4 millilitres (prepubertal is 1 to 3 mL; 4 mL or greater indicates central pubertal onset).

probes.q: What is the chronological sequence of secondary sexual characteristic development in boys?
probes.a: Testicular enlargement, followed by pubic hair growth, penile lengthening and broadening, peak linear growth spurt, axillary/facial hair, and spermarche.

probes.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with adult-length penis and Tanner stage 3 pubic hair, but bilateral testicular volumes are only 2 mL. What does this signify?
probes.a: Peripheral (pseudoisosexual) precocious puberty; the small testes prove the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is inactive, indicating excess adrenal or exogenous androgens (such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia or adrenal tumour).

rubric.text: Ensures privacy, gentle technique, and presence of a chaperone
Measures testicular volume bilaterally using a Prader orchidometer
Accurately classifies Tanner genital stage G1 to G5
Accurately classifies Tanner pubic hair stage PH1 to PH5
Identifies discordance between testicular volume and virilization

teach.heading: Tanner male genital stages and testicular volume
Tanner pubic hair stages in boys
Clinical patterns: central versus peripheral puberty in boys

points.d: Driven by pulsatile GnRH release. Testes enlarge first (>=4 mL) because FSH stimulates seminiferous tubules (85 percent of testicular volume) and LH stimulates Leydig cell testosterone.
Virilization (penile growth, pubic hair, accelerated growth) with prepubertal testes (<4 mL) indicates adrenal androgen excess (congenital adrenal hyperplasia, adrenal adenoma) or Leydig cell tumour.
Unlike girls who experience their growth spurt early (stages 2-3), boys experience their peak height velocity late in puberty, during Tanner stages 3 and 4.
Absence of testicular enlargement (<4 mL) by 14 years of age defines delayed puberty in boys, warranting LH, FSH, testosterone, and bone age assessment.

skill.exam.paed.skin_lesions.title: Examination of paediatric skin lesions
skill.exam.paed.skin_lesions.oneLine: Primary lesion morphology, diascopy for purpura, and neurocutaneous marker identification
skill.exam.paed.skin_lesions.why: Paediatric skin eruptions range from benign self-limiting viral exanthems to life-threatening emergencies (meningococcaemia, purpura fulminans) or genetic neurocutaneous syndromes (neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis). Systematic examination prevents fatal delays.

steps.text: Undress the child completely in a warm, well-lit room to examine the entire skin surface, including scalp, flexures, diaper area, palms, and soles.
Identify the primary lesion morphology: flat colour change (macule/patch), solid raised lesion (papule/plaque/nodule), or fluid-filled lesion (vesicle/bulla/pustule).

Measure lesion dimensions with a clear ruler: macule (<1 cm) versus patch (>1 cm); papule (<0.5 cm) versus nodule (>0.5 cm deep) or plaque (broad flat-topped); vesicle (<0.5 cm) versus bulla (>0.5 cm).
Perform diascopy (the glass slide or tumbler test): press a clear glass slide firmly over red or purple lesions to distinguish blanching erythema from non-blanching extravasated blood.
Classify non-blanching purpuric bleeds: petechiae (<2 mm pinhead bleeds), purpura (2 to 10 mm lesions), and ecchymoses (>10 mm confluent bruises).

Screen systematically for neurocutaneous markers: cafe-au-lait macules (>6 lesions >5 mm prepubertal or >15 mm postpubertal indicate neurofibromatosis 1); hypopigmented ash-leaf macules or shagreen patches (tuberous sclerosis); facial port-wine stain (Sturge-Weber syndrome).

skill.exam.paed.skin_lesions.normal: Intact, smooth skin without petechial, vesicular, or dysplastic lesions; isolated birthmarks (e.g. solitary cafe-au-lait spot or lumbosacral Mongolian spot) are benign.
skill.exam.paed.skin_lesions.abnormal: Non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash; multiple (>6) cafe-au-lait macules; hypopigmented macules; generalized vesicular eruption (varicella, herpes); crusted honey-coloured lesions (impetigo).
skill.exam.paed.skin_lesions.significance: Non-blanching petechiae with fever is an immediate medical emergency (invasive meningococcal disease); palpable purpura on buttocks and extensor legs indicates IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura); neurocutaneous markers indicate underlying epilepsy or intracranial tumours.
skill.exam.paed.skin_lesions.practice: Practise performing diascopy using a clean glass slide on erythematous insect bites or flushed skin, noting the immediate blanching. Measure lesion diameters with a millimeter ruler.
pitfalls: Assuming a petechial rash with fever is a mild viral exanthem; fever with petechiae is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise.
Failing to undress the child completely, missing buttock purpura in Henoch-Schonlein purpura or diaper area rashes.
Confusing Mongolian spots (benign congenital lumbosacral dermal melanocytosis) with non-accidental trauma/bruising in infants.

probes.q: What bedside test differentiates inflammatory vascular erythema from purpuric bleeding in the skin?
probes.a: Diascopy (the glass slide or glass tumbler test); erythema blanches under pressure because blood is within intact capillaries, whereas purpura does not blanch because red blood cells have extravasated into tissue.

probes.q: What dimensional cut-offs separate petechiae, purpura, and ecchymoses?
probes.a: Petechiae are pinpoint bleeds less than 2 millimetres; purpura are bleeds measuring 2 to 10 millimetres; ecchymoses are bruises greater than 10 millimetres (1 centimetre).

probes.q: What number and dimensions of cafe-au-lait macules meet the diagnostic criterion for neurofibromatosis type 1 in a prepubertal child?
probes.a: Six or more cafe-au-lait macules greater than 5 millimetres in greatest diameter in prepubertal children (or greater than 15 millimetres in postpubertal individuals).

rubric.text: Undresses child completely to inspect all skin surfaces including flexures
Accurately categorizes primary lesion morphology (macule, papule, vesicle, pustule)
Performs diascopy / blanching test to identify non-blanching purpura
Measures lesion dimensions against standard cut-off definitions
Systematically screens for cafe-au-lait macules and ash-leaf spots

teach.heading: Primary paediatric skin lesion morphology and cut-offs
Purpuric skin lesions: definitions and red flags

points.d: Pinpoint, non-blanching haemorrhages under 2 mm in diameter. Widespread petechiae with fever is a red-flag sign of meningococcaemia or severe thrombocytopenia (ITP, leukaemia).
Non-blanching cutaneous bleeds measuring 2 to 10 mm. Palpable purpura over the buttocks and lower limbs is diagnostic of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura).
Extravasated blood patches greater than 10 mm (bruises). Large spontaneous ecchymoses suggest coagulation factor deficiencies (haemophilia) or child abuse.

teach.heading: Neurocutaneous markers to identify in childhood

points.d: Uniform light brown patches. Six or more measuring >5 mm prepubertal or >15 mm postpubertal indicate neurofibromatosis type 1; look for axillary freckling (Crowe sign).
Lance-ovoid ash-leaf macules (best seen under Wood lamp) or confetti lesions; 3 or more indicate tuberous sclerosis; look for shagreen patch and facial angiofibromas.
Congenital capillary malformation; distribution over the ophthalmic (V1) branch of the trigeminal nerve indicates Sturge-Weber syndrome with leptomeningeal angiomatosis.

skill.exam.paed.resp.inspection.title: Paediatric chest inspection and breathing patterns
skill.exam.paed.resp.inspection.oneLine: Observe respiratory rate, abdominal motion, chest wall recessions, and accessory muscle recruitment before touching the child
skill.exam.paed.resp.inspection.why: Inspection provides the earliest and most sensitive indicators of respiratory distress in paediatric patients. Touching or distressing an infant triggers crying, immediately obscuring baseline respiratory rate, chest wall indrawing, and abdominal dynamics.

steps.text: Observe the undisturbed child in the parent lap or bed under good lighting with the chest exposed.
Count respiratory rate for a full 60 seconds, observing abdominal and thoracic respiratory excursion.
Identify the primary pattern of respiration: predominantly abdominal in infants and young children, becoming thoracoabdominal with maturation.
Inspect chest wall contours for symmetry, pectus excavatum, pectus carinatum, barrel deformity, or rib crowding.
Check for signs of increased work of breathing: nasal flaring (alae nasi), head bobbing, sternal recession, intercostal indrawing, and subcostal retraction.
Inspect for visible apical pulsation, dilated chest veins, thoracic scars, or surgical drain marks.

skill.exam.paed.resp.inspection.normal: Bilaterally symmetrical chest wall expansion, predominantly abdominal respiration in infants and young children, absence of chest wall indrawing or nasal flaring, age-appropriate resting respiratory rate.
skill.exam.paed.resp.inspection.abnormal: Marked subcostal, intercostal, or suprasternal retractions, nasal flaring, head bobbing, asymmetric chest expansion, tachypnoea, barrel deformity, or thoracoabdominal asynchrony (seesaw breathing).
skill.exam.paed.resp.inspection.significance: Subcostal and intercostal retractions reflect elevated work of breathing due to compliant paediatric rib cages. Seesaw breathing indicates severe upper airway obstruction or diaphragmatic fatigue, while asymmetry suggests unilateral pathology like consolidation, pneumothorax, or massive effusion.
skill.exam.paed.resp.inspection.practice: Count resting respiratory rates in ten paediatric patients while seated quietly, documenting breathing pattern and presence or absence of recessions across three distinct age groups.
pitfalls: Counting respiratory rate for only 15 seconds in an infant with physiological periodic breathing.
Examining a crying child without waiting for a calm period, misinterpreting crying-induced tachypnoea as respiratory failure.
Overlooking subtle alae nasi flaring or head nodding in sleepy infants.
Failing to expose the lower rib cage and abdomen adequately, missing severe subcostal indrawing.

probes.q: What is the normal resting respiratory pattern in healthy infants and children under 2 years of age?
probes.a: Predominantly abdominal breathing due to horizontal rib orientation and reliance on the diaphragm.

probes.q: Why do infants develop visible chest wall retractions much earlier than adults during respiratory distress?
probes.a: The paediatric thoracic cage is highly compliant and cartilaginous, so negative intrathoracic pressures pull the chest wall inward.

probes.q: What does thoracoabdominal asynchrony or seesaw breathing signify in a young infant?
probes.a: Severe respiratory fatigue, impending respiratory failure, or severe upper airway obstruction where the chest draws inward as the abdomen expands.

rubric.text: Observes the calm child before touching or causing distress
Counts respiratory rate for a full 60 seconds
Assesses subcostal, intercostal, and suprasternal retractions systematically
Identifies whether breathing pattern is abdominal or thoracoabdominal
Inspects for nasal flaring and head bobbing

teach.heading: Observation before tactile examination
teach.body:
Inspection is the cornerstone of paediatric chest evaluation. Young children and infants quickly become agitated upon being touched by unfamiliar examiners, particularly cold hands or instruments.

Always position the child comfortably, preferably in the parent lap. Observe quiet breathing from a distance to establish true resting respiratory rate and physiological chest dynamics.

teach.heading: Normal dynamics versus signs of distress

rows: Reduces upper airway resistance in distress
Negative pleural pressure on soft ribs
Increased work of breathing, lower tract disease
Significant accessory muscle use in infants

teach.heading: Chest wall contours and symmetry
teach.body:
In infancy, the anteroposterior diameter is nearly equal to the transverse diameter. As the child grows, transverse diameter expands faster, creating the adult oval contour.

Inspect for asymmetry, unilateral flattening, or rib crowding indicating chronic volume loss such as collapse or fibrosis. Inspect for pectus excavatum or pectus carinatum.

skill.exam.paed.resp.palpation.title: Paediatric chest palpation and expansion
skill.exam.paed.resp.palpation.oneLine: Confirm tracheal alignment, locate apex beat, and measure hemithorax expansion with gentle tactile examination
skill.exam.paed.resp.palpation.why: Palpation confirms inspection findings of mediastinal shift and localized volume loss. In infants and young children, a short neck and thick subcutaneous tissue make tracheal palpation challenging, necessitating subtle technique to avoid provoking paroxysms of coughing or distress.

steps.text: Warm both hands thoroughly before touching the child chest wall.
Palpate the trachea gently at the suprasternal notch using the index finger, confirming midline position or deviation (Trail sign).
Locate the apex beat using warmed fingers: in children under 4 to 7 years, the normal position is in the 4th intercostal space medial to the midclavicular line.
Assess chest expansion by placing hands symmetrically over lower chest with thumbs meeting in the midline, watching divergence during inspiration (normal 2 to 5 cm).
Palpate bilateral hemithorax excursion across anterior, axillary, and posterior lung fields to detect unilateral restriction.
Evaluate tactile vocal fremitus by placing the ulnar border of the hand on the chest while the older child says '99' or during spontaneous infant crying.
Palpate for rib tenderness, palpable rhonchi, and pleural friction fremitus.

skill.exam.paed.resp.palpation.normal: Central trachea, apex beat in the 4th intercostal space medial to midclavicular line (in young children), symmetrical chest expansion of 2 to 5 cm, equal bilateral vocal fremitus, absence of tenderness or palpable fremitus.
skill.exam.paed.resp.palpation.abnormal: Tracheal deviation to one side, displaced apex beat, reduced hemithorax expansion on the affected side, localized intercostal tenderness, palpable rhonchi or pleural rub, increased or decreased vocal fremitus.
skill.exam.paed.resp.palpation.significance: Tracheal deviation coupled with apex shift localises mediastinal displacement: shifted towards the lesion in collapse or fibrosis, and away in large effusion or tension pneumothorax. Palpable rhonchi reflect coarse secretions in major conducting airways.
skill.exam.paed.resp.palpation.practice: Practice gentle suprasternal tracheal localisation and apex beat identification in healthy young children, confirming the transition from 4th space to 5th space with increasing age.
pitfalls: Pressing too firmly into the suprasternal notch, triggering coughing and vocal cord spasm in an infant.
Expecting the apex beat in the 5th intercostal space in toddlers, mistaking a normal 4th space apex for abnormal elevation.
Assessing chest expansion with cold hands, provoking defensive abdominal wall tightening.
Omitting tactile vocal fremitus during crying episodes in infants, losing an opportunity to evaluate sound transmission.

probes.q: Where is the normal apex beat located in a healthy child under 4 years of age?
probes.a: In the 4th intercostal space, medial to the midclavicular line.

probes.q: What is the normal range of chest expansion in older children?
probes.a: Normal chest expansion is 2 to 5 cm.

probes.q: How does one distinguish palpable rhonchi from a pleural friction fremitus on chest palpation?
probes.a: Palpable rhonchi frequently change or clear after a vigorous cough, whereas pleural friction fremitus persists and corresponds to the respiratory cycle.

rubric.text: Warms hands thoroughly before touching the child
Gently palpates the trachea at the suprasternal notch
Accurately locates the apex beat in the 4th intercostal space in young child
Evaluates chest expansion and hemithorax symmetry
Tests vocal fremitus or cry fremitus bilaterally

teach.heading: Age-specific landmarks in paediatric palpation
teach.body:
Paediatric thoracic anatomy differs significantly from adult anatomy. In infants and children younger than 4 to 7 years, the heart sits more horizontally within the thoracic cavity.

Consequently, the normal apical impulse is found in the 4th intercostal space medial to the midclavicular line. By 7 years of age, downward cardiac rotation shifts the apex beat to the 5th space.

teach.heading: Tactile fremitus and airway secretions
teach.body:
Tactile vocal fremitus reflects sound conduction from the larynx through patent airways and lung parenchyma to the chest wall. In preverbal children, palpate during crying.

Fremitus increases over consolidated lung with patent bronchus. Palpable rhonchi occur when secretions rattle in large airways, often disappearing after an effective cough.

rows: Reduced in chest wall deformity, severe asthma, effusion
Shifted away in tension pneumothorax, toward in collapse
Shifted away in massive effusion, toward in fibrosis

skill.exam.paed.resp.percussion.title: Paediatric chest percussion technique and notes
skill.exam.paed.resp.percussion.oneLine: Apply light pleximeter percussion from resonant to dull areas, identifying consolidation, effusion, and organ borders
skill.exam.paed.resp.percussion.why: Heavy adult-style percussion reverberates through thin paediatric chest walls, obscuring small areas of dullness and alarming the child. Gentle, wrist-driven percussion accurately outlines lung boundaries, diaphragmatic position, and pleural fluid.

steps.text: Place the middle phalanx of the non-dominant middle finger (pleximeter) firmly against the chest wall, keeping all other fingers raised off the skin to prevent dampening vibrations.
Align the pleximeter parallel to the expected margin of dullness or intercostal spaces.
Strike the pleximeter sharply and lightly using the tip of the dominant middle or index finger (plexor), with movement originating strictly from the relaxed wrist joint.
Withdraw the plexor finger immediately after impact to avoid dampening the generated acoustic note.
Percuss directly onto the clavicles with the fingertip to assess apical lung fields without a pleximeter.
Percuss systematically from areas of known resonance toward areas of suspected dullness, comparing corresponding contralateral regions across anterior, axillary, and posterior zones.
Determine the upper border of liver dullness anteriorly, which normally corresponds to the right 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line.
For axillary percussion, have the child raise arms above head; for posterior percussion, have the child cross arms in front to displace the scapulae laterally.

skill.exam.paed.resp.percussion.normal: Symmetrical resonant percussion note throughout bilateral lung fields, direct clavicular resonance, liver dullness beginning at right 5th intercostal space, tympanitic note over Traube space.
skill.exam.paed.resp.percussion.abnormal: Hyper-resonant note (pneumothorax, hyperinflation in asthma), impaired or dull note (consolidation, atelectasis, pleural thickening, fibrosis), stony dull note (pleural effusion or empyema), obliteration of Traube space.
skill.exam.paed.resp.percussion.significance: Stony dullness is characteristic of pleural effusion, contrasting with the dullness of consolidation which still transmits vibrations. Hyper-resonance indicates excessive air trapping or pneumothorax. Displacement of the upper liver border downward signifies hyperinflation, while upward shift reflects diaphragmatic elevation or collapse.
skill.exam.paed.resp.percussion.practice: Practice light wrist-flick percussion on a firm table and chest wall model, ensuring adjacent non-pleximeter fingers remain elevated and stroke recovery is instantaneous.
pitfalls: Percussing with excessive force on a thin paediatric chest, which vibrates the entire hemithorax and obscures localized lesions.
Leaving adjacent fingers resting on the chest wall, dampening sound waves and creating artificial dullness.
Moving the entire arm or elbow instead of flicking strictly from the wrist.
Failing to ask the child to cross arms across the chest for posterior interscapular percussion.

probes.q: Which anatomical landmark defines the normal upper border of liver dullness in a child?
probes.a: The right 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of a stony dull percussion note in a child with fever and breathlessness?
probes.a: Stony dullness indicates fluid in the pleural space, such as a parapneumonic effusion or empyema.

probes.q: Why must adjacent fingers of the non-dominant hand be lifted off the chest during paediatric percussion?
probes.a: Resting adjacent fingers on the chest wall dampens vibrations, causing false impairment or artificial dullness.

rubric.text: Places pleximeter firmly with adjacent fingers raised off the skin
Delivers crisp percussion strokes originating purely from the wrist
Rebounds plexor finger immediately after contact to avoid sound dampening
Compares symmetrical anatomical areas of both hemithoraces
Identifies the upper border of liver dullness at the right 5th space

teach.heading: Principles of paediatric percussion
teach.body:
Children have thin, compliant chest walls with minimal subcutaneous fat. Heavy percussion transmits sound waves across the mediastinum, causing false resonance or blurring boundaries.

Keep the pleximeter finger parallel to rib spaces and lift adjacent fingers. Deliver two crisp, light taps per station, flicking cleanly from the wrist.

teach.heading: Special percussion boundaries
teach.body:
Percuss downward along the right midclavicular line from resonant lung to find the upper liver margin at the 5th intercostal space.

Traube space over the left lower anterior chest is normally resonant due to the gastric air bubble. Dullness here suggests left pleural effusion, splenomegaly, or full stomach.

skill.exam.paed.resp.auscultation.title: Paediatric chest auscultation and added sounds
skill.exam.paed.resp.auscultation.oneLine: Systematically evaluate breath sound character, symmetrical air entry, crackles, wheezes, and vocal resonance
skill.exam.paed.resp.auscultation.why: Auscultation maps regional airflow, parenchymal consolidation, and airway narrowing. Because children have puerile breath sounds due to thin thoracic walls, unfamiliar examiners frequently misinterpret normal physiological harshness as bronchial breathing.

steps.text: Warm the stethoscope chest-piece thoroughly between palms before applying to the child skin.
Auscultate systematically anteriorly (apices down to 6th rib), laterally in the axillae (to 8th rib), and posteriorly (to 11th rib).
Listen through at least one complete inspiratory and expiratory cycle at each position, comparing symmetrical areas.
Determine breath sound intensity (normal, diminished, or absent) and quality (vesicular, bronchial, or bronchovesicular).
Listen for adventitious added sounds: coarse or fine crepitations (crackles), polyphonic or monophonic rhonchi (wheezes), and pleural friction rubs.
Assess vocal resonance by having the child vocalize ('99' or counting) or listening to cry resonance in infants, checking for bronchophony, whispering pectoriloquy, or aegophony.
Perform specialized tests if hydropneumothorax is suspected: coin test for metallic transmission and succussion splash upon gentle shaking.

skill.exam.paed.resp.auscultation.normal: Puerile vesicular breath sounds (harsh inspiratory sound with quiet, short expiratory phase without a pause), symmetrical bilateral air entry, absence of added sounds, normal vocal resonance.
skill.exam.paed.resp.auscultation.abnormal: Diminished or absent breath sounds, true tubular bronchial breathing with distinct expiratory pause, inspiratory or expiratory crackles, polyphonic wheezes, pleural friction rub, increased vocal resonance with aegophony.
skill.exam.paed.resp.auscultation.significance: True bronchial breathing with crackles indicates consolidation with patent bronchus. Diminished breath sounds with stony dullness indicate pleural effusion, whereas diminished sounds with hyper-resonance indicate pneumothorax. Wheezes reflect diffuse lower airway narrowing.
skill.exam.paed.resp.auscultation.practice: Listen to chest sounds in healthy toddlers to appreciate the normal harshness of puerile vesicular breathing, comparing it with adult vesicular breathing.
pitfalls: Mistaking normal paediatric puerile breath sounds for pathological tubular bronchial breathing.
Auscultating only anteriorly, completely missing bibasilar pneumonia or posterior empyema.
Confusing transmitted upper airway sounds (stridor or rattling secretions) with true intrathoracic crackles or wheezes.
Auscultating over clothing or while the child is shivering or crying continuously.

probes.q: What is puerile breathing in a paediatric patient?
probes.a: Normal harsh vesicular breath sounds heard in young children due to their thin chest wall.

probes.q: How does one distinguish transmitted upper airway rattles from lower airway fine crackles?
probes.a: Upper airway sounds are coarse, loudest over the neck, transmitted throughout the chest, and often clear with throat clearing or coughing.

probes.q: What auscultatory triad indicates lobar consolidation with a patent supplying bronchus?
probes.a: Tubular bronchial breathing, inspiratory crackles, and increased vocal resonance or bronchophony.

rubric.text: Warms stethoscope before placing it on the patient
Auscultates anterior, axillary, and posterior lung zones systematically
Listens through a full inspiratory and expiratory cycle at each site
Distinguishes normal puerile breathing from bronchial breath sounds
Correctly identifies crackles, wheezes, or pleural rubs

teach.heading: The nature of paediatric breath sounds
teach.body:
Breath sounds in infants and children are normally puerile: louder, harsher, and more resonant than in adults. The thin chest wall attenuates higher frequencies far less than an adult wall.

In true bronchial breathing, inspiration and expiration are equal in length with a distinct silent pause between them, and expiration has a tubular quality.

teach.heading: Adventitious sounds in childhood chest disease
Auscultation zones and transmission traps
teach.body:
Sound transmits easily across the small paediatric hemithorax. Stridor or upper airway rattling frequently radiates throughout both lung fields.

Place the stethoscope over the trachea at the neck. If the sound is loudest at the neck and transmitted downwards, it originates in the upper airway.

sources.locator: pneumonia_long_case: clinicalPearls
Auscultation of the Lungs

skill.exam.paed.resp.distress_grunt.title: Assessment of paediatric respiratory distress and audible sounds
skill.exam.paed.resp.distress_grunt.oneLine: Evaluate audible sounds including grunting, stridor, and wheeze, identifying physiological compensation and severity
skill.exam.paed.resp.distress_grunt.why: Audible breathing sounds without a stethoscope alert the clinician to impending respiratory exhaustion or critical airway compromise. Specifically, an expiratory grunt is a compensatory defence against alveolar collapse that demands urgent recognition.

steps.text: Stand near the child and listen for audible breathing sounds before touching or disturbing the child.
Identify an expiratory grunt: a short, low-pitched, repetitive guttural sound occurring at the beginning or end of expiration.
Identify stridor: a harsh, high-pitched monophonic sound heard predominantly during inspiration, indicating extrathoracic upper airway obstruction.
Identify audible wheeze: a continuous, musical, high-pitched sound heard primarily during expiration, indicating intrathoracic airway narrowing.
Check for tachypnoea against age-specific thresholds: over 60 breaths/min in under 2 months, over 50 in 2 to 12 months, over 40 in 1 to 5 years.
Look for positional preference: tripod positioning or neck extension to maintain airway patency.
Assess ability to feed, speak, or cry vigorously, which reflects physiological cardiopulmonary reserve.

skill.exam.paed.resp.distress_grunt.normal: Quiet, effortless respiration without audible sounds at rest, normal respiratory rate for age, ability to feed and vocalize normally.
skill.exam.paed.resp.distress_grunt.abnormal: Audible expiratory grunting, inspiratory or biphasic stridor, audible wheezing, marked tachypnoea, inability to complete feeds or utter full sentences, lethargy or exhaustion.
skill.exam.paed.resp.distress_grunt.significance: Grunting represents expiration against a partially closed glottis to generate physiological positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), preventing alveolar collapse in surfactant deficiency or pneumonia. Its presence signifies moderate to severe parenchymal lung disease or pulmonary oedema.
skill.exam.paed.resp.distress_grunt.practice: Observe clinical recordings of paediatric respiratory distress, training your ear to differentiate an expiratory grunt from inspiratory stridor and crying.
pitfalls: Mistaking an expiratory grunt for a whimpering cry or pain response, missing acute alveolar disease.
Overlooking stridor at rest, assuming airway obstruction is only mild because the child is quiet.
Relying on pulse oximetry alone; a grunting infant may maintain normal oxygen saturation until sudden terminal exhaustion.
Failing to check whether tachypnoea is present during calm sleep versus active crying.

probes.q: What is the physiological mechanism of an expiratory grunt in a child?
probes.a: Expiration against a partially closed glottis to generate positive end-expiratory pressure and maintain alveolar patency.

probes.q: What is the WHO tachypnoea threshold for an infant aged 3 months?
probes.a: 50 breaths per minute or more.

probes.q: How does the timing of stridor help localise the level of airway obstruction?
probes.a: Inspiratory stridor localises to extrathoracic upper airway (larynx, glottis), while biphasic stridor indicates subglottic or tracheal narrowing.

rubric.text: Listens for audible respiratory sounds without a stethoscope
Correctly identifies expiratory grunting and its clinical urgency
Distinguishes upper airway stridor from lower airway wheezing
Applies age-specific tachypnoea thresholds

teach.heading: The pathophysiology of grunting
teach.body:
An expiratory grunt is not a cry. It occurs when a child exhales against a voluntarily closed glottis, suddenly releasing the vocal cords at the end of expiration.

This manoeuvre acts as natural positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). It increases functional residual capacity and prevents microatelectasis in stiff, consolidated lungs.

teach.heading: Age-specific tachypnoea thresholds
teach.body:
Tachypnoea is often the earliest objective indicator of paediatric lower respiratory infection.

WHO guidelines define fast breathing as 60 or more breaths per minute under 2 months, 50 or more from 2 to 12 months, and 40 or more from 1 to 5 years.
