skill.exam.paed.resp.tracheal_shift.title: Mediastinal and tracheal shift in paediatric chest disease
skill.exam.paed.resp.tracheal_shift.oneLine: Evaluate tracheal and apex displacement to differentiate conditions that push, pull, or spare the mediastinum
skill.exam.paed.resp.tracheal_shift.why: Mediastinal position instantly divides unilateral opacity on a chest radiograph or physical exam into collapse versus effusion versus consolidation. Failing to check tracheal and apical displacement leads to dangerous errors such as chest tube insertion into a collapsed lung.

steps.text: Place the child in a symmetrical, supine or 45-degree upright position with the neck slightly extended in the midline.
Inspect the suprasternal notch and neck contours for visible deviation or prominence of one sternocleidomastoid muscle (Trail sign).
Gently slide the tip of the index finger along the trachea down to the suprasternal notch, assessing central position or lateral displacement.
Palpate the apex beat to evaluate concurrent displacement of the lower mediastinum.
Integrate tracheal position with chest expansion and percussion note across both hemithoraces.
Categorise findings into pathologies that push the mediastinum, pull the mediastinum, or cause no shift.

skill.exam.paed.resp.tracheal_shift.normal: Trachea is central in the suprasternal notch, apex beat is in its normal age-appropriate location (4th or 5th space), bilaterally symmetrical chest volume.
skill.exam.paed.resp.tracheal_shift.abnormal: Trachea displaced to the ipsilateral side (with reduced hemithorax volume), trachea displaced to the contralateral side (with increased or normal hemithorax volume), or apex beat shifted in tandem.
skill.exam.paed.resp.tracheal_shift.significance: A tracheal shift towards the side of dullness signifies lung volume loss (collapse, fibrosis, agenesis). Shift away from the side of dullness indicates space-occupying lesions (massive pleural effusion, empyema, diaphragmatic hernia), or away from hyper-resonance in tension pneumothorax. Consolidation causes no mediastinal shift.
skill.exam.paed.resp.tracheal_shift.practice: Palpate the trachea in a calm child, noting that minor postural rotation of the head can simulate false deviation.
pitfalls: Examining the trachea with the child head turned to one side, producing a spurious tracheal deviation.
Assuming consolidation shifts the trachea; uncomplicated consolidation maintains normal volume and a central trachea.
Forgetting to palpate the apex beat, which confirms whether the entire mediastinum has shifted or only the cervical trachea.
Missing subtle tracheal deviation in short-necked infants by failing to feel deep in the suprasternal notch.

probes.q: Name two paediatric pulmonary conditions that push the trachea away to the opposite side.
probes.a: Massive pleural effusion and tension pneumothorax.

probes.q: What is Trail sign on examination of the neck?
probes.a: Prominence of the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle on the side to which the trachea is deviated.

probes.q: A child has dullness over the entire right hemithorax. How does tracheal position differentiate collapse from effusion?
probes.a: The trachea shifts towards the right in collapse due to volume loss, but shifts towards the left in effusion due to fluid mass effect.

rubric.text: Ensures the child head and neck are strictly aligned in the midline
Gently palpates the trachea at the suprasternal notch
Correlates tracheal deviation with apex beat displacement
Correctly categorises shift direction as push, pull, or no shift

teach.heading: The physics of mediastinal displacement
teach.body:
The paediatric mediastinum is exceptionally mobile and compliant. Volume loss on one side pulls the mediastinal structures towards the disease.

Conversely, space-occupying accumulations of fluid or pressurized gas push the mediastinum across to the opposite, healthy hemithorax.

teach.heading: Clinical differentiation at the bedside
teach.body:
When examining an opaque hemithorax, always check the trachea and apex first.

If the trachea is pulled towards the lesion, the lung is deflated (collapse). If pushed away, fluid or gas occupies the pleural cavity.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.inspection_palpation.title: Paediatric precordial inspection and palpation
skill.exam.paed.cvs.inspection_palpation.oneLine: Inspect for precordial bulge and visible impulses, then palpate the apex, parasternal border, and thrills
skill.exam.paed.cvs.inspection_palpation.why: Chronic cardiac enlargement in infants and young children deforms the soft, cartilaginous anterior chest wall, producing a diagnostic precordial bulge. Palpating the precordium identifies ventricular hypertrophy, thrills, and palpable valve closures before auscultation.

steps.text: Position the child supine or reclined at 45 degrees with adequate thoracic exposure under gentle, warm lighting.
Inspect the precordium tangentially from the foot of the bed and from the right side for asymmetry or visible precordial bulge.
Inspect for visible pulsations at the apex, left parasternal area, epigastrium, and suprasternal notch.
Palpate the apical impulse with warmed fingertips: note location (4th intercostal space medial to midclavicular line in children under 7 years, 5th space thereafter).
Characterize the apical impulse: localized versus diffuse, tapping (palpable S1 in mitral stenosis) versus heaving (volume overload or hypertrophy).
Place the heel of the right hand firmly over the lower left parasternal edge to assess a left parasternal heave (right ventricular hypertrophy).
Palpate for palpable heart sounds: palpable S1 at apex, palpable P2 in the left 2nd intercostal space (pulmonary arterial hypertension).
Palpate for thrills over the apex, left sternal border, aortic, and pulmonary areas using the palmar aspect of the metacarpophalangeal joints.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.inspection_palpation.normal: Symmetrical precordium without bulge, apex beat in 4th intercostal space medial to midclavicular line (in under 7 years), absence of parasternal heave, thrills, or palpable heart sounds.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.inspection_palpation.abnormal: Visible precordial bulge, displaced apex beat (lateral or inferior), heaving or hyperdynamic apical impulse, left parasternal heave, palpable P2, systolic or diastolic thrill.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.inspection_palpation.significance: A precordial bulge indicates chronic cardiomegaly present since infancy while the chest wall was flexible. A left parasternal heave confirms right ventricular hypertrophy or severe dilatation, often seen in large left-to-right shunts or pulmonary stenosis. A thrill confirms a murmur of at least grade 4 intensity.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.inspection_palpation.practice: Palpate the precordium in children of different ages, feeling for the transition of the apex beat from the 4th to the 5th intercostal space and practicing detection of a subtle parasternal lift.
pitfalls: Searching for the apex beat in the 5th space in an infant or toddler, misidentifying a normal 4th space apex as displaced.
Using fingertips instead of the heel of the hand to test for a parasternal heave, confusing intercostal muscle twitching with true ventricular lift.
Overlooking a precordial bulge by examining only from above rather than looking tangentially along the chest surface.
Failing to warm hands prior to palpation, inducing abdominal wall guarding and tachycardia.

probes.q: What does a visible precordial bulge indicate in a young child?
probes.a: Chronic cardiomegaly present during infancy when the rib cage and sternum are pliable and compliant.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of a palpable second heart sound in the left second intercostal space?
probes.a: A palpable P2 indicates pulmonary arterial hypertension.

probes.q: How does one distinguish a hyperdynamic left ventricular impulse from a right ventricular parasternal heave?
probes.a: Left ventricular heave lifts the apex downward and laterally, whereas right ventricular hypertrophy lifts the heel of the hand placed at the left lower sternal border.

rubric.text: Inspects the chest wall tangentially for precordial bulge and pulsations
Accurately identifies apex beat location and character
Palpates for left parasternal heave using the heel of the hand
Systematically palpates for thrills across all cardiac areas
Checks for palpable S1 and P2

teach.heading: The pliable paediatric precordium
teach.body:
The infant rib cage is largely cartilaginous and malleable. If a cardiac chamber becomes chronically enlarged during the first two years of life, the chest wall molds outward around it.

This precordial bulge is an unmistakable sign of longstanding cardiomegaly, commonly due to large congenital left-to-right shunts.

rows: Left ventricular pressure or volume overload
Heel of hand at left sternal edge
Turbulent flow, murmur grade 4 or higher

teach.heading: Apex beat trajectory with somatic growth
teach.body:
In infants and young children, the diaphragm is relatively elevated, placing the heart in a transverse orientation.

The apex beat is normally in the 4th intercostal space, medial to the midclavicular line. As the thorax elongates around age 7, it moves to the 5th space.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.pulses_bp.title: Paediatric pulse and blood pressure evaluation
skill.exam.paed.cvs.pulses_bp.oneLine: Assess rhythm, volume, radio-femoral synchrony, four-limb blood pressure, and pulse pressure
skill.exam.paed.cvs.pulses_bp.why: Missing femoral pulse delay or diminution allows coarctation of the aorta to escape detection until severe hypertension, heart failure, or intracranial haemorrhage occurs. Blood pressure measurement in children requires correct cuff sizing to prevent spurious readings.

steps.text: Palpate peripheral pulses bilaterally: radial, brachial, femoral, and dorsalis pedis.
In infants, prioritize brachial and femoral pulses, as the radial pulse is small and easily obscured.
Perform simultaneous radio-femoral palpation (or brachio-femoral in infants) to evaluate for radio-femoral delay or volume discrepancy.
Note pulse rate, rhythm, and volume: check for bounding or collapsing (water-hammer) pulse in patent ductus arteriosus or aortic regurgitation.
Select an appropriate blood pressure cuff: the inflatable bladder width must cover at least 40% of mid-arm circumference, and bladder length must encircle 80% to 100% of arm.
Measure blood pressure in the right upper arm and compare with lower limb pressure in suspected coarctation or congenital heart disease.
Calculate pulse pressure (systolic minus diastolic pressure) and mean arterial pressure (diastolic plus one-third of pulse pressure).

skill.exam.paed.cvs.pulses_bp.normal: Symmetrical pulses in all four extremities, simultaneous radial and femoral impulses without delay, lower limb blood pressure equal to or slightly higher than upper limb, normal age-appropriate pulse pressure.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.pulses_bp.abnormal: Weak or absent femoral pulses, distinct radio-femoral delay, upper limb hypertension with lower limb hypotension, bounding water-hammer pulse (wide pulse pressure), weak thready pulse (narrow pulse pressure).
skill.exam.paed.cvs.pulses_bp.significance: Radio-femoral delay with lower extremity hypotension is pathognomonic of coarctation of the aorta. Bounding pulses with wide pulse pressure indicate runoff lesions such as patent ductus arteriosus, aortic regurgitation, or arteriovenous malformation. Narrow pulse pressure indicates severe aortic stenosis or cardiogenic shock.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.pulses_bp.practice: Practice simultaneous brachio-femoral palpation in infants, and calibrate blood pressure cuff selection against measured arm circumferences.
pitfalls: Using a blood pressure cuff that is too narrow, which produces falsely elevated blood pressure readings.
Failing to palpate femoral pulses routinely in every hypertensive or unwell child.
Attempting to palpate the radial pulse in a chubby infant instead of the easily accessible brachial artery.
Ignoring postural variations and anxiety-induced blood pressure elevation without allowing rest.

probes.q: What physical finding on pulse examination strongly suggests coarctation of the aorta?
probes.a: Radio-femoral delay with weak or absent femoral pulses compared to upper limb pulses.

probes.q: What is the consequence of using a blood pressure cuff with too small a bladder width?
probes.a: It artificially overestimates the child blood pressure, causing false-positive hypertension.

probes.q: Why is the pulse pressure widened in a child with a large patent ductus arteriosus?
probes.a: Diastolic runoff into the pulmonary circulation drops diastolic pressure, while left ventricular stroke volume increases systolic pressure.

rubric.text: Palpates both brachial and femoral pulses systematically
Performs simultaneous radio-femoral or brachio-femoral palpation
Selects correct blood pressure cuff based on arm dimensions
Measures four-limb blood pressure when cardiac disease is suspected
Assesses pulse volume, water-hammer character, and pulse pressure

teach.heading: The mandatory femoral pulse check
teach.body:
Femoral pulse palpation is non-negotiable in paediatrics. The femoral artery is palpated midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis.

Palpate the right radial and right femoral artery at the exact same moment. Normally they arrive synchronously; delay indicates coarctation of the aorta.

teach.heading: Blood pressure cuff physics in children
teach.body:
A cuff that is too small requires excessive pneumatic pressure to compress the underlying brachial artery, yielding falsely high numbers.

Ensure bladder width covers roughly 40% of arm circumference at midpoint, and bladder length encircles 80% to 100% of the upper arm circumference.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.auscultation.title: Paediatric cardiac auscultation and heart sounds
skill.exam.paed.cvs.auscultation.oneLine: Auscultate four cardiac areas to assess S1, physiological versus pathological S2 splitting, and extra sounds
skill.exam.paed.cvs.auscultation.why: Paediatric heart auscultation requires discriminating normal physiological variations from life-threatening structural anomalies. Normal children frequently exhibit physiological splitting of S2 and a physiological third heart sound; mistaking these for pathology leads to unnecessary anxiety and procedures.

steps.text: Auscultate with the child calm, using the diaphragm for high-pitched sounds and the bell lightly for low-pitched sounds.
Listen systematically at the four classical areas: mitral (apex), tricuspid (left lower sternal edge), pulmonary (left 2nd intercostal space), and aortic (right 2nd intercostal space).
Identify the first heart sound (S1), which coincides with the carotid pulse upstroke and is best heard at the apex.
Evaluate the second heart sound (S2) at the pulmonary area: listen for respiratory variation (A2 and P2 fusing on expiration and splitting on inspiration).
Distinguish physiological splitting from fixed wide splitting (atrial septal defect), single S2 (tetralogy of Fallot, transposition, pulmonary atresia), or loud P2 (pulmonary arterial hypertension).
Listen for extra sounds: physiological third heart sound (S3, common in healthy children), fourth heart sound (S4, always pathological), ejection clicks, and opening snaps.
Auscultate over the neck (carotid bruits and benign venous hum) and into the axilla and back.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.auscultation.normal: Normal S1, physiological respiratory splitting of S2 (widens on inspiration, single on expiration), normal intensity P2, absence of clicks or snaps, soft physiological S3 may be present in healthy children.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.auscultation.abnormal: Wide fixed split S2, single loud S2, abnormally accentuated P2, pathological S4, systolic ejection click, diastolic opening snap, pericardial friction rub.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.auscultation.significance: Wide fixed splitting of S2 is the hallmark of an atrial septal defect. A single loud S2 occurs when only one semilunar valve is audible (aortic in pulmonary atresia or severe TOF) or aortic valve is anterior (TGA). A loud P2 confirms elevated pulmonary artery pressures.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.auscultation.practice: Listen to S2 in a seated, calmly breathing child, tracking the subtle separation of A2 and P2 during deep inspiration.
pitfalls: Auscultating a tachypnoeic or crying infant without identifying S1 by simultaneous carotid or femoral palpation.
Confusing an innocent venous hum at the neck base with an intracardiac continuous murmur.
Missing the wide fixed split of S2 in an atrial septal defect by listening only at the apex rather than the pulmonary area.
Applying the bell with excessive pressure against the chest wall, turning it into an artificial diaphragm and obliterating low-frequency sounds.

probes.q: What congenital cardiac defect is characterized by a wide, fixed splitting of the second heart sound?
probes.a: Atrial septal defect (ASD).

probes.q: What is the mechanism of a venous hum in healthy children, and how can it be abolished at the bedside?
probes.a: Turbulent flow in internal jugular veins; abolished by turning the head, compressing the jugular vein, or lying supine.

probes.q: Why is the second heart sound single in a child with severe tetralogy of Fallot?
probes.a: The pulmonary component (P2) is extremely soft or inaudible due to severe right ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

rubric.text: Times S1 with carotid pulse or apex impulse
Analyses S2 splitting characteristics at the pulmonary area
Auscultates mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary, and aortic areas systematically
Identifies presence of S3, clicks, snaps, or rubs
Tests for venous hum by neck compression or position change

teach.heading: The second heart sound as the paediatric key
teach.body:
Auscultation of S2 at the left 2nd intercostal space is the single most informative element of paediatric auscultation.

S2 consists of aortic (A2) followed by pulmonary (P2) closure. Inspiration delays P2 and hastens A2, producing normal physiological splitting.

teach.heading: S2 splitting patterns in congenital heart disease

rows: Splits on inspiration, closes on expiration
Constant RV stroke volume across cycle
No audible split in any phase
Inaudible P2 or single semilunar trunk
P2 equal to or louder than A2 at apex

teach.heading: Benign innocent sounds: venous hum and S3
teach.body:
A venous hum is a benign continuous murmur heard under the right clavicle in healthy preschool children.

It is caused by turbulent venous blood entering the superior vena cava. It disappears immediately when the child lies flat or when the jugular vein is gently compressed.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.murmurs.title: Paediatric cardiac murmur grading and characterisation
skill.exam.paed.cvs.murmurs.oneLine: Grade systolic and diastolic murmurs from 1 to 6, evaluate radiation, and differentiate innocent from pathological murmurs
skill.exam.paed.cvs.murmurs.why: Over 50% of healthy children have an innocent heart murmur at some stage. Accurately characterizing the murmur prevents inappropriate cardiac invalidism and unnecessary referrals while ensuring serious structural malformations are promptly recognized.

steps.text: Auscultate the murmur systematically to define its epicentre (where it is loudest on the chest wall).
Determine murmur timing: systolic (early, midsystolic ejection, pansystolic/holosystolic, late) versus diastolic (early decrescendo, mid-diastolic rumbling) versus continuous.

Grade murmur intensity using the 6-point Levine scale: Grade 1 (very faint), Grade 2 (quiet but easily heard), Grade 3 (loud without thrill), Grade 4 (loud with palpable thrill), Grade 5 (heard with stethoscope rim lifted), Grade 6 (audible without stethoscope touching chest).
Map radiation: into the axilla (mitral regurgitation), into the neck/carotids (aortic stenosis), or through to the back (coarctation, pulmonary branch stenosis).

Perform dynamic manoeuvres: roll child into left lateral decubitus and listen at the apex with the bell for mitral murmurs; have child sit up, lean forward, and exhale while listening with diaphragm for aortic regurgitation.
Evaluate characteristics of innocent murmurs: Still murmur (vibratory or musical midsystolic at lower left sternal edge, soft, varies with posture) versus pathological murmurs.
Apply Nada criteria to determine likelihood of organic heart disease: one major (systolic murmur grade 3 or higher, diastolic murmur, cyanosis, CCF) or two minor criteria.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.murmurs.normal: No murmur, or a soft (grade 1 to 2), vibratory, midsystolic innocent murmur (e.g. Still murmur) that diminishes on standing, with normal S2 and absence of clicks, thrills, or symptoms.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.murmurs.abnormal: Any diastolic murmur, pansystolic murmur, continuous murmur (except venous hum), murmur of grade 4 or higher (accompanied by thrill), systolic ejection click, fixed split S2, radiation to back or axilla.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.murmurs.significance: Pansystolic murmurs indicate ventricular septal defect, mitral regurgitation, or tricuspid regurgitation. Diastolic murmurs are almost universally pathological. Innocent murmurs are soft, musical or vibratory, midsystolic, change with posture, and occur with entirely normal heart sounds.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.murmurs.practice: Listen to examples of musical Still murmur and compare them with the harsh pansystolic murmur of a ventricular septal defect, practicing the 6-point Levine grading scale.
pitfalls: Labelling a loud, harsh, or pansystolic murmur as innocent without evaluating for radiation, S2 split, or thrills.
Failing to auscultate in the left lateral position with the bell, completely missing the low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur of mitral stenosis.
Failing to have the child lean forward in expiration to listen for the soft early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation.
Neglecting to examine pulses and blood pressure when an ejection systolic murmur is heard, missing coarctation.

probes.q: At what intensity grade does a heart murmur become accompanied by a palpable thrill?
probes.a: Grade 4 out of 6 (or higher).

probes.q: What are the classic features of an innocent Still murmur in a child?
probes.a: Midsystolic, musical or vibratory quality, grade 1 to 2 intensity, loudest at left lower sternal border, changes with posture, with normal heart sounds.

probes.q: State two major Nada criteria that indicate organic heart disease in a child.
probes.a: Presence of a systolic murmur grade 3 or greater, any diastolic murmur, cyanosis, or congestive cardiac failure.

rubric.text: Identifies murmur timing (systolic, diastolic, continuous) and epicentre
Grades murmur accurately from 1 to 6 using Levine criteria
Maps murmur radiation to axilla, neck, and back
Performs left lateral and leaning forward manoeuvres with appropriate bell/diaphragm
Distinguishes innocent murmurs from organic heart disease using Nada criteria

rows: Very faint, audible only with effort
Loud murmur, easily heard across precordium
Loud murmur, accompanied by a thrill
Audible with stethoscope tilted, one edge off skin
Audible with stethoscope lifted entirely off chest

teach.heading: Differentiating innocent from organic murmurs
teach.body:
Innocent murmurs are typically midsystolic, soft (grade 1 to 2), vibratory or musical, localized to the left sternal edge, and vary markedly with posture.

Pathological murmurs are often harsh or blowing, pansystolic or diastolic, grade 3 or higher, radiate broadly, and coexist with abnormal S2 or clicks.

teach.heading: Nada criteria for paediatric heart disease
teach.body:
Presence of one major criterion (grade 3+ systolic murmur, diastolic murmur, cyanosis, congestive heart failure) or two minor criteria confirms heart disease.

Minor criteria include systolic murmur under grade 3, abnormal S2, abnormal ECG, abnormal chest radiograph, or abnormal blood pressure.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.heart_failure_ie.title: Paediatric congestive heart failure and endocarditis signs
skill.exam.paed.cvs.heart_failure_ie.oneLine: Detect paediatric heart failure through the infant clinical triad and screen for endocarditis stigmata
skill.exam.paed.cvs.heart_failure_ie.why: Congestive cardiac failure in infants does not present with adult signs like ankle oedema and orthopnoea. It presents with feeding difficulty, excessive forehead sweating, tachypnoea, and tender hepatomegaly. Recognizing these signs early prevents cardiogenic collapse.

steps.text: Observe infant feeding behavior: history of prolonged feeding times (over 30 minutes), frequent pauses, and profuse forehead perspiration during feeds.
Count resting heart rate and respiratory rate to assess tachycardia and tachypnoea.
Palpate the liver edge below the right costal margin to assess tender hepatomegaly, the primary sign of systemic venous congestion in young children.
Auscultate the heart for an S3 or S4 gallop rhythm and tachycardia.
Auscultate lung bases for fine inspiratory crackles (pulmonary congestion).
Examine facial features for periorbital oedema (paediatric equivalent of dependent oedema).

Perform systematic search for infective endocarditis (IE) signs: fever, pallor, petechiae on palate and conjunctivae, splinter haemorrhages under nails, Osler nodes (painful pulps), Janeway lesions (painless palms/soles), splenomegaly, and Roth spots on fundoscopy.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.heart_failure_ie.normal: Normal resting heart rate, respiratory rate, liver span, absence of gallop rhythm or crackles, normal feeding without sweating, absence of petechiae or peripheral emboli.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.heart_failure_ie.abnormal: Tachycardia, tachypnoea, tender hepatomegaly extending greater than 2 to 3 cm below right costal margin, gallop rhythm, periorbital puffiness, crackles, splenomegaly, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.heart_failure_ie.significance: In infants, tachycardia, tachypnoea, and hepatomegaly form the diagnostic triad of congestive cardiac failure. Infective endocarditis peripheral stigmata represent immune complex vasculitis or septic microemboli, indicating active bacteremia complicating underlying structural heart disease.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.heart_failure_ie.practice: Rehearse infant liver palpation and measurement below the right costal margin, correlating it with resting respiratory rate to detect early cardiac decompensation.
pitfalls: Looking for bilateral ankle oedema as a marker of heart failure in an infant; oedema in infants manifests in the periorbital region and presacral area.
Attributing feeding difficulty and forehead sweating solely to gastro-oesophageal reflux, missing severe left-to-right shunt heart failure.
Forgetting to palpate the spleen in a child with a known congenital murmur who presents with unexplained fever.
Dismissing persistent tachypnoea during sleep as behavioral excitement.

probes.q: What clinical triad constitutes the classic presentation of congestive heart failure in an infant?
probes.a: Tachycardia, tachypnoea, and tender hepatomegaly.

probes.q: Where does dependent oedema typically manifest in a recumbent infant with congestive cardiac failure?
probes.a: Periorbital oedema and presacral oedema, rather than ankle oedema.

probes.q: How do Janeway lesions differ from Osler nodes in physical examination?
probes.a: Janeway lesions are painless erythematous macules on palms and soles, whereas Osler nodes are painful, tender nodules on the finger or toe pads.

rubric.text: Assesses infant heart failure triad: heart rate, respiratory rate, and liver size
Inquires into feeding interruptions and forehead perspiration
Auscultates for cardiac gallop rhythm and pulmonary crackles
Inspects periorbital and presacral areas for oedema
Screens systematically for peripheral endocarditis signs

teach.heading: The infant heart failure presentation
teach.body:
Feeding is the infant equivalent of an exercise tolerance test. Sucking requires substantial cardiac output and oxygen consumption.

An infant in heart failure feeds with difficulty, taking frequent rest pauses, sweating profusely across the forehead, and failing to finish feeds within 30 minutes.

rows: Resting heart rate exceeding upper age limit
Firm, tender liver edge >2 to 3 cm below RCM
Third heart sound producing horse-trot rhythm

teach.heading: Peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis
teach.body:
In children with preexisting structural lesions (VSD, bicuspid aortic valve, TOF), endocardial damage creates a nidus for bacteremia.

Examine the hands, feet, conjunctivae, and oral mucosa for petechiae, splinter haemorrhages, painless Janeway macules, and tender Osler nodes.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.cyanosis.title: Paediatric cyanosis evaluation and hyperoxia test
skill.exam.paed.cvs.cyanosis.oneLine: Distinguish central from peripheral cyanosis, assess mucosal beds, and perform the hyperoxia test
skill.exam.paed.cvs.cyanosis.why: Cyanosis in a neonate or infant is an emergency requiring immediate differentiation between cyanotic congenital heart disease and primary pulmonary pathology. Misdiagnosis delays life-saving ductal prostaglandin therapy or ventilatory intervention.

steps.text: Inspect mucosal membranes in warm, bright daylight: tongue, palatal mucosa, and buccal membranes (central cyanosis) versus nose tip, earlobes, and distal digits (peripheral cyanosis).
Touch the distal extremities: assess whether hands and feet are warm (central cyanosis) or cold with poor perfusion (peripheral cyanosis / acrocyanosis).
Check capillary refill time (CFT) over the sternum or distal nailbed: normal refill time is under 3 seconds.
Inspect the nailbeds and digits for clubbing, which indicates chronic central cyanosis of at least 3 to 6 months duration.
Perform the hyperoxia test in a cyanotic infant: administer 100% inspired oxygen for 10 minutes and measure arterial PaO2 or pre-ductal saturation.
Interpret hyperoxia response: arterial PaO2 rising above 150 mm Hg rules out cyanotic heart disease, while failure to rise above 100 mm Hg indicates right-to-left intracardiac shunting.
Assess response to warming: peripheral cyanosis clears with gentle limb warming, whereas central cyanosis persists unchanged.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.cyanosis.normal: Pink tongue and oral mucosa, warm pink extremities, capillary refill time under 3 seconds, absence of digital clubbing, PaO2 rising well above 150 mm Hg on 100% oxygen.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.cyanosis.abnormal: Blue discolouration of the tongue and buccal mucosa, persistently cold blue extremities with delayed CFT, digital clubbing, arterial PaO2 remaining below 100 mm Hg despite 100% oxygen.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.cyanosis.significance: Central cyanosis requires at least 3 to 5 g/dL of deoxygenated haemoglobin in systemic circulation, reflecting right-to-left shunting or severe alveolar ventilation-perfusion mismatch. The hyperoxia test is the critical discriminator: intracardiac shunts bypass alveolar oxygen, failing to increase PaO2.
skill.exam.paed.cvs.cyanosis.practice: Inspect the mucosal membranes of healthy infants, appreciating the distinction between benign newborn acrocyanosis and true central cyanosis of the tongue.
pitfalls: Relying on finger or toe colour alone, mistaking physiological acrocyanosis in a cold infant for congenital heart disease.
Failing to inspect the tongue and mucosal lining of the mouth, which are the only dependable sites for central cyanosis.
Assuming severe anaemia cannot cause cyanosis; severely anaemic infants cannot generate 5 g/dL of deoxygenated haemoglobin and will not look blue despite profound hypoxia.
Measuring capillary refill in a freezing environment without warming the extremity first.

probes.q: What anatomical site is the most reliable clinical indicator of central cyanosis in an infant?
probes.a: The tongue and buccal oral mucosa.

probes.q: What is normal capillary refill time in a child, and where should it be measured?
probes.a: Normal capillary refill time is under 3 seconds, measured over the sternum or finger pulp.

probes.q: How does the hyperoxia test distinguish cyanotic heart disease from pulmonary parenchymal disease?
probes.a: On 100% oxygen, arterial PaO2 rises above 150 mm Hg in pulmonary disease, but remains low (under 100 mm Hg) in fixed right-to-left cardiac shunts.

rubric.text: Inspects tongue and buccal mucosa in bright lighting
Assesses warmth of distal extremities and capillary refill time
Explains and interprets the 100% oxygen hyperoxia challenge
Checks fingers and toes for chronic cyanotic clubbing
Distinguishes acrocyanosis by response to limb warming

teach.heading: The physiological basis of cyanosis
teach.body:
Cyanosis requires at least 3 to 5 g/dL of reduced (deoxygenated) haemoglobin in capillary blood.

A severely anaemic infant with a haemoglobin of 6 g/dL may suffer fatal tissue hypoxia without ever turning blue, because they cannot form 5 g/dL of reduced haemoglobin.

teach.heading: The hyperoxia challenge test
teach.body:
In a cyanotic newborn, administer 100% oxygen for 10 minutes.

In pulmonary disease, high alveolar oxygen overcomes diffusion barriers, driving PaO2 above 150 mm Hg. In cyanotic heart disease, deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs, keeping PaO2 low.

skill.exam.paed.gi.oral_upper.title: Paediatric oral cavity and upper gastrointestinal examination
skill.exam.paed.gi.oral_upper.oneLine: Inspect lips, dentition, tongue, buccal mucosa, and pharynx without triggering distress or gagging
skill.exam.paed.gi.oral_upper.why: The oral cavity provides direct visualization of systemic, nutritional, and infectious diseases in children, including thrush, measles Koplik spots, scurvy, dehydration, and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Leaving oral examination to the end avoids early distress during abdominal evaluation.

steps.text: Defer the oral examination until after abdominal palpation and auscultation have been completed peacefully.
Inspect the lips: check for angular stomatitis (riboflavin/iron deficiency), cheilitis, cleft lip, herpes vesicles, and perioral hyperpigmentation (Peutz-Jeghers syndrome).
Examine the gums: inspect for gingivitis, scorbutic bleeding gums, gingival hypertrophy (leukaemia, phenytoin), and lead lines.
Count primary or permanent teeth: check for delayed eruption, dental caries, enamel hypoplasia, and mottling (fluorosis).

Inspect the tongue: check hydration (dryness in dehydration), ventral pallor, sublingual icterus, geographic tongue, strawberry tongue (Kawasaki disease, scarlet fever), and oral candidiasis (thrush).
Inspect buccal mucosa with a pen torch: look for aphthous ulcers, Koplik spots (measles opposite lower molars), and melanin macules.
Depress the tongue gently to inspect tonsils (hypertrophy, exudates, membranes) and posterior pharyngeal erythema.

skill.exam.paed.gi.oral_upper.normal: Moist pink mucosa, absence of ulceration or thrush, healthy gums without bleeding, age-appropriate eruption of primary or permanent teeth, non-inflamed tonsils and pharynx.
skill.exam.paed.gi.oral_upper.abnormal: White curdy plaques of oral thrush (cannot be easily scraped off), angular stomatitis, swollen bleeding gums, Koplik spots, strawberry tongue, perioral freckling, severe dental caries, enlarged tonsils with exudate.
skill.exam.paed.gi.oral_upper.significance: Oral thrush is common in infants but in older children suggests immunodeficiency or inhaled corticosteroid use. Koplik spots are pathognomonic of measles, appearing 24 to 48 hours before the exanthem. Perioral pigmentation suggests Peutz-Jeghers polyposis.
skill.exam.paed.gi.oral_upper.practice: Examine the oral cavity in a cooperative child by turning it into a game ('roar like a lion'), inspecting mucosal surfaces swiftly and methodically.
pitfalls: Inserting a wooden tongue depressor at the very start of the clinical encounter, terrifying the child and preventing abdominal palpation.
Confusing retained milk curds on the tongue with oral thrush; milk curds wipe away easily without leaving a raw bleeding mucosal surface.
Forgetting to lift the tongue to look for sublingual jaundice and frenulum ulcers in whooping cough.
Overlooking subtle tonsillar membranes or petechiae on the soft palate.

probes.q: How can one clinically distinguish oral thrush (Candida) from normal milk curds on an infant tongue?
probes.a: Milk curds scrape off easily without bleeding, whereas thrush plaques adhere firmly and leave an inflamed, bleeding base when removed.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of perioral pigmentation in a child with recurrent abdominal pain?
probes.a: Perioral pigmentation suggests Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder with hamartomatous intestinal polyps prone to intussusception.

probes.q: What mucosal finding is pathognomonic of early measles, and where is it located?
probes.a: Koplik spots: tiny bluish-white spots on an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars.

rubric.text: Leaves oral cavity examination until after peaceful abdominal palpation
Inspects lips, gums, and teeth systematically
Evaluates tongue for moisture, pallor, thrush, and sublingual icterus
Inspects buccal mucosa for ulcers, pigmentation, and Koplik spots
Inspects tonsillar pillars and posterior pharyngeal wall

teach.heading: Sequence and child cooperation
teach.body:
Never examine the throat first. Inspecting the oral cavity often requires a tongue depressor, which triggers the gag reflex and immediate crying.

Keep the pen torch and spatula out of sight until the child abdomen and chest have been thoroughly evaluated in a calm state.

rows: White adherent plaques on red base

teach.heading: Dentition timeline in children
teach.body:
Deciduous (milk) teeth begin erupting around 6 months with the lower central incisors. All 20 primary teeth are present by 2 to 3 years.

Permanent dentition begins around 6 years with the first molars and shedding of incisors, completing 32 teeth in young adulthood.

skill.exam.paed.gi.inspection.title: Paediatric abdominal inspection and topography
skill.exam.paed.gi.inspection.oneLine: Map the nine abdominal regions, evaluate contour, respiratory movements, and visible peristalsis
skill.exam.paed.gi.inspection.why: Abdominal inspection reveals physiological contours and life-threatening surgical emergencies before hands touch the abdomen. A scaphoid abdomen in a newborn indicates diaphragmatic hernia, while visible gastric peristalsis signals pyloric stenosis.

steps.text: Place the child supine with the abdomen fully exposed from nipples to mid-thighs, keeping the child warm and reassured.
Identify the anatomical topography: epigastrium, umbilical region, hypogastrium, and bilateral hypochondriac, lumbar, and iliac regions.
Inspect abdominal contour at eye level: normal toddler abdomen is gently protuberant (pot-belly); note scaphoid (sunken) or distended abdomen.
Inspect flank fullness: full flanks suggest significant ascites or large bilateral retroperitoneal masses.
Watch abdominal wall motion during respiration: healthy infants demonstrate synchronous abdominal movement with respiration.
Inspect the umbilicus: note position (central, shifted, or everted), presence of umbilical hernia, erythema, discharge, or granuloma.
Look across the upper abdomen under tangential lighting for visible peristalsis (e.g. left-to-right gastric peristaltic waves in pyloric stenosis).
Inspect for dilated superficial abdominal veins (and check flow direction: upward in IVC obstruction, downward in SVC obstruction, caput medusae in portal hypertension).
Inspect all hernial orifices (inguinal, femoral, umbilical) and examine external genitalia for undescended testes or hydrocoele.

skill.exam.paed.gi.inspection.normal: Gently protuberant (pot-belly) in toddlers due to weak musculature and lordosis, symmetrical movement with respiration, central inverted umbilicus, absence of visible peristalsis, dilated veins, or hernial bulges.
skill.exam.paed.gi.inspection.abnormal: Scaphoid abdomen, generalized distension, full flanks, restricted abdominal movement with respiration (peritonitis), everted umbilicus, visible left-to-right peristalsis, caput medusae, visible pulsating mass.
skill.exam.paed.gi.inspection.significance: A scaphoid abdomen in a breathless neonate signifies congenital diaphragmatic hernia with abdominal viscera displaced into the thorax. Visible gastric peristalsis with non-bilious projectile vomiting is classic for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Restricted abdominal movement indicates acute peritonitis.
skill.exam.paed.gi.inspection.practice: Inspect abdominal shapes in children across various ages (infant, preschooler, older child), noting the normal transition from toddler pot-belly to flat contour.
pitfalls: Labelling the normal protuberant abdomen of a healthy toddler as pathological ascites or abdominal distension.
Failing to expose the inguinal regions, completely missing an incarcerated inguinal hernia causing intestinal obstruction.
Inspecting the abdomen from a standing position rather than bending down to view tangentially at bed level.
Ignoring localized asymmetrical bulging in the flanks or suprapubic area.

probes.q: What does a scaphoid abdomen in a newborn infant with respiratory distress strongly suggest?
probes.a: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (abdominal contents herniated into the thoracic cavity).

probes.q: What is the direction of visible peristaltic waves in infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
probes.a: Left to right across the epigastrium.

probes.q: Why is the normal toddler abdomen gently protuberant ('pot-belly')?
probes.a: Due to weak abdominal wall musculature, physiological lumbar lordosis, and a relatively large liver size.

rubric.text: Exposes the abdomen from nipples to mid-thighs while maintaining warmth
Inspects abdominal contour at eye level from the side and foot of the bed
Assesses symmetry of abdominal wall movement with respiration
Inspects umbilicus and checks for dilated superficial veins
Systematically inspects inguinal regions and external genitalia

teach.heading: Normal paediatric abdominal shape
teach.body:
A toddler abdomen looks very different from an adult abdomen. In infants and young children under 3 to 4 years, a prominent protuberant belly is normal.

This contour results from weak anterolateral abdominal muscles, normal lumbar lordosis, and the relatively large size of normal abdominal organs.

teach.heading: The importance of groin and genital inspection
teach.body:
Never conclude abdominal inspection without checking hernial orifices and genitalia.

An irritable, vomiting infant may have an incarcerated indirect inguinal hernia. Inspect both groins for swelling and confirm bilateral descended testes.

skill.exam.paed.gi.liver.title: Paediatric liver palpation and span measurement
skill.exam.paed.gi.liver.oneLine: Palpate from the right iliac fossa upwards, assess edge characteristics, and measure age-specific liver span
skill.exam.paed.gi.liver.why: A palpable liver edge is a normal finding in healthy infants and toddlers, extending up to 2 cm below the costal margin. Failing to distinguish normal physiological palpable liver from true hepatomegaly leads to extensive unnecessary hepatic evaluations.

steps.text: Warm hands thoroughly and ask the child to flex hips and knees slightly to relax the anterior abdominal wall.
Place the palmar surface of the examining hand flat in the right iliac fossa, pointing fingers toward the right costal margin.
Move the hand gently upwards 1 cm at a time towards the right costal margin with each expiration, pausing during inspiration to feel the liver edge descend.
When the liver edge is felt, measure its distance in centimetres below the right costal margin in the midclavicular line.
Note edge characteristics: sharp versus rounded, surface (smooth versus nodular), consistency (soft, firm, or rock-hard), and tenderness.
Verify that fingers cannot insinuate between the upper border of the mass and the costal margin (confirming liver origin).
Percuss down from the right 3rd intercostal space in the midclavicular line to define the upper border of liver dullness (normally at right 5th ICS).
Calculate total liver span by measuring the vertical distance between the percussed upper border and the palpated lower border.
Grade hepatomegaly below the costal margin: mild (under 4 cm), moderate (5 to 7 cm), massive (greater than 7 cm).

skill.exam.paed.gi.liver.normal: Liver edge palpable 1 to 2 cm below right costal margin in infants and children under 4 to 5 years; smooth, soft, non-tender with a sharp edge; normal liver span: under 1 year (4 to 5 cm), 1 to 5 years (6 to 7 cm), 5 to 12 years (8 to 9 cm).
skill.exam.paed.gi.liver.abnormal: Liver extending greater than 2 to 3 cm below right costal margin, rounded or blunt edge, firm or hard consistency, nodular surface, tenderness, increased liver span, or displaced upper border.
skill.exam.paed.gi.liver.significance: Differentiating true hepatomegaly from a pushed-down liver (pseudopatomegaly) requires measuring liver span: in hyperinflation (severe asthma, bronchiolitis), the upper border is pushed down to the 6th or 7th space with normal span. True hepatomegaly increases liver span.
skill.exam.paed.gi.liver.practice: Palpate the liver edge in cooperative infants, measuring distance below the costal margin and percussing the upper border at the 5th space.
pitfalls: Starting palpation immediately beneath the costal margin, completely missing a massively enlarged liver extending down into the pelvis.
Confusing a liver pushed downward by hyperinflated lungs (in bronchiolitis or asthma) with true pathological hepatomegaly.
Poking with stiff fingertips instead of using the flat palmar surface of relaxed, warm fingers.
Failing to percuss the upper border of liver dullness, missing thoracic processes pushing the liver downward.

probes.q: What is the normal liver span in a child aged 1 to 5 years?
probes.a: 6 to 7 cm.

probes.q: How does one distinguish a truly enlarged liver from pseudopatomegaly due to bronchiolitis?
probes.a: By percussing the upper border of liver dullness: in pseudopatomegaly, the upper border is displaced downwards with a normal liver span.

probes.q: What are the common paediatric causes of massive hepatomegaly extending more than 7 cm below the costal margin?
probes.a: Storage disorders (Gaucher, glycogen storage disease), haematological malignancies (leukaemia), and severe chronic portal hypertension or hepatoma.

rubric.text: Positions child with flexed knees and hips to relax abdominal wall
Starts palpation in the right iliac fossa and ascends towards the costal margin
Evaluates liver edge, surface, consistency, and tenderness
Percusses upper border of liver dullness at the right 5th intercostal space
Calculates total liver span and correlates with age-specific normal ranges

teach.heading: The physiological palpable liver in childhood
teach.body:
In infants and young children under 4 to 5 years, feeling a liver edge 1 to 2 cm below the right costal margin is completely normal.

The edge should feel soft, smooth, non-tender, and sharp. True hepatomegaly is diagnosed only when liver span is increased for age.

teach.heading: Normal liver span by paediatric age group
True hepatomegaly versus pseudopatomegaly
teach.body:
In infants with bronchiolitis or severe asthma, hyperinflated lungs depress the diaphragm.

This pushes a normal-sized liver downward into the abdomen. Percussing the upper border reveals it at the 6th or 7th space, proving liver span is normal.

skill.exam.paed.gi.spleen.title: Paediatric spleen palpation and distinguishing from renal mass
skill.exam.paed.gi.spleen.oneLine: Palpate along the spino-umbilical line, feel for the splenic notch, and differentiate from a left kidney mass
skill.exam.paed.gi.spleen.why: A palpable spleen in a child always demands careful differentiation from an enlarged left kidney or retroperitoneal mass. Unlike the liver, a normal spleen is not palpable in older children; in neonates and healthy infants, a soft tip is occasionally felt within 1 to 2 cm of the costal margin.

steps.text: Ensure the child is relaxed, warm, and lying supine with hips and knees slightly flexed.
Place the right hand flat in the right iliac fossa, aligning fingers diagonally toward the left costal margin along the spino-umbilical line.
Support the child left lower ribcage from behind with the left hand, gently lifting the flank forward.
Advance the examining hand 1 cm at a time during expiration, pausing during inspiration to feel the descending splenic pole.
If not palpable supine, turn the child onto the right lateral position with the left knee flexed over the right leg, allowing gravity to bring the spleen forward.

When an enlarged organ is felt, identify defining splenic characteristics: presence of a splenic notch on the anterior border, inability to insinuate fingers between mass and costal margin, movement inferomedially with inspiration, and dullness to percussion.

Differentiate from an enlarged left kidney: test for bimanual ballottement (positive in kidney, negative in spleen), check if fingers can insinuate above mass, check for resonant overlying band of colonic gas, and check if mass crosses midline.
Grade splenomegaly below the left costal margin: mild (under 2 cm), moderate (2 to 7 cm), massive (greater than 7 cm).

skill.exam.paed.gi.spleen.normal: Spleen not palpable in older children; soft tip may be palpable within 1 to 2 cm of left costal margin in healthy neonates and infants; normal resonance over Traube space.
skill.exam.paed.gi.spleen.abnormal: Palpable firm or hard spleen extending beyond 2 cm below left costal margin, obliterated Traube space, tender splenic enlargement, massive splenomegaly extending past the umbilicus into the right iliac fossa.
skill.exam.paed.gi.spleen.significance: Mild splenomegaly occurs in acute infections (typhoid, viral hepatitis, malaria, infective endocarditis). Moderate to massive splenomegaly suggests portal hypertension (extrahepatic portal vein obstruction, cirrhosis), storage diseases (Gaucher), thalassaemia major, visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), or leukaemia.
skill.exam.paed.gi.spleen.practice: Practice the bimanual splenic palpation technique along the spino-umbilical line and rehearse turning into the right lateral decubitus position.
pitfalls: Palpating straight up the left flank rather than moving diagonally along the spino-umbilical axis, missing an enlarged spleen that grows inferomedially toward the right iliac fossa.
Confusing an enlarged hydronephrotic or Wilms tumour left kidney with a spleen; failing to test for bimanual ballottement.
Pressing too deeply and forcefully, causing pain and pushing the soft spleen deeper away from the examining fingertips.
Neglecting to percuss Traube space before palpation to detect early splenic enlargement.

probes.q: Along which anatomical axis does the paediatric spleen enlarge?
probes.a: Along the spino-umbilical line (from left hypochondrium towards the umbilicus and right iliac fossa).

probes.q: Name three physical signs that distinguish an enlarged spleen from an enlarged left kidney.
probes.a: Presence of a splenic notch, inability to get above the mass, dullness to percussion, moves inferomedially, and not bimanually ballotable.

probes.q: What are the common causes of massive splenomegaly (>7 cm below costal margin) in Indian children?
probes.a: Thalassaemia major, extrahepatic portal vein obstruction (EHPVO), visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), chronic myeloid leukaemia, and Gaucher disease.

rubric.text: Palpates diagonally from right iliac fossa along spino-umbilical line
Supports the left lower rib cage with the non-dominant hand
Turns child into right lateral position if spleen is not felt supine
Systematically distinguishes spleen from enlarged kidney using physical criteria
Measures and grades splenomegaly in centimetres below costal margin

rows: Resonant band of colon in front

teach.heading: Technique of splenic palpation
teach.body:
The spleen enlarges along the spino-umbilical line towards the right iliac fossa. Always start palpating in the right iliac fossa.

Support the lower posterior ribs with your left hand. If a spleen tip is not felt, turn the child 45 degrees onto the right side.

teach.heading: Grading and aetiology in Indian context
teach.body:
Mild splenomegaly (<2 cm) is typical of acute infections like typhoid, malaria, and dengue. Moderate splenomegaly (2 to 7 cm) points to portal hypertension.

Massive splenomegaly (>7 cm) in Indian paediatrics suggests thalassaemia major, EHPVO, visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), or storage disease.

skill.exam.paed.gi.ascites.title: Paediatric ascites detection and grading
skill.exam.paed.gi.ascites.oneLine: Detect free peritoneal fluid using the puddle sign, shifting dullness, and fluid thrill across severity grades
skill.exam.paed.gi.ascites.why: Abdominal distension in children has diverse causes, from functional constipation and organomegaly to tense ascites. Correctly selecting and executing ascites manoeuvres according to fluid volume avoids diagnostic delays in nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, and peritonitis.

steps.text: Inspect the abdomen for abdominal distension with fullness in the flanks and an everted or flattened umbilicus.
Percuss radially from the resonant central abdomen (umbilicus) outwards towards the flanks to establish baseline flank dullness.

For minimal fluid (<150 ml), perform the puddle sign: have the child rest in knee-elbow (or prone) position for 3 minutes, place stethoscope over dependent umbilical area, and flick the flank lightly while moving stethoscope towards the flank.

For moderate fluid (~500 ml), perform shifting dullness: with child supine, percuss from umbilicus into the left flank until resonance becomes dull; keep finger at the dullness point, ask child to roll onto right side, wait 30 seconds, and percuss again.
Note that the dull note shifts to resonance, and subsequent percussion of the newly dependent right flank reveals dullness.

For massive fluid (~1500 ml), elicit a fluid thrill: place the child or an assistant hand firmly along the midline of the abdomen to dampen abdominal wall fat waves; flick one flank while feeling for a fluid wave with the palm resting on the opposite flank.
Grade ascites: Grade I (mild, detected only by ultrasound or puddle sign), Grade II (moderate, shifting dullness positive, no fluid thrill), Grade III (massive/tense, positive fluid thrill).

skill.exam.paed.gi.ascites.normal: Resonant abdomen with tympany over bowel loops, non-dull flanks, negative puddle sign, negative shifting dullness, absence of fluid thrill.
skill.exam.paed.gi.ascites.abnormal: Shifting dullness, positive puddle sign, fluid thrill with tense distension, everted umbilicus with stretched shiny skin.
skill.exam.paed.gi.ascites.significance: Shifting dullness indicates at least moderate peritoneal fluid collection. A fluid thrill confirms massive or tense ascites, requiring evaluation for nephrotic syndrome, chronic liver disease with portal hypertension, congestive heart failure, or tuberculous peritonitis.
skill.exam.paed.gi.ascites.practice: Practice the shifting dullness technique, ensuring adequate pause (30 seconds) after rolling the patient to allow viscous peritoneal fluid to redistribute.
pitfalls: Attempting to elicit a fluid thrill in mild ascites, which requires massive fluid (>1500 ml) to generate an acoustic wave.
Eliciting a fluid thrill without damping the anterior abdominal wall with an assistant hand, mistaking subcutaneous fat vibrations for fluid.
Failing to wait 30 seconds after turning the patient during shifting dullness, percussing before fluid has gravitated down.
Confusing a grossly distended urinary bladder or huge ovarian cyst with free peritoneal ascites.

probes.q: What physical sign is used to detect minimal amounts of ascites (<150 ml) in a child?
probes.a: The puddle sign (examined in the knee-elbow position).

probes.q: Why must an assistant hand be pressed firmly on the midline when testing for a fluid thrill?
probes.a: To dampen and prevent transmission of acoustic waves through subcutaneous abdominal wall fat.

probes.q: What are the common paediatric causes of Grade III tense ascites in Indian clinical practice?
probes.a: Nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis with portal hypertension, extrahepatic portal vein obstruction with hypoalbuminaemia, and tuberculous peritonitis.

rubric.text: Inspects abdominal contours, flank fullness, and umbilicus
Executes puddle sign correctly for minimal peritoneal fluid
Performs shifting dullness with correct wait time and repositioning
Tests for fluid thrill with midline hand damping abdominal fat waves
Accurately assigns ascites grade (Grade I, II, or III)

teach.heading: The mechanics of shifting dullness
teach.body:
Free peritoneal fluid gravitates to the dependent flanks, floating gas-filled loops of bowel centrally around the umbilicus.

Percuss from the resonant centre to the dull flank. When the patient rolls onto the opposite side, bowel loops float up and fluid shifts down, turning the dull area resonant.

teach.heading: Common paediatric aetiologies in India
teach.body:
In children, nephrotic syndrome is the single most common cause of painless generalized ascites.

Other important causes include chronic liver disease, extrahepatic portal vein obstruction (EHPVO), and tuberculous peritonitis.

skill.exam.paed.gi.palpation_percussion.title: Paediatric abdominal palpation and acute abdomen signs
skill.exam.paed.gi.palpation_percussion.oneLine: Assess tenderness, distinguish voluntary guarding from rigidity, test rebound, and auscultate bowel sounds
skill.exam.paed.gi.palpation_percussion.why: Evaluating an acute abdomen in a young child is one of the most demanding clinical challenges in paediatrics. Differentiating voluntary guarding (fear and ticklishness) from involuntary rigidity (true peritonitis) determines whether a child requires emergent surgical laparotomy or conservative medical care.

steps.text: Warm hands thoroughly and converse reassuringly with the child; flex the child hips and knees to relax the abdominal musculature.
Observe the child facial expression and eye movements throughout palpation rather than staring exclusively at the abdomen.
Begin with gentle, superficial palpation in the quadrant furthest away from the site of reported pain.
Palpate each of the nine regions systematically, assessing for localized warmth, hyperaesthesia, and tenderness.

Distinguish voluntary guarding (abdominal wall softens when child takes a breath or during distraction) from true involuntary muscular rigidity (board-like stiffness that persists during inspiration).
Test for rebound tenderness gently by pressing slowly and deeply, then releasing suddenly, or by gently tapping the bed or heels (heel-strike test in older children).
Palpate for deep abdominal masses: check renal angles, iliac fossae (intussusception sausage-shaped mass, appendicular lump), and suprapubic region (distended bladder).
Auscultate for bowel sounds: listen around the umbilicus for normal peristaltic sounds (normally 2 to 3 sounds per minute); auscultate for a full 3 minutes before declaring bowel sounds absent.
Auscultate for vascular bruits (hepatic bruit in hepatoma/haemangioma, renal artery bruit in hypertension) and venous hum in portal hypertension.

skill.exam.paed.gi.palpation_percussion.normal: Soft, non-tender abdomen without guarding or rigidity, no masses, bowel sounds present (2 to 3 per minute), absence of vascular bruits.
skill.exam.paed.gi.palpation_percussion.abnormal: Localized tenderness (e.g. McBurney point), involuntary muscular rigidity, rebound tenderness, palpable sausage-shaped mass with empty right iliac fossa (Dance sign in intussusception), absent bowel sounds (paralytic ileus), or high-pitched tinkling rushes (mechanical obstruction).
skill.exam.paed.gi.palpation_percussion.significance: Involuntary rigidity and rebound tenderness confirm parietal peritoneal inflammation (peritonitis from ruptured appendix or perforation). A palpable tender sausage-shaped mass in an infant with red-currant jelly stools confirms intussusception. Absent bowel sounds signify generalised peritonitis or ileus.
skill.exam.paed.gi.palpation_percussion.practice: Practice the distraction technique during abdominal palpation: talk about toys or family while palpating with one hand and feeling the abdominal rectus muscle soften during inspiration.
pitfalls: Palpating the painful quadrant first, causing distress and reflex abdominal spasm that makes the rest of the examination impossible.
Confusing voluntary guarding due to ticklishness with surgical peritonitis.
Declaring bowel sounds absent after listening for only 15 seconds.
Failing to watch the child face during palpation, missing involuntary grimacing.

probes.q: How does an examiner distinguish voluntary guarding from involuntary muscular rigidity in a child?
probes.a: Voluntary guarding relaxes during inspiration, gentle distraction, or knee flexion, whereas involuntary rigidity remains constantly stiff and board-like.

probes.q: How long must an examiner listen before stating that bowel sounds are truly absent?
probes.a: A full 3 minutes.

probes.q: What clinical features characterise the abdominal mass in an infant with ileocaecal intussusception?
probes.a: A sausage-shaped, curved, slightly tender mass in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium, with an empty right iliac fossa (Dance sign).

rubric.text: Watches the child face continuously during abdominal palpation
Begins palpation in the area furthest away from reported pain
Accurately differentiates voluntary guarding from involuntary rigidity
Auscultates bowel sounds for adequate duration (normal 2 to 3 per minute)
Palpates for appendicular lump or intussusception mass

teach.heading: The art of paediatric abdominal palpation
teach.body:
A frightened or ticklish child tenses their abdominal muscles defensively. If you push into a tense belly, you cannot feel visceral pathology.

Warm your hands, seat the parent nearby, and rest your hand flat on the abdomen. Talk gently and watch the child eyes. Feel the muscle relax on each exhalation.

rows: Softens with distraction and deep inspiration
Pain on rapid release of deep pressure

teach.heading: Auscultation of peristalsis and bruits
teach.body:
Normal bowel sounds occur at a frequency of 2 to 3 sounds per minute. Listen near the umbilicus for up to 3 minutes before declaring sounds absent.

High-pitched tinkling rushes indicate mechanical obstruction. An epigastric or hepatic bruit suggests arteriovenous malformation or vascular tumour.

skill.exam.paed.cns.higher_mental_gcs.title: Paediatric mental status and modified Glasgow Coma Scale
skill.exam.paed.cns.higher_mental_gcs.oneLine: Evaluate sensorium, age-appropriate social milestones, and the modified paediatric Glasgow Coma Scale
skill.exam.paed.cns.higher_mental_gcs.why: Standard adult coma scoring fails in preverbal children because they cannot speak or obey verbal commands. The modified paediatric Glasgow Coma Scale replaces adult verbal and motor responses with developmentally appropriate behaviours like smiling, tracking, crying, and spontaneous movement.

steps.text: Observe spontaneous interaction with parents: note alertness, social smile, eye contact, and vocalizations (cooing, babbling).
Assess state of consciousness along the spectrum: alert, drowsy, obtunded, stuporous, or in light versus deep coma.
Evaluate orientation to time, place, and person in cooperative older children; in infants, assess recognition of primary caregivers.
Test memory (immediate recall, recent events, remote milestones) and language comprehension according to developmental age.
Score Eye Opening (1 to 4): 4 spontaneous, 3 to speech/sound, 2 to pain, 1 none.
Score Verbal Response (1 to 5): 5 smiles/coos/oriented, 4 irritable cry/confused, 3 inappropriate crying/inconsolable, 2 grunts/incomprehensible sounds, 1 none.
Score Motor Response (1 to 6): 6 spontaneous purposeful movement, 5 withdraws to touch, 4 withdraws to pain, 3 abnormal flexion (decorticate), 2 abnormal extension (decerebrate), 1 flaccid/none.
Total the paediatric GCS score (range 3 to 15) and note decorticate (arms flexed, legs extended) versus decerebrate (all limbs extended and pronated) posture.

skill.exam.paed.cns.higher_mental_gcs.normal: Alert, engaging playfully with parents, normal social responsiveness, age-appropriate verbalization, purposeful movement, modified PGCS score of 15.
skill.exam.paed.cns.higher_mental_gcs.abnormal: Inconsolable irritable cry, lack of visual tracking or eye contact, modified PGCS score under 15 (score 8 or less indicates severe coma requiring airway protection), decorticate or decerebrate posturing.
skill.exam.paed.cns.higher_mental_gcs.significance: A paediatric GCS score of 8 or less indicates severe cerebral dysfunction and loss of protective airway reflexes. Decorticate posturing indicates destructive lesions above the red nucleus (cerebral hemispheres/diencephalon), whereas decerebrate posturing indicates midbrain or upper brainstem disruption with poorer prognosis.
skill.exam.paed.cns.higher_mental_gcs.practice: Practice scoring video clips of acute paediatric encephalopathy, rapidly categorizing verbal and motor responses into the modified PGCS matrix.
pitfalls: Applying the adult GCS verbal criteria to a preverbal infant, incorrectly assigning a low verbal score to a normally babbling toddler.
Confusing an irritable, inconsolable cry from raised intracranial pressure with normal hunger crying.
Failing to check pupillary reactivity and brainstem reflexes when evaluating an encephalopathic child.
Assessing responsiveness in a heavily sedated or paralyzed child without documenting medication effects.

probes.q: What total score on the modified paediatric Glasgow Coma Scale defines severe coma and loss of protective airway reflexes?
probes.a: A score of 8 or less (out of 15).

probes.q: How does the verbal response scoring in the modified paediatric GCS accommodate preverbal infants?
probes.a: It substitutes cooing, smiling, and consolability for words; score 5 is coos and babbles, 4 is irritable cry, 3 is inconsolable cry, 2 is grunting.

probes.q: What anatomical difference separates decorticate posturing from decerebrate posturing?
probes.a: Decorticate involves damage above the red nucleus (cortex/thalamus) with arm flexion, while decerebrate involves damage below the red nucleus (brainstem) with arm extension.

rubric.text: Observes child baseline interaction with primary caregiver
Scores eye opening response accurately from 1 to 4
Applies paediatric verbal criteria (cooing, babbling, cry) from 1 to 5
Assesses motor response (purposeful, withdrawal, decorticate, decerebrate) from 1 to 6
Differentiates decorticate flexion from decerebrate extension

teach.heading: Adapting mental status evaluation to child development
teach.body:
Mental status in a preverbal child is evaluated through behavior: how the infant looks at the mother, tracks colorful objects, reaches for toys, and responds to soothing voices.

A child who refuses to make eye contact, displays paradoxical irritability (crying harder when held), or lies motionless demands urgent evaluation.

teach.heading: Decorticate versus decerebrate posturing
teach.body:
Decorticate rigidity reflects corticospinal tract interruption above the red nucleus: the upper limbs are flexed, adducted, and internally rotated, while lower limbs are extended.

Decerebrate rigidity indicates deeper lesions disrupting the midbrain: all four extremities are rigidly extended, with teeth clenched and neck extended.

skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_visio.title: Paediatric cranial nerves: olfactory, optic, and visual function
skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_visio.oneLine: Assess olfactory patency, age-appropriate visual acuity, confrontation fields, pupils, and fundus
skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_visio.why: Cranial nerves I and II provide crucial localization of raised intracranial pressure and anterior visual pathway pathology. Testing vision in children requires age-appropriate adaptation, moving from preferential looking and tracking in infants to optotypes and confrontation in older children.

steps.text: Test cranial nerve I (olfactory): ensure nasal passages are clear; with child eyes closed, occlude one nostril and present non-pungent familiar scents (coffee, orange peel, soap); never use pungent stimulants like ammonia which stimulate CN V.
Assess gross visual function in infants: observe fixing and following of colorful toys or mother face; test menace reflex (blinking to sudden hand approach, develops around 3 to 4 months).

Test visual acuity in pre-schoolers with picture optotypes, and in children over 5 years using the Snellen chart positioned at 6 metres (normal acuity 6/6; record as d/D where d is distance of testing and D is row distance).

Test visual fields using the confrontation method (sitting 3 feet opposite the cooperative child over 3 years old, bringing a wiggling finger or red target from periphery to centre while child fixes on examiner nose).
Test colour vision using Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates in children older than 3 to 4 years.
Evaluate pupillary responses: size, symmetry, direct light reflex, consensual light reflex, and accommodation reflex (constriction when shifting focus from distant to near object).
Perform direct ophthalmoscopy in a darkened room: inspect optic disc (margins, colour, physiological cup), retinal vessels, and search for papilloedema or retinal haemorrhages.

skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_visio.normal: Intact non-pungent scent identification, age-appropriate visual acuity (6/6 in older child), full visual fields, brisk direct and consensual pupillary light reflexes, sharp flat pink optic disc margins.
skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_visio.abnormal: Anosmia, visual acuity impairment, visual field defect (hemianopia), afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil), sluggish or dilated fixed pupil, optic disc swelling with blurred margins and lost pulsations (papilloedema).
skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_visio.significance: Papilloedema signifies raised intracranial pressure, demanding urgent neuroimaging before considering lumbar puncture. A unilateral dilated, unreactive pupil in an encephalopathic child indicates uncal herniation with compression of third nerve parasympathetic fibres.
skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_visio.practice: Practice confrontation visual field testing using a brightly coloured toy puppet as a target in preschool children, keeping the child attention centred.
pitfalls: Using pungent substances like peppermint or ammonia to test olfaction, which stimulate trigeminal mucosal nociceptors rather than olfactory nerves.
Performing confrontation fields with the child eyes shifting away from the central fixation target.
Forgetting to dim room lights during fundoscopy, causing pupillary miosis that prevents adequate visualization of the optic disc.
Assuming an uncooperative infant is blind without testing fixation and following in quiet conditions.

probes.q: Why should pungent substances like ammonia never be used to test olfactory nerve function?
probes.a: Ammonia stimulates trigeminal (CN V) pain and temperature fibres in the nasal mucosa rather than olfactory (CN I) receptors.

probes.q: What is the normal visual acuity on a standard Snellen chart, and what does 6/18 mean?
probes.a: Normal is 6/6; 6/18 means the patient reads at 6 metres what a normal eye can read at 18 metres.

probes.q: What are the earliest ophthalmoscopic signs of papilloedema in raised intracranial tension?
probes.a: Loss of spontaneous venous pulsations at the disc margin, blurring of nasal disc margins, and optic disc hyperaemia.

rubric.text: Uses non-pungent scent with each nostril tested separately
Applies developmental vision assessment (tracking, pictures, or Snellen chart)
Executes confrontation visual field testing correctly
Tests direct, consensual, and accommodation pupillary reflexes
Inspects optic disc for blurring, pallor, or papilloedema

teach.heading: Developmental maturation of vision
teach.body:
Neonates demonstrate crude light perception and follow moving faces at 20 to 30 cm. By 3 to 4 months, infants reliably fix and follow and demonstrate visual menace.

Visual acuity improves rapidly, reaching adult 6/6 equivalent between 3 and 5 years of age.

teach.heading: Snellen chart principles
teach.body:
Visual acuity is expressed as d/D. Here d represents the distance at which letters are read (6 metres in British practice), and D represents the distance at which a normal eye reads them.

Normal vision is 6/6. If the child can only read the top line at 6 metres, acuity is recorded as 6/60.

skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_bulba.title: Paediatric cranial nerves: oculomotor to hypoglossal examination
skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_bulba.oneLine: Examine ocular motility, facial symmetry, bulbar motor function, and apply the clinical Rule of 17
skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_bulba.why: Cranial nerves III through XII control eye movements, facial expression, airway protection, and swallowing. Brainstem encephalitis, raised intracranial pressure, and skull base pathologies cause discrete cranial nerve palsies that require rapid anatomical localization.

steps.text: Test CN III, IV, and VI (oculomotor, trochlear, abducens): inspect head posture; check for ptosis, strabismus, and nystagmus; perform cover-uncover test; have child follow a colorful target through six cardinal positions of gaze (remember LR6, SO4).

Test CN V (trigeminal): inspect temporalis and masseter muscles; palpate muscle contraction while child bites down; check jaw deviation on opening (lateral pterygoids); test facial sensation in ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular divisions; test corneal reflex and jaw jerk.

Test CN VII (facial): observe spontaneous symmetry during smiling, crying, or resting; ask older child to wrinkle forehead (frontalis), close eyes tightly against resistance (orbicularis oculi), show teeth, blow cheeks (buccinator), and test taste on anterior two-thirds of tongue.
Note upper motor neuron (spares forehead due to bilateral corticobulbar innervation) versus lower motor neuron facial palsy (paralyses both upper and lower face with Bell phenomenon).
Test CN VIII (vestibulocochlear): test gross hearing by whispering or rubbing fingers; in older children perform tuning fork tests (air vs bone conduction).

Test CN IX and X (glossopharyngeal and vagus): assess speech for nasal twang; ask about dysphagia or nasal regurgitation of fluids; inspect palate at rest and during phonation ('ah'), noting uvula deviation away from paralysed side; test gag reflex gently.
Test CN XI (spinal accessory): inspect trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles; have child shrug shoulders against downward resistance and turn head laterally against resistance.

Test CN XII (hypoglossal): inspect tongue inside the mouth for wasting and fasciculations; have child protrude tongue, noting deviation towards the paralysed side; test lateral tongue strength inside each cheek.
Apply the Rule of 17 for quick recall: nerves whose sum is 17 behave alike (10+7=17: uvula and angle of mouth deviate to the opposite side; 12+5=17: tongue and jaw deviate to the same side).

skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_bulba.normal: Full conjugate eye movements without nystagmus or strabismus, symmetrical facial movements with equal forehead wrinkling, intact palate elevation with central uvula, strong shoulder shrug, straight midline tongue protrusion without wasting.
skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_bulba.abnormal: Strabismus, diplopia, ptosis, sixth nerve palsy (inability to abduct eye), unilateral facial weakness, uvula deviation away from affected side, nasal regurgitation, weak shoulder shrug, tongue deviation towards affected side with fasciculations.
skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_bulba.significance: A sixth nerve palsy in a child with headache and vomiting is a classic false-localizing sign of raised intracranial pressure due to its long intracranial course. Unilateral LMN facial palsy with ear vesicles indicates Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Tongue fasciculations indicate anterior horn cell disease like spinal muscular atrophy.
skill.exam.paed.cns.cranial_nerves_bulba.practice: Practice the rapid cranial nerve survey in a cooperative child, turning it into a mirroring game ('copy my funny faces: squeeze eyes, blow cheeks, poke out tongue').
pitfalls: Failing to observe spontaneous infant smiling or crying, attempting to force deliberate facial expressions in a preverbal toddler.
Confusing UMN and LMN facial palsy; forehead wrinkling is preserved in UMN lesions because of bilateral cortical representation.
Testing tongue deviation while the child tongue is still inside the mouth; the tongue must be protruded to evaluate hypoglossal deviation.
Overlooking the sixth nerve as a non-localizing sign of raised intracranial pressure.

probes.q: Explain the clinical Rule of 17 regarding cranial nerve palsies.
probes.a: Nerves summing to 17 deviate similarly: 7 and 10 deviate to the opposite side (mouth and uvula); 5 and 12 deviate to the same side (jaw and tongue).

probes.q: Why is the upper face (forehead) spared in an upper motor neuron seventh nerve palsy?
probes.a: The frontalis and upper facial muscles receive bilateral corticobulbar innervation from both cerebral hemispheres.

probes.q: Why is isolated unilateral sixth cranial nerve palsy considered a false-localizing sign in paediatric neurology?
probes.a: The abducens nerve has a long, tortuous intracranial course over the petrous temporal bone, making it susceptible to compression by generalized raised ICP without focal brainstem pathology.

rubric.text: Tests extraocular movements and screens for ptosis and strabismus
Distinguishes upper motor neuron from lower motor neuron facial weakness
Inspects palatal movement and uvula alignment on phonation
Inspects tongue for fasciculations and assesses midline protrusion
Applies the Rule of 17 for cranial nerve deviation patterns

teach.heading: UMN versus LMN facial nerve weakness
teach.body:
In LMN facial palsy (Bell palsy), all muscles on the ipsilateral side of the face are paralysed, including the frontalis: the child cannot wrinkle the forehead or close the eye.

In UMN facial palsy (stroke, hemispheric tumor), the forehead is completely spared because the motor nucleus of the upper face receives bilateral hemispheric fibers.

teach.heading: The clinical Rule of 17 for cranial deviations
Clinical mechanics of deviation
teach.body:
In tenth nerve palsy, the intact contralateral palatoglossus pulls the uvula across to the healthy side.

In twelfth nerve palsy, the healthy genioglossus pushes the tongue forward and unopposed across the midline, directing it towards the paralysed side: the tongue always points to the lesion.
