skill.exam.paed.cns.motor_tone_power.title: Paediatric motor examination: muscle bulk, tone, and power
skill.exam.paed.cns.motor_tone_power.oneLine: Measure limb circumferences, assess muscle tone and neonatal signs, and grade voluntary power from 0 to 5
skill.exam.paed.cns.motor_tone_power.why: Distinguishing upper motor neuron spasticity from lower motor neuron or muscular hypotonia dictates the entire neurodiagnostic trajectory. In young infants, evaluation of tone through passive manoeuvres like the scarf sign and heel-to-ear test provides the primary window into neuromuscular integrity.

steps.text: Observe the posture and attitude of the limbs at rest: note frog-leg hypotonic posture, hemiparetic flexed posture, or scissoring of the lower limbs.
Inspect muscle bulk and nutrition for symmetry, generalized wasting, focal atrophy, or pseudohypertrophy of calves.
Measure limb circumferences at fixed distances from bony landmarks: mid-arm, mid-forearm, mid-thigh, and mid-calf.
Assess muscle tone in older children: ask child to relax and move joints passively through full flexion and extension at wrists, elbows, knees, and ankles.

Characterize hypertonia: spasticity (clasp-knife: velocity-dependent resistance collapsing suddenly, UMN lesion) versus rigidity (lead-pipe or cogwheel: constant velocity-independent resistance throughout movement, extrapyramidal lesion).
In infants, evaluate tone using developmental passive manoeuvres: scarf sign (elbow does not cross midline in normal tone, crosses freely in hypotonia), heel-to-ear test, and popliteal angle.

Test muscle power using the MRC 0 to 5 scale: Grade 0 (no movement), Grade 1 (flicker/trace), Grade 2 (movement with gravity eliminated), Grade 3 (movement against gravity), Grade 4 (movement against partial resistance), Grade 5 (normal power).
Test power functionally in young children: observe getting up from floor (Gowers sign), running, jumping on one foot, and climbing stairs.

skill.exam.paed.cns.motor_tone_power.normal: Symmetrical muscle bulk, normal resting limb posture, normal resistance to passive movement without clasp-knife catch or flaccidity, scarf sign with elbow stopping at midline, full Grade 5 power in all major muscle groups.
skill.exam.paed.cns.motor_tone_power.abnormal: Hypotonia (floppy infant, frog-leg posture, scarf sign crossing midline), spasticity (clasp-knife catch with adductor spasm), muscle wasting, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gowers sign, weakness graded below 5.
skill.exam.paed.cns.motor_tone_power.significance: Upper motor neuron lesions cause spastic hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and preserved bulk. Lower motor neuron or myopathic lesions cause flaccid hypotonia, early wasting, and hyporeflexia. Pseudohypertrophy of calves with positive Gowers sign is classic for Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
skill.exam.paed.cns.motor_tone_power.practice: Practice eliciting the scarf sign and popliteal angle in infants, correlating passive resistance with active movements and muscle bulk.
pitfalls: Testing tone while the child is actively crying or resisting, mistaking voluntary resistance for pathological spasticity.
Assessing muscle power with the MRC scale in a toddler who cannot comprehend formal resistance instructions; use functional play observations instead.
Measuring limb circumference at arbitrary levels rather than measured distances from bony landmarks, creating false asymmetry.
Overlooking subtle distal muscle wasting in the hands or feet.

probes.q: What does MRC muscle power Grade 3 signify?
probes.a: Active movement against gravity, but not against resistance.

probes.q: What is the normal limit of the scarf sign in a term infant?
probes.a: The infant elbow does not cross the midline of the chest.

probes.q: How does spasticity differ from rigidity on passive movement of a limb?
probes.a: Spasticity is velocity-dependent with a clasp-knife catch (UMN), whereas rigidity is velocity-independent with constant lead-pipe or cogwheel resistance throughout (extrapyramidal).

rubric.text: Observes resting attitude and limb posture for frog-leg or scissoring
Measures limb circumferences symmetrically from fixed bony landmarks
Assesses muscle tone through passive movement and identifies spasticity or hypotonia
Executes infant tone manoeuvres (scarf sign, heel-to-ear) correctly
Grades muscle power from 0 to 5 or evaluates functional motor tasks

teach.heading: MRC scale for muscle power grading

rows: No visible or palpable voluntary contraction
Moves across bed, cannot lift off bed
Can lift limb off bed, yields to any resistance

teach.heading: Tone assessment in infants: scarf sign and popliteal angle
teach.body:
In the newborn and infant, passive tone reflects gestational maturity and central nervous system integrity.

To test the scarf sign, draw the infant hand across the chest towards the opposite shoulder. In a normal term infant, the elbow does not cross the sternum. In hypotonia, it wraps easily past the contralateral axillary line.

teach.heading: Spasticity versus rigidity
teach.body:
Spasticity originates in the pyramidal (corticospinal) tract. It is velocity-dependent: rapid passive stretching triggers a sudden 'clasp-knife' catch, followed by release.

Rigidity originates in the extrapyramidal system (basal ganglia). Resistance is uniform throughout the range of motion (lead-pipe) or ratchets smoothly (cogwheel).

skill.exam.paed.cns.reflexes.title: Paediatric deep tendon and superficial reflexes
skill.exam.paed.cns.reflexes.oneLine: Elicit deep tendon reflexes, test clonus and Jendrassik reinforcement, and evaluate the plantar response
skill.exam.paed.cns.reflexes.why: Reflex testing localises neurological pathology to the upper versus lower motor neuron. Understanding that an extensor plantar response is completely physiological in healthy infants under 2 years prevents misdiagnosing normal infant development as corticospinal tract disease.

steps.text: Place the child in a relaxed, comfortable position with limbs supported and muscles limp.
Tap the tendon briskly with a paediatric reflex hammer, observing both muscle contraction and joint displacement.
Test deep tendon reflexes (DTRs): biceps (C5-C6), supinator/brachioradialis (C5-C6), triceps (C6-C7), knee jerk (L3-L4), and ankle jerk (S1).
Grade DTR intensity from 0 to 4+: 0 (absent), 1+ (sluggish/reinforcement only), 2+ (normal briskness, like normal ankle jerk), 3+ (very brisk, like normal knee jerk), 4+ (hyperactive with clonus).
Use Jendrassik reinforcement if reflexes appear absent: have older child hook fingers together and pull apart on command while you tap the tendon.
Test for patellar and ankle clonus: dorsiflex the ankle sharply and maintain dorsiflexion pressure; count beats (sustained clonus of 4 or more beats is pathological).

Elicit superficial reflexes: abdominal reflexes (stroke lightly with wooden stick from periphery toward umbilicus in epigastric T6-T9, umbilical T9-T10, and hypogastric T10-T12 quadrants; absent in UMN lesions).
Test cremasteric reflex in males (stroke upper inner thigh, normal response is brisk elevation of ipsilateral testis, root L1).

Elicit the plantar reflex (S1): stroke the lateral aspect of the sole from heel forward across the metatarsal pad; note flexor versus extensor response (extensor Babinski sign is normal up to 2 years of age).

skill.exam.paed.cns.reflexes.normal: Symmetrical 2+ deep tendon reflexes, unsustained clonus (1 to 2 beats in neonates), intact abdominal reflexes, extensor plantar response physiological under 2 years of age, flexor plantar response after 2 years.
skill.exam.paed.cns.reflexes.abnormal: Areflexia (0) in Guillain-Barre syndrome or spinal muscular atrophy, hyperreflexia (4+) with sustained clonus in cerebral palsy, absent abdominal reflexes, extensor plantar response persisting after 2 years of age.
skill.exam.paed.cns.reflexes.significance: Hyperreflexia with sustained clonus and extensor plantar after age 2 indicates upper motor neuron corticospinal disruption. Hyporeflexia or areflexia indicates lower motor neuron pathology, peripheral neuropathy, or myopathy.
skill.exam.paed.cns.reflexes.practice: Practice eliciting knee and ankle jerks in children with minimal hammer impact, feeling the muscle belly contract directly with your thumb resting over the tendon.
pitfalls: Diagnosing an upper motor neuron lesion in an 11-month-old infant based solely on an extensor Babinski response; it is normal up to 2 years.
Tapping with a cold, heavy adult reflex hammer without resting an examining thumb over the paediatric tendon, causing pain and withdrawal.
Calling reflexes absent without attempting reinforcement manoeuvres like Jendrassik.
Stroking the medial sole or ball of the foot during plantar testing, which elicits a grasping reflex rather than Babinski.

probes.q: Up to what age is an extensor plantar response (Babinski sign) considered normal and physiological in a child?
probes.a: Up to 2 years of age (due to incomplete myelination of the corticospinal tracts).

probes.q: What spinal nerve root levels are evaluated by the knee jerk and ankle jerk respectively?
probes.a: Knee jerk evaluates L3 and L4; ankle jerk evaluates S1.

probes.q: What is Jendrassik manoeuvre, and what physiological mechanism underlies it?
probes.a: Reinforcement manoeuvre where the patient interlocks flexed fingers and pulls apart, decreasing descending presynaptic inhibition on spinal motor neurons.

rubric.text: Applies proper reflex hammer technique with tendon cushioned by examiner thumb
Accurately tests and grades DTRs (biceps, knee, ankle) on 0 to 4+ scale
Tests for sustained ankle clonus with rapid dorsiflexion
Tests abdominal and cremasteric superficial reflexes
Interprets plantar reflex correctly based on child age (under or over 2 years)

rows: Very brisk response, may indicate UMN lesion
Abnormal; sustained clonus, definitive UMN lesion

teach.heading: Spinal root values of paediatric reflexes

rows: Flexor (>2 yr); extensor normal in <2 yr

teach.heading: The developing corticospinal tract and Babinski sign
teach.body:
Myelination of the corticospinal tracts is incomplete at birth and continues throughout infancy.

An extensor plantar response (dorsiflexion of great toe with fanning of other toes) is normal and expected up to 2 years of age. Beyond 2 years, myelination is complete and the plantar response becomes flexor.

skill.exam.paed.cns.sensory.title: Paediatric sensory examination and dermatomal mapping
skill.exam.paed.cns.sensory.oneLine: Map key landmark dermatomes and test spinothalamic, posterior column, and cortical modalities in children
skill.exam.paed.cns.sensory.why: Sensory examination in young children requires patience and ingenuity, as subjective appreciation of touch and pain easily fluctuates with fear or fatigue. Establishing landmark dermatomes localises spinal cord transection, transverse myelitis, and peripheral neuropathies.

steps.text: Gain the child confidence first; turn sensory testing into a painless game ('let us play a guessing game with closed eyes').
Test spinothalamic sensation: touch skin lightly with a wisp of cotton wool (light touch), compare with warm and cool test tubes (temperature), and use a blunt pinhead for superficial pain.
Map sensory levels against key landmark dermatomes: thumb (C6), nipple line (T4), xiphisternum (T7), umbilicus (T10), inguinal crease (L1), big toe (L4), and perianal region (S3-S4).
Test posterior column modalities: vibration sense using a 128 Hz tuning fork over distal bony prominences (great toe IP joint, medial malleolus, tibial tuberosity, ASIS, radial styloid).
Test joint position sense (proprioception): grasp the sides of the child big toe or thumb gently, demonstrating 'up' and 'down' with eyes open, then testing with eyes closed.
Perform Romberg test in standing child: observe stability with feet together and eyes open, then note swaying or falling when eyes are closed (positive Romberg: sensory ataxia).
In cooperative school-age children, test cortical sensations: stereognosis (identifying coin, key, or marble in hand), graphesthesia (identifying numbers drawn on palm), and two-point discrimination.

skill.exam.paed.cns.sensory.normal: Symmetrical perception of light touch, temperature, and pinprick; accurate perception of 128 Hz vibration and joint position sense; negative Romberg test; intact stereognosis.
skill.exam.paed.cns.sensory.abnormal: Sensory level across the trunk (delineating spinal cord pathology), stocking-glove sensory loss (peripheral polyneuropathy), positive Romberg sign (sensory ataxia), astereognosis (contralateral parietal lobe lesion).
skill.exam.paed.cns.sensory.significance: A distinct sensory level on the trunk establishes the precise anatomical level of a compressive spinal lesion (transverse myelitis, spinal tumour, or Pott spine). Dissociated sensory loss (loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch and vibration) indicates central cord lesions like syringomyelia.
skill.exam.paed.cns.sensory.practice: Practice the Romberg test and joint position sense demonstration on a partner, ensuring you hold only the lateral borders of the digit to avoid giving pressure clues.
pitfalls: Holding the dorsal and plantar surfaces of the toe during position sense testing, providing tactile clues that mask true proprioceptive loss.
Using sharp needles that frighten the child, causing withdrawal and terminating the examination prematurely.
Attempting complex cortical testing in a fatigued or uncooperative preschooler.
Forgetting to test perianal sensation (S3-S5) in suspected acute spinal cord compression (cauda equina syndrome).

probes.q: What key anatomical landmarks correspond to the T4, T10, and C6 dermatomes?
probes.a: T4 corresponds to the nipple line, T10 corresponds to the umbilicus, and C6 corresponds to the thumb.

probes.q: What frequency tuning fork is standard for neurological vibration sense testing, and why?
probes.a: 128 Hz tuning fork; it produces sustained low-frequency vibration optimal for bone conduction rather than audible pitch.

probes.q: What is a positive Romberg test, and what sensory pathway does it evaluate?
probes.a: Loss of balance with eyes closed while standing with feet together; it indicates posterior column (proprioceptive) impairment.

rubric.text: Introduces sensory testing non-threateningly with demonstration before testing
Accurately maps key landmark dermatomes (C6, T4, T10, L4, S3-S4)
Tests 128 Hz vibration on bony points and joint position sense correctly
Conducts Romberg test with examiner arms positioned to ensure patient safety
Tests stereognosis or graphesthesia in age-appropriate children

teach.heading: Key landmark dermatomes in paediatric neurology

rows: Conus medullaris and sacral cord function

teach.heading: Testing proprioception without cheating
teach.body:
When testing joint position sense, never grasp the top and bottom of the toe. Pressure receptors will tell the child which direction you are pushing, even if position sense is gone.

Grasp only the lateral borders of the distal phalanx. Move the digit up or down 1 to 2 millimetres and ask the child with eyes closed.

teach.heading: Sensory ataxia versus cerebellar ataxia
teach.body:
Romberg test differentiates sensory ataxia from cerebellar ataxia. Standing requires two of three inputs: vision, proprioception, and vestibular balance.

In sensory ataxia, closing the eyes eliminates visual compensation, causing immediate instability. In cerebellar ataxia, the patient is unsteady even with eyes open.

skill.exam.paed.cns.cerebellar.title: Paediatric cerebellar signs and coordination testing
skill.exam.paed.cns.cerebellar.oneLine: Evaluate intention tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, pendular reflexes, and scanning speech
skill.exam.paed.cns.cerebellar.why: Cerebellar disorders in children range from acute post-infectious cerebellitis to posterior fossa tumours (medulloblastoma, astrocytoma). Recognizing cerebellar signs localises pathology specifically to the midline vermis (truncal ataxia) versus cerebellar hemispheres (appendicular dysmetria).

steps.text: Observe speech for cerebellar scanning dysarthria (slow, staccato speech with unnatural pauses and explosive syllable pronunciation).
Inspect eyes in primary gaze and lateral gaze for cerebellar nystagmus (coarse, gaze-evoked, with fast component towards the direction of gaze).
Test upper limb coordination with the finger-to-nose test: have child touch examiner moving fingertip and their own nose repeatedly, looking for intention tremor and dysmetria (past-pointing).
Test rapid alternating movements for dysdiadochokinesia: have child rapidly pronate and supinate hands on thighs or screw in an imaginary light bulb.

Test Holmes rebound phenomenon: have child flex forearm against resistance, then abruptly release; normal antagonist contraction arrests movement, while cerebellar dysfunction causes unchecked limb recoil.
Evaluate lower limb coordination using the heel-to-knee-to-shin test: have child place heel on opposite knee and slide it smoothly down the tibial crest to the big toe.

Elicit the pendular knee jerk: with legs dangling freely over bed edge, tap the patellar tendon; the normal limb arrests after 1 to 2 oscillations, while a hypotonic cerebellar limb swings back and forth like a pendulum.
Test gait: observe tandem walking (heel-to-toe walking) and assess for broad-based, reeling ataxic gait (falling towards the side of a hemispheric lesion).

skill.exam.paed.cns.cerebellar.normal: Smooth coordinated movements, accurate finger-to-nose targeting without tremor, rapid rhythmic pronation-supination, prompt arrest on rebound test, smooth heel-shin slide, non-pendular knee jerks, steady tandem gait.
skill.exam.paed.cns.cerebellar.abnormal: Intention tremor (worsens as finger approaches target), dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, positive rebound phenomenon, decomposition of movement, pendular knee jerk, scanning dysarthria, truncal or limb ataxia.
skill.exam.paed.cns.cerebellar.significance: Vermis lesions (such as medulloblastoma) produce prominent truncal ataxia, broad-based reeling gait, and titubation of the head with little or no limb dysmetria. Cerebellar hemisphere lesions (such as juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma) cause ipsilateral limb dysmetria, intention tremor, and nystagmus.
skill.exam.paed.cns.cerebellar.practice: Rehearse demonstrating the finger-nose test and rapid hand-patting at child eye level, turning coordination tasks into playful games.
pitfalls: Confusing an intention tremor (which amplifies at the endpoint of voluntary movement) with a resting Parkinsonian tremor or physiological jitteriness.
Testing heel-to-shin in a child who has significant pyramidal weakness, attributing motor clumsiness to cerebellar ataxia.
Forgetting that cerebellar lesions cause signs on the IPSILATERAL side of the body, unlike cerebral lesions which are contralateral.
Missing midline vermis lesions by testing only finger-to-nose and neglecting to observe sitting balance and gait.

probes.q: What is intention tremor, and how does it behave as the target is reached?
probes.a: A kinetic tremor absent at rest that intensifies and becomes coarse as the hand reaches the intended target.

probes.q: What is dysdiadochokinesia, and how is it tested clinically?
probes.a: Inability to perform rapid alternating movements smoothly; tested by rapid pronation and supination of the hands.

probes.q: How does the anatomical localization differ between truncal ataxia and appendicular limb ataxia?
probes.a: Truncal ataxia localises to the midline cerebellar vermis, whereas appendicular limb ataxia localises to the cerebellar hemispheres.

rubric.text: Executes finger-to-nose test assessing for intention tremor and dysmetria
Tests rapid alternating movements (pronation-supination)
Conducts heel-to-knee-to-shin coordination testing in lower limbs
Evaluates knee jerk for pendular swinging oscillations
Assesses tandem walking and truncal balance

teach.heading: Cerebellar functional anatomy: vermis versus hemispheres
teach.body:
The cerebellar vermis occupies the midline and controls axial balance, posture, and locomotion.

The cerebellar hemispheres control ipsilateral limb coordination and fine motor planning. A lesion in the right hemisphere causes ataxia in the right arm and leg.

rows: Inability to judge distance and velocity
Failure of rapid muscle group alternation
Loss of cerebellar tone and damping

teach.heading: Acute ataxia in paediatric clinical practice
teach.body:
In toddlers, acute ataxia most commonly represents post-infectious acute cerebellitis following varicella or enterovirus infection, which resolves spontaneously.

However, persistent or worsening ataxia accompanied by morning headaches, vomiting, or papilloedema warrants immediate MRI to rule out a posterior fossa tumor.

skill.exam.paed.cns.meningeal.title: Paediatric meningeal irritation signs and raised intracranial tension
skill.exam.paed.cns.meningeal.oneLine: Elicit neck rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski signs, and identify infant indicators of meningitis and raised pressure
skill.exam.paed.cns.meningeal.why: Acute bacterial and tuberculous meningitis remain life-threatening paediatric emergencies where delay in recognition causes death or devastating neurological handicap. Classic adult meningeal signs are frequently absent in young infants under 12 to 18 months, who manifest subtle signs like a bulging fontanelle.

steps.text: In infants, inspect and palpate the anterior fontanelle while the child is upright and quiet: note bulging, fullness, or abnormal tension (normal fontanelle is flat or slightly depressed and pulsatile).
Observe infant behaviour: look for paradoxical irritability (cries more when comforted or handled due to meningeal stretching), high-pitched cry, and neck retraction or opisthotonos.

Test for neck rigidity: place hands behind child occiput and gently flex the cervical spine forward towards the chest; note involuntary resistance and muscle spasm (normal child chin touches sternum easily).
Test Kernig sign: with child supine, flex hip to 90 degrees and knee to 90 degrees; attempt to extend the knee; note resistance and pain caused by hamstring spasm beyond 135 degrees.
Test Brudzinski neck sign: during passive flexion of the neck, observe involuntary flexion of both hips and knees (positive neck sign).
Test Brudzinski contralateral leg sign: passively flex one hip and knee; note involuntary flexion of the contralateral hip and knee.

Screen for raised intracranial pressure: check for projectile vomiting without preceding nausea, Macewen cracked-pot sign on skull percussion, setting-sun eye sign, and Cushing triad (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respirations).

skill.exam.paed.cns.meningeal.normal: Full painless neck flexion allowing chin to touch chest, flat soft pulsatile fontanelle in infants, knee extension with flexed hip without resistance, negative Brudzinski signs.
skill.exam.paed.cns.meningeal.abnormal: Marked neck stiffness, positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, tense bulging anterior fontanelle, paradoxical irritability, opisthotonos, setting-sun sign, projectile vomiting, Cushing triad.
skill.exam.paed.cns.meningeal.significance: Positive meningeal signs indicate irritation and stretching of inflamed leptomeninges and spinal nerve roots (bacterial meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage). Tense fontanelle and Cushing triad indicate severely raised intracranial pressure where immediate lumbar puncture is contraindicated.
skill.exam.paed.cns.meningeal.practice: Practice the gentle neck flexion and Kernig manoeuvres on pediatric training models, ensuring movements are gentle and never forced against extreme resistance.
pitfalls: Palpating the anterior fontanelle while the infant is actively screaming or crying, which causes physiological bulging in healthy infants.
Relying on neck stiffness to exclude meningitis in an infant under 12 months; infants frequently present without classical meningeal signs.
Performing a lumbar puncture in a child with signs of impending herniation (Cushing triad, fixed unreactive pupil, focal deficit).
Confusing cervical lymphadenitis or retroverted torticollis with true generalized meningeal neck stiffness.

probes.q: What is Kernig sign, and what anatomical mechanism causes it?
probes.a: Pain and resistance when attempting to extend the knee with the hip flexed at 90 degrees, caused by hamstring spasm from inflamed spinal nerve roots.

probes.q: What is paradoxical irritability in an infant with suspected meningitis?
probes.a: The infant cries more when held and comforted by parents, because movement and handling stretch the inflamed meninges.

probes.q: What three clinical parameters constitute Cushing triad in acutely raised intracranial pressure?
probes.a: Hypertension (widened pulse pressure), bradycardia, and irregular respirations.

rubric.text: Palpates anterior fontanelle with infant calm and seated upright
Gently tests passive neck flexion towards the sternum
Elicits Kernig sign with hip flexed at 90 degrees
Checks for Brudzinski neck sign and contralateral leg sign
Screens for signs of herniation risk (fontanelle, pupils, Cushing triad)

teach.heading: The pathophysiology of meningeal signs
teach.body:
Inflammation of the arachnoid and pia mater irritates nerve roots traversing the subarachnoid space.

Flexing the neck or extending the knee pulls on these inflamed spinal roots. The body reflexively contracts the extensor neck muscles and hamstrings to prevent painful mechanical stretching.

teach.heading: Meningeal signs in infants versus older children
Red flags contraindicating immediate lumbar puncture
teach.body:
Lumbar puncture must be deferred if signs of impending cerebral herniation exist.

Key contraindications include unequal or non-reactive pupils, Cushing triad (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular breathing), focal neurological deficits, and local infection at the puncture site.

skill.exam.paed.cns.gait_movement.title: Paediatric gait patterns and involuntary movements
skill.exam.paed.cns.gait_movement.oneLine: Evaluate gait development, recognize hemiparetic, spastic, and waddling gaits, and elicit Gowers sign
skill.exam.paed.cns.gait_movement.why: Gait analysis synthesizes motor, sensory, cerebellar, and musculoskeletal systems in action. In children, spotting Gowers sign or a waddling Trendelenburg gait provides the earliest clue to progressive neuromuscular dystrophies before overt disability occurs.

steps.text: Observe the child walking barefoot across an open space, viewing from the front, from behind, and from the side.
Differentiate normal toddler gait (wide-based, slight outward rotation of feet, arms in high-guard position) from mature adult-type gait (achieved by 3 to 4 years of age).
Identify hemiparetic gait: circumduction of the affected leg with upper limb flexed, adducted, and held rigid.
Identify spastic diplegic gait: scissoring of knees due to adductor spasm, walking on tiptoes with flexion at hips and knees.
Identify ataxic gait: broad-based, reeling, uncoordinated steps with irregular swaying and difficulty turning.
Identify waddling gait (myopathic/Trendelenburg gait): bilateral pelvic drop and lateral trunk sway due to proximal gluteus medius weakness.
Elicit Gowers sign: have child sit on the floor and ask them to stand up without assistance; note if child turns prone, rises onto hands and knees, and 'climbs up their own legs' using their hands.
Inspect for involuntary movements: chorea (rapid, non-rhythmic, jerky), athetosis (slow, writhing distal movements), dystonia (sustained twisting postures), tremors (resting vs action), and tics.

skill.exam.paed.cns.gait_movement.normal: Age-appropriate steady gait, smooth reciprocal arm swing, narrow base of support after age 4, ability to stand from the floor effortlessly in one fluid motion without using hands on thighs, absence of involuntary movements.
skill.exam.paed.cns.gait_movement.abnormal: Hemiparetic circumduction, spastic scissoring, broad-based ataxic reeling, high-stepping foot-drop gait, waddling gait, positive Gowers sign, choreoathetosis, dystonic posturing.
skill.exam.paed.cns.gait_movement.significance: Gowers sign is the hallmark of proximal muscle weakness, classically seen in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. A spastic scissoring gait indicates bilateral corticospinal damage typical of spastic diplegic cerebral palsy. Sydenham chorea presents with rapid purposeless involuntary movements in acute rheumatic fever.
skill.exam.paed.cns.gait_movement.practice: Observe children rising from the floor from a supine position, contrasting normal abdominal and quadriceps spring with the hand-climbing Gowers sequence.
pitfalls: Diagnosing pathological ataxia in an 18-month-old toddler who has a normal physiological wide-based gait.
Dismissing mild toe-walking as a behavioral habit without assessing heel-cord tightness and ankle clonus.
Forgetting to have the child rise from the floor, missing early proximal muscle dystrophy when casual walking appears nearly normal.
Confusing choreic movements in acute rheumatic fever with behavioral restlessness or tics.

probes.q: What is Gowers sign, and what underlying pathological process does it signify?
probes.a: The child rises from the floor by climbing up their own thighs with their hands; indicates proximal muscle weakness (e.g. Duchenne muscular dystrophy).

probes.q: What is a scissoring gait, and what clinical condition is it classically associated with?
probes.a: Excessive adduction of the thighs causing knees to cross over each other like scissors; associated with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy.

probes.q: How does chorea differ from athetosis on physical inspection?
probes.a: Chorea consists of rapid, jerky, involuntary, non-rhythmic movements; athetosis consists of slow, continuous, sinuous, writhing movements of distal limbs.

rubric.text: Observes child walking barefoot from front, back, and side
Accurately identifies hemiparetic, scissoring, ataxic, or waddling gait
Tests the child ability to stand up from the floor to elicit Gowers sign
Screens for chorea, athetosis, dystonia, and tremors
Distinguishes normal toddler gait from true cerebellar or sensory ataxia

rows: Pelvic drop and lateral trunk sway
Common peroneal nerve palsy, CMT disease

teach.heading: The Gowers sign sequence
teach.body:
Gowers sign reveals pelvic girdle and proximal hip extensor (gluteus maximus) weakness.

The child rolls prone onto hands and knees, extends knees, pushes hands off the floor onto knees, and walks hands up the shins and thighs to bring the trunk erect.

teach.heading: Involuntary movements in childhood
teach.body:
Chorea features rapid, unpredictable, non-stereotyped jerks flowing from one body part to another.

In India, Sydenham chorea remains an important manifestation of acute rheumatic fever. Differentiate it from tics, which are preceded by an internal premonitory urge.

skill.exam.paed.cns.febrile_seizure.title: Paediatric febrile seizure evaluation and criteria
skill.exam.paed.cns.febrile_seizure.oneLine: Evaluate a child with febrile convulsions, apply the 10 criteria for simple febrile seizures, and identify red flags
skill.exam.paed.cns.febrile_seizure.why: Febrile seizures occur in 2% to 5% of young children and represent the commonest neurological emergency in early childhood. Differentiating benign simple febrile seizures from complex febrile seizures or bacterial meningitis avoids unnecessary neuroimaging while ensuring CNS infections are never missed.

steps.text: Obtain a detailed history of the convulsion: exact age of child, fever onset, duration of seizure, seizure semiology (generalized vs focal), and number of episodes in 24 hours.

Verify the 10 criteria for a Simple Febrile Seizure: age 6 months to 5 years, neurologically normal child prior to onset, absence of CNS infection, occurrence within 24 hours of fever onset, generalized tonic-clonic semiology, duration under 10 to 15 minutes, single episode in 24 hours, no postictal neurological deficit, and normal recovery.
Perform a thorough physical examination to identify the fever source: inspect ears (otitis media), throat (pharyngotonsillitis), chest, and urine.
Examine for meningeal irritation signs: neck stiffness, Kernig sign, Brudzinski signs, and anterior fontanelle tension.
Perform a complete neurological examination: assess level of consciousness, pupillary responses, cranial nerves, tone, and symmetric motor power.
Identify indicators for complex febrile seizure: focal seizure, duration exceeding 15 minutes, or multiple episodes within 24 hours.
Determine indications for lumbar puncture: age under 12 months, incomplete immunisation (Hib, Pneumococcal), child pretreated with antibiotics, persistent lethargy, or any meningeal signs.

skill.exam.paed.cns.febrile_seizure.normal: Complete neurological recovery within 1 hour, normal sensorium, alert and playful, absence of focal weakness (Todd paresis), absence of meningeal signs, identifiable extracranial fever focus.
skill.exam.paed.cns.febrile_seizure.abnormal: Complex febrile seizure features (focal seizure, prolonged >15 minutes, multiple in 24 hours), persistent lethargy or encephalopathy after 1 hour, focal postictal paralysis (Todd paresis), presence of neck rigidity or bulging fontanelle.
skill.exam.paed.cns.febrile_seizure.significance: A simple febrile seizure carries an excellent prognosis with no elevated risk of intellectual disability and minimal risk of subsequent epilepsy. Complex febrile seizures or incomplete recovery require urgent evaluation for bacterial or viral meningoencephalitis, structural lesions, or epilepsy syndromes.
skill.exam.paed.cns.febrile_seizure.practice: Rehearse counseling an anxious parent after a simple febrile seizure, clearly explaining the benign nature, low risk of epilepsy, fever management, and seizure first aid.
pitfalls: Performing routine emergency CT brain or EEG in a child who has met all criteria for a simple febrile seizure and has fully recovered.
Attributing postictal drowsiness persisting beyond 1 to 2 hours solely to the seizure, failing to recognize bacterial meningitis.
Forgetting that prior oral antibiotic therapy masks the classic symptoms and signs of bacterial meningitis.
Prescribing daily continuous long-term anticonvulsants for simple febrile convulsions.

probes.q: What are the three core features that classify a febrile seizure as complex rather than simple?
probes.a: Focal onset, duration greater than 15 minutes, or recurrence of more than one episode within a 24-hour period.

probes.q: What is the typical age range for simple febrile seizures in children?
probes.a: 6 months to 5 years (peaking between 12 and 18 months).

probes.q: Why is a lumbar puncture strongly recommended in an infant under 12 months presenting with a first febrile seizure?
probes.a: Infants under 12 months frequently do not exhibit classical meningeal signs of neck stiffness, making clinical exclusion of bacterial meningitis unreliable.

rubric.text: Elicits exact seizure semiology, duration, and recurrence within 24 hours
Accurately classifies seizure as simple versus complex febrile seizure
Examines thoroughly for neck stiffness, fontanelle fullness, and irritability
Performs systemic examination to identify extracranial fever source
Identifies clinical indications for diagnostic lumbar puncture

rows: Two or more episodes within 24 hours

teach.heading: The 10 criteria for simple febrile seizure
teach.body:
A simple febrile seizure requires: age 6 months to 5 years; normal neurodevelopment; no CNS infection; no metabolic disturbance; onset within 24 hours of fever; generalized semiology; duration <15 minutes; single episode in 24 hours; complete recovery; and often a positive family history.

All 10 criteria must be met to confirm the diagnosis.

teach.heading: Management and investigations policy
teach.body:
Routine blood investigations, EEG, and neuroimaging are not indicated in a child with a simple febrile seizure who has returned to baseline.

Counsel the family on seizure first aid: place child in lateral recovery position, do not insert anything into the mouth, and seek immediate hospital care if seizure exceeds 5 minutes.

skill.hx.paed.neo.maternal_perinatal.title: Maternal and perinatal history
skill.hx.paed.neo.maternal_perinatal.oneLine: Systematic inquiry into antenatal complications, labour progression, delivery mode, and early neonatal transition
skill.hx.paed.neo.maternal_perinatal.why: A newborn is the direct biological continuation of maternal physiology and intrapartum events. Overlooking maternal diabetes, fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, or instrumental delivery leaves early-onset sepsis, hypoglycaemia, and birth trauma unrecognised until severe deterioration occurs.

asks.text: Record maternal age, obstetric score (gravida, para, living children, miscarriages, neonatal deaths), and whether pregnancy was conceived spontaneously or through assisted reproduction.

Inquire about trimester illnesses: first trimester febrile episodes, rash, or drug exposures; second trimester anatomy scan findings; and third trimester gestational diabetes, pregnancy-induced hypertension, or antepartum bleeding.
Establish intrapartum details: duration of rupture of membranes, colour of liquor (clear, blood-stained, or meconium-stained), maternal intrapartum fever, and intrapartum antibiotic administration.
Clarify delivery circumstances: spontaneous vaginal birth, vacuum or forceps assistance, or caesarean section, noting whether emergency or elective and the specific clinical indication.

Ask about immediate post-birth transition: whether the infant cried immediately, required positive-pressure ventilation or intubation, Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes, time to first breastfeed, and passage of meconium and urine.

skill.hx.paed.neo.maternal_perinatal.practice: Role-play taking a comprehensive perinatal history from a mother in the postnatal ward, documenting the obstetric score, maternal risk factors, delivery details, and initial neonatal adaptation.
pitfalls: Recording only the mode of delivery without noting the specific medical or obstetric indication for intervention.
Failing to ask the exact time interval between membrane rupture and delivery, missing prolonged rupture over 18 hours as a primary sepsis risk.
Omitting maternal drug history, such as intrapartum opioids that cause neonatal respiratory depression, or antithyroid medications.

probes.q: Within how many hours after birth should a healthy term newborn pass urine and meconium?
probes.a: A healthy newborn should pass meconium within 24 hours of birth and urine within 48 hours of birth.

probes.q: Why is a rupture of membranes interval exceeding 18 hours clinically significant in neonatal history?
probes.a: Prolonged rupture of membranes allows ascending vaginal bacteria to colonise the amniotic cavity, dramatically increasing the risk of early-onset neonatal sepsis and pneumonia.

probes.q: A mother with poorly controlled gestational diabetes delivers a macrosomic infant. What immediate metabolic and haematological risks must the history anticipate?
probes.a: Severe neonatal hypoglycaemia due to fetal hyperinsulinism, polycythaemia driven by fetal hypoxia, hypocalcaemia, and birth trauma such as shoulder dystocia or brachial plexus injury.

rubric.text: Records maternal age, parity, gravidity, and conception history
Screens for maternal diabetes, hypertension, infections, and drug intake
Inquires about membrane rupture duration, liquor appearance, and delivery indication
Documents immediate cry, resuscitation needed, Apgar scores, and elimination milestones

teach.heading: Why the neonatal history begins in utero
teach.body:
Neonatal pathology rarely starts at delivery. Maternal medical conditions, placental perfusion, and intrapartum events directly shape newborn viability.

A complete neonatal history bridges obstetric events and paediatric care. It identifies infants who need close monitoring for hypoglycaemia, respiratory distress, or systemic infection before symptoms appear.

teach.heading: Key maternal and intrapartum risk factors
Normal neonatal elimination milestones
teach.body:
Over 95 percent of healthy term infants pass meconium within the first 24 hours of life. Failure to pass meconium by 24 hours warrants evaluation for intestinal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus, or an imperforate anus.

Healthy newborns pass urine within 48 hours of life, though most do so within 24 hours. Delayed micturition beyond 48 hours requires assessment for dehydration, renal agenesis, or posterior urethral valves in males.

skill.approach.paed.neo.resuscitation_in.title: Initial steps and thermal control in neonatal resuscitation
skill.approach.paed.neo.resuscitation_in.oneLine: Team preparation, rapid birth assessment, thermal chain maintenance, positioning, and gentle tactile stimulation
skill.approach.paed.neo.resuscitation_in.why: Immediate hypothermia and ineffective airway management at birth trigger pulmonary vasoconstriction, hypoxia, and metabolic acidosis. Executing structured initial steps under a radiant warmer preserves physiological transition and prevents asphyxial injury.

steps.text: Prepare the resuscitation area before delivery: ensure a pre-heated radiant warmer, warm dry towels, functional suction apparatus, stethoscope, and pre-checked bag-mask unit.
Assess three rapid questions immediately upon birth: Is the newborn term? Is the newborn breathing or crying? Does the newborn have good muscle tone?

If the newborn is vigorous with clear amniotic fluid, place skin-to-skin on the maternal chest, dry thoroughly with warm linen, cover with a warm blanket, and delay cord clamping for at least 60 seconds.
If any answer is no, transfer the infant immediately to the radiant warmer, place in a supine position with the neck slightly extended in the sniffing position using a shoulder roll.
Wipe the mouth and nose gently; reserve catheter suction (pressure <100 cmH2O or <50 mmHg) strictly for infants with obvious airway obstruction or those requiring positive-pressure ventilation.
Provide brief tactile stimulation by flicking the soles or rubbing the back gently while removing wet towels to prevent evaporative heat loss.

skill.approach.paed.neo.resuscitation_in.practice: Rehearse the rapid assessment and initial 30-second sequence on a neonatal manikin, practicing sniffing position alignment, towel exchange, and tactile stimulation.
pitfalls: Hyperextending or flexing the newborn neck, which collapses the pliable airway rather than opening it.
Performing routine vigorous oral and tracheal suctioning in clear fluid, which induces reflex bradycardia and mucosal trauma.
Failing to remove wet towels after drying, causing rapid evaporative and conductive hypothermia.

probes.q: What three rapid questions determine whether a newborn requires initial steps at the radiant warmer?
probes.a: Whether the newborn is term, whether the baby is breathing or crying, and whether there is good muscle tone.

probes.q: Why is routine deep or aggressive suctioning avoided in a freshly delivered newborn?
probes.a: Deep vigorous pharyngeal suctioning stimulates vagal afferents, causing reflex bradycardia, laryngeal spasm, and delayed onset of spontaneous respirations.

probes.q: For how long should cord clamping be delayed in uncomplicated term and preterm births, and what benefits does it confer?
probes.a: Delayed cord clamping should be performed for at least 60 seconds. It facilitates placental transfusion, increases neonatal blood volume, enhances iron stores, and reduces intraventricular haemorrhage in preterm infants.

rubric.text: Prepares radiant warmer and verifies equipment before delivery
Assesses gestation, breathing/cry, and muscle tone within 5 seconds
Positions head in sniffing position with shoulder roll
Dries infant thoroughly and discards wet towels promptly
Applies appropriate tactile stimulation without violent shaking

teach.heading: The golden minute and initial assessment
teach.body:
The first 60 seconds after birth are termed the golden minute. During this critical window, the resuscitation team assesses the baby, initiates thermal protection, positions the airway, and starts positive-pressure ventilation if the infant is not breathing effectively.

Three questions guide initial triage: Is the baby born at term? Is the infant crying or breathing? Does the baby possess good muscle tone? If all are affirmative, the infant stays with the mother for routine care.

teach.heading: The thermal chain and prevention of heat loss
teach.body:
Newborns have a large surface area relative to body weight and wet skin, predisposing them to rapid conductive and evaporative cooling. Hypothermia impairs surfactant function, increases oxygen consumption, and produces metabolic acidosis.

Maintain the warm chain: deliver into warm towels, dry immediately, remove wet linen, and use skin-to-skin contact for stable babies or a pre-heated servo-controlled radiant warmer for distressed infants. Bathing is postponed for at least 24 hours.

teach.heading: Airway positioning and selective suction
teach.body:
The neonatal occiput is prominent. When supine, the head flexes forward, obstructing the pharynx. Placing a small shoulder roll (2 cm thick) positions the head in the neutral sniffing posture, aligning the pharyngeal axes.

Routine suctioning is not recommended. Routine suctioning damages fragile mucosa and triggers vagal bradycardia. Wipe the mouth and nose; reserve catheter suction (negative pressure <100 cmH2O or <50 mmHg) for proven obstruction.

skill.approach.paed.neo.bag_mask_ventila.title: Positive pressure ventilation and MR SOPA corrective steps
skill.approach.paed.neo.bag_mask_ventila.oneLine: Administering bag-mask ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths/min and troubleshooting inadequate chest rise
skill.approach.paed.neo.bag_mask_ventila.why: Ventilation is the single most critical and effective intervention in neonatal resuscitation. Failure to establish effective lung inflation within the golden minute perpetuates hypoxia, bradycardia, and hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury.

steps.text: Select an appropriately sized cushioned face mask covering the chin, mouth, and nose without overlapping the eyes.
Position the head in the neutral sniffing posture and apply the mask using the C-grip (thumb and index finger on mask, remaining fingers lifting mandibular ramus).

Initiate positive-pressure ventilation at a rate of 40 to 60 breaths per minute using a self-inflating bag (250 mL or 500 mL) with oxygen concentration of 21 percent for term or 21 to 30 percent for preterm.
Deliver the first inflation at 30 to 40 cmH2O to establish functional residual capacity, followed by subsequent breaths at 15 to 20 cmH2O.
Attach a pulse oximeter probe to the right wrist or palm to monitor pre-ductal oxygen saturation and heart rate.

If chest rise is absent or heart rate does not rise above 100 beats per minute within 15 seconds, immediately execute the MR SOPA sequence: Mask adjustment, Reposition head, Suction mouth and nose, Open mouth, Pressure increase (up to 40 cmH2O), and Alternative airway (endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask).

skill.approach.paed.neo.bag_mask_ventila.practice: Practice two-finger C-grip mask seal and squeezing a 250 mL resuscitation bag at 40 to 60 breaths per minute on an infant manikin, verbally executing the MR SOPA mnemonic.
pitfalls: Pushing the face mask down forcefully onto the eyes or soft tissues of the neck, causing bradycardia and airway occlusion.
Starting chest compressions before establishing effective bilateral ventilation with visible chest excursion.
Using high-concentration 100 percent oxygen routinely for term resuscitation, which causes oxidative reperfusion damage.

probes.q: What is the recommended ventilation rate during neonatal bag-mask resuscitation?
probes.a: The recommended ventilation rate is 40 to 60 breaths per minute.

probes.q: What does the mnemonic MR SOPA stand for when troubleshooting ineffective ventilation?
probes.a: Mask adjustment, Reposition head, Suction mouth and nose, Open mouth, Pressure increase, and Alternative airway.

probes.q: What are the two absolute contraindications to bag-mask ventilation in a depressed newborn?
probes.a: Suspected congenital diaphragmatic hernia (which distends intrathoracic bowel) and a non-vigorous meconium-stained infant requiring direct laryngoscopic inspection.

rubric.text: Selects correct mask size and applies airtight C-grip without ocular pressure
Delivers positive-pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths per minute
Executes MR SOPA corrective algorithm promptly when chest rise is absent
Applies pulse oximeter probe to right wrist for pre-ductal saturation

teach.heading: Indications and parameters for positive-pressure ventilation
teach.body:
Positive-pressure ventilation is indicated when an infant remains apnoeic or gasping, or has a heart rate below 100 beats per minute after the initial steps. It is also indicated for persistent central cyanosis despite supplemental oxygen.

Ventilate at 40 to 60 breaths per minute ('breathe-two-three, breathe-two-three'). Initial inflation of fluid-filled lungs requires 30 to 40 cmH2O pressure; subsequent breaths require 15 to 20 cmH2O.

teach.heading: Oxygen concentration and pre-ductal saturation monitoring
teach.body:
Resuscitation of term infants begins in room air (21 percent oxygen). Preterm infants under 35 weeks gestation begin at 21 to 30 percent blended oxygen. High oxygen concentrations create toxic reactive oxygen species that injure retinal and pulmonary tissues.

Attach the pulse oximeter sensor to the right hand or wrist to measure pre-ductal blood before mixing across the ductus arteriosus. Titrate oxygen to meet normal target saturations: 60 to 65 percent at 1 minute, reaching 85 to 95 percent by 10 minutes.

rows: Eliminate mask leak around mouth and nose
Adjust head to neutral sniffing posture
Suction mouth then nose with bulb or catheter
Open mouth slightly and lift jaw forward
Increase pressure by 5 cmH2O steps up to 40
Generate sufficient pressure to expand alveoli
Insert endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask

skill.approach.paed.neo.airway_intubatio.title: Neonatal endotracheal intubation and meconium airway management
skill.approach.paed.neo.airway_intubatio.oneLine: Laryngoscopy, endotracheal tube sizing, depth calculation, verification, and non-vigorous meconium protocol
skill.approach.paed.neo.airway_intubatio.why: Securing an advanced airway is life-saving when bag-mask ventilation fails, prolonged resuscitation is needed, or congenital diaphragmatic hernia is suspected. Unchecked or repeated prolonged intubation attempts cause severe hypoxaemia, vagal arrest, and airway perforation.

steps.text: Select the correct endotracheal tube size: 2.5 mm for weight <1000 g (<28 weeks), 3.0 mm for 1000 to 2000 g (28 to 34 weeks), 3.5 mm for 2000 to 3000 g (34 to 38 weeks), and 4.0 mm for >3000 g (>38 weeks).
Prepare straight-blade (Miller) laryngoscope: blade size 0 for preterm infants and size 1 for term newborns; confirm bright, reliable light source.
Position newborn in sniffing position; hold laryngoscope in the left hand and insert blade into the right side of mouth, sweeping tongue to left.
Advance blade tip into vallecula or gently lift epiglottis directly; elevate blade upward and forward along the handle axis without levering on the alveolar ridge.
Visualize vocal cords, advance tube from the right corner of mouth between the cords until the vocal cord guide aligns with the cords; complete attempt within 30 seconds.
Calculate tube insertion depth at upper lip using the formula: 6 + weight in kilograms (for example, 2.5 kg infant fixed at 8.5 cm).

Confirm position by observing bilateral symmetrical chest rise, auscultating bilateral axillary breath sounds without gastric distension, checking colourimetric exhaled CO2 detector, and inspecting tube misting.

In infants born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid: if non-vigorous, place under radiant warmer and clear mouth and hypopharynx under direct laryngoscopy; routine tracheal suctioning is not advised unless airway is obstructed.

skill.approach.paed.neo.airway_intubatio.practice: Perform timed endotracheal intubations on a neonatal manikin, practicing blade insertion, cord visualization, tube insertion, and securing the tube at 6 plus weight depth within 30 seconds.
pitfalls: Levering the laryngoscope against the alveolar margin using it as a fulcrum, which injures gums and tooth buds.
Continuing an intubation attempt beyond 30 seconds while the infant desaturates into profound bradycardia.
Intubating the right mainstem bronchus due to advancing the tube too deep, causing unilateral expansion and contralateral atelectasis.

probes.q: What internal diameter endotracheal tube is selected for a newborn weighing 2.5 kg?
probes.a: A 3.5 mm internal diameter endotracheal tube.

probes.q: How is the correct depth of endotracheal tube insertion at the upper lip calculated from the infant weight?
probes.a: The depth of insertion at the upper lip is calculated as 6 plus the infant weight in kilograms (6 + weight in kg).

probes.q: What are the clinical and capnographic indicators confirming correct tracheal tube placement?
probes.a: Symmetrical bilateral chest rise, equal breath sounds in both axillae without gastric sounds, condensation inside the tube, and colour change on an exhaled CO2 detector.

rubric.text: Selects correct tube internal diameter and laryngoscope blade for infant size
Visualizes vocal cords and inserts tube within 30-second time limit
Calculates depth at lip using weight plus 6 and secures tube
Confirms bilateral breath sounds, chest rise, and exhaled CO2 change

teach.heading: Endotracheal tube sizing and depth guidelines
Calculation of insertion depth and fixation
teach.body:
The tip-to-lip distance for endotracheal tube fixation follows the standard NRP formula: depth in centimetres equals 6 plus the baby weight in kilograms.

For example, an infant weighing 1 kg is fixed at 7 cm at the upper lip; a 2.5 kg infant is fixed at 8.5 cm. Securing the tube precisely prevents inadvertent extubation or endobronchial intubation of the right main bronchus.

teach.heading: Protocol for meconium-stained amniotic fluid
teach.body:
Intrapartum suctioning of the mouth and pharynx before delivery of the shoulders is not recommended. Routine tracheal intubation for suctioning in non-vigorous infants born through meconium-stained liquor is also no longer recommended.

If the infant is vigorous, provide routine care with mother. If non-vigorous, place under radiant warmer, inspect pharynx under direct laryngoscopy to clear thick debris, and initiate positive-pressure ventilation promptly if respiration is depressed.

skill.approach.paed.neo.chest_compressio.title: Neonatal chest compressions and circulatory resuscitation
skill.approach.paed.neo.chest_compressio.oneLine: Two-thumb encircling chest compressions at 3:1 ratio, vascular access, and volume/adrenaline management
skill.approach.paed.neo.chest_compressio.why: When severe bradycardia below 60 beats per minute persists despite adequate ventilation, myocardial perfusion falls below critical levels. Coordinated 3:1 compressions restore coronary perfusion pressure, driving spontaneous cardiac electrical and mechanical recovery.

steps.text: Confirm indication: heart rate remains below 60 beats per minute despite 30 seconds of effective positive-pressure ventilation with 100 percent oxygen.
Position yourself at the head or side of the bed; place both thumbs on the lower third of the sternum, just below the inter-nipple line, avoiding the xiphoid.
Encircle the newborn chest with both hands, supporting the infant back with the fingers.

Compress sternum to a depth of approximately one-third of the anteroposterior diameter of the chest (about half to three-quarters of an inch), allowing full chest recoil without lifting thumbs off the skin.

Coordinate compressions and ventilations in a 3:1 ratio: three compressions followed by one breath (90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute, totaling 120 events each minute, rhythm: 'one-and-two-and-three-and-breathe').
Re-evaluate heart rate and rhythm using a 3-lead ECG monitor or auscultation every 60 seconds; discontinue compressions once spontaneous heart rate rises above 60 beats per minute.

If heart rate remains below 60 beats per minute after 45 to 60 seconds of coordinated CPR, prepare emergency umbilical venous catheterization for adrenaline (epinephrine 1:10,000 at 0.1 to 0.3 mL/kg IV followed by 0.5 to 1 mL saline flush; repeat every 3 to 5 minutes).
If hypovolaemic shock or acute intrapartum blood loss is suspected, infuse normal saline at 10 mL/kg IV over 5 to 10 minutes.

skill.approach.paed.neo.chest_compressio.practice: Perform 2 minutes of uninterrupted coordinated CPR on an infant manikin using the two-thumb technique at a 3:1 ratio, calling the cadence and checking pulse after 60 seconds.
pitfalls: Starting chest compressions before confirming effective bilateral lung inflation and audible breath sounds.
Lifting thumbs off the sternum between compressions, losing anatomical positioning and causing sternal or rib injury.
Giving routine sodium bicarbonate or Ringer lactate, which worsen intracellular acidosis and acute mortality.

probes.q: What is the heart rate threshold for initiating chest compressions in a newborn?
probes.a: Heart rate remaining below 60 beats per minute despite 30 seconds of effective positive-pressure ventilation.

probes.q: Why is the two-thumb encircling technique preferred over the two-finger technique for neonatal chest compressions?
probes.a: The two-thumb encircling technique generates higher peak systolic and coronary perfusion pressures, maintains consistent depth, and produces less rescuer fatigue.

probes.q: What is the recommended dose and route for emergency adrenaline in neonatal resuscitation when IV access is established?
probes.a: Adrenaline 1:10,000 solution given intravenously via umbilical venous catheter at 0.1 to 0.3 mL/kg, followed by a 0.5 to 1 mL normal saline flush.

rubric.text: Confirms heart rate below 60 bpm despite effective ventilation before starting CPR
Applies two-thumb encircling grip on lower third of sternum below nipple line
Maintains strict 3:1 ratio achieving 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute
Calculates adrenaline 1:10,000 dose and normal saline volume correctly

teach.heading: Physiology of neonatal chest compressions
teach.body:
Neonatal bradycardia is almost invariably hypoxic in origin, not primary cardiac arrest. Effective ventilation usually restores heart rate within 30 seconds. Compressions are reserved for profound myocardial depression where coronary blood flow has ceased.

The 3:1 compression-to-ventilation ratio delivers 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute (120 total events). This higher ventilation proportion matches the asphyxial pathophysiology of the newborn.

teach.heading: Two-thumb encircling technique vs two-finger method
teach.body:
The two-thumb encircling-hands method is the gold standard. Place both thumbs over the lower third of the sternum (just below the imaginary inter-nipple line) with fingers encircling the torso to support the spine.

Compress one-third of the anteroposterior diameter of the chest. Allow complete chest recoil between compressions to permit ventricular filling. The two-finger method is reserved only when umbilical line placement requires anterior chest access.

skill.exam.paed.neo.ballard_gestational_.title: New Ballard examination for gestational maturity
skill.exam.paed.neo.ballard_gestational_.oneLine: Physical and neuromuscular scoring to determine gestational age from 20 to 44 weeks
skill.exam.paed.neo.ballard_gestational_.why: Maternal dates are often inaccurate or unrecorded. Accurately assessing gestational age using physical and neuromuscular criteria within 12 to 24 hours of birth distinguishes preterm from growth-restricted infants, guiding thermal, nutritional, and monitoring protocols.

steps.text: Perform the neuromuscular examination when the infant is warm, calm, and resting in the supine position.
Assess posture: observe flexion of arms and legs (from full extension 0 to complete flexion 4).
Assess square window: flex the hand at the wrist, exert gentle pressure to minimize angle between palm and forearm without twisting wrist; measure angle (from >90 degrees -1 to 0 degrees 4).
Assess arm recoil: flex forearms for 5 seconds, extend by pulling hands downward, release and observe degree and speed of recoil (score 0 to 4).
Assess popliteal angle: flex thigh on abdomen, gently extend leg until resistance is felt; measure angle behind knee (from 180 degrees -1 to <90 degrees 5).
Assess scarf sign: draw the infant elbow across the chest toward the opposite shoulder, noting relationship of elbow to sternal midline (from across neck -1 to unable to cross midline 4).
Assess heel to ear: hold foot, draw toward ipsilateral ear without forcing; note distance and pelvic tilt (score -1 to 4).

Inspect the six physical maturity signs: skin (gelatinous to cracked/leathery), lanugo (none to thinning to bald), plantar creases (anterior transverse to entire sole), breast bud (imperceptible to raised areola with 5 to 10 mm nodule), eye/ear (fused to firm formed cartilage), and genitalia (male: scrotum flat/smooth to deep rugae with descended testes; female: prominent clitoris to labia majora covering minora).

skill.exam.paed.neo.ballard_gestational_.normal: A term infant (37 to 41 weeks) exhibits flexed resting posture, square window angle near 0 degrees, vigorous arm recoil, popliteal angle <100 degrees, elbow not crossing midline, deep plantar creases over the entire sole, fully formed ear cartilage with instant recoil, and labia majora covering minora or pendulous rugated scrotum with testes descended.
skill.exam.paed.neo.ballard_gestational_.abnormal: Generalized hypotonic extension, wide square window (>60 degrees), absent arm recoil, popliteal angle >150 degrees, elbow easily pulled across contralateral axilla, translucent gelatinous skin, fused eyelids, flat smooth scrotum with undescended testes, or widely exposed clitoris and labia minora.
skill.exam.paed.neo.ballard_gestational_.significance: Identifies preterm gestation (<37 weeks) and separates small-for-gestational-age infants from premature infants of identical birth weight, each carrying radically different disease risks.
skill.exam.paed.neo.ballard_gestational_.practice: Examine a newborn using the New Ballard chart, scoring all six neuromuscular and six physical items to calculate the maturity rating and assign gestational weeks.
pitfalls: Performing the neuromuscular examination when the baby is cold, crying, or within the first hour of birth before recovery from intrapartum stress.
Forcing the popliteal angle or heel-to-ear manoeuvre, which causes pain and triggers defensive extensor hypertonia.
Relying solely on physical signs in an infant exposed to drying radiant heat, which causes artificial skin cracking and peeling.

probes.q: Name three neuromuscular criteria evaluated in the New Ballard Score.
probes.a: Posture, square window at wrist, arm recoil, popliteal angle, scarf sign, and heel to ear.

probes.q: How does the square window angle change as gestational maturity advances from preterm to post-term?
probes.a: The square window angle decreases progressively from over 90 degrees in extreme preterms down to 0 degrees in full-term and post-term infants.

probes.q: A newborn weighs 1.4 kg with deep sole creases, firm ear recoil, and a square window of 0 degrees. What is the clinical classification?
probes.a: The infant is term or near-term but severely small for gestational age (SGA) with intrauterine growth restriction, rather than preterm.

rubric.text: Ensures infant is warm, calm, and rested before scoring tone
Scores posture, square window, arm recoil, popliteal angle, scarf sign, and heel to ear
Scores skin, lanugo, plantar creases, breast bud, ear cartilage, and external genitalia
Sums scores accurately and maps total to gestational age weeks

teach.heading: Development of tone and the New Ballard Score
teach.body:
The New Ballard Score assesses 6 neuromuscular and 6 physical criteria to determine gestational maturity between 20 and 44 weeks. Neuromuscular maturation follows a cephalocaudal direction: tone develops first in the lower extremities and progresses upward to the upper limbs.

Extremely premature infants exhibit passive extension and hypotonia. As gestation advances toward term, active flexor tone develops, reducing the square window, popliteal angle, and scarf sign excursion.

rows: Faint red marks, anterior crease only
Pinna flat, stays folded on release
Firm formed pinna, instant elastic recoil
Scrotum pendulous, deep rugae, testes down

teach.heading: Preterm versus small for gestational age (SGA)
teach.body:
Accurate gestational assessment separates preterm infants from growth-restricted term infants of identical birth weight. Preterm babies have immature physical and neuromuscular scores, thin skin, and are prone to respiratory distress syndrome and apnoea.

Growth-restricted infants exhibit mature physical markers (advanced creases, firm ears) despite low weight, but carry severe risks of perinatal asphyxia, hypoglycaemia, and polycythaemia.

skill.exam.paed.neo.head_skull_trauma.title: Neonatal head, fontanelle, and birth trauma examination
skill.exam.paed.neo.head_skull_trauma.oneLine: Assessing cranial moulding, fontanelle dimensions, and distinguishing caput, cephalhaematoma, and subgaleal bleed
skill.exam.paed.neo.head_skull_trauma.why: Birth trauma and cranial pathology can present deceptively as benign scalp swellings. Failing to differentiate subgaleal haemorrhage from caput succedaneum or cephalhaematoma leads to unrecognised exsanguinating shock and neonatal mortality.

steps.text: Inspect the scalp from above and sides with the infant calm and resting supine in the cot.
Palpate the anterior fontanelle with a warm fingerpad while the infant is upright and not crying; note size (transverse and longitudinal diameters), tension, and normal gentle pulsation.
Palpate cranial sutures (sagittal, coronal, lambdoid) for overriding edges (moulding) or premature synostosis.
Evaluate any scalp swelling: note whether it crosses cranial suture lines, palpate for soft pitting oedema versus tense fluctuance, and identify the timing of appearance.

Differentiate caput succedaneum (diffuse, soft, pitting oedema, present at delivery, crosses suture lines, resolves within days) from cephalhaematoma (subperiosteal collection, limited by suture boundaries, appears hours after birth, firm edge, resolves over weeks).
Carefully exclude subgaleal haemorrhage: extensive, fluctuant, progressive swelling crossing sutures into neck and ears, accompanied by pallor, tachycardia, and falling hematocrit.
Inspect facial symmetry during crying to exclude traumatic facial nerve palsy (loss of nasolabial fold, inability to close eye, mouth pulled to unaffected side).

skill.exam.paed.neo.head_skull_trauma.normal: Anterior fontanelle soft and level with the skull table, measuring 1 to 4 cm in diameter with gentle arterial pulsation; cranial sutures mobile with mild moulding that resolves within 48 hours; no abnormal scalp collections or facial asymmetry.
skill.exam.paed.neo.head_skull_trauma.abnormal: Tense bulging fontanelle (raised ICP, meningitis, intracranial haemorrhage) or deeply depressed fontanelle (severe dehydration); fluctuant swelling crossing sutures with hypovolaemia (subgaleal haematoma); unilateral subperiosteal swelling (cephalhaematoma); facial droop on crying.
skill.exam.paed.neo.head_skull_trauma.significance: Detects intracranial hypertension, guides volume resuscitation in life-threatening extracranial haemorrhage, and anticipates hyperbilirubinaemia resulting from breakdown of extravasated blood in cephalhaematoma.
skill.exam.paed.neo.head_skull_trauma.practice: Palpate the anterior fontanelle in both upright and supine postures; sketch the anatomic planes of caput, cephalhaematoma, and subgaleal bleed.
pitfalls: Palpating the anterior fontanelle while the infant is crying vigorously, mistaking transient physiological fullness for pathological raised intracranial pressure.
Attempting to aspirate a cephalhaematoma, which introduces infection and converts a benign sterile haematoma into an abscess.
Failing to monitor head circumference and blood pressure in subgaleal haemorrhage, where blood loss into the loose aponeurosis exceeds 50 percent of circulating blood volume.

probes.q: Does a cephalhaematoma cross cranial suture lines, and what is its anatomical location?
probes.a: No, a cephalhaematoma does not cross suture lines because it is a subperiosteal collection confined by periosteal attachments to individual cranial bones.

probes.q: Why does a newborn with a large cephalhaematoma have an increased risk of severe neonatal jaundice?
probes.a: The breakdown of extravasated red blood cells within the trapped haematoma produces a large secondary bilirubin load, overwhelming immature neonatal hepatic conjugation.

probes.q: What clinical features distinguish life-threatening subgaleal haemorrhage from caput succedaneum?
probes.a: Subgaleal haemorrhage is a progressive fluctuant mass dissecting beneath the epicranial aponeurosis into the neck, causing expanding head circumference, severe pallor, and hypovolaemic shock.

rubric.text: Palpates anterior fontanelle while infant is calm and sitting upright
Evaluates cranial sutures for mobile moulding versus craniosynostosis
Distinguishes caput succedaneum, cephalhaematoma, and subgaleal bleed
Inspects eye closure and mouth movements during cry for facial palsy

teach.heading: The anterior and posterior fontanelles
teach.body:
The anterior fontanelle is diamond-shaped, situated at the junction of the coronal, sagittal, and frontal sutures. It normally measures 1 to 4 cm in width and closes between 9 and 18 months of age.

The posterior fontanelle is triangular, located at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures, admitting a fingertip at birth and closing by 6 to 8 weeks. A bulging fontanelle signals raised intracranial pressure; a depressed fontanelle signals dehydration.

teach.heading: Birth trauma and peripheral nerve palsies
teach.body:
Moulding is the physiological overlapping of cranial bones along suture lines during vaginal delivery, which resolves spontaneously within 48 to 72 hours. Vacuum extraction and forceps carry increased risks of cephalhaematoma and subgaleal haematoma.

Compression of the facial nerve against the maternal sacral promontory or by forceps blades produces unilateral facial weakness: loss of forehead wrinkling, incomplete eye closure, and mouth deviation away from the affected side when crying.

skill.exam.paed.neo.skin_cord_variations.title: Cutaneous variations and umbilical cord examination
skill.exam.paed.neo.skin_cord_variations.oneLine: Recognising benign physiological neonatal rashes, birthmarks, and umbilical vessel anatomy
skill.exam.paed.neo.skin_cord_variations.why: Harmless physiological neonatal skin lesions are frequently misdiagnosed as serious viral or bacterial infections, resulting in unnecessary maternal anxiety, separation, and inappropriate antibiotic use. Conversely, missing omphalitis or a single umbilical artery leaves severe systemic anomalies undetected.

steps.text: Examine the newborn completely undressed under warm, bright, indirect lighting.
Inspect for vernix caseosa (protective lipid-rich biofilm) and physiological desquamation or peeling, especially marked in post-term infants.

Inspect for benign physiological eruptions: erythema toxicum neonatorum (erythematous macules with central white/yellow papules containing eosinophils, appearing day 2-3), milia (tiny 1-2 mm pearly white keratinous epidermal cysts on nose and chin), and Epstein pearls on the hard palate.

Examine pigmentary and vascular marks: Mongolian spots (congenital dermal melanocytosis, slate-grey macules over lumbosacral region), salmon patches / stork bites (flat pink capillary macules on nape, forehead, and upper eyelids), and cutis marmorata (transient vascular mottling with temperature drops).
Inspect the umbilical cord stump: verify presence of three vessels (two thick-walled muscular umbilical arteries and one thin-walled, larger umbilical vein) within Wharton jelly.
Check the periumbilical skin for signs of omphalitis: periumbilical erythema, oedema, foul-smelling purulent discharge, or tenderness.

skill.exam.paed.neo.skin_cord_variations.normal: Warm, smooth skin with variable physiological peeling, benign erythema toxicum or milia without systemic illness; umbilical cord showing three distinct patent vessels with clean dry base and no surrounding erythema.
skill.exam.paed.neo.skin_cord_variations.abnormal: Extensive pustules with erythematous base containing neutrophils/bacteria, petechiae or purpura (congenital infection, thrombocytopenia), periumbilical redness spreading to abdominal wall (omphalitis), or a single umbilical artery (two-vessel cord).
skill.exam.paed.neo.skin_cord_variations.significance: Single umbilical artery occurs in 0.5 to 1 percent of births and warrants renal ultrasound for occult genitourinary or cardiovascular malformations; omphalitis is a medical emergency that rapidly seeds portal vein thrombophlebitis and septic shock.
skill.exam.paed.neo.skin_cord_variations.practice: Inspect neonatal skin photographs, distinguishing erythema toxicum from staphylococcal pustulosis; examine the cut end of a cord to identify the two arteries and one vein.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting Mongolian spots as non-accidental bruises, causing unjustified distress and investigations.
Applying harmful substances (such as cow dung or soot) to the umbilical stump, predisposing to neonatal tetanus and omphalitis.
Dismissing periumbilical erythema as normal cord drying, missing early omphalitis before cellulitis spreads.

probes.q: How many blood vessels are normally present in the human umbilical cord?
probes.a: Three vessels: two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein.

probes.q: What predominant white blood cell type is found within the pustules of erythema toxicum neonatorum?
probes.a: Eosinophils (demonstrable on Wright or Giemsa stain of a smear from the pustule).

probes.q: What occult congenital malformations are associated with the detection of a single umbilical artery?
probes.a: Renal anomalies (hydronephrosis, renal agenesis), congenital heart defects, and VACTERL association components, warranting abdominal ultrasonography.

rubric.text: Identifies erythema toxicum, milia, and Mongolian spots correctly
Examines umbilical cord stump to confirm two arteries and one vein
Inspects periumbilical margins for erythema, induration, and foul discharge
Advises dry umbilical cord care and warns against harmful topical applications

rows: Flea-bite rash with yellow-white papules on red base
Appears day 2 to 3, self-resolves in 1 to 2 weeks
Pearly white 1 to 2 mm epidermal inclusion cysts
Present on nose and cheeks, exfoliates spontaneously
Blue-grey slate macules over sacrum and buttocks
Dermal melanocyte arrest, fades during childhood
Pale pink capillary macules on nape or eyelids
Fades over 1 to 2 years (nape lesion may persist)

teach.heading: Umbilical cord anatomy and the single umbilical artery
teach.body:
The normal umbilical cord contains two muscular umbilical arteries carrying deoxygenated blood to the placenta and one larger, thin-walled umbilical vein delivering oxygenated blood to the fetus, embedded in Wharton jelly.

A single umbilical artery (two-vessel cord) occurs in roughly 1 percent of births. While often an isolated finding, it is associated with renal agenesis, hydronephrosis, and cardiovascular malformations, indicating renal ultrasonography.

teach.heading: Omphalitis and aseptic cord care
teach.body:
The devitalised tissue of the umbilical cord stump is an ideal culture medium for bacteria, particularly Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Gram-negative bacilli. Omphalitis presents with periumbilical erythema, swelling, tenderness, and malodorous discharge.

Infection can rapidly spread via the umbilical vessels to produce portal vein thrombosis and fatal sepsis. WHO and IAP recommend clean, dry cord care for institutional births, avoiding all traditional topical applications.
