skill.exam.paed.neo.chest_respiratory_cv.title: Neonatal respiratory and cardiovascular examination
skill.exam.paed.neo.chest_respiratory_cv.oneLine: Evaluation of respiratory rate, recession signs, grunting, femoral pulses, and transitional murmurs
skill.exam.paed.neo.chest_respiratory_cv.why: Neonatal cardiorespiratory failure develops rapidly because of high oxygen consumption, compliant chest walls, and persistent transitional shunts. Timely recognition of tachypnoea, retractions, expiratory grunting, or absent femoral pulses catches critical congenital heart disease and respiratory distress syndrome before arrest.

steps.text: Observe respiration for a full 60 seconds with the infant resting quietly; count respiratory rate (normal 40 to 60 breaths per minute; tachypnoea >60/min).
Inspect for signs of respiratory distress: nasal flaring, subcostal retractions, intercostal indrawing, sternal recession, and head nodding in synchrony with inspiration.
Listen without stethoscope at the cot side for an expiratory grunt (a protective sound produced by forced expiration against a partially closed glottis to maintain functional residual capacity).
Auscultate bilateral lung fields across anterior, lateral, and posterior chests, checking for symmetrical air entry, crackles, or wheezing.
Inspect and palpate the precordium: determine apex beat (normally 4th intercostal space, lateral to midclavicular line), feel for hyperdynamic impulses or parasternal thrills.
Auscultate heart sounds (S1, S2, physiological splitting) and evaluate any murmur (soft systolic murmurs in the first 24 to 48 hours are often transitional flow or closing ductus arteriosus).

Simultaneously palpate right brachial and bilateral femoral pulses: compare timing and amplitude to detect radio-femoral delay or diminished femoral pulses (characteristic of coarctation of the aorta).

skill.exam.paed.neo.chest_respiratory_cv.normal: Respiratory rate 40 to 60 breaths per minute, quiet effortless breathing without retractions or grunting; clear bilateral vesicular breath sounds; heart rate 120 to 160 beats per minute; strong, synchronous brachial and femoral pulses with no precordial heave or cyanosis.
skill.exam.paed.neo.chest_respiratory_cv.abnormal: Tachypnoea >60 breaths per minute, moderate-to-severe chest indrawing, audible expiratory grunt, unilateral absent air entry (pneumothorax, diaphragmatic hernia), heart rate <100 or >180 bpm, loud or harsh pan-systolic/continuous murmurs, or absent/weak femoral pulses.
skill.exam.paed.neo.chest_respiratory_cv.significance: Differentiates transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN) and respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) from life-threatening conditions such as congenital diaphragmatic hernia, tension pneumothorax, and duct-dependent critical congenital heart lesions.
skill.exam.paed.neo.chest_respiratory_cv.practice: Count resting respiratory rate for 60 seconds in a calm newborn; simultaneously palpate the brachial and femoral pulses, comparing volume and timing.
pitfalls: Counting respiratory rate for only 15 seconds, which misinterprets normal neonatal periodic breathing as tachypnoea or apnoea.
Relying solely on heart murmurs to assess congenital heart disease, missing severe duct-dependent lesions that present with cyanosis or shock without any murmur.
Omitting femoral pulse palpation, leaving critical coarctation of the aorta undetected until acute cardiovascular collapse occurs on ductal closure.

probes.q: What is the normal resting respiratory rate in a healthy term newborn?
probes.a: The normal resting respiratory rate is 40 to 60 breaths per minute.

probes.q: What is the physiological mechanism and clinical significance of an expiratory grunt in a distressed neonate?
probes.a: An expiratory grunt is generated by exhaling against a partially closed vocal glottis, which creates intrinsic positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to prevent alveolar collapse.

probes.q: A 2-day-old infant becomes suddenly pale and tachypnoeic with absent femoral pulses and poor lower limb perfusion. What lesion must be suspected and urgently treated?
probes.a: Severe coarctation of the aorta or interrupted aortic arch, which manifested as acute duct-dependent cardiogenic shock when the patent ductus arteriosus closed.

rubric.text: Counts respiratory rate for full 60 seconds in resting state
Inspects systematically for nasal flaring, retractions, and grunting
Auscultates bilateral breath sounds in anterior, lateral, and back fields
Simultaneously palpates brachial and femoral pulses bilaterally

teach.heading: Mechanics of breathing and signs of respiratory distress
teach.body:
Neonates have high chest wall compliance and horizontal ribs, making intercostal stabilization less efficient. When work of breathing increases, negative intrathoracic pressure sucks the compliant ribs inward, producing prominent subcostal and intercostal retractions.

Tachypnoea (>60 breaths/min) is the earliest and most sensitive sign of respiratory distress. Grunting is an active compensatory manoeuvre to preserve functional residual capacity in surfactant-deficient or fluid-filled lungs.

teach.heading: Transitional circulation and neonatal murmurs
teach.body:
At birth, clamping of the umbilical cord increases systemic vascular resistance, while first breaths expand lungs and cause pulmonary vascular resistance to drop precipitously. This reverses the fetal right-to-left shunt across the ductus arteriosus.

Transient systolic murmurs heard in the first 24 to 48 hours frequently represent physiological closing ductus flow or peripheral pulmonary branch stenosis. However, any loud, harsh, or diastolic murmur warrants urgent echocardiography.

skill.exam.paed.neo.abdomen_genitalia_sp.title: Neonatal abdominal, genitourinary, and spinal examination
skill.exam.paed.neo.abdomen_genitalia_sp.oneLine: Palpating visceral margins, evaluating umbilical ring, external genitalia, anal patency, and neural tube integrity
skill.exam.paed.neo.abdomen_genitalia_sp.why: Congenital anomalies of the gastrointestinal tract, urinary system, genitalia, and neural tube frequently present with subtle physical signs in the first 24 hours. Missing an imperforate anus, ambivalence of genitalia, or open spinal dysraphism leads to bowel perforation, adrenal crisis, or permanent neurologic deficit.

steps.text: Inspect abdominal contour: note normal fullness and protuberance; check for scaphoid abdomen (suggestive of diaphragmatic hernia) or gross distension (intestinal obstruction, peritonitis).

Inspect anterior abdominal wall for defects: omphalocele (midline defect with herniated viscera covered by peritoneal membrane) versus gastroschisis (full-thickness paraumbilical defect with exposed, thickened bowel loops).

Palpate abdomen gently with warm flat fingers: assess liver edge (normally soft, smooth, palpable 1 to 2 cm below right costal margin) and spleen tip (palpable in up to 10 percent of healthy newborns); palpate for renal poles in both flanks.

Inspect external genitalia in male infants: confirm bilateral testicular descent into the scrotum, inspect scrotal rugosity, evaluate urethral meatus position on glans tip (check for hypospadias; defer circumcision), and note physiological non-retractile phimosis.

Inspect external genitalia in female infants: examine labia majora (covering labia minora in term infants), check for mucoid vaginal discharge or pseudomenses (benign maternal oestrogen withdrawal), and inspect for hymenal tags.
Assess for ambiguous genitalia: clitoromegaly, micropenis, bifid scrotum, or non-palpable gonads, which require urgent endocrine evaluation for congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
Inspect the perineum to verify anal patency and position; observe for passage of normal dark green meconium within 24 hours of birth.

Turn infant prone to inspect entire vertebral column from occiput to coccyx: check for midline defects, tufts of hair, haemangiomas, sinus tracts, or deep sacral dimples (>5 mm depth, >25 mm from anal verge).

skill.exam.paed.neo.abdomen_genitalia_sp.normal: Soft, slightly protuberant abdomen without tenderness or distension; liver edge 1 to 2 cm below right costal margin; patent anus at normal anatomical location; male with descended testes and apical urethral meatus; female with labia majora covering minora; straight intact spine with no neural defects.
skill.exam.paed.neo.abdomen_genitalia_sp.abnormal: Scaphoid or severely distended abdomen, palpable abnormal mass, omphalocele, gastroschisis, absent anal opening, ambiguous genitalia (hypospadias with undescended testes, clitoromegaly), myelomeningocele, or deep atypical sacral dimple.
skill.exam.paed.neo.abdomen_genitalia_sp.significance: Detects intestinal atresia and anorectal malformations before feeds cause perforation; prevents salt-wasting death from congenital adrenal hyperplasia; triggers neuro-imaging for closed spinal dysraphism.
skill.exam.paed.neo.abdomen_genitalia_sp.practice: Palpate the liver and spleen margins in a relaxed supine newborn; inspect the perineum to verify anal patency; inspect the midline spine down to the coccyx.
pitfalls: Forcefully retracting the neonatal foreskin, which produces painful micro-tears and acquired pathological phimosis (physiological phimosis is normal at birth).
Measuring rectal temperature with a glass thermometer to confirm anal patency, risking rectal laceration and perforation.
Assigning gender to an infant with ambiguous genitalia before genetic and endocrine workup excludes congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

probes.q: What is the normal palpable extent of the neonatal liver below the right costal margin?
probes.a: The liver edge is normally palpable 1 to 2 cm below the right costal margin in healthy newborns.

probes.q: What anatomical features differentiate an omphalocele from gastroschisis?
probes.a: An omphalocele is a midline umbilical ring defect covered by a membrane (peritoneum and amnion) with the cord inserting onto the sac; gastroschisis is a full-thickness paraumbilical defect (usually right-sided) with no covering membrane, leaving bowel exposed directly to air.

probes.q: Why is bilateral non-palpable testes in a phenotypically male newborn considered a potential medical emergency?
probes.a: The infant may be a genetic female (46,XX) with congenital adrenal hyperplasia and severe virilisation, at imminent risk of a life-threatening salt-wasting adrenal crisis with shock and hyperkalaemia.

rubric.text: Inspects contour for distension or scaphoid shape and checks umbilical ring
Palpates liver edge and checks for splenomegaly and abnormal abdominal masses
Assesses testicular descent, urethral meatus, or labia and screens for ambiguity
Confirms anal patency and inspects midline spine for dysraphism markers

teach.heading: Normal neonatal abdominal features vs surgical anomalies
teach.body:
The neonatal abdomen is naturally protuberant because of weak abdominal musculature and large relative liver volume. A soft, non-tender liver edge is palpable 1 to 2 cm below the right costal margin in midclavicular line.

A scaphoid abdomen points to congenital diaphragmatic hernia, where viscera have herniated into the pleural cavity. Progressive distension indicates gastrointestinal obstruction (such as duodenal atresia or Hirschsprung disease) or necrotising enterocolitis.

rows: Onto apex of the hernial sac

teach.heading: Evaluation of genitalia, anus, and spinal integrity
teach.body:
In males, confirm bilateral scrotal testes and apical urethral meatus. In hypospadias, the meatus opens on the ventral surface; do not circumcise, as prepuce is needed for repair. Ambiguous genitalia warrants emergency endocrine workup for congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

Verify anal patency and meconium passage within 24 hours. Inspect the spine: a sacral dimple deeper than 5 mm, located more than 25 mm above the anus, or accompanied by a tuft of hair or haemangioma requires ultrasound to exclude occult spinal dysraphism.

skill.exam.paed.neo.hip_ddh.title: Examination for developmental dysplasia of the hip
skill.exam.paed.neo.hip_ddh.oneLine: Screening hip instability using Barlow, Ortolani, and Galeazzi manoeuvres
skill.exam.paed.neo.hip_ddh.why: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) produces no pain or functional impairment in the neonatal period. If missed at the newborn screening, painless dislocation results in permanent leg length discrepancy, abnormal waddling gait, and early crippling osteoarthritis requiring major reconstructive surgery.

steps.text: Place the calm, undressed newborn supine on a firm, flat examination surface with hips and knees flexed.
Review risk factors: the 4 Fs (Firstborn, Female sex accounting for 80 percent of cases, Family history of DDH, and Feet-first / breech presentation).
Inspect thighs and gluteal folds for asymmetry; compare leg lengths (Galeazzi test: flex both knees with feet flat on table, observing for discrepancy in knee heights).

Perform the Barlow test to detect a dislocatable hip: grasp the infant thigh between thumb along medial aspect and long fingers over the greater trochanter; adduct hip towards midline while applying gentle posterior pressure ('Barlow pushes back / dislocates').
Feel for a sensation of the femoral head sliding or popping out of the acetabulum posteriorly.

Perform the Ortolani test to reduce a dislocated hip: abduct the hip outward toward the examination table while exerting upward anterior pressure on the greater trochanter with the fingertips ('Ortolani out / reduces').
Feel for a distinct palpable 'clunk' as the femoral head slips back into the acetabular cup (a benign high-pitched ligamentous 'click' is non-pathological).
Examine one hip at a time, keeping the contralateral pelvis stabilized with the opposite hand; never use excessive force.

skill.exam.paed.neo.hip_ddh.normal: Symmetrical thigh and gluteal skin folds; equal knee heights on Galeazzi testing; full, smooth hip abduction beyond 70 degrees bilaterally without clunks, instability, or resistance.
skill.exam.paed.neo.hip_ddh.abnormal: A palpable clunk on abduction (positive Ortolani sign) or palpable dislocation on adduction and posterior pressure (positive Barlow sign); asymmetric abduction limitation (<60 degrees); unequal knee heights on Galeazzi test.
skill.exam.paed.neo.hip_ddh.significance: Identifies unstable or dislocated hips in the neonatal window when dynamic Pavlik harness splinting achieves over 90 percent success, avoiding operative open reduction.
skill.exam.paed.neo.hip_ddh.practice: Perform Barlow and Ortolani manoeuvres on a pediatric hip model, practicing gentle single-hip stabilization and feeling the difference between a ligamentous click and a reduction clunk.
pitfalls: Examining both hips simultaneously, which prevents stabilization of the pelvis and misses subtle unilateral instability.
Mistaking harmless, high-pitched soft-tissue or ligamentous clicks for the deep, palpable reduction clunk of an unstable hip.
Applying forceful pressure during the Barlow manoeuvre, which can damage the acetabular labrum or femoral head cartilage.

probes.q: What are the four classic risk factors (the 4 Fs) associated with developmental dysplasia of the hip?
probes.a: Firstborn child, Female sex (accounting for 80 percent of cases), Family history of DDH, and Feet-first (breech) presentation.

probes.q: What mechanical actions distinguish the Barlow manoeuvre from the Ortolani manoeuvre?
probes.a: The Barlow test adducts the hip and applies gentle posterior pressure to provoke dislocation; the Ortolani test abducts the hip and lifts the greater trochanter anteriorly to reduce a dislocated femoral head back into the acetabulum.

probes.q: A 4-week-old female infant born by breech delivery has an equivocal hip click on examination. What investigation is indicated, and why is plain radiography avoided at this age?
probes.a: Dynamic hip ultrasonography (Graf technique) is the investigation of choice. Plain X-rays are unhelpful before 4 to 6 months of age because the femoral head and acetabulum are predominantly cartilaginous and not yet ossified.

rubric.text: Positions infant supine on firm surface with pelvic stabilization
Inspects skin creases and checks knee height symmetry with Galeazzi test
Performs Barlow test (adduction and posterior force) gently on each hip
Performs Ortolani test (abduction and anterior lift) feeling for reduction clunk

teach.heading: Pathophysiology and the 4 F risk factors
teach.body:
Developmental dysplasia of the hip encompasses a spectrum from mild acetabular dysplasia to established dislocation. Intrauterine packaging constraints and maternal relaxin hormones produce ligamentous laxity.

The 4 F risk factors are Firstborn, Female (accounting for 80 percent of DDH), Family history, and Feet-first (breech presentation). Breech infants with a positive family history warrant screening ultrasound at 4 to 6 weeks of age regardless of physical examination.

rows: Hip flexed, adducted; gentle posterior pressure
Hip flexed, abducted; anterior lift on trochanter
Reduces a dislocated hip back into joint
Both hips flexed to 90 deg with feet flat on bed

teach.heading: Clicks versus clunks and imaging milestones
teach.body:
Distinguish benign clicks from pathological clunks. Fine, high-pitched clicks stem from innocuous movement of the ligamentum teres or fascia lata over bony prominences. A true reduction clunk is a deep, palpable thud as the femoral head clears the acetabular rim.

Prior to 4 to 6 months, the femoral head is radiolucent unossified cartilage, making plain radiographs unreliable. Dynamic hip ultrasonography (measuring the alpha angle) is the gold standard diagnostic tool.

skill.exam.paed.neo.primitive_reflexes.title: Primitive neonatal reflexes and neurological integrity
skill.exam.paed.neo.primitive_reflexes.oneLine: Testing Moro, grasp, rooting, tonic neck, and stepping reflexes to evaluate brainstem and spinal pathways
skill.exam.paed.neo.primitive_reflexes.why: Primitive reflexes reflect the integrity of the subcortical and brainstem motor pathways at birth. An absent, depressed, or persistent primitive reflex serves as the earliest physical marker of hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, brachial plexus avulsion, or cerebral palsy.

steps.text: Ensure the newborn is warm, awake, and quiet in a non-crying state before beginning the reflex examination.

Test the rooting and sucking reflex: gently stroke the perioral skin at the angle of the mouth; observe the baby turn the head toward the stimulus, open the mouth, and latch (onset 32 weeks, integrates by 3 to 4 months).
Test the palmar grasp reflex: place your index finger into the baby palm from the ulnar side; observe strong, symmetrical finger flexion gripping your finger (onset 32 weeks, integrates by 3 months).

Test the plantar grasp reflex: press your thumb against the ball of the infant foot behind the toes; observe plantarflection of all toes curling around your thumb (onset birth, integrates by 9 months).
Test the Moro reflex (head drop method): support the infant head and chest in a semi-upright posture; allow the head to drop backward abruptly by 1 to 2 cm into your waiting hand.

Observe the two phases of Moro: Phase 1 is rapid symmetrical abduction and extension of both upper limbs with opening of the hands; Phase 2 is slow adduction and flexion of the arms in an embrace, often followed by a cry (onset 32 weeks, integrates by 3 to 4 months).

Test the asymmetrical tonic neck reflex (ATNR): with the infant supine, gently rotate the head to one side for 15 seconds; observe extension of arm and leg on the face side and flexion on the occiput side ('fencing posture', onset 36 weeks, integrates by 3 to 5 months).
Evaluate tone and traction: perform pull-to-sit from wrists, observing head lag and momentary head control.

skill.exam.paed.neo.primitive_reflexes.normal: Brisk, symmetrical Moro reflex with full abduction and subsequent adduction; strong bilateral palmar and plantar grasps; vigorous rooting and sucking; transient fencing posture that the infant can readily break out of.
skill.exam.paed.neo.primitive_reflexes.abnormal: Absent or depressed Moro reflex (severe birth asphyxia, intracranial haemorrhage, severe sedation); asymmetrical Moro (clavicle fracture, Erb-Duchenne brachial plexus injury, hemiparesis); persistent obligatory ATNR beyond 6 months (hallmark of spastic cerebral palsy).
skill.exam.paed.neo.primitive_reflexes.significance: Differentiates central encephalopathy from localized birth trauma and provides a reliable functional baseline for neurodevelopmental prognosis.
skill.exam.paed.neo.primitive_reflexes.practice: Perform Moro, palmar grasp, rooting, and ATNR manoeuvres on an infant under supervision, noting phase completion and symmetry.
pitfalls: Testing primitive reflexes in a screaming or deeply sleeping baby, which distorts resting tone and suppresses responses.
Performing the Moro reflex by shaking the cot or pulling the limbs, which is frightening and non-standardised compared to the supported head-drop method.
Dismissing an asymmetrical Moro response as minor irritability, failing to diagnose a fractured clavicle or Erb palsy.

probes.q: At what gestational age does the Moro reflex appear, and by what age does it normally disappear?
probes.a: The Moro reflex appears at around 32 weeks of gestation and integrates (disappears) by 3 to 4 months of postnatal age.

probes.q: What clinical entities must be investigated when an asymmetrical Moro reflex is detected in a newborn?
probes.a: Fractured clavicle, fractured humerus, or brachial plexus injury (such as Erb-Duchenne palsy C5-C6), and less commonly unilateral cerebral infarction.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of a persistent, obligatory asymmetrical tonic neck reflex (ATNR) beyond 6 months of age?
probes.a: A persistent obligatory ATNR indicates failure of cortical motor inhibition and is a strong clinical marker for spastic cerebral palsy and upper motor neuron injury.

rubric.text: Verifies infant is awake, calm, and warm before reflex elicitation
Elicits Moro reflex using safe supported head-drop method
Systematically assesses symmetry of upper limb movement in Moro response
Demonstrates palmar grasp, plantar grasp, and rooting reflexes correctly

teach.heading: Chronological timeline of primitive neonatal reflexes
The Moro reflex: anatomy and phases
teach.body:
The Moro reflex is a vestibular response triggered by sudden movement of the head in relation to the torso. It consists of two distinct phases: Phase 1 is rapid extension and abduction of both upper extremities with fingers spreading; Phase 2 is slower adduction and flexion of the limbs in an embracing motion, often ending in a cry.

A complete, brisk, symmetrical response proves integrity of the brainstem, vestibular nuclei, and cervical spinal cord.

teach.heading: Pathological reflex patterns and asymmetry
teach.body:
A depressed or absent Moro reflex indicates generalized central nervous system depression from hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, severe infection, or maternal sedation.

An asymmetrical Moro reflex is an urgent diagnostic clue. If one arm fails to abduct, palpate the clavicle for crepitus and tenderness (fracture) and inspect the arm for the characteristic 'waiter tip' adducted and internally rotated posture of Erb palsy (C5-C6 nerve roots).

skill.exam.paed.neo.jaundice_kramer.title: Clinical assessment of neonatal jaundice and Kramer rule
skill.exam.paed.neo.jaundice_kramer.oneLine: Cephalocaudal dermal blanching assessment, zone estimation, and distinguishing physiological from pathological jaundice
skill.exam.paed.neo.jaundice_kramer.why: Unconjugated bilirubin in the newborn is neurotoxic and can cross the blood-brain barrier to cause acute bilirubin encephalopathy and irreversible kernicterus. Visual inspection using dermal blanching provides rapid bedside screening to trigger urgent serum bilirubin quantification and phototherapy.

steps.text: Examine the newborn completely undressed in natural daylight or under well-balanced white fluorescent light.
Apply gentle digital pressure with your thumb or finger over a bony prominence for 2 to 3 seconds to blanch cutaneous capillaries, then lift finger and inspect underlying dermal colour.

Examine dermal icterus in a cephalocaudal direction according to Kramer zones: Zone 1 (head and neck, estimated bilirubin ~5 mg/dL), Zone 2 (chest down to umbilicus, ~10 mg/dL), Zone 3 (lower abdomen and thighs to knees, ~12 mg/dL), Zone 4 (arms and lower legs below knees, ~15 mg/dL), Zone 5 (palms and soles, >15 mg/dL).
Inspect the sclerae and oral mucosa: note that clinical icterus becomes visible in neonates only when serum bilirubin exceeds 5 to 7 mg/dL (in contrast to adults where threshold is >2 mg/dL).

Differentiate physiological from pathological jaundice by checking the four pathological criteria: appearance within the first 24 hours of life, rate of rise exceeding 5 mg/dL per day (or 0.2 mg/dL/hour), total bilirubin exceeding phototherapy threshold, or persistence beyond 14 days in term (21 days in preterm).
Inspect stool and urine colour: dark staining yellow urine and pale clay-coloured stools indicate conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (cholestasis, biliary atresia).
Screen for acute bilirubin encephalopathy red flags: poor feeding, lethargy, high-pitched cry, loss of Moro reflex, alternating hypotonia and hypertonia, retrocollis, and opisthotonus.

skill.exam.paed.neo.jaundice_kramer.normal: No jaundice in the first 24 hours; mild cephalic jaundice appearing on day 2 to 3, peaking at 10 to 12 mg/dL by day 4 to 5, resolving by day 10 to 14, with normal golden-yellow stools, clear urine, and vigorous feeding.
skill.exam.paed.neo.jaundice_kramer.abnormal: Jaundice visible within 24 hours of birth; progression to Kramer zones 4 or 5 (involving hands and feet); high direct bilirubin (>2 mg/dL or >20% of total); pale acholic stools; or signs of acute encephalopathy.
skill.exam.paed.neo.jaundice_kramer.significance: Identifies severe hyperbilirubinaemia requiring urgent total serum bilirubin measurement, phototherapy, or double-volume exchange transfusion to prevent kernicterus.
skill.exam.paed.neo.jaundice_kramer.practice: Examine infants under daylight using finger blanching over forehead, chest, thighs, and soles to map the Kramer zone; compare with laboratory serum bilirubin.
pitfalls: Assessing jaundice in poor artificial yellow light or dark skin without blanching, underestimating severe hyperbilirubinaemia.
Dismissing jaundice appearing in the first 24 hours of life as physiological (jaundice in the first 24 hours is always pathological).
Failing to fractionate total serum bilirubin, overlooking direct hyperbilirubinaemia from life-threatening biliary atresia.

probes.q: At what serum bilirubin concentration does jaundice become clinically detectable in a newborn compared with an adult?
probes.a: Jaundice becomes detectable in a newborn when total serum bilirubin exceeds 5 to 7 mg/dL, whereas in adults it becomes visible above 2 mg/dL.

probes.q: According to Kramer scale, what anatomical region corresponds to dermal Zone 5, and what bilirubin level does it signify?
probes.a: Zone 5 comprises the palms and soles, indicating a high total serum bilirubin concentration exceeding 15 mg/dL.

probes.q: What four clinical criteria define pathological jaundice in a newborn infant?
probes.a: Appearance within the first 24 hours of life, rate of rise exceeding 5 mg/dL per day, total bilirubin crossing the phototherapy threshold, and persistence beyond 14 days in term or 21 days in preterm infants.

rubric.text: Examines naked infant under daylight using finger blanching technique
Assigns cephalocaudal progression correctly through Kramer zones 1 to 5
Screens for onset within 24 hours, rapid progression, and prolonged duration
Checks for acholic stools, dark urine, lethargy, poor feeding, and encephalopathy

teach.heading: Mechanisms of neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
teach.body:
Over 60 percent of term and 80 percent of preterm newborns develop clinical jaundice during the first week of life. This high incidence stems from three interrelated physiological factors.

First, increased production due to higher red cell mass and shorter red cell lifespan (70 to 90 days vs 120 days in adults). Second, defective hepatic uptake and low UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity. Third, enhanced enterohepatic reabsorption driven by intestinal beta-glucuronidase.

rows: Lower abdomen and thighs to knees
Arms and lower legs below knees

teach.heading: Physiological versus pathological jaundice
teach.body:
Physiological jaundice appears between 36 and 72 hours, peaks on day 4 to 5 (day 7 in preterms) at <12 to 15 mg/dL, and clears by day 10 to 14. The baby is vigorous and feeds well.

Pathological jaundice appears within 24 hours, rises >5 mg/dL/day, exceeds treatment thresholds, or persists beyond 2 weeks. Haemolysis (Rh/ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency) and sepsis are common causes requiring urgent serum bilirubin testing.

skill.approach.paed.neo.infant_feeding_b.title: Breastfeeding initiation, technique, and milk composition
skill.approach.paed.neo.infant_feeding_b.oneLine: Promoting early skin-to-skin, assessing latch and positioning, and evaluating breast milk phases and composition
skill.approach.paed.neo.infant_feeding_b.why: Suboptimal breastfeeding technique and delayed initiation are the leading causes of early neonatal dehydration, excessive weight loss, breastfeeding jaundice, and hypernatraemic dehydration. Mastering feeding assessment ensures successful lactation and protects infant survival.

steps.text: Promote early initiation: place newborn skin-to-skin on the mother chest immediately at delivery and support initiation of breastfeeding within the first hour of birth (within 2 hours following caesarean section).
Assess maternal and infant positioning: mother comfortable, infant head and body in a straight line, facing the breast with nose opposite nipple, infant whole body supported close to mother.
Evaluate the four signs of good latch: more areola visible above the upper lip than below, mouth opened widely, lower lip turned outward (everted), and baby chin touching the breast.
Observe sucking dynamics: initial rapid shallow sucks stimulating the milk ejection reflex, followed by slow, deep sucks with audible swallowing pauses.

Explain breast milk progression to parents: colostrum (<4 days, thick yellowish fluid rich in secretory IgA, lactoferrin, and white cells, low in fat), transitional milk (4 to 14 days), and mature milk (>14 days, higher in calories, lactose, and fat).

Explain foremilk versus hindmilk: foremilk (released at the start of feed, watery, rich in protein and lactose to quench thirst) versus hindmilk (released towards end of feed, rich in fat to provide satiety and energy).

Differentiate human milk from cow milk: human milk has lower protein (1.1 g/100 mL versus 3.3 g/100 mL in cow milk) with predominantly whey (whey:casein 60:40 versus 20:80 in cow milk, forming soft, easily digestible curd), higher carbohydrate (lactose 7.0 g/100 mL versus 4.8 g/100 mL), and highly bioavailable iron despite low absolute quantity.

Confirm clinical signs of breastfeeding adequacy: baby feeds 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, appears content after feeds, wets 6 or more nappies daily after day 3, passes mustard-yellow seedy stools, and regains birth weight by day 10 to 14.

skill.approach.paed.neo.infant_feeding_b.practice: Observe a mother feeding her newborn; systematically score positioning and the four signs of attachment; counsel on foremilk-hindmilk balance.
pitfalls: Advising scheduled rigid feeds rather than demand feeding based on early hunger cues (rooting, hand-to-mouth movements).
Giving prelacteal feeds (sugar water, honey, animal milk), which disrupt gut microbiome colonization and increase infection risks.
Switching the infant to the second breast after a few minutes, which denies the baby energy-dense, fat-rich hindmilk and causes frothy lactose overload stools.

probes.q: What are the four clinical signs of a good latch during breastfeeding?
probes.a: More areola visible above the upper lip, mouth opened widely, lower lip everted (curled outward), and the baby chin touching the breast.

probes.q: How does the protein composition of human breast milk differ from cow milk?
probes.a: Human milk contains 1.1 g/100 mL of protein with a 60:40 whey to casein ratio, producing soft digestible curds, whereas cow milk contains 3.3 g/100 mL with an 80:20 casein to whey ratio, forming tough curds and imposing a high renal solute load.

probes.q: What clinical parameters demonstrate adequate milk intake in an exclusively breastfed newborn by day 5 of life?
probes.a: Passing 6 or more pale, wet nappies per day, passing soft yellow seedy stools, settling calmly for 2 to 3 hours between feeds, and regaining birth weight by 10 to 14 days of age.

rubric.text: Verifies infant head and body alignment facing breast
Checks all four signs of good latch (areola, wide mouth, everted lip, chin touching)
Explains colostrum value, foremilk thirst quenching, and hindmilk satiety
Assesses feeding frequency, urine output, stool transition, and weight trajectory

teach.heading: Attachment signs and suckling biomechanics
teach.body:
Effective suckling requires attachment of the infant mouth to the maternal areola, not just the nipple tip. When correctly attached, the nipple is drawn deep into the baby pharynx while the tongue compresses the lactiferous sinuses against the hard palate.

The four attachment signs are: more areola visible above than below, mouth opened widely, lower lip turned outward, and chin resting firmly against the breast tissue.

teach.heading: Human breast milk versus animal milk

rows: Cow milk has high renal solute load, tough curd
Human milk lactose aids brain growth and gut acidity

teach.heading: Phases of breast milk and feed progression
teach.body:
Lactation evolves through three stages: colostrum (<4 days, packed with secretory IgA, lactoferrin, and maternal antibodies that coat the gut mucosa); transitional milk (4 to 14 days, rising fat and calorie content); and mature milk (>14 days).

During a single feed, foremilk satisfies thirst with high water and lactose content. As the feed proceeds, hindmilk releases concentrated milk fats to induce satiety and fuel brain development.

skill.annex.paed.neo.definitions.title: Neonatal definitions and classifications
skill.annex.paed.neo.definitions.oneLine: Standard chronological, gestational, birth weight, and intrauterine growth definitions
skill.annex.paed.neo.definitions.why: Inconsistent neonatal definitions lead to diagnostic confusion, inappropriate clinical triage, and incorrect statistical reporting. Standardised criteria establish universal thresholds for prematurity, low birth weight, and growth restriction.
skill.annex.paed.neo.definitions.practice: Classify five clinical vignettes with birth weight and gestational age into preterm, term, or post-term, and AGA, SGA, or LGA categories.
pitfalls: Equating low birth weight (<2500 g) exclusively with prematurity, overlooking term small-for-gestational-age infants.
Confusing the early neonatal period (<7 days) with the total neonatal period (<28 days).
Measuring gestational age from conception rather than from the first day of the last menstrual period.

probes.q: What chronological age boundaries define the early neonatal period and the total neonatal period?
probes.a: The early neonatal period is birth to less than 7 completed days of life; the total neonatal period is birth to less than 28 completed days of life.

probes.q: What birth weight cut-offs define low birth weight (LBW), very low birth weight (VLBW), and extremely low birth weight (ELBW)?
probes.a: Low birth weight is under 2500 grams, very low birth weight is under 1500 grams, and extremely low birth weight is under 1000 grams.

probes.q: How are small for gestational age (SGA) and large for gestational age (LGA) defined against population centiles?
probes.a: Small for gestational age is a birth weight below the 10th centile for gestational age; large for gestational age is a birth weight above the 90th centile for gestational age.

rubric.text: Applies 7-day and 28-day boundaries for early and late neonatal periods
Distinguishes preterm (<37 weeks), term (37 to 41 weeks), and post-term (>42 weeks)
Categorises birth weight into LBW (<2500 g), VLBW (<1500 g), and ELBW (<1000 g)
Identifies AGA, SGA, and LGA using the 10th and 90th population centiles

rows: Birth to less than 28 days (<28 days)
Birth to less than 7 days (<7 days)

skill.annex.paed.neo.apgar_score.title: Apgar scoring system at 1 and 5 minutes
skill.annex.paed.neo.apgar_score.oneLine: Standardised 10-point scoring of newborn physiological transition and resuscitation response
skill.annex.paed.neo.apgar_score.why: Apgar scoring provides a rapid, objective, reproducible assessment of newborn clinical status and the adequacy of resuscitation efforts at 1 and 5 minutes after birth. Failing to record structured Apgar scores obscures the trajectory of neonatal recovery.
skill.annex.paed.neo.apgar_score.practice: Watch videos of neonatal delivery; assign 1-minute and 5-minute Apgar scores across all 5 parameters; document score in standard obstetric format.
pitfalls: Waiting for the 1-minute Apgar score before initiating resuscitation (resuscitation must begin immediately within the golden minute).
Assigning an appearance score of 2 in an infant with blue hands and feet (acrocyanosis earns a score of 1).
Using the Apgar score alone to predict long-term neurological outcome or diagnose birth asphyxia.

probes.q: What five physiological parameters comprise the Apgar score?
probes.a: Activity (muscle tone), Pulse (heart rate), Grimace (reflex irritability), Appearance (skin colour), and Respiration (respiratory effort).

probes.q: What Apgar score range indicates a severely depressed newborn requiring immediate resuscitation?
probes.a: An Apgar score of 0 to 3 (or less than 4) indicates severe depression requiring immediate active resuscitation.

probes.q: Why is the Apgar score an inappropriate tool for deciding when to initiate neonatal resuscitation in the delivery room?
probes.a: Resuscitation must begin immediately within the first 30 to 60 seconds if the baby is apnoeic or bradycardic; waiting for the 1-minute Apgar score delays life-saving ventilation.

rubric.text: Evaluates all 5 Apgar components: heart rate, effort, tone, reflex, colour
Assigns 0, 1, or 2 accurately according to clinical criteria
Records scores at 1 and 5 minutes, continuing at 5-minute intervals if <7
Initiates resuscitation immediately without waiting for timed Apgar score

teach.heading: The Apgar scoring components and scale
Clinical interpretation and extended scoring
teach.body:
Scores of 7 to 10 indicate a vigorous newborn who requires only routine care. Scores of 4 to 6 indicate moderate depression requiring thermal protection, tactile stimulation, and positive-pressure ventilation.

Scores below 4 (<4) signal severe depression requiring immediate advanced resuscitation. If the 5-minute score remains below 7, continue assigning scores every 5 minutes until two successive scores reach 7 or higher, up to 20 minutes.

teach.heading: Clinical limitations of the Apgar score
teach.body:
The Apgar score reflects physiological transition at a single point in time, but it is not a tool to initiate resuscitation. Never delay bag-mask ventilation to wait for the 1-minute score.

Apgar scores can be falsely depressed by prematurity, congenital neuromuscular disorders, maternal anaesthesia, or airway malformations without true hypoxic-ischaemic asphyxia. Cord blood gas analysis is required to document metabolic acidaemia.

skill.annex.paed.neo.ballard_score.title: New Ballard gestational maturity scoring chart
skill.annex.paed.neo.ballard_score.oneLine: Reference scoring table for neuromuscular and physical maturity from 20 to 44 weeks gestation
skill.annex.paed.neo.ballard_score.why: The New Ballard Score extends gestational age evaluation down to 20 weeks of gestation, providing a validated tool to assign maturity ratings when ultrasound dating is absent or unreliable.
skill.annex.paed.neo.ballard_score.practice: Using a completed New Ballard worksheet, sum neuromuscular and physical points; read the maturity rating table to calculate the exact gestational age.
pitfalls: Scoring physical signs in an infant who has been under radiant warmers for >24 hours (skin cracks and appears falsely mature).
Measuring the square window angle while twisting or pronating the wrist.
Failing to record the time of examination (scores are most accurate between 12 and 24 hours of postnatal age).

probes.q: What total New Ballard score corresponds to 40 completed weeks of gestation?
probes.a: A total score of 40 points corresponds to 40 weeks of gestation.

probes.q: What is the lowest gestational age and corresponding score evaluated by the New Ballard scoring chart?
probes.a: A score of -10 corresponds to 20 weeks of gestation.

probes.q: How does popliteal angle scoring change from extreme prematurity (24 weeks) to full term (40 weeks)?
probes.a: The popliteal angle decreases from 180 degrees (score -1) in extreme prematurity down to less than 90 degrees (score 5) in term infants due to developing flexor hamstring tone.

rubric.text: Applies -1 to 5 scale for posture, square window, recoil, popliteal, scarf, heel-to-ear
Applies -1 to 5 scale for skin, lanugo, plantar, breast, eye/ear, genitalia
Sums all 12 items and correctly maps total score (-10 to 50) to gestational weeks

rows: Moderate flexion of hips and knees (2-3)
Full flexion of arms and legs, adducted (4)

skill.annex.paed.neo.respiratory_distres.title: Downes and Silverman-Anderson respiratory distress scoring systems
skill.annex.paed.neo.respiratory_distres.oneLine: Objective clinical scoring systems to grade respiratory distress severity in term and preterm neonates
skill.annex.paed.neo.respiratory_distres.why: Subjective evaluation of respiratory difficulty is unreliable and leads to delayed escalation of respiratory support. Standardised clinical scoring using Downes score for all neonates and Silverman-Anderson score for preterm infants stratifies distress severity to guide oxygen therapy, CPAP, and mechanical ventilation.
skill.annex.paed.neo.respiratory_distres.practice: Examine a tachypnoeic newborn at the bedside; calculate Downes score and Silverman-Anderson score; identify the correct clinical escalation step.
pitfalls: Scoring grunting as absent without using a stethoscope to listen directly over the larynx or trachea.
Failing to reassess the score every 30 to 60 minutes after initiating CPAP or oxygen therapy.
Assuming an infant with falling respiratory rate and decreasing retractions is improving when exhausted and developing hypercapnic respiratory failure.

probes.q: What five clinical parameters constitute the Downes respiratory distress score?
probes.a: Respiratory rate, cyanosis, chest retractions, grunting, and air entry.

probes.q: What total score on the Downes scale signifies severe respiratory distress requiring urgent neonatal intensive care and positive pressure support?
probes.a: A Downes score greater than 8 indicates severe respiratory distress and impending respiratory failure.

probes.q: In the Silverman-Anderson score, what clinical sign represents paradoxical or see-saw respiration, and why does it occur?
probes.a: See-saw breathing is simultaneous chest sinking while the abdomen expands during inspiration, caused by diaphragmatic excursion overcoming an unstable, highly compliant thoracic cage.

rubric.text: Calculates Downes score across rate, cyanosis, retractions, grunting, and air entry
Applies Silverman-Anderson score to evaluate preterm thoracoabdominal synchrony
Correctly classifies distress as mild (<5), moderate (5-8), or severe (>8)
Links score threshold to oxygen, bubble CPAP 5 cmH2O, or invasive ventilation

teach.heading: Clinical score stratification and intervention thresholds
teach.body:
On the Downes scale: a score <5 indicates mild distress manageable with thermal support and humidified low-flow oxygen; a score of 5 to 8 indicates moderate distress warranting bubble CPAP at 5 cmH2O; a score >8 signifies severe distress requiring immediate endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.

On the Silverman-Anderson scale: 0 indicates no distress, 1 to 3 mild distress, 4 to 6 moderate distress, and 7 to 10 impending respiratory failure.

skill.proc.paed.lumbar_puncture.title: Paediatric lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid collection
skill.proc.paed.lumbar_puncture.oneLine: Safe positioning, landmark identification at L3-L4 or L4-L5, and avoiding herniation risks
skill.proc.paed.lumbar_puncture.why: Lumbar puncture provides essential diagnostic access to cerebrospinal fluid in suspected central nervous system infections, neonatal sepsis, and leukaemia. Performing it without screening for raised intracranial pressure risks fatal tonsillar herniation, while improper technique leads to traumatic taps that confound interpretation.

steps.text: Exclude absolute contraindications before beginning: check for signs of raised intracranial pressure (altered sensorium, unequal pupils, bradycardia with hypertension, papilloedema), focal neurological signs, local skin sepsis at the puncture site, and severe coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia.

Position the child in lateral recumbency on a firm flat surface with the back aligned vertically at the edge of the bed. An assistant flexes the hips and knees while maintaining neck extension to preserve airway patency.
Locate the intercristal Tuffier line connecting the superior borders of the iliac crests, which crosses the spine at the L3-L4 interspace. Select the L3-L4 or L4-L5 intervertebral space.
Cleanse the skin with antiseptic solution in widening concentric circles and drape sterilely. Infiltrate 1 percent lignocaine into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue if time permits.

Insert a 22 G or 24 G spinal needle with stylet in the midline, directing the needle slightly cephalad towards the umbilicus. Advance slowly until a subtle release of resistance is felt as the ligamentum flavum and dura are pierced.

Withdraw the stylet periodically to check for clear CSF flow. Collect 5 to 10 drops per sterile tube into 3 separate tubes for cell counts, biochemistry (protein, glucose), and microbiology (Gram stain, culture). Reinsert the stylet before withdrawing the needle.
Apply firm sterile pressure over the puncture site for 2 minutes and apply an adhesive dressing. Keep the child supine for 30 to 60 minutes and monitor vital signs closely.

skill.proc.paed.lumbar_puncture.practice: Practise identifying the L3-L4 intercristal landmark on a pediatric spinal manikin while maintaining correct lateral positioning and needle angulation.
pitfalls: Excessive neck flexion during restraint of infants, which causes acute airway compromise and hypoxaemia.
Performing lumbar puncture in the presence of focal neurological deficits, papilloedema, or cardiorespiratory instability without prior neuroimaging.
Advancing the spinal needle without a stylet, which risks introducing epidermal tissue plugs into the spinal canal.

probes.q: Which anatomical intervertebral spaces are safe for lumbar puncture in children and why?
probes.a: The L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace. In infants and children, the spinal cord terminates lower than in adults (near L2-L3 in neonates), so puncturing below L3 avoids direct cord trauma.

probes.q: What rule helps distinguish a traumatic tap from true pathological CSF pleocytosis?
probes.a: Allow 1 white blood cell for every 500 red blood cells, and a protein increase of 1 mg/dL for every 1000 red blood cells per cubic millimetre.

probes.q: Why must neck flexion be avoided when positioning a small infant for lumbar puncture?
probes.a: Hyperflexion of the neck in small infants can occlude the compliant upper airway, leading to acute hypoxaemia and bradycardia. Only the hips and knees should be flexed.

rubric.text: Screens for raised intracranial pressure, focal neurological deficits, cardiorespiratory compromise, and local skin infection before the procedure
Positions child in lateral recumbency with hips flexed and neck extended to protect the airway
Accurately identifies the intercristal line at L3-L4 and selects the L3-L4 or L4-L5 intervertebral space
Uses a spinal needle with stylet, directs needle towards umbilicus, and reinserts stylet prior to needle withdrawal
Maintains sterile haemostasis, applies dressing, and orders post-procedure neurological and vital observation

teach.heading: Indications and safety screening
teach.body:
Lumbar puncture is indicated for suspected meningitis, encephalitis, neonatal sepsis evaluation, staging of paediatric acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, and intrathecal chemotherapy.

Absolute contraindications include space-occupying lesions with mass effect, unequal pupils, papilloedema, local lumbar infection, and severe uncorrected bleeding diatheses.

teach.heading: Anatomical landmarks and needle selection
teach.body:
The spinal cord terminates around L2 to L3 in infants and reaches the adult L1-L2 level only during early childhood. The intercristal line connecting the top of the iliac crests identifies L3-L4.

A 22 G or 24 G needle with a matched stylet is chosen. The stylet prevents pushing epidermal plugs into the subarachnoid space, which could develop into spinal epidermoid tumours.

teach.heading: Interpretation of traumatic taps
teach.body:
When blood is encountered, clearing across sequential collection tubes suggests a traumatic tap rather than subarachnoid haemorrhage.

To correct for peripheral blood contamination, subtract 1 leukocyte for every 500 erythrocytes per cubic millimetre, and deduct 1 mg/dL of protein for each 1000 erythrocytes per cubic millimetre.

skill.proc.paed.nasogastric_tube.title: Paediatric nasogastric and feeding tube insertion
skill.proc.paed.nasogastric_tube.oneLine: Length estimation by nose-earlobe-xiphoid measurement, gentle insertion, and verification of gastric position
skill.proc.paed.nasogastric_tube.why: Enteral tubes provide essential access for enteral nutrition, drug delivery, and gastric decompression in intestinal obstruction. Tracheal misplacement can lead to fatal aspiration pneumonia or pneumothorax if feeds are infused without reliable gastric verification.

steps.text: Select the appropriate tube calibre: 6 to 8 French for neonates, 8 to 10 French for infants, and 12 to 16 French for older children. Check nostril patency and clear any secretions.

Estimate the required insertion distance using the nose-earlobe-xiphoid (NEX) method: measure from the tip of the child's nose to the earlobe, and then down to the tip of the xiphoid process. Mark the target distance on the tube with tape or note the printed centimetre marking.
Swaddle infants securely to prevent arm movement. Position older children sitting upright or at 45 degrees with the head in a neutral or slightly flexed position.
Lubricate the tip with water-soluble lubricant or sterile water. Gently advance the tube along the floor of the chosen nasal passage perpendicular to the face.

When the tube reaches the posterior pharynx, encourage swallowing in older children or offer a pacifier in infants to facilitate oesophageal entry. Advance steadily until the marked measurement reaches the nostril.
Halt immediately and withdraw the tube if the child coughs persistently, becomes cyanotic, chokes, or exhibits respiratory distress, indicating tracheal misplacement.

Verify gastric placement before administering any fluid: aspirate gastric contents with a syringe and test with pH indicator paper (pH should be 5.5 or lower). Auscultation of a whoosh over the epigastrium during air insufflation is supplementary and not sufficient alone.
Secure the tube to the upper lip and cheek with hypoallergenic adhesive tape without applying traction or pressure necrosis to the nasal alar cartilage.

skill.proc.paed.nasogastric_tube.practice: Rehearse measuring the NEX distance on a paediatric simulator, passing the tube along the nasal floor, and interpreting pH test paper from simulated aspirate.
pitfalls: Failing to confirm gastric placement with pH testing and relying solely on epigastric auscultation, which can sound similar over the lung.
Taping the tube under tension against the nasal nostril rim, leading to pressure necrosis of the alar cartilage.
Continuing advancement despite cough, choking, or desaturation, resulting in bronchial intubation.

probes.q: How is the insertion length for a paediatric nasogastric tube measured?
probes.a: Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe, and then from the earlobe to the xiphoid process (the NEX measurement).

probes.q: What size of feeding tube is typically selected for a neonate compared with an older child?
probes.a: Size 6 to 8 French for a neonate, and size 12 to 16 French for an older child.

probes.q: Why is epigastric auscultation of an air bolus alone not considered definitive proof of gastric tube placement?
probes.a: Air insufflated into the bronchus or oesophagus can transmit sounds easily across the infant chest wall to the epigastrium, mimicking gastric placement. Testing aspirate pH (5.5 or less) or radiography is needed.

rubric.text: Selects appropriate tube calibre and accurately measures the nose-earlobe-xiphoid distance
Lubricates tip and advances gently along nasal floor without upward force, pausing if respiratory distress occurs
Aspirates fluid and checks pH of 5.5 or lower to confirm gastric placement before feeding
Secures tube to the cheek avoiding alar tension and records the centimetre mark at the nostril

teach.heading: Indications and tube selection
teach.body:
Enteral tubes serve diagnostic and therapeutic functions. Diagnostic uses include gastric lavage for toxicology, gastric aspirate for acid-fast bacilli in suspected tuberculosis, and checking patency in suspected tracheo-oesophageal fistula.

Therapeutic uses include gavage feeding in prematurity or malnutrition, gastric decompression in bowel obstruction, and oral rehydration delivery.

teach.heading: Anatomical measurement and insertion path
teach.body:
The distance from the nares to the stomach is measured by the nose-earlobe-xiphoid pathway. In neonates, 6 to 8 French tubes are preferred; older children use 12 to 16 French.

The tube must travel along the floor of the nose directly backwards, avoiding the upward tilt towards the cribriform plate which can cause painful mucosal trauma and epistaxis.

teach.heading: Verification of gastric placement
teach.body:
Auscultating an air bolus over the epigastrium is unreliable in infants because acoustic transmission across small thoracic dimensions can disguise tracheal placement.

First-line verification is checking that aspirated fluid turns indicator paper acidic with a pH of 5.5 or less. In doubtful or high-risk cases, a chest-abdominal radiograph confirms the tip lies below the diaphragm.

skill.proc.paed.bone_marrow_aspiration.title: Paediatric bone marrow aspiration technique
skill.proc.paed.bone_marrow_aspiration.oneLine: Posterior superior iliac spine landmarking, needle stabilization, and marrow film preparation
skill.proc.paed.bone_marrow_aspiration.why: Bone marrow aspiration provides definitive cytological evaluation of marrow architecture in haematological malignancies, aplastic anaemia, immune thrombocytopenia, and metabolic storage disorders. Inadequate technique causes dry taps, cortical transfixion, or painful soft tissue injury.

steps.text: Review indications (unexplained cytopenias, suspected acute leukaemia, staging lymphomas, storage diseases) and check coagulation profile and platelet support requirements.

Identify the primary site: the posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) is the safest site across all paediatric ages. In infants under 1 year, the anteromedial aspect of the proximal tibia may be considered as an alternative.
Position the child in prone or lateral decubitus position with adequate sedation and analgesia. Palpate and mark the bony prominence of the posterior superior iliac spine.
Clean the skin with chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine in widening concentric circles and drape sterilely. Infiltrate 1 to 2 percent lignocaine down to and including the periosteum.

Select a paediatric bone marrow aspiration needle (Salah or Jamshidi type) with an securely locked inner stylet. Grasp the needle handle in the palm with the index finger extended along the shaft to prevent uncontrolled penetration.

Introduce the needle through the skin and advance perpendicular to the posterior superior iliac spine. Rotate the needle clockwise and counterclockwise with firm downward pressure until a distinct give or loss of resistance indicates cortex penetration into the cancellous marrow cavity.

Remove the inner stylet. Attach a 5 mL or 10 mL syringe and aspirate sharply to obtain 0.2 to 0.5 mL of marrow particles. Warn the assistant that the child will experience brief deep ache during suction.
Replace the stylet before withdrawing the needle. Apply firm sterile pressure over the puncture site for at least 5 minutes until complete haemostasis is achieved, followed by a pressure dressing.
Immediately expel the aspirate onto clean glass slides to identify marrow spicules and make thin feather-edged wedge smears before clot formation occurs.

skill.proc.paed.bone_marrow_aspiration.practice: Rehearse hand grip, perpendicular bone alignment, and gentle rotational advancement on a paediatric bone model, followed by rapid slide spreading of simulated marrow spicules.
pitfalls: Penetrating through both anterior and posterior bony cortices due to uncontrolled force without an index finger guard on the shaft.
Aspirating excessive marrow volume (greater than 1 mL), which hemodilutes the sample with peripheral sinusoidal blood and distorts differential counts.
Delaying slide preparation so that the aspirate clots within the syringe before spicules can be identified and smeared.

probes.q: What is the preferred anatomical site for bone marrow aspiration in children?
probes.a: The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS).

probes.q: Why should only a small volume (0.2 to 0.5 mL) of marrow be aspirated initially?
probes.a: Aspirating larger volumes pulls in peripheral venous blood, causing hemodilution that masks true marrow cellularity and blasts.

probes.q: Which site may be used in an infant under 1 year of age if the posterior iliac spine is inaccessible?
probes.a: The anteromedial surface of the proximal tibia, 1 to 2 cm below the tibial tuberosity.

rubric.text: Correctly palpates and marks the posterior superior iliac spine as the primary aspiration site
Infiltrates local anaesthetic down to the periosteum and confirms adequate depth of analgesia
Maintains locked inner stylet and stabilizes shaft with index finger to prevent over-penetration
Aspirates a small volume (0.2 to 0.5 mL) to prevent peripheral blood hemodilution
Rapidly prepares multiple particle-rich glass slide smears before clotting begins

teach.heading: Indications and site selection
teach.body:
Paediatric bone marrow aspiration is essential in evaluating acute leukaemias, aplastic anaemia, staging neuroblastoma and lymphoma, refractory thrombocytopenia, and storage disorders.

The posterior superior iliac spine offers the thickest marrow bed with minimal risk of adjacent organ or vascular injury. The sternum is strictly avoided in children due to the risk of cardiac transfixion.

teach.heading: Instrument parts and puncture mechanics
teach.body:
The aspiration needle features an outer cannula with cutting bevel, an inner matched stylet with a locking cap, and an ergonomic grip. The stylet prevents bone fragments from occluding the bore.

The physician grips the handle in the palm while bracing the index finger along the shaft. Advancing with controlled rotary motion prevents sudden slippage through the posterior cortex.

teach.heading: Smear technique and spicule identification
teach.body:
A quick suction yields greyish particulate grains called marrow spicules. Immediately tilting the slide drains away excess red blood, leaving spicules adherent to the surface.

A second glass slide gently drags the spicules into a feathered wedge smear. Additional aspirate is placed in EDTA for flow cytometry and heparin for cytogenetics.

skill.proc.paed.liver_biopsy.title: Paediatric percutaneous liver biopsy approach
skill.proc.paed.liver_biopsy.oneLine: Safety screening, Trucut needle technique, and post-procedure right lateral monitoring
skill.proc.paed.liver_biopsy.why: Percutaneous liver biopsy provides definitive histopathological diagnosis in obscure hepatomegaly, chronic hepatitis, storage disorders, and neonatal cholestasis. Ignoring strict haemostatic contraindications leads to catastrophic intraperitoneal haemorrhage or biliary peritonitis.

steps.text: Review haematological prerequisites: verify platelet count is above 40,000 to 50,000 per cubic millimetre and prothrombin time / INR is within 3 seconds of control (INR <1.5). Exclude severe anaemia.

Confirm absence of absolute contraindications: hydatid cyst (risk of fatal anaphylaxis), vascular malformations or haemangiomas, pyogenic abscess, marked ascites, and extrahepatic biliary obstruction.
Select ultrasound guidance or identify the intercostal puncture site: typically the 8th or 9th intercostal space in the mid-axillary line during suspended expiration to avoid lung laceration.
Administer deep procedural sedation with local anaesthetic infiltration of the skin, intercostal space, and liver capsule.
Make a small skin nick with a scalpel blade. Introduce a paediatric Trucut needle with cutting cannula retracted over the inner notched stylet.
Advance the needle through the intercostal space just above the lower rib margin to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle. Penetrate the liver capsule.

Advance the notched inner specimen rod into liver parenchyma, immediately slide the outer cutting sheath forward to slice and capture the tissue core, and withdraw the entire unit in one continuous motion.
Inspect the specimen: place in formalin for histology, sterile saline for molecular assays, or glutaraldehyde for electron microscopy according to indication.

Apply a sterile pressure dressing over the puncture site and immediately position the child in the right lateral decubitus position for 2 to 4 hours to compress the liver puncture against the lateral chest wall.
Enforce strict bed rest for 6 to 12 hours with frequent vital signs monitoring (pulse and blood pressure every 15 minutes for the first hour, then every 30 minutes) to detect occult bleeding.

skill.proc.paed.liver_biopsy.practice: Simulate the two-step mechanical firing of a Trucut needle on a soft tissue phantom, practising rapid capsule penetration and tissue capture.
pitfalls: Performing percutaneous biopsy in a child with an unrecognised hydatid cyst, precipitating fatal anaphylactic shock.
Advancing the needle along the inferior rib border, lacerating the intercostal artery and causing heavy chest wall haematoma.
Failing to maintain the child in the right lateral decubitus position post-procedure, increasing the risk of intraperitoneal bleeding.

probes.q: What platelet count threshold is generally required before performing a paediatric liver biopsy?
probes.a: A platelet count of at least 40,000 to 50,000 per cubic millimetre.

probes.q: Why is hydatid disease an absolute contraindication to percutaneous needle biopsy?
probes.a: Puncturing a hydatid cyst can release antigenic cyst fluid into the peritoneum, causing life-threatening anaphylaxis and secondary abdominal hydatid seeding.

probes.q: Why is the child placed in the right lateral decubitus position following a liver biopsy?
probes.a: Lying on the right side uses the child's body weight to compress the liver puncture site against the lateral ribs, facilitating mechanical haemostasis.

rubric.text: Verifies platelet count (>40,000-50,000) and INR (<1.5) and excludes hydatid disease and vascular lesions
Introduces needle immediately above the upper border of the lower rib to protect intercostal vessels
Operates the Trucut needle smoothly with swift specimen capture and single-pass withdrawal
Places child in right lateral decubitus position and initiates vital signs protocol to detect occult haemorrhage

teach.heading: Indications and absolute contraindications
teach.body:
Percutaneous liver biopsy investigates unexplained hepatomegaly, chronic hepatitis B or C, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson disease, storage disorders, and neonatal cholestasis.

Absolute contraindications include prolonged coagulation (INR > 1.5), severe thrombocytopenia (<40,000/cu.mm), hydatid cyst, vascular haemangioma, tense ascites, and pyogenic abscess.

teach.heading: Trucut mechanism and anatomical approach
teach.body:
The Trucut needle uses a 2 cm specimen notch on an inner rod and an outer hollow cutting sleeve. Advancing through the 8th or 9th intercostal space at the mid-axillary line traverses the diaphragm into liver parenchyma.

The needle must pass over the upper edge of the lower rib to avoid the subcostal groove containing intercostal vessels and nerve.

teach.heading: Post-procedure monitoring and complications
teach.body:
The most feared complication is intraperitoneal haemorrhage or subcapsular haematoma. Biliary leakage and pneumothorax can also occur.

Positioning the child on the right side creates direct tamponade against the thoracic wall. Monitoring blood pressure and heart rate detects early hypovolaemic shock.

skill.proc.paed.inhaler_devices.title: Paediatric inhaler devices and nebuliser administration
skill.proc.paed.inhaler_devices.oneLine: Age-appropriate delivery: MDI with valved spacer and mask under 4, spacer alone at 4-12, and nebuliser setup
skill.proc.paed.inhaler_devices.why: Inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids are the cornerstone of paediatric asthma management. Using an MDI without an age-appropriate spacer or mask causes 80 to 90 percent of medication to deposit in the oropharynx, leading to therapeutic failure and local side effects.

steps.text: Select the age-appropriate delivery interface: children under 4 years require a metered dose inhaler (MDI) with a valved holding chamber (spacer) and closely fitting face mask; children aged 4 to 12 years use an MDI with a spacer and mouthpiece; children over 12 years can use an MDI alone or dry powder inhaler (DPI) if inspiratory technique is adequate.
Prepare the MDI: remove the dust cap, inspect the mouthpiece for foreign objects, shake the canister vigorously 4 to 5 times, and prime into the air if unused for several days.
Assemble the spacer: fit the MDI nozzle into the rubber port of the spacer holding chamber.
Apply the face mask gently over the child's nose and mouth to achieve an airtight seal without air leaks around the cheeks or bridge of the nose.

Depress the canister once to release a single puff into the chamber. Allow the young child to breathe normally through the spacer for 5 to 6 breaths (tidal breathing technique). Never fire multiple puffs into the chamber simultaneously.

For children using a mouthpiece: ask the child to exhale gently away from the spacer, seal lips tightly around the mouthpiece, fire one puff, and take a slow, deep breath in over 3 to 5 seconds followed by a 10-second breath hold.
Wait at least 30 to 60 seconds before delivering a second puff, shaking the canister again between puffs.
Instruct the child to rinse the mouth with water and spit it out after inhaling corticosteroid medications to prevent oral candidiasis and dysphonia.

For jet nebulisation in severe acute asthma: place 2.5 to 5.0 mg salbutamol respirator solution in the medication cup, add normal saline to reach a 3 to 4 mL fill volume, connect to oxygen source running at 6 to 8 litres per minute, and deliver via face mask over 10 to 15 minutes.

skill.proc.paed.inhaler_devices.practice: Demonstrate assembling a valved spacer, checking mask seal on a manikin, timing 5 tidal breaths per puff, and cleaning the spacer with warm soapy water without scrub-drying.
pitfalls: Firing two or three puffs rapidly into the spacer holding chamber before the child inhales, which causes aerosol aggregation and drops lung delivery by half.
Wiping the inside of a plastic spacer dry with a cloth, generating electrostatic charge that traps drug particles on the plastic wall.
Using an unsealed face mask or allowing a gap between mask and nose, which reduces inhaled lung deposition by over 80 percent.

probes.q: What interface is mandatory when administering an MDI to a child under 4 years of age?
probes.a: A metered dose inhaler connected to a valved spacer with an airtight face mask.

probes.q: Why must multiple puffs not be fired into a spacer simultaneously?
probes.a: Multiple puffs create aerosol turbulence and particle collision, causing medication droplets to impact against the spacer wall and halving delivered drug dose.

probes.q: What gas flow rate and total solution volume are needed to operate a jet nebuliser effectively?
probes.a: An oxygen or air flow of 6 to 8 litres per minute with a total chamber fill volume of 3 to 5 mL.

rubric.text: Selects appropriate interface by age: MDI with spacer and mask (<4 yr), spacer with mouthpiece (4-12 yr), or DPI (>4 yr)
Shakes canister and delivers strictly one puff per inhalation cycle without compounding doses
Ensures airtight mask seal and allows 5-6 tidal breaths or a 10-second breath hold
Counsels mouth rinsing and spitting after corticosteroid inhalation to prevent oral thrush

teach.heading: Device choice by developmental age
teach.body:
Inhaled medications require particle sizes of 1 to 5 micrometres to reach bronchioles.

Children under 4 years lack breath coordination and require an MDI with a valved spacer and mask. Children aged 4 to 12 years use a spacer with mouthpiece. Dry powder inhalers (DPIs like Rotahaler) generate resistance requiring high inspiratory effort and are reserved for children over 4 to 5 years.

teach.heading: Spacer mechanics and static prevention
teach.body:
Valved holding chambers slow high-velocity spray from MDIs, allowing propellant evaporation into respirable particles while retaining coarse droplets that cause oral thrush.

Plastic spacers acquire electrostatic charge if scrubbed dry with cloths. Spacers should be washed in mild detergent, rinsed, and allowed to air-dry to preserve electrical neutrality.

teach.heading: Jet nebuliser operational principles
teach.body:
Jet nebulisers use the Venturi effect: high-velocity gas (6 to 8 L/min) pulls liquid through a capillary tube and smashes it against a baffle plate into a polydisperse aerosol.

Effective atomisation requires a liquid volume of 3 to 5 mL. Delivering salbutamol takes 10 to 15 minutes. In severe acute attacks, oxygen is the driving gas of choice.

skill.proc.paed.pefr.title: Peak expiratory flow rate measurement and zone interpretation
skill.proc.paed.pefr.oneLine: Technique in children over 5 years, best of three attempts, and traffic light zones
skill.proc.paed.pefr.why: Peak expiratory flow rate provides an objective assessment of variable expiratory airflow limitation and response to treatment. In acute asthma, clinical assessment alone understates obstruction; PEFR detects impending respiratory deterioration before overt respiratory failure occurs.

steps.text: Verify eligibility: the child must be at least 5 years old and capable of understanding and performing maximal forced expiration.
Inspect the peak flow meter: ensure the mouthpiece is clean and unobstructed. Slide the red indicator marker down to zero at the bottom of the scale.

Instruct the child to stand up straight. Explain the manoeuvre: breathe in as deeply as possible, put the mouthpiece in the mouth, and blow out as hard and fast as you can like blowing out birthday candles.

Ensure the child takes a maximal inspiration to total lung capacity, places the mouthpiece between the teeth, and seals the lips tightly without covering the exhaust holes with fingers or obstructing the hole with the tongue.
Have the child deliver a single, forceful, explosive expiration lasting about 1 second. Read and record the value indicated by the marker.
Reset the marker to zero and repeat the procedure twice more, allowing a brief rest between attempts. Record the highest of the three acceptable readings as the official PEFR.

Compare the recorded peak flow to the child's personal best or predicted normal value based on height formulae: for boys, (2.96 multiplied by height in cm) minus 110; for girls, (3.43 multiplied by height in cm) minus 178.

Categorise into asthma management zones: Green zone (greater than 80 percent of personal best) indicates good control; Yellow zone (50 to 80 percent) indicates acute exacerbation requiring bronchodilator step-up; Red zone (less than 50 percent) signals severe obstruction requiring urgent emergency hospital care.

skill.proc.paed.pefr.practice: Demonstrate the zeroing, standing position, lip seal, and sharp explosive expiration on a mini-Wright peak flow meter, and calculate the height-based predicted normal for a 120 cm child.
pitfalls: Allowing the child to spit or cough into the mouthpiece, which propels the marker artificially high without reflecting true lung volume.
Recording the average of three attempts instead of the highest valid reading.
Permitting an incomplete inspiration or loose lip seal, leading to falsely low PEFR values that mimic severe bronchospasm.

probes.q: What is the minimum age at which peak expiratory flow rate measurement is reliable in children?
probes.a: Children aged 5 years and above.

probes.q: How many attempts should be performed, and which reading is recorded?
probes.a: Perform 3 attempts and record the highest reading.

probes.q: What are the percentage cut-offs for the Green, Yellow, and Red zones in peak flow action plans?
probes.a: Green zone is greater than 80 percent of personal best; Yellow zone is 50 to 80 percent; Red zone is less than 50 percent.

rubric.text: Slides indicator to zero and checks mouthpiece for obstruction prior to each blow
Ensures standing position, full deep inspiration, airtight lip seal, and explosive 1-second blast
Repeats 3 times and correctly selects the highest value rather than the average
Accurately categorises value into Green (>80%), Yellow (50-80%), or Red (<50%) zones and links to clinical action

teach.heading: Physiological principles and indications
teach.body:
Peak expiratory flow rate measures the maximal airflow generated during forced expiration from full lung inflation. It reflects large-airway calibre and effort-dependent expiratory muscle strength.

PEFR is indicated in children over 5 years to quantify asthma severity, evaluate bronchodilator reversibility, recognise diurnal variability, and guide home action plans.

teach.heading: Measurement technique and reproducibility
teach.body:
The child must stand upright to maximize diaphragmatic excursion. A tight lip seal around the mouthpiece is essential, ensuring the tongue does not occlude the orifice.

Three technically acceptable blows are obtained. The highest reading is recorded. A difference greater than 20 L/min between blows suggests poor effort or inconsistent technique.

rows: Inhaled salbutamol and step up controller
Immediate salbutamol and urgent hospital care
