skill.proc.paed.mantoux_test.title: Tuberculin skin testing and Mantoux technique
skill.proc.paed.mantoux_test.oneLine: Intradermal injection of 0.1 mL tuberculin PPD, 6-10 mm wheal, and induration reading at 48-72 hours
skill.proc.paed.mantoux_test.why: The Mantoux tuberculin skin test detects delayed-type cell-mediated hypersensitivity to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens. Subcutaneous injection rather than intradermal placement produces false negatives, while measuring erythema instead of induration leads to misclassification of infection.

steps.text: Screen the child: confirm absence of high fever, extensive dermatitis at the test site, or documented previous severe necrotic tuberculin reaction. Note any live viral vaccines given within the preceding 4 weeks, which can suppress tuberculin reactivity.
Select a sterile 1 mL tuberculin syringe with a 26 G or 27 G short-bevel needle. Draw exactly 0.1 mL of Purified Protein Derivative (PPD) solution containing 1 TU or 2 TU PPD RT23 with Tween 80.
Position the child's left forearm supported comfortably on a flat surface, volar aspect facing upward, free from rashes, scars, or superficial veins.
Clean the skin with an alcohol swab and allow to air dry completely. Moisture or residual antiseptic can inactivate the protein antigen.

Stretch the forearm skin taut with the non-dominant hand. Insert the needle almost parallel to the skin at a 5 to 15 degree angle with the bevel pointing upward, advancing just enough to cover the bevel within the dermis.

Inject the 0.1 mL solution slowly. Confirm the immediate appearance of a pale, elevated, well-demarcated wheal with distinct orange-peel (peau d'orange) follicular pitting measuring 6 to 10 mm in diameter.
If no wheal forms or fluid leaks subcutaneously, withdraw the needle and repeat on the other forearm or at least 5 cm away from the first site.
Dab any blood drop gently without rubbing. Do not apply an adhesive bandage, ointment, or pressure to the site. Instruct the family to keep the site clean and dry.

Schedule the reading strictly between 48 and 72 hours post-injection. Inspect under good lighting and palpate across the forearm with the fingertips from outside towards the centre to identify margins of induration.

Use the ballpoint pen technique: roll a pen towards the induration from both sides; resistance halts the pen at the margins. Measure the transverse diameter of palpable induration across the long axis of the forearm in millimetres using a clear plastic ruler. Do not measure redness.

skill.proc.paed.mantoux_test.practice: Practise intradermal injection technique on an orange skin or intradermal training pad, achieving a 6 to 10 mm discrete wheal, and measure simulated induration with a caliper.
pitfalls: Injecting subcutaneously instead of intradermally, which fails to produce a wheal and yields a false-negative result.
Measuring surrounding erythema instead of palpable, raised induration, which falsely overestimates test positivity.
Reading the test before 48 hours or after 72 hours, missing the peak of delayed-type cell-mediated hypersensitivity.

probes.q: What volume and dose of tuberculin PPD is administered, and into which skin layer?
probes.a: 0.1 mL containing 1 TU or 2 TU of PPD RT23, injected strictly intradermally.

probes.q: At what time window should the Mantoux test be read, and what physical feature is measured?
probes.a: Read between 48 and 72 hours, measuring the transverse diameter of palpable induration in millimetres (not erythema).

probes.q: What induration cut-off defines a positive Mantoux test in a malnourished child or a child with HIV?
probes.a: An induration of 5 mm or greater is considered positive in children with HIV, severe acute malnutrition, or immunosuppression.

rubric.text: Uses a 1 mL tuberculin syringe and draws precisely 0.1 mL of tuberculin PPD solution
Inserts needle at 5-15 degrees bevel up and raises an immediate 6-10 mm pale peau d'orange wheal
Instructs family not to rub or cover the site and confirms reading return between 48 and 72 hours
Measures transverse diameter of induration in millimetres using ruler or pen technique, excluding erythema

teach.heading: Principles of the tuberculin skin test
teach.body:
The Mantoux test measures delayed-type hypersensitivity mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes. Following intradermal injection of tuberculin protein, memory T cells release cytokines recruiting macrophages over 48 to 72 hours.

This cellular infiltration forms a palpable, firm induration. Erythema represents transient vascular dilation and is not correlated with tuberculosis infection.

teach.heading: Injection technique and wheal confirmation
teach.body:
A 1 mL tuberculin syringe with a 26 G needle is used on the volar aspect of the forearm. The needle enters at 5 to 15 degrees into the papillary dermis.

Injecting 0.1 mL must raise a discrete, pale wheal measuring 6 to 10 mm with visible hair follicle pits (peau d'orange). Absence of a wheal indicates subcutaneous leakage requiring immediate re-administration.

rows: HIV, severe malnutrition, organ transplant, recent close TB contact
Children <4 yr, high-risk medical conditions, general paediatric population in India

skill.proc.paed.growth_chart_plotting.title: Plotting and interpreting paediatric growth charts
skill.proc.paed.growth_chart_plotting.oneLine: Plotting dots on WHO and IAP percentile curves, corrected age for prematurity, and recognising growth faltering
skill.proc.paed.growth_chart_plotting.why: Serial plotting of anthropometric measures on standard growth charts is the most sensitive tool to identify growth failure, acute wasting, or pathological stunting before physical signs develop. Plotting errors or failing to correct for prematurity leads to incorrect diagnostic interventions or missed failure to thrive.

steps.text: Select the correct sex-specific growth chart: WHO Child Growth Standards (pink for girls, blue for boys) for children aged 0 to 5 years, and revised IAP growth charts for older children aged 5 to 18 years.
Calculate the child's exact age: determine completed weeks for infants under 3 months, completed months for infants 3 to 24 months, and completed years and quarter-years thereafter.

In premature infants born before 37 weeks of gestation, calculate gestational corrected age (chronological age minus weeks of prematurity). Plot anthropometric parameters on the corrected age axis until 2 years of age for weight and 3 years for height and head circumference.

Obtain accurate anthropometric data: naked weight on a calibrated digital infant scale, recumbent crown-heel length on an infantometer for children under 2 years, standing height on a stadiometer for children aged 2 and older, and occipitofrontal head circumference with a non-stretchable tape.

Locate the precise age along the horizontal axis. Move vertically to align with the measured value on the vertical axis. Mark a single, crisp, distinct dot at the exact intersection using a sharp pencil.
Connect consecutive plotted points with a straight line to visualize the child's individual growth curve. Avoid drawing curved or smoothed lines between distant points.

Compare the trajectory with standard percentile curves (3rd, 15th, 50th, 85th, 97th) or Z-score lines (-3, -2, -1, 0, +1, +2, +3). Assess whether the child is tracking parallel to centiles or deviating.

Screen for growth faltering: identify a flat growth curve (no weight gain over two consecutive monthly measurements), a downward trajectory, or crossing two major centile channels downward, prompting nutritional and clinical investigation.

skill.proc.paed.growth_chart_plotting.practice: Plot weight, height, and head circumference for a 9-month-old infant born at 32 weeks gestation, correctly adjusting for prematurity and identifying if growth tracks parallel to the 15th centile.
pitfalls: Failing to correct for prematurity in an infant born at 28 to 34 weeks, misdiagnosing healthy preterm catch-up as severe failure to thrive.
Using standing height charts for an infant measured recumbently, creating a false 1 to 2 cm drop in height.
Evaluating a single isolated anthropometric plot instead of reviewing the longitudinal trajectory over time.

probes.q: Which growth charts are recommended by the WHO and Government of India for children aged 0 to 5 years?
probes.a: The WHO Child Growth Standards charts.

probes.q: How is corrected age calculated for a preterm infant, and up to what age is it used?
probes.a: Corrected age equals chronological age minus weeks of prematurity (40 minus gestational age at birth); it is used until 2 to 3 years of age.

probes.q: What pattern of trajectory on a growth chart defines growth faltering?
probes.a: A flat or falling weight curve over two consecutive visits, or crossing two major centile lines downwards.

rubric.text: Selects sex-appropriate WHO (0-5 yr) or IAP (5-18 yr) growth chart
Calculates and plots on gestational corrected age for preterm infants under 2 years
Accurately plots age on horizontal axis and measurement on vertical axis with neat dot
Interprets trajectory relative to centile channels and recognises flat curve or crossing centiles

teach.heading: Growth standards versus growth references
teach.body:
The WHO Child Growth Standards (0 to 5 years) describe how healthy children should grow under optimal environmental, nutritional, and health conditions, establishing a prescriptive standard.

In India, the revised Indian Academy of Pediatrics (IAP) charts are utilized for children aged 5 to 18 years to reflect physiological pubertal timing and genetic height potentials.

teach.heading: Corrected age calculation for prematurity
teach.body:
Infants born before 37 weeks of gestation must be plotted using corrected age to prevent false classification of malnutrition.

Corrected age is calculated by subtracting the weeks of prematurity from chronological age. For example, a 6-month-old infant born at 32 weeks has 8 weeks (2 months) of prematurity, so growth is plotted at 4 months.

teach.heading: Trajectory interpretation and warning patterns
teach.body:
A single point shows nutritional status at one moment, but trajectory indicates velocity. Normal growth parallels centile lines.

A horizontal curve (no gain), a downward curve (weight loss), or crossing two major centile lines downwards (such as dropping from the 50th to below the 15th centile) signifies acute growth faltering requiring urgent evaluation.

skill.ix.paed.cxr_approach.title: Systematic interpretation of the paediatric chest radiograph
skill.ix.paed.cxr_approach.oneLine: Assessing inspiratory adequacy, rotation, exposure, cardiothoracic ratio, and the ABCDE reading framework
skill.ix.paed.cxr_approach.why: Paediatric chest radiographs differ substantially from adult films due to thymic shadows, compliant chest walls, and rapid respiratory rates. Expiratory or rotated films mimic cardiomegaly and lung consolidation, leading to misdiagnosis of pneumonia and unnecessary antibiotics.
skill.ix.paed.cxr_approach.practice: Review five paediatric chest radiographs: count anterior and posterior ribs above the diaphragm, assess rotation from clavicular symmetry, calculate the cardiothoracic ratio, and identify the normal thymic sail sign.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting an expiratory film as diffuse pneumonia or pulmonary congestion when fewer than 6 anterior ribs are visible above the diaphragm.
Mistaking the normal triangular thymic shadow (sail sign or wave sign) for right upper lobe consolidation or mediastinal mass.
Diagnosing cardiomegaly on an anteroposterior (AP) supine film of an infant using adult cardiothoracic ratio cut-offs.

probes.q: How many anterior or posterior ribs should be visible above the right hemidiaphragm on a well-inspired paediatric chest radiograph?
probes.a: 6 anterior ribs or 9 to 10 posterior ribs above the right diaphragmatic dome.

probes.q: What is the normal upper limit of the cardiothoracic ratio on a chest radiograph in infants and children?
probes.a: Up to 0.55 in children and up to 0.60 in neonates and young infants on an AP film (compared to 0.50 in adults).

probes.q: How do you distinguish a normal thymic shadow from pathological mediastinal adenopathy on a paediatric chest X-ray?
probes.a: The thymus has smooth or wavy lateral borders (spinnaker sail sign or wave sign of Mulstein), does not displace the trachea, and merges smoothly with the cardiac silhouette without mass effect.

rubric.text: Evaluates technical adequacy: projection (AP vs PA), inspiratory effort (6 anterior / 9-10 posterior ribs), rotation, and penetration
Calculates cardiothoracic ratio and applies paediatric threshold (<0.55 in children, <0.60 in infants)
Follows systematic review: Airway, Bones, Cardiac, Diaphragm/Pleura, and Extrathoracic tissues
Distinguishes normal physiological thymic shadow (sail sign) from upper lobe consolidation

teach.heading: Technical adequacy: inspiration, rotation, and exposure
teach.body:
In neonates and young infants who cannot stand, an anteroposterior (AP) supine view is standard. Once the child sits or stands unsupported, a posteroanterior (PA) view is obtained.

A satisfactory inspiratory film shows the dome of the right diaphragm at the level of the 6th anterior rib or 9th to 10th posterior rib. In under-inflation, crowded bronchovascular markings mimic pneumonia.

teach.heading: Rotation and exposure evaluation
teach.body:
Rotation is assessed by ensuring equal distance between the medial ends of the clavicles and the thoracic vertebral spinous processes.

On a correctly exposed film, intervertebral disc spaces are faintly visible through the upper cardiac shadow down to T3 or T4. Overexposure burns out delicate lung parenchymal markings.

teach.heading: Cardiothoracic ratio and the paediatric thymus
teach.body:
The cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) is the maximal transverse cardiac diameter divided by the internal thoracic diameter at the diaphragm. Normal CTR is up to 0.55 in children and up to 0.60 in neonates.

The normal thymus is prominent under 2 years, appearing as a triangular sail-like density in the right superior mediastinum (sail sign) or exhibiting gentle rib indentations (wave sign).

skill.ix.paed.cxr_pneumonia_collapse.title: Paediatric chest X-ray: consolidation, collapse, and the silhouette sign
skill.ix.paed.cxr_pneumonia_collapse.oneLine: Identifying air bronchograms, lobar collapse signs, and localising lesions using the cardiac and diaphragmatic borders
skill.ix.paed.cxr_pneumonia_collapse.why: Differentiating alveolar consolidation from atelectasis and localising pulmonary opacities are core competencies in managing paediatric lower respiratory tract infections. The silhouette sign localises opacities to the middle lobe or lingula without requiring lateral radiographs.
skill.ix.paed.cxr_pneumonia_collapse.practice: Examine radiographs showing right middle lobe consolidation, left lower lobe collapse, and pleural effusion, mapping the obliteration of cardiac and diaphragmatic borders.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise that right middle lobe collapse obscures the right heart border while lower lobe collapse obscures the hemidiaphragm.
Confusing volume loss in collapse (tracheal and mediastinal shift towards the lesion) with mass effect in pleural effusion or pneumothorax (shift away).
Assuming every pulmonary opacity is bacterial pneumonia and missing foreign body aspiration causing post-obstructive atelectasis.

probes.q: What is the silhouette sign on a chest radiograph, and what anatomical lesion does obliteration of the right cardiac border indicate?
probes.a: The silhouette sign is the loss of a normal anatomical boundary when adjacent tissue has identical radiographic density. Loss of the right heart border indicates right middle lobe consolidation or collapse.

probes.q: Which anatomical lobe is affected when the left heart border is obscured on a frontal chest radiograph?
probes.a: The lingular segment of the left upper lobe.

probes.q: How do you distinguish pulmonary collapse from a large pleural effusion on chest radiograph when both produce opaque hemithorax?
probes.a: Collapse causes volume loss with tracheal, cardiac, and mediastinal shift towards the affected side; pleural effusion causes mass effect with mediastinal shift away from the lesion.

rubric.text: Identifies radiographic hallmarks of consolidation: homogenous opacity, ill-defined margins, and air bronchograms
Applies the silhouette sign to localise lesion: right heart border (RML), left heart border (lingula), hemidiaphragm (lower lobe)
Evaluates signs of collapse: rib crowding, elevated hemidiaphragm, and mediastinal shift towards opacity
Screens for complications including pleural effusion, pneumatocele, lung abscess, or cavitation

teach.heading: Consolidation and the air bronchogram
teach.body:
Alveolar consolidation occurs when inflammatory exudate replaces alveolar air. Radiographically, this appears as an ill-defined patchy or homogenous opacity.

Air-filled bronchi traversing non-aerated alveoli stand out as branching tubular lucencies known as air bronchograms, confirming that the pathology resides within the lung parenchyma rather than the pleural space.

teach.heading: The silhouette sign in lobar localisation
teach.body:
Two structures of identical water density in contact eliminate their shared radiographic interface. This silhouette sign localises disease precisely on a frontal film.

Obliteration of the right cardiac border indicates right middle lobe disease. Obliteration of the left cardiac border indicates lingular segment disease. Obliteration of the posterior hemidiaphragm indicates lower lobe disease.

skill.ix.paed.cxr_chd.title: Paediatric chest X-ray in congenital heart disease
skill.ix.paed.cxr_chd.oneLine: Distinguishing plethoric from oligaemic lung fields, cardiac silhouettes, and the boot-shaped heart
skill.ix.paed.cxr_chd.why: Chest radiography provides immediate classification of congenital heart disease into acyanotic versus cyanotic lesions based on cardiomegaly and pulmonary blood flow. Recognizing increased pulmonary vascularity (plethora) or decreased vascularity (oligaemia) narrows complex congenital lesions to two primary physiological pathways.
skill.ix.paed.cxr_chd.practice: Review chest radiographs of ventricular septal defect and Tetralogy of Fallot: assess pulmonary plethora versus oligaemia, measure the cardiothoracic ratio, and identify the upturned cardiac apex.
pitfalls: Failing to evaluate the peripheral one-third of the lung fields, where visible pulmonary vessels indicate true pulmonary plethora.
Confusing the boot-shaped heart of Tetralogy of Fallot (normal or mildly enlarged heart with upturned apex) with marked cardiomegaly.
Overlooking an associated right-sided aortic arch, which is present in 25 percent of children with Tetralogy of Fallot.

probes.q: What radiographic appearance of pulmonary blood flow is typical of left-to-right cardiac shunts such as VSD or PDA?
probes.a: Pulmonary plethora (increased pulmonary vascular markings extending into the peripheral third of the lung fields).

probes.q: Describe the characteristic cardiac silhouette in Tetralogy of Fallot on a frontal chest radiograph.
probes.a: The boot-shaped heart (coeur-en-sabot), characterized by right ventricular hypertrophy lifting the apex above the diaphragm, a concavity at the pulmonary artery bay, and oligaemic lung fields.

probes.q: What does pulmonary oligaemia indicate on a paediatric chest radiograph, and which cyanotic heart defect is the classic example?
probes.a: Decreased pulmonary blood flow due to right ventricular outflow tract obstruction; Tetralogy of Fallot is the classic example.

rubric.text: Classifies pulmonary vascularity correctly into plethoric (increased) or oligaemic (decreased)
Assesses cardiac chamber enlargement and measures cardiothoracic ratio (>0.55 indicating cardiomegaly)
Recognises the boot-shaped heart of Tetralogy of Fallot: upturned apex and hollow pulmonary bay
Determines the side of the aortic arch and tracheal indentation

teach.heading: Evaluating pulmonary vascularity: plethora versus oligaemia
teach.body:
Pulmonary vascularity is the most critical feature on a cardiac radiograph. In pulmonary plethora, end-on pulmonary vessels are larger than the accompanying bronchus and extend into the lateral third of the thorax.

Plethora indicates high pulmonary blood flow typical of left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, PDA) or cyanotic lesions with unrestricted flow (TGA, truncus arteriosus).

teach.heading: Pulmonary oligaemia and cyanotic heart disease
teach.body:
Pulmonary oligaemia appears as abnormally dark, hyperlucent lung fields with small, stringy, attenuated hilar vessels.

Oligaemia indicates severe obstruction to pulmonary blood flow, classically observed in Tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary atresia, and tricuspid atresia. It confirms that cyanosis is due to reduced pulmonary perfusion.

skill.ix.paed.neck_croup_epiglottitis.title: Soft tissue neck radiograph in acute paediatric stridor
skill.ix.paed.neck_croup_epiglottitis.oneLine: AP steeple sign in viral croup versus lateral thumbprint sign in acute epiglottitis
skill.ix.paed.neck_croup_epiglottitis.why: Acute inflammatory upper airway obstruction is a life-threatening emergency in young children. Distinguishing subglottic narrowing in croup from supraglottic swelling in acute epiglottitis prevents catastrophic airway instrumentation, while ensuring unnecessary imaging never delays airway stabilization in an unstable child.
skill.ix.paed.neck_croup_epiglottitis.practice: Review AP and lateral soft tissue neck films of croup and epiglottitis: identify subglottic pencil-tipping, inspect the vallecula and epiglottic shadow, and check the retropharyngeal space width.
pitfalls: Sending an agitated child with acute stridor and suspected epiglottitis unescorted to the radiology suite, precipitating acute complete airway obstruction.
Misinterpreting physiological retropharyngeal soft tissue thickening on an expiratory neck film as a retropharyngeal abscess.
Relying on radiographs to diagnose croup when the clinical triad of barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor is already diagnostic.

probes.q: What classic sign is seen on an AP soft tissue neck radiograph in a child with viral croup?
probes.a: The steeple sign (or pencil-tip sign), representing symmetrical subglottic tracheal narrowing.

probes.q: What classic sign is seen on a lateral neck radiograph in acute epiglottitis?
probes.a: The thumbprint sign (or thumb sign), caused by an enlarged, rounded, oedematous epiglottis projecting into the pharyngeal airway.

probes.q: Why is radiographic examination contraindicated in an unstable child with suspected epiglottitis?
probes.a: Any distress, crying, or forced neck extension during positioning can trigger acute laryngospasm and complete respiratory arrest; the airway must be secured in the operating theatre first.

rubric.text: Confirms clinical stability and never sends an unstable or struggling child to the radiology suite
Identifies the AP steeple sign of symmetrical subglottic tracheal tapering in croup
Recognises the lateral thumbprint sign of swollen epiglottis and aryepiglottic fold thickening in epiglottitis
Examines retropharyngeal space thickness on true inspiratory extension to exclude retropharyngeal abscess

teach.heading: Clinical safety and role of imaging in stridor
teach.body:
Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is typically a clinical diagnosis. Radiography is reserved for atypical presentations, suspected foreign body aspiration, or failure of standard nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone therapy.

In suspected epiglottitis, imaging is strictly contraindicated if airway compromise is present. A physician skilled in paediatric intubation must accompany the child at all times.

teach.heading: The steeple sign in subglottic croup
teach.body:
On an anteroposterior (AP) neck film, the normal subglottic airway has square shoulders formed by the inferior borders of the vocal cords.

In croup, circumferential oedema of the subglottic mucosa obliterates these lateral shoulders. The lumen tapers gradually into an inverted V-shape resembling a church steeple (steeple sign or pencil-tip sign).

teach.heading: The thumbprint sign in supraglottic epiglottitis
teach.body:
On a true lateral soft tissue neck view, the normal epiglottis appears as a thin, graceful leaflet with an air-filled vallecula anteriorly.

In acute epiglottitis, profound cellulitis expands the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds into a rounded, bulbous soft tissue mass projecting like a thumb into the hypopharynx (thumbprint sign), with obliteration of the vallecula.

skill.ix.paed.axr_acute_abdomen.title: Paediatric abdominal radiograph: intestinal obstruction and perforation
skill.ix.paed.axr_acute_abdomen.oneLine: Air-fluid levels in obstruction, free gas under the diaphragm in perforation, and pneumatosis in NEC
skill.ix.paed.axr_acute_abdomen.why: Plain abdominal radiography is the primary emergent imaging modality for paediatric surgical emergencies, including neonatal intestinal atresia, malrotation with volvulus, intussusception, and necrotising enterocolitis. Recognizing pneumoperitoneum or intramural gas directs urgent laparotomy before intestinal necrosis and septic shock occur.
skill.ix.paed.axr_acute_abdomen.practice: Examine supine and erect paediatric abdominal radiographs: count dilated small bowel loops, assess the step-ladder air-fluid pattern, detect crescentic free gas under the diaphragm, and identify linear pneumatosis intestinalis.
pitfalls: Failing to obtain an erect or cross-table lateral decubitus view when intestinal perforation is suspected, missing small volumes of free peritoneal air.
Misinterpreting normal crying infant aerophagia (diffuse gas throughout the bowel) as mechanical intestinal obstruction.
Overlooking subtle linear or bubbly intramural lucencies of pneumatosis intestinalis in a premature infant with abdominal distension.

probes.q: What radiographic finding on an erect abdominal X-ray indicates intestinal perforation?
probes.a: Free subdiaphragmatic air (pneumoperitoneum), appearing as a crescent of gas under the dome of the diaphragm.

probes.q: What radiographic pattern characterizes mechanical small bowel obstruction on an erect abdominal film?
probes.a: Centrally located dilated bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels arranged in a stepped or step-ladder pattern, and absent rectal gas.

probes.q: What is the hallmark radiographic sign of necrotising enterocolitis (NEC) in a preterm infant?
probes.a: Pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas appearing as linear or bubbly lucencies within the bowel wall), and branching portal venous gas.

rubric.text: Inspects subdiaphragmatic spaces and peritoneal margins on erect/decubitus film to detect free gas
Identifies mechanical obstruction: dilated bowel loops, step-ladder air-fluid levels, and rectal air absence
Scrutinizes bowel wall for pneumatosis intestinalis and liver shadow for branching portal venous gas
Selects appropriate projections: supine and left lateral decubitus in unstable infants

teach.heading: Normal paediatric bowel gas patterns
teach.body:
In healthy newborns, swallowed air reaches the stomach within 15 minutes, small bowel within 3 to 6 hours, and rectum within 12 to 24 hours.

Healthy infants exhibit a mosaic of polygonal gas-filled bowel loops throughout the abdomen without prominent fluid levels. Absence of bowel gas beyond the duodenum signals complete neonatal intestinal atresia (double bubble sign).

teach.heading: Mechanical intestinal obstruction
teach.body:
Mechanical obstruction produces proximal bowel dilation and fluid stasis. On an erect film, air-fluid levels greater than 2 to 3 cm in width arranged in a stepped ladder pattern are diagnostic.

Colonic obstruction exhibits peripheral dilatation with preserved haustra, whereas small bowel loops occupy central abdomen and show circumferential plicae circulares (valvulae conniventes).

teach.heading: Perforation and necrotising enterocolitis
teach.body:
Pneumoperitoneum produces a lucent subdiaphragmatic crescent on erect views, or the football sign (air outlining the entire peritoneal cavity) on supine films.

In necrotising enterocolitis, mucosal breakdown allows gas-producing bacteria to invade the submucosa, generating linear or curvilinear intramural lucencies known as pneumatosis intestinalis.

Digestive System: Evaluation of the Acute Pediatric Abdomen and Intestinal Obstruction

skill.ix.paed.xray_rickets.title: Radiographic evaluation of paediatric rickets
skill.ix.paed.xray_rickets.oneLine: Metaphyseal cupping, fraying, splaying, widened physis, and distinguishing active from healing rickets
skill.ix.paed.xray_rickets.why: Skeletal radiographs of the wrist and knee provide objective confirmation of nutritional and metabolic rickets. Identifying metaphyseal cupping, fraying, and splaying confirms active failure of mineralization, while observing the provisional line of calcification documents therapeutic response to vitamin D and calcium.
skill.ix.paed.xray_rickets.practice: Examine wrist and knee radiographs of active rickets: measure the distance between the epiphysis and metaphysis, identify metaphyseal cupping and fraying, and detect the reappearance of the zone of provisional calcification during healing.
pitfalls: Ordering whole-body skeletal surveys instead of focused radiographs of the most rapidly growing growth plates (distal radius and ulna, knee).
Mistaking normal physiological cortical bowing of toddler legs for rachitic deformities without evaluating metaphyseal mineralization.
Failing to recognise greenstick or pseudo-fractures (Looser zones) along the inner cortical margins.

probes.q: What are the three classic radiographic changes at the metaphysis in active rickets?
probes.a: Cupping (concavity of the metaphysis), fraying (irregular, brush-like margins), and splaying (widening of the metaphyseal end).

probes.q: Which anatomical sites are the most sensitive for demonstrating early radiographic signs of rickets and why?
probes.a: The wrists (distal radius and ulna) and knees (distal femur and proximal tibia), because these are the most rapidly growing growth plates in infancy and early childhood.

probes.q: What is the earliest radiographic sign that rickets is healing after vitamin D treatment?
probes.a: Reappearance of a dense, white transverse line of provisional calcification across the metaphysis separated from the shaft by a radiolucent band.

rubric.text: Identifies the classic rachitic triad at the growth plate: cupping, fraying, and splaying
Measures increased radiolucent distance between the epiphyseal ossification centre and metaphysis
Evaluates diaphyseal rarefaction, cortical thinning, bowing deformities, and greenstick fractures
Recognises the zone of provisional calcification as proof of therapeutic healing after vitamin D therapy

teach.heading: Pathophysiology and optimal radiographic views
teach.body:
Rickets is a disease of growing bone caused by failure of osteoid mineralization at the epiphyseal plate. Consequently, radiographic signs are most prominent at rapidly growing skeletal sites.

The single best view is a posteroanterior (PA) radiograph of the wrist showing the distal radius and ulna. Radiographs of the knees (distal femur and proximal tibia) provide supplementary sensitivity.

teach.heading: The classic metaphyseal radiographic triad
teach.body:
Under normal conditions, the metaphysis terminates in a crisp, smooth transverse margin. In rickets, accumulation of non-calcified osteoid causes distinct changes:

1. Cupping: the metaphyseal margin becomes concave rather than flat. 2. Fraying: the border loses definition, appearing ragged and brush-like. 3. Splaying: the metaphyseal end expands transversely due to weight-bearing stress on unmineralised bone.

teach.heading: Physis widening and healing response
teach.body:
The radiolucent zone between the epiphyseal ossification centre and the metaphysis widens significantly due to hypertrophy of non-calcified cartilage cells.

Within 2 to 3 weeks of initiating therapeutic vitamin D, calcium salts deposit in the unmineralized osteoid, producing a dense white line known as the zone of provisional calcification, proving biological healing.

skill.annex.paed.normal_biochemical_valu.title: Paediatric normal biochemical and physiological reference values
skill.annex.paed.normal_biochemical_valu.oneLine: Serum electrolytes, calcium, glucose, renal indices, ABG parameters, and urine output thresholds
skill.annex.paed.normal_biochemical_valu.why: Children are not small adults: their normal electrolyte concentrations, metabolic rates, acid-base balances, and renal clearance values vary dynamically with age. Applying adult reference intervals to infants results in missed hyponatraemia, overlooked hypoglycaemia, and inappropriate fluid prescription.
skill.annex.paed.normal_biochemical_valu.practice: Look up serum sodium, potassium, calcium, blood glucose, creatinine, and arterial blood gas values for an infant and child, and calculate hourly urine output in mL/kg/hour for a 12 kg toddler.
pitfalls: Applying adult serum creatinine cut-offs (such as 1.0 mg/dL) to an infant, missing advanced renal impairment when normal infant creatinine is 0.3 to 0.4 mg/dL.
Tolerating blood glucose levels between 40 and 50 mg/dL in young children when normal fasting values should exceed 50 to 60 mg/dL.
Calculating total urine volume without dividing by body weight and elapsed hours, obscuring true oliguria (less than 1 mL/kg/hour).

probes.q: What is the normal urine output in millilitres per kilogram per hour in children?
probes.a: Normal urine output is greater than 1 mL/kg/hour (oliguria is defined as less than 1 mL/kg/hour in infants and children).

probes.q: What are the normal reference ranges for serum sodium and potassium in children?
probes.a: Serum sodium is 135 to 150 mEq/L; serum potassium is 3.5 to 5.5 mEq/L.

probes.q: What are normal arterial blood gas (ABG) values for pH, PaCO2, and HCO3 in children?
probes.a: pH is 7.38 to 7.42; PaCO2 is 35 to 45 mm Hg; HCO3 is 22 to 28 mEq/L.

rubric.text: Applies paediatric reference values for sodium (135-150), potassium (3.5-5.5), and calcium (8.5-11 mg/dL)
Evaluates paediatric serum glucose (50-100 mg/dL) and age-adjusted creatinine (0.3-1.0 mg/dL)
Correctly references normal arterial blood gas values: pH 7.38-7.42, PaCO2 35-45, PaO2 80-100, HCO3 22-28
Calculates weight-based urine output and identifies oliguria (<1 mL/kg/h) or anuria (<0.5 mL/kg/h)

teach.heading: Arterial blood gas and urine output thresholds
Urine output thresholds in paediatric monitoring
teach.body:
Urine output must always be quantified per kilogram per hour (mL/kg/h).

Normal urine output in children is greater than 1 mL/kg/h. Oliguria is defined as less than 1 mL/kg/h, indicating prerenal hypoperfusion or renal failure. Anuria is less than 0.5 mL/kg/h. Polyuria exceeds 4 mL/kg/h, seen in diabetes insipidus or osmotic diuresis.

Reference Values: Laboratory Values in Pediatrics

skill.annex.paed.csf_analysis.title: Paediatric cerebrospinal fluid reference values and disease profiles
skill.annex.paed.csf_analysis.oneLine: Normal CSF across ages, distinguishing pyogenic, tuberculous, and viral profiles, and the traumatic tap correction
skill.annex.paed.csf_analysis.why: Prompt differentiation of bacterial, tuberculous, and viral central nervous system infections depends entirely on rapid cerebrospinal fluid cytology and biochemistry. Misinterpreting normal neonatal protein elevation or failing to calculate simultaneous CSF-to-blood glucose ratio leads to missed meningitis or unnecessary antimicrobial therapy.
skill.annex.paed.csf_analysis.practice: Compare simulated CSF laboratory reports for acute pyogenic, tuberculous, and viral meningitis against normal paediatric reference values, and apply the traumatic tap formula to correct a bloody CSF sample.
pitfalls: Interpreting CSF glucose in isolation without measuring simultaneous blood glucose, missing a low CSF-to-blood ratio in hyperglycaemic patients.
Applying adult CSF protein cut-offs (<40 mg/dL) to a neonate, in whom normal protein can physiologically reach up to 100 to 120 mg/dL.
Discarding a bloody CSF sample as uninterpretable instead of calculating the ratio of white to red blood cells (1 WBC per 500 RBCs).

probes.q: What is the normal cerebrospinal fluid leukocyte count and protein concentration in an infant over 1 month of age?
probes.a: Fewer than 5 leukocytes per cubic millimetre (all lymphocytes) and protein 10 to 40 mg/dL.

probes.q: What CSF findings characterize tuberculous meningitis in children?
probes.a: Marked lymphocytic pleocytosis (L > N), markedly elevated protein (often 100 to 500 mg/dL or higher), very low glucose (less than one-third of blood glucose), and a cobweb coagulum on standing.

probes.q: What normal CSF-to-blood glucose ratio is expected, and what threshold confirms hypoglycorrachia?
probes.a: Normal CSF glucose is roughly two-thirds (60 to 70 percent) of simultaneous blood glucose; a ratio below 0.5 (or below 0.6 in neonates) confirms hypoglycorrachia.

rubric.text: Applies age-adjusted normal CSF ranges: child (<5 cells, 10-40 mg/dL protein) vs neonate (up to 10-20 cells, up to 120 mg/dL protein)
Identifies pyogenic meningitis: marked neutrophil pleocytosis, very high protein, and markedly decreased glucose
Differentiates TBM (very high protein, low glucose, cobweb coagulum) from viral meningitis (normal glucose, moderate protein)
Applies traumatic tap correction: subtracts 1 WBC per 500 RBCs and 1 mg/dL protein per 1000 RBCs

teach.heading: Cerebrospinal fluid profiles in central nervous system infections
Traumatic tap interpretation and specific features
teach.body:
When a needle pierces a subdural venous plexus, blood enters the CSF. To distinguish true pleocytosis from peripheral contamination:

Allow 1 WBC per 500 RBCs. Deduct 1 mg/dL of protein per 1000 RBCs. In tuberculous meningitis, a delicate cobweb or spider-web coagulum forms when refrigerated, reflecting abundant fibrinogen.

skill.annex.paed.biomedical_waste.title: Biomedical waste segregation and colour coding in paediatric practice
skill.annex.paed.biomedical_waste.oneLine: Segregating anatomical, contaminated plastic, sharps, glass, and municipal waste under national guidelines
skill.annex.paed.biomedical_waste.why: Improper segregation of hospital waste transmits blood-borne pathogens (HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C) to healthcare workers and causes environmental contamination. Sorting at source into colour-coded containers is a statutory clinical standard and critical safety competency.
skill.annex.paed.biomedical_waste.practice: Classify 10 clinical items from a paediatric ward encounter (used cannula, blood-stained cotton swab, vaccine vial, scalp vein needle, medicine wrapper) into their respective colour-coded disposal receptacles.
pitfalls: Discarding needles or sharps into red or yellow plastic bags instead of puncture-proof white translucent containers, causing needle-stick injuries to handling staff.
Disposing of unsoiled paper wrappers, fruit peels, and food cartons into yellow bags, massively inflating expensive hazardous waste incineration volume.
Recapping used needles before disposal, which is the primary cause of preventable accidental percutaneous punctures.

probes.q: Which colour-coded receptacle is designated for anatomical waste and soiled cotton or gauze dressings?
probes.a: Yellow non-chlorinated plastic bags.

probes.q: Where should contaminated intravenous infusion sets, catheters, and plastic syringes without needles be discarded?
probes.a: Red plastic bags (for recyclable contaminated plastic waste).

probes.q: What container is mandatory for disposal of used needles, scalpels, and lancets?
probes.a: White translucent, puncture-proof, tamper-proof, and leak-proof sharps containers.

rubric.text: Immediately drops needles and blades into white puncture-proof sharps container without recapping
Routes anatomical waste, blood, body fluid-soaked cotton, and swabs into yellow incineration bags
Places recyclable plastics (IV tubing, catheters, urine bags, syringe barrels) into red bags
Directs broken medicine ampoules to blue boxes and general food/packaging waste to black/green bins

teach.heading: Principles of segregation at source
teach.body:
Biomedical waste management requires that waste be segregated at the exact point of generation. Once mixed, non-hazardous waste becomes hazardous, multiplying infection risks and incineration costs.

Healthcare staff must dispose of items immediately into dedicated receptacles without temporary storage on countertops or bedside trays.

rows: Soiled cotton, blood dressings, anatomical tissues
Contaminated plastics: IV sets, tubing, catheters, urine bags
Sharps: needles, syringes with fixed needles, scalpels, blades
Broken glassware, medicine vials, ampoules, metallic implants

teach.heading: Sharps handling and municipal waste
teach.body:
Needles must never be recapped, bent, broken, or handled by hand. Immediately after use, needles are placed directly into a white puncture-proof sharps container or destroyed using a needle burner.

Black or green bins are reserved exclusively for non-biomedical municipal waste (food scraps, vegetable peels, paper packaging, unsoiled cartons).

Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules: Guidelines for Colour-Coded Waste Segregation

skill.annex.paed.poisoning_antidotes.title: Paediatric emergency toxicology and antidote reference
skill.annex.paed.poisoning_antidotes.oneLine: Specific antidotes, dosing rationale, and emergency protocols for acute paediatric poisonings
skill.annex.paed.poisoning_antidotes.why: Accidental poisoning is a leading paediatric toxicological emergency. While general supportive stabilization (airway, breathing, circulation) is universally vital, timely administration of specific antidotes reverses cellular hypoxia, prevents irreversible hepatic or neurological necrosis, and prevents mortality.
skill.annex.paed.poisoning_antidotes.practice: Match 10 clinical toxin scenarios (paracetamol overdose, organophosphate cholinergic crisis, opioid apnea, iron ingestion) with their specific antidote, route, and clinical endpoint of therapy.
pitfalls: Withholding N-acetylcysteine in paracetamol overdose while awaiting delayed laboratory results when the ingestion occurred more than 8 hours prior.
Titrating atropine in organophosphate poisoning by pupil size alone instead of clearing of bronchial secretions and airway resistance.
Administering flumazenil routinely in mixed drug overdoses with tricyclic antidepressants, precipitating refractory fatal seizures.

probes.q: What is the specific antidote for acute acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning?
probes.a: N-acetylcysteine (NAC).

probes.q: What two drugs are used in the management of acute organophosphate poisoning?
probes.a: Atropine (antimuscarinic to dry secretions) and pralidoxime (oxime to reactivate acetylcholinesterase).

probes.q: Which oral antidote is used for autonomic storm in severe scorpion sting envenomation in India?
probes.a: Prazosin (alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist).

rubric.text: Identifies N-acetylcysteine as antidote for paracetamol and explains replenishment of glutathione
Administers atropine titrated to clear chest secretions and adds pralidoxime for nicotinic effects
Selects naloxone for opioid-induced hypoventilation and flumazenil for pure benzodiazepine coma
Identifies desferrioxamine for iron, BAL/EDTA for lead and arsenic, and methylene blue for methaemoglobinaemia

teach.heading: Principles of antidotal therapy in children
teach.body:
Supportive management following airway, breathing, and circulation takes precedence in all paediatric poisonings.

Antidotes act by competitive receptor antagonism (naloxone, flumazenil), biochemical replenishment (N-acetylcysteine for glutathione), heavy metal chelation (desferrioxamine, BAL), or toxin conversion (methylene blue).

rows: Completion of protocol and normal ALT
Central cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, metHb >30%
Maintain urine output to avoid nephrotoxicity

skill.tx.paed.resuscitation_drugs.title: Paediatric emergency resuscitation pharmacology
skill.tx.paed.resuscitation_drugs.oneLine: Adrenaline, atropine, adenosine, calcium gluconate, and sodium bicarbonate in paediatric life support
skill.tx.paed.resuscitation_drugs.why: Cardiac arrest in children is typically secondary to progressive asphyxia rather than primary ventricular arrhythmias. Rapid administration of weight-appropriate emergency resuscitation drugs re-establishes coronary and cerebral perfusion, while dosing errors cause severe hypertension, arrhythmias, or irreversible neurological death.

steps.text: Recognize cardiac arrest (unresponsiveness, absent breathing or agonal gasps, absent central pulse within 10 seconds). Start high-quality CPR (100 to 120 compressions per minute, compression-to-ventilation ratio 15:2 with 2 rescuers) and provide 100 percent oxygen via bag-valve-mask.
Establish rapid vascular access: place a peripheral IV catheter; if vascular access is not achieved within 60 to 90 seconds, insert an intraosseous (IO) needle into the proximal anteromedial tibia.

For cardiac arrest (asystole, pulseless electrical activity, or shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation/pulseless VT): administer adrenaline (epinephrine) 1:10,000 solution at 0.1 mL/kg (10 micrograms/kg) IV or IO. Flush immediately with 5 mL of normal saline. Repeat every 3 to 5 minutes as long as pulselessness persists.

For symptomatic bradycardia with poor perfusion unresponsive to oxygenation and ventilation: administer adrenaline 0.1 mL/kg of 1:10,000 IV/IO. If bradycardia is vagally mediated or secondary to primary AV block, administer atropine 0.02 mg/kg IV/IO (minimum dose 0.1 mg, maximum single dose 0.5 mg).

For supraventricular tachycardia (narrow-complex tachycardia, heart rate >220/min in infants or >180/min in children, no P waves, no heart rate variability): after failed vagal manoeuvres, administer adenosine 0.1 mg/kg (maximum initial dose 6 mg) as a rapid IV push over 1 to 2 seconds into a large proximal vein, immediately followed by a rapid 5 to 10 mL normal saline flush. If no conversion after 2 minutes, double the dose to 0.2 mg/kg (maximum 12 mg).

For documented hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, or calcium-channel blocker toxicity: administer 10 percent calcium gluconate 1 mL/kg (100 mg/kg) slowly IV over 10 minutes with continuous electrocardiographic monitoring. Stop the infusion if bradycardia develops.

For severe prolonged arrest with documented profound metabolic acidosis or hyperkalaemic arrest: administer sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mEq/kg (1 to 2 mL/kg of 8.4 percent solution) slow IV bolus, only after adequate alveolar ventilation is fully established to blow off generated carbon dioxide.

For emergency volume resuscitation in haemorrhagic shock or severe anaemia: administer packed red blood cells at 10 to 15 mL/kg, fresh frozen plasma at 10 mL/kg for coagulopathy, and platelet concentrate at 1 unit per 10 kg body weight for severe thrombocytopenia with active bleeding.

skill.tx.paed.resuscitation_drugs.dosingNote: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses here are quoted from the cited national or guideline document so a student can check them; the treating team's own protocol and the current formulary decide what is given.
skill.tx.paed.resuscitation_drugs.practice: Calculate the exact volume in millilitres of adrenaline 1:10,000, atropine, adenosine, and 10 percent calcium gluconate for an 8 kg infant in emergency resuscitation on paper.
pitfalls: Injecting the concentrated 1:1000 adrenaline solution IV instead of the diluted 1:10,000 resuscitation solution, delivering a fatal tenfold overdose.
Administering adenosine via a slow peripheral drip instead of an immediate rapid bolus followed by a rapid saline flush, causing enzymatic breakdown in blood before reaching the heart.
Infusing sodium bicarbonate without adequate bag-mask ventilation, which causes intracellular acidosis as generated CO2 diffuses across cell membranes.

probes.q: What is the intravenous dose and concentration of adrenaline (epinephrine) in paediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation?
probes.a: 0.1 mL/kg of 1:10,000 solution (equal to 10 micrograms/kg) given IV or IO every 3 to 5 minutes.

probes.q: How must adenosine be administered in supraventricular tachycardia, and why?
probes.a: Rapid IV push over 1 to 2 seconds followed immediately by a rapid 5 to 10 mL saline flush, because its plasma half-life is under 10 seconds.

probes.q: What volume of packed red blood cells (PCV) is infused for emergency paediatric transfusion?
probes.a: 10 to 15 mL/kg, which typically raises the haemoglobin concentration by roughly 3 g/dL.

rubric.text: Administers adrenaline 1:10,000 at 0.1 mL/kg IV/IO with saline flush every 3-5 minutes during pulseless arrest
Delivers adenosine 0.1 mg/kg as a rapid 1-2 second push followed by immediate rapid saline flush
Infuses 10% calcium gluconate slowly over 10 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring
Ensures adequate alveolar ventilation prior to sodium bicarbonate administration to prevent CO2 retention

teach.heading: Adrenaline pharmacodynamics in paediatric arrest
teach.body:
Adrenaline is the primary pharmacological agent in paediatric cardiac arrest. Its alpha-1 adrenergic vasoconstrictor effect increases aortic diastolic pressure, driving coronary and cerebral perfusion.

The resuscitation dose is 0.1 mL/kg of 1:10,000 solution (10 mcg/kg). Higher doses do not improve survival to discharge and exacerbate myocardial oxygen demand.

teach.heading: Adenosine kinetics and administration technique
teach.body:
Adenosine acts on A1 receptors in the AV node, causing transient conduction block that breaks re-entrant supraventricular tachycardias.

Because erythrocyte adenosine deaminase degrades the drug with a half-life under 10 seconds, it must be injected as a rapid IV push into the most proximal vein available, followed instantly by a 5 to 10 mL saline flush.

rows: Repeat every 3-5 min with saline flush
Min dose 0.1 mg, max single 0.5 mg
Rapid push with immediate saline flush

skill.tx.paed.anticonvulsants.title: Medical management of paediatric acute seizures and status epilepticus
skill.tx.paed.anticonvulsants.oneLine: Stepwise emergency algorithm: first-line benzodiazepines, second-line IV loading, and neonatal phenobarbitone
skill.tx.paed.anticonvulsants.why: Prolonged convulsive seizures lasting more than 5 minutes become increasingly refractory to standard therapy and cause excitotoxic neuronal death, cerebral oedema, and systemic hyperpyrexia. Implementing a timed, stepwise protocol terminates seizures promptly while avoiding respiratory depression.

steps.text: 0 to 5 minutes (Emergency stabilization): maintain airway, position child in recovery position, deliver 100 percent oxygen via non-rebreather mask, and check bedside capillary blood glucose immediately. If hypoglycaemic, administer 2 mL/kg of 10 percent dextrose IV bolus.

5 to 10 minutes (First-line benzodiazepine): if generalised convulsion persists beyond 5 minutes, administer IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg) slowly over 2 minutes, or IV diazepam 0.2 to 0.3 mg/kg (maximum 10 mg) at a rate of 2 mg per minute.
If intravenous access is not yet secured: administer per-rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg (maximum 10 mg) using a syringe or rectal tube, or buccal midazolam 0.2 to 0.3 mg/kg.

10 to 15 minutes (Second benzodiazepine dose): if convulsion continues at 10 minutes, repeat the same dose of benzodiazepine once only. Prepare bag-valve-mask and suction equipment at the bedside to manage possible respiratory depression.

15 to 30 minutes (Second-line non-sedating loading infusion): if seizure continues at 15 minutes (established status epilepticus), initiate second-line IV infusion over 15 to 20 minutes without waiting for a third benzodiazepine dose. Options include: IV levetiracetam 40 to 60 mg/kg (maximum 3000 mg), IV fosphenytoin or phenytoin 20 mg/kg diluted in normal saline (infusion rate not exceeding 1 mg/kg/min or 50 mg/min; never mix in dextrose), or IV sodium valproate 20 to 40 mg/kg.

Neonatal seizure exception: in neonates (under 28 days of life), the first-line anticonvulsant of choice is intravenous phenobarbitone 20 mg/kg loading dose infused slowly over 15 minutes. If seizures persist, give an additional 10 to 20 mg/kg (up to 40 mg/kg total) before adding phenytoin.

Greater than 30 minutes (Refractory status epilepticus): if seizure activity continues beyond 30 minutes, alert paediatric intensive care, prepare for endotracheal intubation, and initiate continuous IV anaesthetic infusions (midazolam infusion 0.1 to 2 mg/kg/h or propofol or thiopentone).

skill.tx.paed.anticonvulsants.dosingNote: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses here are quoted from the cited national or guideline document so a student can check them; the treating team's own protocol and the current formulary decide what is given.
skill.tx.paed.anticonvulsants.practice: Rehearse the timed 0-5-10-15-30 minute status epilepticus protocol for an 18 kg child, calculating exact volumes for IV lorazepam, rectal diazepam, IV levetiracetam, and phenytoin.
pitfalls: Administering more than two doses of benzodiazepines before initiating second-line anticonvulsants, causing severe respiratory arrest without stopping the seizure.
Diluting phenytoin in 5 percent dextrose solution, causing immediate crystallization and loss of active drug in the IV tubing.
Failing to check capillary blood glucose immediately, treating hypoglycaemic convulsions with repeated antiepileptic drugs instead of dextrose.

probes.q: What is the first-line medication class for terminating an acute convulsive seizure lasting more than 5 minutes in a child?
probes.a: Benzodiazepines (intravenous lorazepam, intravenous/rectal diazepam, or buccal midazolam).

probes.q: What is the drug of first choice for neonatal seizures, and what is its loading dose?
probes.a: Intravenous phenobarbitone, at a loading dose of 20 mg/kg.

probes.q: Why must phenytoin never be diluted in 5 percent dextrose solution?
probes.a: Dextrose solutions have an acidic pH that causes phenytoin to precipitate immediately into insoluble crystals, blocking the infusion and preventing drug delivery.

rubric.text: Assesses airway, breathing, and bedside glucose (0-5 min) before drug administration
Administers first-line benzodiazepine (lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg or diazepam 0.2-0.3 mg/kg) at 5 min
Limits benzodiazepine to a maximum of two doses to prevent respiratory depression
Initiates second-line non-sedating antiepileptic (levetiracetam, phenytoin, or valproate) by 15 min
Selects phenobarbitone (20 mg/kg IV) as the specific first-line loading drug in neonatal seizures

teach.heading: Physiological rationale for timed intervention
teach.body:
Prolonged seizures cause GABA-A receptor internalization and NMDA receptor upregulation, rendering benzodiazepines progressively ineffective after 15 to 30 minutes.

Simultaneously, hyperpyrexia, systemic lactic acidosis, and massive cerebral metabolic demand exhaust cellular energy stores. Early protocolized termination protects cognitive function.

rows: Airway, oxygen, bedside blood glucose check
Treat glucose <50 mg/dL with 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg
IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg or IV diazepam 0.2-0.3 mg/kg
Rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg if no IV line

teach.heading: Neonatal seizures and drug compatibility rules
teach.body:
In neonates, GABA-A receptor activation produces excitatory rather than inhibitory chloride currents, making phenobarbitone (20 mg/kg IV) superior to benzodiazepines.

Phenytoin requires an alkaline pH for solubility. Infusing phenytoin in 5 percent dextrose precipitates microcrystals, risking fatal embolisation. Phenytoin must be diluted exclusively in normal saline.

asks.text: Name, age and sex of the child, and who is giving the history.
Reliability of the informant, usually the mother, and who looks after the child by day.
Residence, rural or urban, and distance from the nearest hospital.
Socioeconomic background and parental occupation, which affect nutrition, overcrowding and follow-up.
Immunisation status in brief, to be detailed later, since infection risk runs through this disease.

skill.history.nephrotic.particulars.body: Particulars in a puffy child do more work than in most paediatric cases, because age alone shifts the likely cause before any symptom is weighed.
keyPoints: Age is the single most informative particular. Disease beginning in the preschool years is most often the idiopathic, steroid-sensitive form. Onset in the first year of life points towards a congenital or genetic cause, and onset in later childhood or adolescence should prompt a search for secondary or atypical disease.
Sex and birth order matter less for the diagnosis, but record them exactly, since referral letters and growth charts follow this child for years through repeated relapses.
Note who brings the child and who noticed the swelling first. The mother usually reports the morning puffiness, and her account of the sequence is the backbone of the history.
Residence and distance from care decide follow-up planning from the first visit. A family that travels far needs urine dipsticks at home and a clear written plan for relapse, not just a prescription.
skill.history.nephrotic.particulars.oneLine: Age first, informant next, distance from care last
pitfalls: Writing the age without the informant, so a later reader cannot judge the history.
Treating particulars as booking clerical work and missing that preschool onset is itself a diagnostic clue.

probes.a: The typical age group for idiopathic steroid-sensitive disease, with onset in infancy or adolescence counting as atypical.
probes.q: What does the age of onset tell you in a child with nephrotic-range swelling?

probes.a: Who noticed the swelling, who looks after the child, and how far the family lives from the hospital, because relapse care depends on it.
probes.q: Beyond age and sex, what two particulars change your management plan?

sources.locator: nephrotic_syndrome_paediatric: clinicalPearls
Nephrotic syndrome: age distribution and classification

skill.history.nephrotic.particulars.title: Particulars of the oedematous child
skill.history.nephrotic.particulars.why: Age sets the pre-test probability of steroid-sensitive disease before a single symptom is described, and the informant and distance from care decide how relapse follow-up can realistically be organised.

asks.text: Past episodes of similar swelling, and how each episode was treated and how long it lasted.
Recent infections: sore throat, skin sores, urinary complaints, tuberculosis contact, and worm infestation.
Immunisation history in full, including pneumococcal vaccine, since these children carry extra infection risk.
Dietary recall with salt intake, appetite, and any recent weight gain the mother noticed on the same clothes.
Drugs the child takes or recently took, including steroids, and any known drug allergy.
Family history of kidney disease, swelling, early hearing loss, or consanguinity.

skill.history.nephrotic.background.body: The background history sorts triggers from mimics and prepares the ground for steroids: what set this off, what the immune status is, and what runs in the family.
keyPoints: Ask about each past episode of swelling in detail. A first episode is worked up differently from a relapse, and the response to earlier steroids predicts the response now.

Ask about recent sore throat, skin sores and dark or cola-coloured urine. A nephritic illness after streptococcal infection is the closest mimic, and it announces itself through blood and pressure rather than pure swelling.
Take the full immunisation history. Children with nephrotic syndrome are prone to pneumococcal infection, and missing vaccines change the prevention plan.
Record the diet with salt in mind rather than protein alone. Added salt worsens oedema, while overzealous protein restriction harms a growing child, so find out what the child actually eats.
List every drug, recent or current. Steroids already taken elsewhere, diuretics, and nephrotoxic medicines all alter the picture and the plan.

Draw out the family kidney story, including consanguinity. Disease in infancy, deafness, or several affected relatives points towards inherited causes that need referral rather than repeated steroid courses.
skill.history.nephrotic.background.oneLine: Triggers, vaccines, salt, drugs and the family kidney story
pitfalls: Skipping the immunisation history and only discovering the missing pneumococcal vaccine during a febrile episode.
Missing a recent sore throat with dark urine, which reframes the whole case as nephritic.
Forgetting consanguinity and family deafness, the quiet clues to inherited disease.

probes.a: Whether this is a first episode or a relapse, and how earlier episodes responded to steroids.
probes.q: What past-history question most changes your plan in a swollen child?

probes.a: Recent streptococcal sore throat or skin sores with dark urine and raised pressure, favouring a nephritic mimic.
probes.q: Which recent infection history would make you doubt nephrotic syndrome?

probes.a: Consanguinity, infantile onset, deafness or several affected relatives, suggesting inherited disease needing referral.
probes.q: What family history points away from simple steroid-sensitive disease?

skill.history.nephrotic.background.title: Background history in nephrotic syndrome
skill.history.nephrotic.background.why: Relapse versus first episode, vaccine gaps, salt load and family patterns each change the immediate plan, and none of them can be recovered from the presenting complaint alone.

asks.text: Where the swelling was first noticed, and the exact day-by-day spread from face to legs to belly.
Morning versus evening pattern: worse around the eyes on waking, worse in the feet by evening.
Urine: frothy appearance, colour, volume passed, and any burning, bedwetting or cola-coloured urine.
Weight change: recent gain noticed on the same clothes or scale, and appetite alongside it.
Associated features: belly pain, breathlessness, cough, fever, vomiting, loose stools, or reduced play.
Trigger in the preceding weeks: fever, cold, sore throat, skin sores, or a recent vaccination.
What treatment has already been given: diuretics, steroids, antibiotics, or home remedies.

skill.history.nephrotic.illness.body: The history of a nephrotic child is the story of swelling told in order, with the urine as the second witness. Sequence matters more than any single symptom.
keyPoints: Start where the mother started: puffiness around the eyes noticed in the morning. Trace its spread to the feet, legs and belly over days to weeks, since a nephrotic course builds gradually rather than overnight.
Ask about the morning-evening shift. Oedema that is periorbital on waking and settles to the dependent parts by evening is the classic rhythm, and it helps separate renal swelling from other causes.
Ask directly about frothy urine and urine volume. Parents report swelling, not urine findings, yet persistent froth and reduced volume are the bedside echoes of heavy protein loss.
Ask about weight gain on the same scale or the same clothes. A child who eats poorly but gains weight is retaining fluid, and serial weights later become the simplest monitor of response.
Ask about belly pain with fever, breathlessness, and reduced urine output. These are complication alarms: infection of ascitic fluid, fluid around the lungs, and failing kidney function.
Ask what triggered this episode. An upper respiratory infection commonly precedes both first presentation and relapse, which is why the history routinely begins with a cold two weeks back.
Record treatment already taken. Diuretics started elsewhere mask the oedema, and steroids already given change both the urine findings and the urgency of referral.
skill.history.nephrotic.illness.oneLine: Swelling in sequence, urine as second witness, triggers and alarms
pitfalls: Accepting generalised swelling without fixing where it began and how it spread.
Never asking about the urine, so the protein leak goes unmentioned until the laboratory reports it.
Missing fever with belly pain, the alarm for infection of the ascitic fluid.

probes.a: Periorbital puffiness on waking spreading to dependent parts, with frothy urine and reduced volume.
probes.q: Describe the typical opening story of childhood nephrotic syndrome.

probes.a: Infection of the ascitic fluid, pleural effusion, or deteriorating renal function needing urgent review.
probes.q: Fever with belly pain in an oedematous child suggests what?

probes.a: An upper respiratory infection in the preceding weeks commonly precedes first presentation and relapse.
probes.q: What trigger commonly precedes the swelling?

sources.locator: nephrotic_syndrome_paediatric: clinicalPearls

skill.history.nephrotic.illness.title: History of the nephrotic illness
skill.history.nephrotic.illness.why: The sequence of swelling plus the urine story separates nephrotic from nephritic and nutritional oedema at the bedside, days before the laboratory confirms it.

skill.presentation.nephrotic.case.body: Present in a fixed order and keep it to about two minutes for a focused case. The listener should be able to reach nephrotic syndrome before you say it.
keyPoints: Open with the problem representation: a preschool child, swelling built over weeks with a morning-evening rhythm, and the urine findings. One or two sentences.
Give the relevant positives in order: periorbital onset, spread, froth, weight gain, ascites, then the relevant negatives: no haematuria, normal pressure, preserved function.
State the response pattern and episode number, since a first episode and a fourth relapse are presented differently.
Close with the plan: urine quantification done, steroids proposed with counselling on relapse, salt advice, vaccines reviewed, and home dipstick monitoring explained.

A worked example: This 4-year-old boy, first episode, has generalised pitting oedema with ascites that built over three weeks, with frothy urine and a 2 kg weight gain. Pressure is normal, urine shows heavy protein without red cells, and albumin is low. In summary this is childhood nephrotic syndrome with no atypical features, for which I propose confirming the workup and starting oral steroids with relapse counselling.
skill.presentation.nephrotic.case.oneLine: Two minutes, ending with the response pattern and the plan
pitfalls: Presenting in the order the history was collected rather than age, tempo, syndrome, atypical markers, pattern.
Omitting the episode number and response pattern, leaving the plan hanging.
Forgetting the home dipstick and vaccine plan, which is what the family actually takes home.

probes.a: Age clue, tempo with diurnal rhythm, syndrome in abstract terms, atypical markers or their absence, and the response pattern.
probes.q: What five elements does a nephrotic case presentation carry in order?

skill.presentation.nephrotic.case.title: Presenting the nephrotic child
skill.presentation.nephrotic.case.why: The consultant judges the case on structure as much as content, and a presentation that ends with the response pattern and a home plan shows the student is managing a relapsing illness, not just describing swelling.

skill.hx.acute.stool.title: Stool history in acute diarrhoea
skill.hx.acute.stool.oneLine: Onset, frequency, consistency, blood, mucus and what comes with the motions
skill.hx.acute.stool.why: The stool history separates watery from inflammatory diarrhoea at the first sitting, and that separation decides whether stool culture has any role and whether antibiotics can even be considered. Frequency and duration also feed directly into the dehydration assessment.

asks.text: When did the loose motions start, and was the onset sudden or gradual.
How many loose stools in the last 24 hours, and how does that compare with the usual pattern.
What do the stools look like: watery, bulky, frothy, and whether they conform to the shape of the container.
Is there visible blood or mucus in the stool, and is the blood fresh red or altered.
Is there straining, urgency, or a frequent urge with little passed.
Is there vomiting, and does it precede the diarrhoea or follow it.
How is urine output: usual volume, decreased, or not passed for many hours.
Is the child thirstier than usual, drinking eagerly, or unable to drink.

teach.heading: Start with onset and frequency
teach.body:
Ask when the loose motions began and how many have been passed in the last 24 hours. Three or more loose or watery stools in a day defines diarrhoea, and an illness under two weeks sits in the acute infectious frame.

Record the trajectory too: rising frequency with vomiting points to rapid fluid loss, while a static low frequency over many days points elsewhere.

teach.heading: Describe the stool itself
points: Watery stools with no blood suggest a small bowel enterotoxin process.
Visible blood or mucus suggests large bowel inflammation or invasion, which is dysentery.
Profuse pale watery stools in large volume raise cholera in an outbreak setting.
Bulky pale stools suggest a malabsorptive process rather than an acute infection.

teach.heading: Ask what travels with the diarrhoea
teach.body:
Vomiting before the diarrhoea with a very short gap after a suspect meal suggests preformed toxin. Fever favours invasive disease. Decreased urine, excessive thirst and lethargy are dehydration signals, not separate complaints.

Always close with blood and mucus asked directly: families often do not volunteer it.

pitfalls: Accepting loose without asking watery or formed, so a change in frequency is never established.
Never asking directly about blood or mucus, which the family may not think worth mentioning.
Recording vomiting and diarrhoea without establishing which came first.

probes.q: What stool finding defines dysentery rather than watery diarrhoea?
probes.a: Visible blood or mucus in the stool, pointing to large bowel inflammation or invasion.

probes.q: Why do you ask about urine output in a child with diarrhoea?
probes.a: Decreased urine or no urine for many hours is an early marker of dehydration and feeds the severity grading.

probes.q: Vomiting started within hours of a suspect meal, before any diarrhoea, with no fever. What does the timing suggest?
probes.a: Preformed toxin food poisoning, which has the shortest incubation and prominent vomiting without fever.

skill.hx.acute.risk.title: Risk and background history in diarrhoea
skill.hx.acute.risk.oneLine: Age, feeding, water, contacts and drugs that change the risk and the plan
skill.hx.acute.risk.why: Two children with identical stools carry different risks: an exclusively breastfed six month old and a malnourished eighteen month old on diluted top feeds do not have the same illness. The background also names the source to fix at home, so this admission is not repeated next month.

asks.text: Age in months, birth weight, and whether growth has been faltering.
Feeding: exclusive breastfeeding, mixed feeds, dilution of top milk, and whether feeding continued during this illness.
Drinking water source, storage, boiling, and toilet and handwashing at home.
Rotavirus immunisation and whether the routine schedule is complete.
Sick contacts with loose motions, recent travel, and foods eaten outside the home.
Drugs already given: antibiotics, antimotility syrups, and any traditional remedies.
Past similar episodes, past admission for diarrhoea, and known illness such as immunodeficiency.

teach.heading: Age and nutrition set the risk
teach.body:
Diarrhoea with moderate dehydration in an infant under two years, especially with fever beyond a day, bloody stools or a prolonged course, marks higher risk. Malnutrition and faulty feeding, such as over diluted top milk, both predispose to infection and worsen its course.

Ask feeding without judgement: what milk, how mixed, how often, and whether anything was stopped because of this illness.

teach.heading: Water, sanitation and contacts
points: Unsafe water, poor storage and absent handwashing explain recurrence and must be fixed before discharge.
A household contact with similar motions suggests a shared source or person to person spread.
Very small infective doses allow person to person spread for some organisms, while others need growth in food first.
Recent travel widens the organism list and raises the chance of an inflammatory cause.

teach.heading: Drugs and immunisation
teach.body:
Ask what has already been given: recent antibiotics raise Clostridioides difficile as a cause, and antimotility drugs can prolong fever and shedding in some infections. Record rotavirus immunisation and the rest of the schedule, since prevention belongs in the discharge plan.

Past admissions for the same complaint hint at an underlying cause that this episode may share.

pitfalls: Skipping the feeding history, so over diluted top milk is missed as the remediable cause.
Not asking about drugs already given, including antibiotics that change the differential.
Forgetting rotavirus immunisation, which belongs in every diarrhoea discharge plan.

probes.q: Name three background facts that raise the risk in a child with diarrhoea.
probes.a: Age under two years, malnutrition or faulty feeding, and unsafe water or poor sanitation, with incomplete immunisation and recent antibiotics adding risk.

probes.q: The child received a course of antibiotics last week for a cough. Why does that matter now?
probes.a: Recent antibiotics disturb the gut flora and raise antibiotic associated colitis, including Clostridioides difficile, as a cause of the current diarrhoea.

skill.present.acute.diarrhoea.title: Presenting the dehydrated child
skill.present.acute.diarrhoea.oneLine: Age, feeds, stools, dehydration grade and plan in under two minutes
skill.present.acute.diarrhoea.why: A dehydration case is won or lost on whether the grade and the plan are stated together: the consultant should hear the classification and the fluid order in the same breath, with the evidence that earned the grade listed before it.

teach.heading: Open with age, feeds and tempo
teach.body:
State age in months, feeding pattern and the tempo: days of loose stools with frequency, vomiting and urine output. These three decide urgency before any sign is listed.

Name the stool character and any blood or mucus early, since dysentery changes the investigation plan.

teach.heading: Grade with the signs that earned it
teach.body:
List the dehydration signs found: general condition, eyes, tears, tongue, thirst and skin pinch, then state the grade they add up to. Never state a grade without its signs.

Add weight, nutritional state and the fontanelle in an infant, since each modifies the reading of the signs.

teach.heading: Close with plan and prevention
points: State the WHO plan, A, B or C, with the fluid, volume and time frame.
State feeding, zinc and what was deliberately not given, such as routine antibiotics.
State red flags explained to the mother and the follow up arrangement.
State the source fixed at home: water, sanitation or feeding.

pitfalls: Stating a dehydration grade without listing the signs that earned it.
Omitting feeding and immunisation, so prevention never enters the plan.
Closing without red flags and follow up, leaving the mother unprepared.

probes.q: What must a dehydration case presentation contain that a generic case presentation need not?
probes.a: The dehydration grade with its supporting signs, and the WHO plan with fluid, volume and time frame, stated together.

skill.hx.anaemia.particulars.title: Particulars of the pale child
skill.hx.anaemia.particulars.oneLine: Age, informant, community and consanguinity before the symptoms
skill.hx.anaemia.particulars.why: In inherited anaemia the particulars carry diagnostic weight: age of onset separates major from later nutritional causes, community hints at carrier rates, and consanguinity with an affected relative can establish recessive inheritance before a test is ordered.
skill.hx.anaemia.particulars.body: Particulars in a pale child record more than name and age: they fix the informant, the community background, and the marriage pattern that recessive disease needs.

asks.text: Age in months or years, and who noticed the paleness first with how reliable the account is.
Informant name and relation, usually the mother, with who else cares for the child through the day.
Community and residence, since carrier rates cluster in certain communities and regions.
Consanguinity of the parents, asked directly and without judgement, with the exact relation.
Birth order with the health of siblings, including any sibling on transfusions or lost in infancy.
Socioeconomic background and anganwadi or school attendance, which set what follow up is feasible.

keyPoints: Record age in months for infants: pallor from the second half of the first year favours thalassaemia major as fetal haemoglobin falls.
Name the informant and reliability: a mother who tracks feeds and milestones gives a usable tempo, a changing cast of carers does not.
Ask consanguinity plainly: recessive disease needs carrier parents, and the question is routine, not accusatory.
Map siblings and cousins: a transfused cousin or a lost infant sibling is often the first hard evidence of inheritance.
Note community background neutrally: some communities carry higher trait rates, which raises pre-test probability without stereotyping care.
pitfalls: Recording age in years for an infant, blurring the 8-month onset that points to major disease.
Skipping consanguinity from discomfort, losing the pedigree that counsel depends on.
Never asking about siblings, so a transfused cousin goes unmentioned until the HPLC returns.

probes.q: What six particulars do you record first in a pale child?
probes.a: Exact age, informant with reliability, community and residence, consanguinity, sibling health, and socioeconomic background with anganwadi attendance.

probes.q: Why does age in months matter more here than in a fever case?
probes.a: Pallor from the second half of the first year marks the fall of fetal haemoglobin and points to thalassaemia major.
