skill.hx.anaemia.illness.title: History of the anaemic illness
skill.hx.anaemia.illness.oneLine: Pallor in sequence, feeds and pica, jaundice, transfusions and alarms
skill.hx.anaemia.illness.why: The anaemia story separates nutritional from inherited causes at the bedside: feeds and pica with no organ enlargement against pallor since infancy with a big spleen and a transfused relative. Sequence and diet do what no single symptom can.
skill.hx.anaemia.illness.body: The history of a pale child is told in order from first paleness, through feeds and cravings, to jaundice, transfusions and alarms.

asks.text: When the paleness was first noticed and how it has progressed, sudden or creeping, steady or episodic.
Feeds in a day: breast, bottle quantity and dilution, age at weaning, and meat, egg and green intake.
Pica: craving for earth, chalk, raw rice or ice, with what is eaten and how often.
Worms passed, deworming given, and black or bloody stools with nose or gum bleeding and bruises.
Yellow eyes or dark urine, episodic or steady, with gallstone colic in older children.
Breathlessness and tiredness in play, poor weight gain, and repeated fevers with their pattern.
Blood transfusions before, admissions, and iron tonics given with whether the pallor answered.
Alarms: persistent fever with bleeding or bone pain, rapidly swelling belly, or breathlessness at rest.

keyPoints: Fix onset against fetal haemoglobin: pallor creeping in after 6 months with poor growth favours major disease.
Quantify milk: prolonged bottle feeds of diluted milk with little else is the classic iron lack setup.
Ask pica directly: earth or chalk craving is volunteered rarely but reported often when asked.
Separate steady from episodic yellow: steady pallor from infancy is thalassaemic, episodic jaundice with dark urine is haemolytic.
Record transfusion and iron history as results: non-response to iron is an indication to test, prior transfusion changes every baseline.
Close with alarms: fever with bleeding or bone pain warns of marrow disease, breathlessness at rest warns of cardiac strain.
pitfalls: Accepting pallor without fixing onset, so infancy onset hides inside a vague months-long story.
Never quantifying milk feeds, missing the commonest reversible cause in the room.
Filing non-response to iron as non-compliance instead of testing for thalassaemia.

probes.q: What feed history defines the iron lack setup?
probes.a: Prolonged bottle feeds of diluted milk with delayed weaning and little meat, egg or green intake.

probes.q: How does the jaundice story separate thalassaemia from haemolytic mimics?
probes.a: Steady pallor since infancy without yellow fits thalassaemia major; episodic yellow eyes with dark urine fits G6PD lack or immune haemolysis.

probes.q: Iron tonic for two months with no improvement. What next?
probes.a: Stop repeating the tonic: check haemoglobin response formally, send iron studies with ferritin, and work up thalassaemia with film and HPLC.

skill.hx.anaemia.background.title: Background history in the anaemic child
skill.hx.anaemia.background.oneLine: Birth, diet, immunisation, drugs and the family pedigree
skill.hx.anaemia.background.why: Background decides whether pallor is nutritional, inherited or a warning of marrow disease: diet recall with milk load, past transfusions, drugs already tried, and a three-generation pedigree each change the workup before blood is drawn.
skill.hx.anaemia.background.body: Background history covers birth and growth, diet and immunisation, past illness with drugs, and family, in that order.

asks.text: Birth: term or preterm, birth weight, cry at birth, and neonatal jaundice or admissions.
Growth and development: anganwadi weights, milestones, and comparison with siblings at the same age.
Diet recall for yesterday with milk quantity, plus tea with meals, which blocks iron absorption.
Immunisation card review with vitamin A doses and deworming dates.
Past illness: malaria, prolonged fever, tuberculosis contact, known kidney or liver disease.
Drugs: iron tonics with duration and response, antimalarials, recent oxidant drugs, and home remedies.
Family pedigree across three generations: pallor, transfusions, jaundice, gallstones young, and infant deaths.

keyPoints: Read the birth weight and neonatal course: low birth weight with early pallor compounds every later cause.
Do a real diet recall: tea with meals and milk-only days explain iron lack that tonics alone will not fix.
Review the immunisation card yourself: missed pneumococcal vaccine matters before any splenectomy decision.
List every drug with response: iron without response is the commonest clue to thalassaemia in the records.
Draw three generations: transfusions, young gallstones and infant deaths mark recessive and haemolytic families.
Ask tuberculosis contact and malaria: both keep anaemia company and change the investigation list.
pitfalls: Accepting a festival day as a diet recall, so tea and milk load are undercounted.
Trusting the card is complete without reading it, missing the vaccines a splenectomy plan assumes.
Stopping the pedigree at parents, so the transfused cousin who names the disease stays hidden.

probes.q: What seven background areas do you cover in a pale child?
probes.a: Birth with growth, diet recall with milk and tea, immunisation card, past illness, drugs with response, and a three-generation family pedigree.

probes.q: Why do you ask about tea with meals?
probes.a: Tea taken with meals blocks iron absorption, so a milk-and-tea diet explains iron lack that tonics alone will not correct.

skill.present.anaemia.child.title: Presenting the anaemic child
skill.present.anaemia.child.oneLine: Two minutes, ending with the form, the burden and the family plan
skill.present.anaemia.child.why: The consultant judges the case on structure as much as content, and in inherited anaemia the presentation must carry tempo, transfusion history and family risk or the plan cannot be set.
skill.present.anaemia.child.body: Present in a fixed order and keep it to about two minutes for a focused case. The listener should reach thalassaemia major before you name it.
keyPoints: Open with the problem representation: age, pallor since infancy with growth faltering, organ enlargement, and the informant. One or two sentences.
Give the relevant positives in order: pallor tempo, bossing, liver and spleen size, film and HPLC pattern, then the relevant negatives: no jaundice, no bleeding, no blasts.
State transfusion history and iron studies: transfusion-naive with normal ferritin frames every next step.
Name the form with the burden: major with growth and iron status, and what stays local versus what goes to haematology.
Close with the family plan: carrier parents, sibling screening, antenatal counsel for future pregnancies, and follow up records shared with the medical college.

A worked example: This 3-year-old boy, reported by his mother, has pallor since 8 months with poor weight gain, frontal bossing and a firm 5 cm spleen, without jaundice or bleeding. Blood shows severe microcytic anaemia with target cells, normal ferritin and near absent HbA with very high HbF. In summary this is beta thalassaemia major, transfusion-naive, for which I propose haematology referral for transfusion planning with chelation, and carrier screening with antenatal counsel for the family.
pitfalls: Presenting in the order the history was collected rather than age, tempo, syndrome, burden, family.
Omitting transfusion history and ferritin, leaving the plan without its frame.
Forgetting sibling screening and antenatal counsel, which is what the family actually takes home.

probes.q: What six elements does an anaemia case presentation carry in order?
probes.a: Age with tempo, syndrome with positives and negatives, transfusion and iron frame, form with burden, referral split, and the family screening plan.

skill.hx.bacterial.risk_factors.title: Meningitis risk and exposure history
skill.hx.bacterial.risk_factors.oneLine: Immunisation gaps, crowding, recent infections and contacts that raise the odds of bacterial meningitis
skill.hx.bacterial.risk_factors.why: Bacterial meningitis strikes some children far more readily than others, and the risk sits in facts the routine history can miss: an unimmunised infant in a crowded home with a recent ear discharge is a different patient from a fully immunised only child. Asking these questions takes a minute and changes both the urgency and the prevention plan for the household.

asks.text: Ask for the exact age in months or years, since risk and likely organisms change sharply between neonates, infants and older children.
Ask which vaccines the child has received and check the card: pentavalent including Hib, pneumococcal conjugate, and any meningococcal vaccine.
Ask about the household: number of rooms and people sleeping together, hostel or barrack stay, and recent contact with anyone with fever, rash or a stiff neck.
Ask about infections in the past fortnight: ear discharge, sinus pain, pneumonia, or a recent head injury, skull fracture or neurosurgery.
Ask about recurrent meningitis clues: repeated episodes, persistent watery nasal discharge after trauma, known immunodeficiency, sickle cell disease or absent spleen.
Ask about tuberculosis contact: anyone at home with prolonged cough, weight loss or treatment for tuberculosis.
Ask about the current drug history: antibiotics already given before arrival, steroids, and any known drug allergy.

skill.hx.bacterial.risk_factors.body: Take the risk history as a focused supplement once the presenting complaint is clear. Confirm age, immunisation, crowding and contacts, recent local infections, and anything that suggests recurrence or tuberculosis.
keyPoints: Age sets the organism list: neonates face Group B streptococcus and gut gram negative organisms, while older infants and children face pneumococcus, meningococcus and, where unimmunised, Haemophilus influenzae type b.
Check the immunisation card rather than memory: missing Hib or pneumococcal doses leaves the child open to preventable meningitis and signals catch-up vaccination for siblings too.
Crowding matters because meningococcus and pneumococcus spread through close respiratory contact, so ask who shares the sleeping room and whether anyone nearby is ill.
A recent ear discharge, sinusitis, pneumonia or head injury gives bacteria a direct route to the meninges and should be asked about in every case.
Repeat episodes point to an anatomical leak or an immune defect and need referral to a higher centre rather than another identical course of treatment.
A tuberculosis contact in a child with a subacute course shifts the differential towards tuberculous meningitis early, while it is still treatable.
pitfalls: Accepting fully immunised on memory without seeing the card.
Skipping the crowding and contact questions, so household prophylaxis is never considered.
Missing prior antibiotics given before arrival, which then makes a negative culture misleading.
Treating a second episode exactly like the first without looking for a leak or immune cause.

probes.q: Which two vaccines on the routine schedule most directly protect against bacterial meningitis, and how do you verify them?
probes.a: Hib containing pentavalent vaccine and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, verified against the written immunisation card rather than memory.

probes.q: A child has had meningitis twice in a year. What history changes your plan?
probes.a: Ask about head injury with watery nasal discharge suggesting a cerebrospinal fluid leak, and about immunodeficiency, sickle cell disease or absent spleen, then refer for specialist evaluation of the cause.

skill.present.bacterial.meningitis_case.title: Presenting the child with suspected meningitis
skill.present.bacterial.meningitis_case.oneLine: Tempo, consciousness, meningeal signs, rash and the CSF, in under two minutes
skill.present.bacterial.meningitis_case.why: A meningitis presentation fails when it reads as a list of symptoms rather than an argument for urgency. The consultant needs the tempo in hours, the state of consciousness, the discriminating signs and the CSF profile in a fixed order, because each of those changes what happens in the next hour.
skill.present.bacterial.meningitis_case.body: Present in a fixed order and keep it under two minutes. The listener should be able to state your diagnosis and your next step before you announce either.
keyPoints: Open with age in months or years, immunisation status, and tempo: a previously well child with fever for a stated number of hours or days.
State consciousness and systemic state next: alert, drowsy or unresponsive, with pulse, blood pressure and perfusion, since shock changes everything.
Give the discriminating findings: neck stiffness, Kernig or Brudzinski signs, fontanelle state in an infant, any rash and whether it fades on pressure.
Quote the CSF profile as cells with differential, protein, and glucose against simultaneous blood glucose, then state what pattern that fits.
State the diagnosis with the likely focus, name the one closest alternative you excluded and the finding that excludes it, then state the immediate plan.
pitfalls: Starting with the CSF report before the listener knows the child.
Omitting immunisation status, which the listener needs to judge the likely organism.
Describing a rash without saying whether it fades on pressure.
Quoting CSF glucose without the simultaneous blood glucose beside it.
Ending on the diagnosis with no statement of urgency or next step.

probes.q: What must the opening sentence of a meningitis presentation contain?
probes.a: Age, immunisation status, and the tempo of the illness in hours or days in a previously well child.

probes.q: Why quote simultaneous blood glucose alongside every CSF glucose you present?
probes.a: Because only the ratio shows true hypoglycorrhachia, and a low CSF glucose beside an unknown blood glucose cannot distinguish bacterial or tuberculous meningitis from hyperglycaemia.

skill.hx.severe.illness.title: History of the SAM illness
skill.hx.severe.illness.oneLine: Oedema, appetite and silent infection: the three threads of the SAM history
skill.hx.severe.illness.why: The SAM history sorts three things at once: whether oedema is present, whether appetite survives, and whether infection is hiding without fever. Those three answers decide complicated versus uncomplicated disease, which is the single most consequential branch in management.

teach.heading: Start with the swelling
teach.body:
Ask when the swelling was first noticed and where it began. Nutritional oedema starts in the feet, then climbs to the legs and hands, and reaches the face last. It is bilateral, painless, and pits on pressure.

Ask about weight change alongside it. A child who gains weight rapidly while looking thinner in the limbs is gaining fluid, not flesh, and that fluid masks the true wasting underneath.

teach.heading: Appetite is the triage question
teach.body:
Ask exactly what the child ate yesterday and today, and whether breastfeeding continues. Then ask how eagerly the child eats: finishing a ready-to-use feed with interest counts as a pass, while refusal or needing to be forced counts as failure.

Poor appetite in a child who otherwise meets SAM criteria means complicated disease and admission, even when the child looks relatively alert. Appetite, not appearance, is the gate.

teach.heading: Feeding history and the diarrhoea loop
teach.body:
Ask about exclusive breastfeeding to six months, the age at which complementary feeds began, and what those feeds are: thin dal water and diluted animal milk are classic risk feeds, and bottle feeding adds infection to undernutrition.

Ask about loose stools in detail: frequency, blood or mucus, and how many similar episodes preceded this illness. Each bout of diarrhoea strips weight off a child who had none to spare, and persistent diarrhoea beyond two weeks points to underlying enteropathy or immunodeficiency.

teach.heading: Infection is often silent, so hunt for it
teach.body:
Do not accept the absence of fever as the absence of infection. Children with SAM mount poor febrile responses, so ask directly about cough, fast breathing, ear discharge, skin sores, burning on passing urine, and unusual sleepiness or refusal to play.

Ask about tuberculosis contact, any chronic cough in the household, measles in the past three months, and parental illness or death. Where the local prevalence warrants it, ask about HIV risk in the parents, since advanced immunodeficiency and SAM travel together.

asks.text: Swelling: when first noticed, where it began, and how far it has spread, plus whether it pits on pressure.
Weight change: rapid gain with swelling (fluid) versus steady thinning of limbs and buttocks (wasting).
Appetite: exact intake yesterday and today, breastfeeding, and eagerness versus refusal of feeds.
Feeding: exclusive breastfeeding to six months, age and content of complementary feeds, dilution, bottle use.
Diarrhoea: frequency, blood or mucus, duration, and number of previous similar episodes.
Silent infection: cough, fast breathing, ear discharge, skin sores, burning urine, lethargy, recent measles.
Contacts: TB contact, chronic cough at home, parental illness, and HIV risk where relevant.

probes.q: What are the three threads of the SAM history?
probes.a: The oedema story, the appetite story, and the hunt for silent infection.

probes.q: A mother reports her swollen child is eating less each day. Why does that change the plan?
probes.a: Poor appetite makes this complicated SAM, which needs inpatient stabilisation rather than community care.

probes.q: Why do you ask about infection even when the child has no fever?
probes.a: Children with SAM often fail to mount fever, so serious infection hides behind normal temperature and must be sought by symptoms and contacts.

skill.hx.severe.particulars.title: Particulars of the wasted or swollen child
skill.hx.severe.particulars.oneLine: Age in months, growth-monitoring trail, and the household behind the child
skill.hx.severe.particulars.why: SAM lives in an age window and a household pattern: the 6 to 59 month weaning window, low birth weight behind it, and a growth chart that usually warned weeks before the mother noticed. Particulars that capture all three turn a thin child into an explainable event.

teach.heading: Age in months sets the criteria
teach.body:
Record age in completed months, not years, because the diagnostic thresholds are month specific. The peak window is 6 to 59 months, when complementary feeding begins and infections cluster.

Infants under 6 months are assessed differently, since MUAC and weight-for-height cut-offs do not apply to them in the same way, and adolescents need BMI-for-age rather than these charts. Getting the window right avoids applying the wrong standard.

teach.heading: The growth-monitoring trail
teach.body:
Ask where the child was weighed last: the anganwadi growth chart, the immunisation clinic, or a previous admission. A flattened or falling curve over two or more visits predates the visible illness and tells you how long this has been building.

Ask how the child reached you: referred from anganwadi growth monitoring, brought by the mother, or transferred from another facility. Referred children arrive earlier in the course, on average, than self-presented ones.

teach.heading: The household behind the child
teach.body:
Record birth order, birth weight, and whether the birth was preterm or twin, since low birth weight children start growth from behind and never catch up without help. Ask about surviving siblings and any sibling death, which marks both shared risk and maternal depletion.

Record parental occupation, maternal literacy, and ration or anganwadi take-home support. These are not social decoration: they predict whether the discharge plan of frequent feeding and follow-up weighing can actually happen at home.

asks.text: Age in completed months, and whether the child falls in the 6 to 59 month window.
Growth trail: anganwadi chart, last weighing, direction of the curve, and referral source.
Birth: birth weight, preterm or twin birth, and place of delivery.
Household: birth order, sibling deaths, parental occupation and literacy, ration or take-home support.

probes.q: Why is age recorded in months in a SAM case?
probes.a: Because the diagnostic thresholds and feeding norms are month specific, and the peak risk window is 6 to 59 months.

probes.q: What does a flattened anganwadi growth curve add to the story?
probes.a: It dates the failure: growth faltering weeks before visible wasting or oedema, and shows this is chronic undernutrition tipping over, not an acute event.

skill.present.severe.case.title: Presenting the SAM child
skill.present.severe.case.oneLine: Age, wasting versus oedema, appetite, phase: then the plan
skill.present.severe.case.why: The consultant needs four facts in the first thirty seconds: how old, wasting or oedema or both, appetite kept or lost, and therefore complicated or not. A presentation that buries appetite in the middle has buried the admission decision.

teach.heading: Open with the four triage facts
teach.body:
State age in months, the phenotype in one phrase (severe wasting, bilateral oedema to the legs, or both), the appetite result, and the resulting label of complicated or uncomplicated SAM. One or two sentences.

Name the grade alongside: weight-for-height band or MUAC zone with the oedema grade, so the listener can picture severity before hearing a single symptom.

teach.heading: Positives in order, then the discriminating negatives
teach.body:
Give anthropometry first, then oedema extent, then hair, skin and liver clues, then complications found: hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, dehydration, or infection. End the body with feeding and immunisation gaps that explain it.

State the negatives that exclude mimics: urine output and froth against nephrotic syndrome, no chronic cough or contact against tuberculosis, alertness and normal development against chronic systemic disease.

teach.heading: Close with the phase and the home plan
teach.body:
State the management phase: stabilisation with cautious feeds and complication watch, or rehabilitation with catch-up feeding and stimulation. Name the infection screen sent and micronutrients started.

Close with follow-up: daily weights in stabilisation, weekly in rehabilitation, the anganwadi or nutrition rehabilitation centre link, immunisation catch-up, and what brings the child back urgently.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
This 22-month-old girl has marasmic kwashiorkor with bilateral pedal oedema, a MUAC in the red zone, and failed appetite, making this complicated SAM.

She is hypothermic with a cough but no fever, for which I have sent blood counts and a chest film, and started stabilisation feeds with warming, empirical antibiotics, and micronutrients without iron.

probes.q: What four facts open a SAM case presentation?
probes.a: Age in months, wasting versus oedema phenotype, appetite kept or lost, and the complicated or uncomplicated label.

probes.q: Why does the presentation grade oedema and MUAC before describing symptoms?
probes.a: Because the grade carries the diagnosis and severity on its own, so the listener judges everything after it against a fixed severity anchor.

skill.hx.birth.asphyxia_illness.title: History of the asphyxiated newborn's illness
skill.hx.birth.asphyxia_illness.oneLine: Labour, liquor, first cry and resuscitation told in time order
skill.hx.birth.asphyxia_illness.why: The cause of a flat newborn is written in the hours before and minutes after birth, not in the baby's face on the ward. A history that runs in strict time order from labour pains to the first cry to the resuscitation table separates an intrapartum insult from sepsis or a metabolic trap.

asks.text: Ask when labour pains began, how long they lasted, where delivery happened and who conducted it, including any delay in reaching the facility.
Ask about the waters: when they broke, the colour and smell of the liquor, and whether it was thickly meconium stained.
Ask exactly what happened at birth: whether the baby cried at once, the colour and tone, and how many minutes passed before the first cry or breath.
Ask what resuscitation was given and in what order: drying and warmth, clearing the airway, bag and mask breaths, chest compressions, any drug through the cord, and oxygen.
Ask for the Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes and whether the baby needed continued help after 5 minutes.
Ask how the baby behaved after stabilising: alertness, suck, cry, limb movements, any fit, jitteriness, apnoea or blue spells.
Ask about feeds since birth: when breastfeeding started, how the baby sucks, and whether urine and stool have been passed.

skill.hx.birth.asphyxia_illness.practice: Take this history from the mother on the postnatal ward with the case sheet open, and read back the timeline to her to confirm each interval.
pitfalls: Accepting cried after some time without pinning down the minutes, so a brief delay and a true asphyxial insult read the same.
Recording bag and mask without asking whether the chest rose and the heart rate picked up, which is the only proof ventilation worked.
Forgetting the liquor entirely, and with it the clue that points to aspiration and infection risk.

probes.q: What four antenatal questions fix the risk before labour starts?
probes.a: The gestational age, whether the fluid is clear, how many babies are expected, and whether any additional risk factor is present.

probes.q: Why do you ask the liquor colour before you ask about the resuscitation?
probes.a: Thick meconium staining explains a non-vigorous baby and warns of aspiration and infection, so it frames everything the resuscitation then had to overcome.

probes.q: The mother says the baby cried late but she cannot say how late. What do you do?
probes.a: Anchor with events: length of pushing, who else entered the room, when the bag and mask appeared, and cross-check with the case sheet Apgar times.

teach.heading: Run the clock from pains to first cry
teach.body:
Fix the timeline first: when pains began, when the waters broke, how long pushing lasted, and the minutes from birth to first cry or breath. An insult that grows through a prolonged second stage with thick liquor reads differently from a sudden cord event in an otherwise smooth labour.

Confirm each interval twice, once from the mother's story and once from the case sheet or referral slip.

teach.heading: Liquor, tone and cry are the three witnesses
teach.body:
Green, thick or foul liquor points to in-utero stress, aspiration and ascending infection. A baby born limp, blue and silent needed resuscitation by definition, while a baby who cried at once and pinked up was vigorous even if the labour looked alarming.

Ask colour, tone and cry as three separate facts, because families merge them into one memory of a difficult birth.

teach.heading: Resuscitation in order, with proof it worked
points: What was done, in order: drying and warmth, airway positioning, bag and mask breaths, compressions, cord medication, oxygen.
Whether it worked: chest rise with each breath, heart rate climbing, spontaneous breaths returning, saturation improving.
What the scores say: Apgar at 1 and 5 minutes, and whether help was still needed after 5 minutes, which marks severity better than any single number.

Neonatal resuscitation: history and assessment

skill.hx.birth.asphyxia_risks.title: Maternal and intranatal risk history for asphyxia
skill.hx.birth.asphyxia_risks.oneLine: The background that made this birth dangerous: mother, pregnancy and labour risks
skill.hx.birth.asphyxia_risks.why: Asphyxia is rarely a bolt from a clear sky; anaemia, hypertension, infection, post-term gestation and prolonged labour stack the odds long before the first cry. A risk history taken for every flat baby finds the preventable cause and tells the mother what to change next pregnancy.

asks.text: Ask maternal age, parity, previous stillbirths or neonatal deaths, and abortions, since a bad obstetric past predicts a risky present.
Ask about this pregnancy's care: number of checkups, tetanus doses, iron tablets taken, weight gain, and scans with their findings.
Ask about maternal illness: anaemia, high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid illness, fever or urinary infection, and every drug taken.
Ask about labour risks: post-term dates, twin pregnancy, reduced foetal movements, bleeding, headache with swelling of feet, or convulsions.
Ask about rupture and infection: hours since the waters broke, fever in labour, foul liquor, and any antibiotic given before delivery.
Ask about the road to care: distance from home to the facility, who decided to shift, and the time lost before skilled help arrived.

skill.hx.birth.asphyxia_risks.practice: Complete the antenatal card with the mother beside you, ticking each risk as present or absent so none is skipped in a hurried ward round.
pitfalls: Stopping at a normal card entry for blood pressure while missing the headache and foot swelling the mother never volunteered.
Calling the pregnancy low risk because checkups were regular, while prolonged rupture with fever sat unasked in labour.
Blaming the birth attendant alone and never recording the hours lost on the road, so the same delay repeats.

probes.q: Which maternal conditions must you ask about in every asphyxia history?
probes.a: Anaemia, high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid illness, fever or urinary infection, and every drug taken in pregnancy.

probes.q: Why does the number of hours since the waters broke change your plan?
probes.a: Prolonged rupture lets vaginal bacteria ascend into the womb, so early-onset sepsis joins asphyxia on the differential and antibiotics enter the plan.

probes.q: A mother with regular checkups still delivers a severely asphyxiated baby. Where do you look?
probes.a: At labour itself and the road to care: prolonged second stage, thick meconium, cord events, maternal fever, and hours lost before skilled help arrived.

teach.heading: The mother is the first half of the baby
teach.body:
Age and parity, prior stillbirth or neonatal death, and illnesses of this pregnancy set the baseline risk. Anaemia thins the oxygen reserve, hypertension and diabetes injure the placenta, and infection seeds the liquor, so each must be asked by name.

Record drugs as carefully as diseases: labour painkillers given near delivery can flatten the newborn's first breaths.

teach.heading: Labour turns risk into injury
teach.body:
Post-term gestation, twins, poor foetal movements, prolonged rupture with fever, and a long second stage are the intranatal risks that convert a fragile reserve into frank asphyxia. Meconium in the liquor is both a marker of past stress and a threat of aspiration.

Ask the road story too: distance, decision and delay, because the preventable cause of the next asphyxia is often transport, not medicine.

teach.heading: Close the loop for the next pregnancy
points: Name the risks found, in plain words, so the family carries them to the next antenatal card.
State what changes next time: early booking, planned facility birth, and no home wait once pains strengthen.
Record advice for the interval before the next pregnancy: spacing, iron and pressure checks before the next conception.

Birth asphyxia: maternal and foetal risk factors

skill.present.birth.asphyxia_case.title: Presenting the asphyxiated newborn
skill.present.birth.asphyxia_case.oneLine: One perinatal sentence, then resuscitation, current state and plan
skill.present.birth.asphyxia_case.why: An asphyxia case presented as a loose story buries the insult under ward events. A fixed order that opens with gestation, insult and resuscitation lets the listener grade severity before you name it, which is exactly what the examiner listens for.
skill.present.birth.asphyxia_case.practice: Present an admitted newborn in under two minutes to your unit chief, ending with the grade and the plan before being asked.
pitfalls: Starting with today's feeds and weight while the labour, liquor and minutes to first cry wait till the end.
Quoting Apgar scores without saying what resuscitation they bracket, so the numbers float free of meaning.
Closing without a grade or a cooling decision, leaving the most time-critical judgement unsaid.

probes.q: What opens the presentation of an asphyxiated newborn?
probes.a: One perinatal sentence: gestation, birth weight, the insult in brief, and the resuscitation given.

probes.q: Which negatives must you state, and why?
probes.a: No prolonged rupture with fever, no foul liquor beyond meconium, no maternal drug near delivery, and no dysmorphism or anomaly, because each excludes sepsis, drugs or a syndrome mimicking asphyxia.

probes.q: How do you close the presentation?
probes.a: With the working diagnosis and grade, the gases and brain picture so far, and the plan: support, sepsis cover, cooling decision, counsel and follow up.

teach.heading: Open with one perinatal sentence
teach.body:
Term, weight, insult, resuscitation: this term 2.7 kg boy, born through thick meconium after a prolonged second stage, limp and silent, cried after bag and mask breaths with Apgar 3 at 1 minute and 6 at 5 minutes. One sentence carries gestation, insult, response and severity.

Follow with the current state in one more: now 8 hours old, lethargic with a weak suck and one brief fit.

teach.heading: Positives that prove, negatives that exclude
points: Positives in order: the labour course, liquor state, minutes to cry, resuscitation steps, Apgar pair, then today's tone, reflexes, fits and organ signs.
Negatives that exclude mimics: no prolonged rupture with fever, no foul liquor, no maternal drug near delivery, no anomaly or dysmorphism, glucose checked.
Numbers that grade: Apgar pair, cord gas acidosis, current saturation, temperature and glucose.

teach.heading: Close with grade and plan
teach.body:
Name the working diagnosis with its grade: birth asphyxia with moderate encephalopathy. Then the plan in the same breath: supportive care with saturation and glucose targets, blood culture with antibiotics until sepsis is excluded, cooling decision within hours, mother counselled on danger signs, and neurodevelopmental follow up booked.

End where the examiner wants you: what you will recheck tonight and what would change the grade.

asks: Exact age in months, and whether the child falls between 6 months and 5 years.
Past fits: any fit with fever before, and crucially any fit WITHOUT fever, which points away from febrile seizures entirely.
Family history: febrile fits or epilepsy in parents, siblings, or close blood relatives.
Development so far: age at sitting, walking and first words, and any slowing or loss of milestones already gained.
Immunisation: vaccines taken on time, any missed doses, and the vaccine card seen, since incomplete protection lowers the threshold for excluding meningitis.
The fever itself: runny nose, cough, ear tugging, vomiting, loose stools, burning urine, or rash, to name the illness carrying the fever.
Medicines already given: antipyretic syrups, antibiotics, or leftover medicines from home, and any fit-preventing medicine the family may be using.
skill.hx.febrile.risks.body: Place the fit inside the child: exact age, past fits with and without fever, fits in blood relatives, development so far, vaccine protection, and the illness carrying the fever.
keyPoints: Fix the exact age first. Febrile seizures cluster between 6 months and 5 years, peaking between 12 and 18 months, so age inside that window raises the likelihood and age outside it should prompt a wider search.
Ask about every past fit, and separate fits with fever from fits without. A single prior afebrile seizure moves the child out of the febrile seizure definition and towards epilepsy.
Ask the family history directly. Febrile fits and epilepsy run in families, and a positive history in a parent or sibling both explains the tendency and helps counsel about recurrence.

Check development and vaccines in the same breath. A developmentally normal, fully immunised child with a clear fever focus is reassuring; delay or missed vaccines raise the chance of central infection hiding behind the fever.
Name the fever. Most fits ride on ordinary viral illnesses of the nose, throat, ear or gut, and finding the focus both explains the fever and decides whether an antibiotic has any role.
Record medicines already given. An antipyretic does not prevent fits, antibiotics started elsewhere can mask meningitis, and some families use daily fit medicines that need stopping under guidance.
skill.hx.febrile.risks.oneLine: Age, family history, development, immunisation, and what the fever was
pitfalls: Calling the fit febrile without asking whether a fit without fever ever happened.
Skipping the family history, losing both the explanation and the recurrence counselling.
Accepting fully immunised without seeing the card, then missing the infant who needs a meningitis hunt.

probes.a: Between 6 months and 5 years, peaking between 12 and 18 months of age.
probes.q: What is the typical age window for febrile seizures?

probes.a: A prior fit without fever moves the diagnosis away from febrile seizures and towards epilepsy.
probes.q: Which single history answer would take febrile seizure off the table?

probes.a: A positive family history of febrile fits or epilepsy, young age at the first fit raise the chance of another.
probes.q: What in the background raises the chance that the fit comes back?

Febrile seizures: risk factors and recurrence

skill.hx.febrile.risks.title: Risk factors and background of the fitting child
skill.hx.febrile.risks.why: A fit with fever in a neurologically normal toddler from a family of fever fits is routine; the same fit in a developmentally slow infant with missed vaccines is a meningitis hunt. The background decides the urgency.

asks: Who saw the fit from the start, and whether they were with the child when the fever began or only when the shaking started.
Fever before the fit: how the fever was noticed, how high it felt, and how soon after the fever the fit began.
What the fit looked like: whole body stiffening and jerking versus one side only, eyes or head turning to one side, lip smacking, or a brief limp collapse.
Duration by the clock: when the shaking started and stopped, and whether anyone timed it rather than guessed.
How many fits in the last day, and the gap between one fit and the next.
The recovery: sleepy or confused afterwards, how long before the child was back to normal, and any weakness of one side after waking.
Colour and breathing during the fit, wetting or soiling, biting of tongue or cheek, and what the family did while it lasted.
skill.hx.febrile.seizure_story.body: Take the fit apart in order: the fever that came first, exactly what the movements looked like, how the minutes were counted, whether it came back within a day, and how the child woke up afterwards.
keyPoints: Start with the witness. Only someone who watched from the start can say whether the movements were generalised or focal and how long they lasted, and the whole classification rests on exactly that.
Fix the fever-fit sequence. The fit typically follows within a day of fever starting, and a fit that precedes any fever or comes days into the illness needs a different explanation.
Describe the movements precisely: generalised stiffening and rhythmic jerking of the whole body versus twitching confined to one side, deviation of eyes or head, or automatisms such as lip smacking.
Time the fit by the clock. Under 15 minutes favours simple; past that, or more than one fit within 24 hours, the fit is complex and the workup changes.
Record the recovery. Brief sleepiness that clears within the hour fits a simple fit; prolonged drowsiness, confusion, or a one-sided weakness afterwards points to brain infection or injury.
skill.hx.febrile.seizure_story.oneLine: Fever timing, what the fit looked like, how long it lasted, and the recovery
pitfalls: Accepting shook for a while without pinning generalised versus focal and minutes by the clock.
Forgetting to ask whether the fit came back later the same day, which alone makes it complex.
Mistaking a long sleep after the fit for recovery when the child is actually still encephalopathic.

probes.a: Focal movements, a fit lasting past 15 minutes, or more than one fit within 24 hours.
probes.q: What three features in the story make a febrile seizure complex rather than simple?

probes.a: The fit comes with fever, usually within a day of the fever starting.
probes.q: How are the fever and the fit related in time?

probes.a: Only a witness can say whether the movements were generalised or focal and how long they lasted, and the diagnosis rests on exactly that.
probes.q: Why does the witness account outrank every test in this diagnosis?

sources.locator: febrile_seizure: clinicalPearls
Febrile seizures: clinical features

skill.hx.febrile.seizure_story.title: History of the febrile fit
skill.hx.febrile.seizure_story.why: Simple and complex febrile seizures are separated entirely by the story: duration, type, recurrence within a day, and recovery. No test makes the distinction, so the witness account is the diagnosis.

skill.present.febrile.case.body: Present in a fixed order and keep it to about two minutes for a focused case. The listener should be able to call the fit simple before you say it.
keyPoints: Open with the problem representation: age, normal development or not, a single fit with fever, and the fever focus. One or two sentences.
Give the criteria count in order: generalised type, minutes by the clock, single episode in the day, and full recovery within the hour.
State the relevant negatives: no fit without fever, no meningeal signs, no focal deficit, alert now, and glucose checked where relevant.
Name the fever focus and the vaccine position, since an unnamed fever leaves the meningitis question open.

Close with the plan: reassurance with recurrence counselling, first-aid teaching for the next fit, an antipyretic for comfort, safety-net advice, review with the vaccine card, and no daily fit medicine.

A worked example: This 18-month-old boy with normal development had a single generalised fit lasting about 3 minutes within hours of fever from a viral upper respiratory illness. He recovered fully within the hour, has no meningeal signs and no focal deficit, and his glucose is normal. In summary this is a simple febrile seizure, for which I propose reassurance with first-aid teaching, an antipyretic for comfort, safety-net advice, and review with the vaccine card.
skill.present.febrile.case.oneLine: Age, fit-fever sequence, criteria count, negatives, and the home plan
pitfalls: Presenting the fit without the clock time, leaving the simple versus complex question unanswered.
Omitting the negatives, so the listener cannot tell meningitis was excluded.
Closing without the home plan, which is what the family actually takes away.

probes.a: Age with development, fit-fever sequence with the clock time, the criteria count, the relevant negatives, and the home plan.
probes.q: What five elements does a febrile fit presentation carry in order?

Febrile seizures: counselling and follow-up

skill.present.febrile.case.title: Presenting the child after a febrile fit
skill.present.febrile.case.why: The consultant judges the case on structure as much as content, and a presentation that counts the criteria, states the negatives, and ends with the home plan shows the student excluded meningitis instead of assuming it away.

skill.hx.neonatal.jaundice_story.title: History of the yellow newborn
skill.hx.neonatal.jaundice_story.oneLine: Clock time of onset, spread down the body, feeding and output
skill.hx.neonatal.jaundice_story.why: The hour the yellow appeared and how fast it travelled down the body decides whether this is expected settling or disease. A mother remembers both exactly, so the student who asks for the clock time and the lowest yellow point usually knows the category before any laboratory result.

asks.text: Ask the exact age in hours or days when the yellow was first noticed, and who in the family noticed it first.
Ask where the yellow was first seen and how far down the body it has travelled, from the face toward the chest, belly, limbs and finally the palms or soles.

Ask about feeding in detail: how often the baby feeds through day and night, how long each feed lasts, whether the baby wakes on its own for feeds, and whether the mother feels the breast empty after a feed.
Ask about urine and stools: the number of wet nappies in a day, the colour of the urine, and whether the stools are golden yellow or pale, chalky and clay coloured.
Ask about the baby's behaviour: unusual sleepiness, difficulty waking for feeds, a weak or unusually shrill cry, fever, vomiting, or any stiffness, arching of the back, or jerky movements.
Ask about the birth events that colour the story: the weeks of gestation, the birth weight, the place of delivery, and any scalp swelling, bruise, or instrumental help during delivery.
Ask what has been done so far: exposure to sunlight as treatment, any blood test of bilirubin with its value and trend, and whether light treatment was started or advised at another facility.

teach.heading: The clock comes first
teach.body: Yellow on the first day of life is never expected and always means disease, most often blood group mismatch with rapid red cell breakdown. Yellow that appears on the second or third day, spreads slowly, and sits with a vigorous feeder is commonly the expected pattern. Yellow that deepens fast, reaches the limbs and soles early, or is still deepening after two weeks points to disease needing urgent testing.

teach.heading: Feeding and output name the mechanism
teach.body: A sleepy baby that feeds rarely and passes little urine with dark colour is taking in too little milk, which slows stool passage and returns more bilirubin to the blood. Golden yellow stools with clear urine fit unconjugated jaundice from breakdown or immature clearance. Pale chalky stools with yellow staining urine mean conjugated pigment is blocked from the gut and point to liver or bile duct disease needing referral.

teach.heading: Alarm answers that change the hour
points: A baby too sleepy to wake for feeds, with a weak suck or a shrill cry, is showing early brain effects of bilirubin and needs same-day testing.
Arching of the back or neck, stiffness alternating with floppiness, or fits mean advanced brain involvement and need emergency care.
Fever, poor weight gain, vomiting, or a red umbilical stump beside the yellow suggest infection driving the jaundice.
Pale stools with dark urine at any age need a direct bilirubin test and early referral, since bile duct blockage is repaired against the clock.

pitfalls: Recording yellow as present or absent without the day of onset, so first-day disease and third-day settling read the same.
Asking about feeding as good or poor instead of feeds per day, minutes per feed, waking behaviour and wet nappies.
Forgetting stool and urine colour, which is the only history that separates blocked bile from ordinary newborn jaundice.

probes.q: Which two facts of the jaundice story fix its timing?
probes.a: The exact age in hours or days when yellow was first noticed, and how far down the body it has since travelled.

probes.q: How does the feeding and output history separate poor intake jaundice from bile duct blockage?
probes.a: Poor intake shows infrequent feeds with few wet nappies and dark urine but yellow stools, while blockage shows pale chalky stools with yellow staining urine at any intake.

probes.q: Which behaviour answers in a yellow baby demand same-day escalation?
probes.a: Excessive sleepiness with failure to wake for feeds, a shrill cry, arching or stiffness, and fits, which mark bilirubin effects on the brain.

sources.locator: neonatal_jaundice_bilirubin_long_case: clinicalPearls
Neonatal jaundice: history and feeding assessment

skill.hx.neonatal.jaundice_risks.title: Risk factors behind the yellow baby
skill.hx.neonatal.jaundice_risks.oneLine: Blood groups, the previous child, gestation, bruising and intake
skill.hx.neonatal.jaundice_risks.why: Most pathological jaundice is predictable before the baby turns yellow: a mismatched blood group, an earlier jaundiced sibling, prematurity, a bruise that is being reabsorbed, and poor milk intake each raise the risk. The student who collects these risks knows which baby needs an early bilirubin test rather than reassurance.

asks.text: Ask the blood groups of the mother and the baby where known, and whether any antibody or Coombs testing was done during pregnancy or after birth.
Ask about previous children: any sibling who turned deeply yellow, needed light treatment or exchange of blood, or has ongoing anaemia or an enzyme deficiency.
Ask the family pattern: known anaemia running in the family, favism or avoidance of certain beans and drugs, or relatives with early removal of the spleen.
Ask the gestation in completed weeks and the birth weight, since early and small babies clear bilirubin slowly and turn yellow more often.
Ask about the labour and delivery: prolonged labour, forceps or vacuum help, scalp swelling or bruising anywhere on the baby, and delayed first cry or resuscitation.
Ask about the mother's health and medicines: diabetes or thyroid illness, induced labour, and any drug given to mother or baby around birth.
Ask about passage of the first dark stool and urine, any vomiting or delay in stooling, and whether feeds were delayed or supplemented with anything other than breast milk.

teach.heading: Blood groups and the previous child
teach.body: A mother of group O with a baby of group A or B, or a Rh negative mother with a Rh positive baby, risks antibody breakdown of the baby's red cells, fastest when a previous pregnancy was already affected. A sibling who needed light treatment or blood exchange is the strongest warning that this baby will follow the same course and needs testing on day one.

teach.heading: Bruises, gestation and intake
teach.body: A scalp swelling or bruise is a hidden load of red cells that breaks down into bilirubin over days, so an instrumental delivery explains yellow that appears after discharge. Early and small babies conjugate slowly and feed poorly, which together raise and prolong the yellow. Delayed first stool and infrequent feeds return more bilirubin to the blood through the gut.

teach.heading: Maternal illness and family clues
teach.body: Babies of diabetic mothers, and babies with delayed stooling or poor activity, carry extra risk and deserve closer watch. A family story of favism, drug-triggered anaemia, or lifelong mild jaundice with anaemia points to inherited red cell defects that declare themselves in the first week. Thyroid illness in the baby prolongs jaundice and is tested when yellow outstays two weeks.

pitfalls: Skipping the sibling history, which is the single fastest predictor of a haemolytic course in the new baby.
Recording gestation as term or preterm without completed weeks and birth weight, which decide the testing threshold.
Missing an instrumental delivery and scalp swelling, so a preventable bilirubin load reads as unexplained.

probes.q: Which blood group pairings raise the risk of haemolytic jaundice?
probes.a: A group O mother with a group A or B baby, and a Rh negative mother with a Rh positive baby.

probes.q: Why does a scalp swelling after instrumental delivery worsen jaundice days later?
probes.a: The collected blood breaks down slowly and releases its pigment load into the circulation over days, adding to the newborn bilirubin.

probes.q: A sibling needed blood exchange for jaundice. What does this change for the new baby?
probes.a: It predicts the same haemolytic course, so the baby needs blood group and antibody testing with an early bilirubin measurement rather than routine reassurance.

skill.present.neonatal.jaundice.title: Presenting the jaundiced neonate
skill.present.neonatal.jaundice.oneLine: Hours of age first, then zone, trend, feeding and cause
skill.present.neonatal.jaundice.why: A neonatal presentation fails when age is given in days while the disease moves in hours. The listener needs hours of age with gestation and weight, the lowest yellow zone with the bilirubin trend, feeding and output, and the cause statement with red flags, in that order.
skill.present.neonatal.jaundice.body: Present in a fixed order and keep it to about two minutes. The listener should be able to name haemolytic disease before you say the blood groups.
keyPoints: Open with hours of age, gestation in completed weeks, birth and current weight, and place of delivery: a 70-hour-old term baby weighing 2.9 kg, delivered normally at the district hospital.
State the tempo in one breath: yellow first noticed at a named hour, now reaching a named zone, with the bilirubin values and their rise across repeat tests.
Give feeding and output next: feeds per day, waking behaviour, wet nappies, and stool and urine colour, since these carry the mechanism.
Close with the cause statement: blood groups with antibody result, bruising or sibling pattern, red flags present or absent, and the plan of repeat testing, light treatment or referral.

A worked example: this 70-hour-old term boy, birth weight 2.9 kg, turned yellow at 30 hours with colour now to the thighs. Mother is group O and the baby group B with a positive antibody test. Bilirubin has risen steeply across two tests. He feeds eight times a day but sleepily, with yellow stools and clear urine. In summary this is pathological jaundice from ABO mismatch needing urgent light treatment with exchange readiness.
pitfalls: Giving age in days when the thresholds, the rise rate and the trend all run in hours.
Listing examination zones without the bilirubin values and their direction, leaving the plan unsupported.
Omitting feeding, stool colour and red flags, which removes the mechanism and the urgency from the story.

probes.q: What order does a jaundiced neonate presentation follow?
probes.a: Hours of age with gestation and weight, tempo with zone and bilirubin trend, feeding and output, then the cause statement with red flags and plan.

skill.hx.neonatal.sepsis_risks.title: Sepsis risk factors in the newborn
skill.hx.neonatal.sepsis_risks.oneLine: Which mothers and which babies carry the highest risk of neonatal sepsis
skill.hx.neonatal.sepsis_risks.why: Sepsis in a neonate is often suspected before it is proved, and the background decides how hard you look. A baby with ruptured membranes of long duration, maternal fever, prematurity or an invasive line starts with a far higher pre-test probability, so the same mild lethargy means something different in that baby than in a well term infant with a clean perinatal history.

asks.text: Ask the mother whether she had fever, shivering, burning on passing urine, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge in the days before delivery.
Ask how many hours before birth the waters broke, whether the liquor looked green or smelt foul, and how long labour lasted.
Ask where the baby was born, who conducted the delivery, and whether the cord was cut with a clean blade and nothing applied to the stump.
Ask the gestation and birth weight, and whether the baby cried at once or needed bag and mask help, suction, or admission after birth.
For a baby already in the nursery, ask about intravenous lines, a ventilator or oxygen support, heel pricks, and any procedures done so far.
Ask about feeding from birth: time of first breastfeed, whether feeds have been regular, and any top feeds, prelacteal feeds, or animal milk given.
Ask about older siblings or previous newborn deaths in the family, and about overcrowding or a recent infection at home.

teach.heading: Maternal risks point to early onset disease
teach.body:
Early onset sepsis follows infection ascending from the birth canal, so the maternal story matters most in the first three days. Ask after fever near delivery, membranes ruptured for more than 18 hours, foul-smelling or meconium-stained liquor, prolonged or obstructed labour, and repeated unclean vaginal examinations.

A home birth with an unclean blade, resuscitation with unclean hands or tubes, and prelacteal feeds given before the first breastfeed all add risk in the Indian setting. Each of these is a question, not an accusation, and the mother usually answers plainly when asked directly.

teach.heading: Neonatal risks point to late onset disease
teach.body:
Late onset sepsis is acquired after birth, from the nursery, the ward, or the home. Prematurity and low birth weight below 2500 g carry the highest risk, because the skin and gut barriers are thin and the immune responses are immature. Resuscitation at birth, intravenous lines, ventilatory support, and long nursery stays add further risk.

Overcrowding, poor hand hygiene on the postnatal ward, and a sick contact at home complete the picture you must ask after. Group the answers as you take them: maternal and birth canal factors argue for early onset disease, while nursery, line, and home factors argue for late onset disease.

teach.heading: How the risk groups change your threshold
teach.body:
A preterm, low birth weight baby with membranes ruptured long before birth sits at the top of the risk ladder, and even soft signs in that baby deserve a full workup. A well term baby with none of these risks and a clean history can be watched while causes with a clearer story are considered.

Record gestation, birth weight, membrane rupture interval, and procedures in the first lines of your notes. These four facts do more work than any single examination finding in deciding whether this baby is worked up for sepsis.

probes.q: Name three maternal or labour risk factors for early onset neonatal sepsis.
probes.a: Fever near delivery, membranes ruptured for more than 18 hours, and foul-smelling liquor, with prolonged labour as a further factor.

probes.q: Which babies carry the highest risk of late onset sepsis, and why?
probes.a: Preterm and low birth weight babies, especially those with intravenous lines or ventilatory support, because their barriers are thin and their immune responses are immature.

probes.q: A term baby, clean hospital birth, day 6 fever with a discharging umbilical stump. Which risk group does this fit?
probes.a: Late onset disease from the home or ward environment, with the infected cord stump as the likely portal of entry rather than the birth canal.

skill.hx.neonatal.sepsis_course.title: History of the possibly septic neonate
skill.hx.neonatal.sepsis_course.oneLine: Poor feeding, changed activity, and temperature instability in the words of the mother
skill.hx.neonatal.sepsis_course.why: A neonate cannot localise a complaint, so sepsis presents as a change in behaviour rather than a symptom list. The mother notices that the baby feeds less, sleeps more, feels hot or cold, or cries differently. Unless you ask after each behaviour in turn, with time anchors, the story stays vague and the illness looks milder than it is.

asks.text: Ask when the baby last fed well, how the current feed compares in time and vigour, and whether feeds have become shorter, weaker, or refused.
Ask whether the baby is less active or more sleepy than before, harder to wake for feeds, or limp when picked up.
Ask whether the baby has felt hot with fever or cold to touch, and whether the hands and feet look pale, blue, or mottled.
Ask about breathing: fast breathing, noisy breathing, pauses in breathing, or a grunting sound with each breath.
Ask whether the cry has changed: weak, high-pitched, irritable, or inconsolable, and whether the baby has had jerky movements or fits.
Ask about vomiting, a swollen or tight abdomen, loose stools, blood in the stools, and how many wet nappies the baby passes in a day.
Ask about the umbilical stump: redness spreading to the skin around it, swelling, foul smell, or a yellow discharge.
Ask about yellow colour of the eyes or skin, pale stools or dark urine, bleeding from any site, or a rash with spots that do not fade.
Anchor every change to time: when the baby was last completely well, and whether the course has been hours or days.

teach.heading: Behaviour change is the presenting complaint
teach.body:
Think in behaviours, not organs. The classic story is a baby who fed well until yesterday, now sucks weakly, sleeps through feed times, and must be woken. Add temperature instability in either direction: fever in a term baby, or hypothermia with cold hands and feet in a preterm or very young infant.

Ask the mother to compare with the baby's own best day, not with other babies. A mother who says he takes half the feed and falls asleep at the breast has given you the diagnosis of poor feeding, even if she does not use those words.

teach.heading: Red flag behaviours that escalate the urgency
teach.body:
Respiratory signs carry the most weight at the bedside: fast breathing, chest indrawing, grunting, apnoea, or a need for oxygen. Next come neurological signs: a weak or high-pitched cry, blank staring, jerky movements, frank convulsions, a bulging fontanelle, or a baby who has become floppy or unresponsive.

Abdominal signs point towards gut involvement: vomiting, distension, blood in the stools, or a tender abdomen. Umbilical redness spreading beyond the stump with discharge marks omphalitis, a common portal for late onset sepsis. Bleeding, widespread spots that do not fade, and grey mottled skin mark severe disease with shock.

teach.heading: What the history must exclude while it builds
teach.body:
While building the sepsis story, ask the few questions that let you test the mimics later: birth asphyxia and resuscitation at birth, exact day of life when symptoms began, urine output and stools, jaundice course, and any medicines, ghutti, or home remedies given.

Note medicines by name, because some home preparations sedate the baby and mimic lethargy. Record the day of life of onset precisely: illness from birth suggests an early onset or perinatal cause, while a well interval of several days before deterioration fits late onset sepsis.

probes.q: A mother says her 6-day-old baby is dull and not feeding. What three behaviours do you ask after first?
probes.a: Feeding pattern and vigour, activity and wakefulness, and temperature change with colour of the hands and feet.

probes.q: Which history features mark severe or complicated neonatal sepsis?
probes.a: Apnoea or grunting with respiratory distress, convulsions or a bulging fontanelle, abdominal distension with blood in the stools, bleeding or non-fading spots, and shock with cold mottled skin.

probes.q: Why does the exact day of life of onset matter in the history?
probes.a: Illness from birth suggests an early onset or perinatal cause such as birth asphyxia, while a well interval of days before deterioration fits late onset sepsis acquired after birth.

skill.present.neonatal.sepsis_case.title: Presenting the septic neonate
skill.present.neonatal.sepsis_case.oneLine: Day of life, gestation, weight, portal, and plan in under three minutes
skill.present.neonatal.sepsis_case.why: A neonatal case presentation fails when it reads like an adult history with the ages changed. The consultant needs the day of life, the gestation and weights, the risk ladder, and the portal of entry before anything else, because those four facts decide whether this is early or late onset disease and how urgent the plan is.

teach.heading: The opening line carries the case
teach.body:
Open with age in days, sex, gestation, birth weight and current weight, informant, and the syndrome with its onset. A strong opening sounds like this: a 6-day-old term male baby, birth weight 2.5 kg, brought by the mother with two days of poor feeding, lethargy, and fever, currently showing features of late onset sepsis with omphalitis.

State early or late onset in the opening line itself, with the reasoning in one phrase: illness from birth with maternal risk factors, or a well interval of days with a postnatal portal. The listener should know your diagnostic position within thirty seconds.

teach.heading: Antenatal, natal, and postnatal in that order
teach.body:
Give antenatal history crisply: maternal age, parity, antenatal visits, maternal fever or urinary infection, and membrane rupture interval. Then natal: place of birth, mode of delivery, gestation, birth weight, cry at birth, and any resuscitation or nursery admission.

Then postnatal: feeding from birth, passage of urine and stools, immunisation at birth, weight trend, and the day-by-day course of the current illness. Group positives together and keep negatives short: no maternal fever, no prolonged rupture, cried at birth, no lines or ventilation.

teach.heading: Findings, screen, and plan to close
teach.body:
Present examination as appearance and vitals first, then the portal and systemic findings: cord stump with spreading redness and discharge, temperature, perfusion, respiratory signs, tone and fontanelle, abdomen, and weight. Quote the sepsis screen and cultures as pending or resulted, with what each result would change.

Close with a one-line summary, the diagnosis with onset type, severity, and the plan: blood culture before antibiotics, empiric cover, supportive care, monitoring, and referral level. End by naming what you will watch for in the next hours: feeding, alertness, perfusion, and apnoea.

probes.q: What four facts must the opening line of a neonatal sepsis presentation contain?
probes.a: Day of life with sex, gestation with birth weight and current weight, the informant, and the syndrome with its onset type.

probes.q: How do you order the background of a neonatal presentation?
probes.a: Antenatal, then natal, then postnatal course, grouping positives together and keeping negatives short.

skill.hx.rheumatic.cardiac.title: Cardiac symptom history in a child
skill.hx.rheumatic.cardiac.oneLine: Feeding, play, colour and posture tell you what the heart is doing
skill.hx.rheumatic.cardiac.why: A young child never complains of orthopnoea or palpitations in those words. The heart declares itself through interrupted feeds, play that stops early, slow weight gain and changes in colour or posture, so the history has to ask about daily life rather than adult symptoms.

asks.text: Note the informant, usually the mother, and how closely she has observed the child during feeds and play.
Ask how the child breathes during feeds and play: interrupted feeds, sweating on the forehead while feeding, needing rest during play, or keeping up with other children.
Ask about breathlessness lying flat, waking breathless at night, and how many pillows the child prefers, in the family's own words.
Ask about awareness of the heartbeat, chest pain or fainting, especially during play or excitement, and what the child was doing each time.
Ask about colour changes: blue lips or tongue when crying or feeding, pale or grey episodes, and whether the child squats or bends the knees up to rest.
Ask about growth and infections: weight gain over months, frequent chest infections, and days of school missed.
Date any sore throat that came before this illness: throat pain with fever, pain on swallowing, treatment taken, and sore throats in siblings or classmates around the same time.

skill.hx.rheumatic.cardiac.practice: Take the cardiac symptom history from the mother of a child with a murmur, covering feeds, play, colour, posture and the dated sore throat, and write the complaints in chronological order.
pitfalls: Asking a mother whether her child has orthopnoea and recording no when she does not know the word, instead of asking about pillows and night waking.
Recording palpitations as present without asking what the child was doing, so excitement and fear get labelled as arrhythmia.
Forgetting to date the sore throat, which removes the one fact that links a later arthritis or murmur to rheumatic fever.

teach.heading: Feeding, play and growth are the child's effort tolerance
teach.body:
An adult is asked about stairs and distance. A child is asked about feeds and play. A baby who tires at the breast, sweats on the forehead while feeding, or takes much longer over a feed is describing exertional breathlessness.

An older child who sits out games, lags behind friends on the way to school, or has fallen off the growth curve over months is describing the same limitation in a different vocabulary. Record what the child can no longer do, not a diagnosis.

teach.heading: Ask about colour and posture, not just breath
points: Blue lips or tongue during crying or feeding point to blood bypassing the lungs, while pale or grey colour with cold limbs points to poor output rather than low oxygen.
Squatting, or drawing the knees up to the chest to rest, is a posture the cyanotic child discovers for relief and should be asked about directly.
Spells of sudden deep blue colour with distress, often on waking or crying, are the cyanotic spell history and need their trigger, duration and recovery described.
Fainting during play or excitement is never just weakness in a child with a murmur and needs the exact activity, warning signs and recovery recorded.

teach.heading: Date the sore throat
teach.body:
Acute rheumatic fever follows a throat infection with group A streptococcus after the throat itself has settled, usually by a matter of weeks. The mother may not connect a forgotten sore throat to today's joint pains, so ask specifically.

Record whether the throat was treated and with what, since an untreated or partially treated episode carries more weight, and ask about sore throats in siblings and classmates, which mark the same crowded spread.

probes.q: The mother says her baby takes very long over feeds and sweats on the forehead. What is the baby telling you?
probes.a: Exertional breathlessness from a cardiac cause: the feed is the baby's exercise, and tiredness with sweating during feeds reflects the effort of breathing against cardiac limitation.

probes.q: Why do you ask a schoolchild with a murmur whether he squats while playing?
probes.a: Squatting is a posture children with cyanotic heart disease discover for relief, so asking about it tests for right to left shunting and spells without using words the family may not know.

probes.q: A child has migratory joint pains today and a sore throat that settled weeks ago. Why does the date of the sore throat matter?
probes.a: Acute rheumatic fever is a delayed immune response that appears weeks after the streptococcal throat infection has settled, so a dated preceding sore throat is the link that makes the joint pains fit rheumatic fever.

rubric.text: Elicits feeds, play and growth as effort tolerance
Asks about colour changes, squatting and spells
Dates the preceding sore throat and its treatment

skill.hx.rheumatic.risk.title: Risk, past and family history in the cardiac child
skill.hx.rheumatic.risk.oneLine: Past attacks, throats, injections, home and birth set the odds before you listen
skill.hx.rheumatic.risk.why: A murmur in a child means something different depending on what came before it: a past attack of rheumatic fever with missed injections points one way, while an unrepaired defect noticed since infancy points another. The background history carries that distinction, and it is lost if the student listens to the chest first.

asks.text: Ask about past episodes of joint pain or swelling: which joints, in what order, how long each lasted, and what treatment helped.
Ask about any past diagnosis of rheumatic fever or heart disease, any monthly injections advised, and how many were actually taken and on time.
Ask about recurrent sore throats in the child and in siblings, and about the home: number of rooms, people sleeping together, school class size, and safe water.

Ask the birth history: illness or fever with rash in pregnancy, place of delivery, birth weight, whether the baby cried at once, and any blue colour, fast breathing or poor feeding in the first weeks.
Ask the family history: heart disease in siblings, sudden deaths in young relatives, marriages within the family, and any known thyroid, diabetic or seizure history that changes drug choices.
Ask about current medicines in the mother's own words, any allergy especially to penicillin injections, and any recent painkillers or steroids that may have masked joint pains or fever.

skill.hx.rheumatic.risk.practice: Take the background history of a child with suspected rheumatic fever, covering past attacks, injections, home crowding, birth and family, and list which facts raise or lower the probability.
pitfalls: Accepting monthly injections are being taken without asking how many were missed, since lapsed prophylaxis is the commonest reason for a second attack.
Recording salicylates or steroids started before the joint pattern declared itself without noting that the picture may now be masked.
Skipping the birth history in a schoolchild, which loses the chance to separate a congenital defect murmuring since infancy from a newly acquired rheumatic murmur.

teach.heading: A past attack changes everything
teach.body:
A child who has already had rheumatic fever is sensitised, and every further streptococcal throat can add fresh valve damage. Ask whether monthly penicillin injections were advised and count the ones actually taken.

Also ask what eased past joint pains. Dramatic relief with salicylates is itself a clue to rheumatic arthritis, while painkillers or steroids started early can mask the migratory pattern the diagnosis depends on.

teach.heading: Crowding, school and throats travel together
points: Record rooms, sleepers per room, siblings and class size: streptococcal throats spread where children sleep and study close together.
Ask about recurrent sore throats in the child and in siblings, since the trigger often moves through the household and the classroom.
Note access to care: distance to the health centre and whether a throat infection gets seen and treated, since untreated episodes carry the risk.
Record safe water, sanitation and nutrition briefly, because the same household carries the other risks a paediatric history always screens for.

teach.heading: Birth and family history point at congenital disease
teach.body:
A murmur noticed in infancy, poor feeding and sweating from the early weeks, or slow weight gain from birth point towards a structural defect present since birth rather than an acquired rheumatic lesion.

Ask about illness with fever and rash in pregnancy, birth weight and cry at birth, heart disease in siblings, and marriages within the family, since these raise the probability of a congenital defect behind today's findings.

probes.q: Why do you count the monthly injections actually taken, rather than just noting they were advised?
probes.a: Because lapsed secondary prophylaxis is the commonest reason for a recurrent attack, so the count of injections actually taken decides whether this illness is a breakthrough on protection or disease in an unprotected child.

probes.q: A child took painkillers for a week before the joints were examined. Why does that matter?
probes.a: Salicylates and steroids can mask the migratory pattern of rheumatic arthritis and suppress fever, so treatment started before the picture declared itself can hide the very features the diagnosis needs.

probes.q: How does the birth history separate a congenital murmur from a rheumatic one in a schoolchild?
probes.a: Features present since infancy, such as a murmur noted early, poor feeding with sweating, or slow weight gain from birth, point to a structural defect present since birth, while a newly noted murmur after sore throats and joint pains points to acquired rheumatic disease.

rubric.text: Elicits past attacks and counts prophylaxis injections taken
Records crowding, school and throat spread in the household
Covers birth history and family heart disease

skill.present.rheumatic.case.title: Presenting the cardiac child
skill.present.rheumatic.case.oneLine: Type, valve, pressure, infection, failure and rhythm in one line
skill.present.rheumatic.case.why: The consultant listening to a cardiac presentation is waiting for one line that carries the whole haemodynamic state. A student who reads out findings in the order they were collected forces the listener to assemble the diagnosis themselves, and loses marks on a case they actually understood.

teach.heading: The diagnosis line comes first
teach.body:
Open with the informant, age and the type of heart disease: rheumatic or congenital, and acyanotic or cyanotic where relevant. Then name the valve and the lesion, evidence of pulmonary hypertension, evidence of infective endocarditis, whether the child is in failure, and the rhythm.

A complete line reads like this: rheumatic heart disease with mitral regurgitation, no evidence of pulmonary hypertension or endocarditis, not in failure, in sinus rhythm. Every clause after the valve answers a management question.

teach.heading: Follow the examination order
points: Give particulars with age in years and months, informant, and the presenting complaints with durations in the mother's words.
Summarise the dated sore throat, past attacks and injections, birth and family history, since these are the facts the diagnosis line depends on.
Present general examination, then the precordium in order: inspection, palpation, pulses and pressures, auscultation with the murmur fully characterised, and failure and endocarditis signs.
Close with other systems, the investigations that confirm and grade, the Jones position where rheumatic fever is suspected, and the plan including prophylaxis and referral.

teach.heading: A worked presentation
teach.body:
A 9 year old boy from a rural household, informant mother, presents with three weeks of shifting pains in the knees and ankles after a sore throat, and a new murmur. Examination shows an apical systolic murmur with a soft mid diastolic murmur, no failure and no endocarditis signs.

Investigations show evidence of recent streptococcal infection with raised inflammatory markers and valvulitis on echocardiography. This is acute rheumatic fever with carditis, and he needs throat eradication, anti-inflammatory cover, registration and long term secondary prophylaxis with cardiology follow up.

probes.q: What six things must the diagnosis line of a cardiac child carry?
probes.a: The type of heart disease, the valve and lesion, evidence of pulmonary hypertension, evidence of infective endocarditis, whether the child is in failure, and the rhythm.

probes.q: Why does the presentation give the diagnosis line before the findings?
probes.a: Because the listener needs the conclusion first to weigh each finding as it comes, and a presentation in collection order forces the consultant to assemble the diagnosis instead of judging it.

rubric.text: States type, valve, pressure, infection, failure and rhythm
Follows the examination order and closes with a plan
