skill.hx.rickets.illness.title: History of the rachitic illness
skill.hx.rickets.illness.oneLine: Bending legs in order, milestones beside them, alarms underneath
skill.hx.rickets.illness.why: Parents report bent legs, not rickets. The student who fixes when the bending began, what the child could do then, and whether fits or bone pain ever appeared can separate a slow nutritional illness from an inherited or renal one before any blood is drawn.

asks.text: When the legs first looked bent, and whether one side or both sides changed together.
Walking and standing: age of first steps, any slowing or refusal to walk that came with the bending.
Bone pain or tenderness: crying on handling, night waking with leg pain, or a limp after play.
What the wrists, ribs and head show at home: wide wrists noticed while dressing, beading along the ribs, a large soft head.
Fits, twitching around the mouth, or spasms of the hands and feet, with the age each happened.
Teeth and growth: age of first tooth, and whether height and weight gain have slowed beside other children.
What treatment has already been given: vitamin drops or syrups, calcium tonics, massage oils, or bone setting.

teach.heading: The bending has a birthday
teach.body: Ask exactly when the legs began to bend, and pin it to something the family remembers, such as a festival or a sibling milestone. Rickets bends legs only after the child bears weight, so bending noticed soon after first steps points to a nutritional cause building through infancy.

teach.heading: Milestones walk beside the legs
teach.body: Take gross motor milestones in the same breath as the bending: age of sitting, standing and first steps, and any recent refusal to walk. A child who walked on time and then slowed with leg pain is telling a different story from one who never walked at all.

teach.heading: Three alarms change the road
points: Fits or carpopedal spasm mean symptomatic low calcium and need urgent correction, not routine replacement.
Fracture after trivial injury means bone too soft for its load and needs protection alongside treatment.
Hair loss over the whole scalp with severe early rickets points toward receptor resistance, which ordinary doses will not overcome.

pitfalls: Recording bow legs without asking when they began, so a birth problem and a nutritional one read the same.
Never asking about fits, so the low calcium declares itself in the ward instead of the history.
Accepting delayed walking as family trait without asking about bone pain and wrist changes.

probes.q: A mother says her toddler has bow legs. What two dates do you fix first?
probes.a: When the bending was first noticed, and the age of first independent steps, since rickets bends legs only once weight bearing begins.

probes.q: Why do you ask about fits and hand spasms in a child with suspected rickets?
probes.a: They signal symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, which needs urgent calcium correction rather than routine vitamin replacement alone.

probes.q: What does total scalp hair loss suggest in an infant with severe rickets?
probes.a: Possible vitamin D receptor resistance, a severe inherited form that responds poorly to ordinary replacement and needs specialist care.

skill.hx.rickets.risk.title: Risk and background history in suspected rickets
skill.hx.rickets.risk.oneLine: Feed, sun, mother, medicines and family: where the deficiency came from
skill.hx.rickets.risk.why: Two children with the same bow legs need different plans when one was exclusively breastfed without supplements indoors and the other takes fits-preventing medicines with a parent who is short. Risk history finds the source and the inherited cases hiding behind it.

asks.text: Feeding: months of exclusive breastfeeding, age at weaning, and current daily milk, ragi, dal and oil intake.
Sunlight and housing: hours outdoors daily, swaddling or covered clothing, and whether the home gets direct sun.
Mother: her diet and sun exposure in pregnancy, calcium or vitamin tablets taken, and any bone pains of her own.
Birth and growth: preterm birth or low birth weight, twin birth, and the anganwadi growth curve since birth.
Medicines and illness: long fits medicines, repeated loose motions, liver or kidney illness, and any steroids given.
Family: short stature or bow legs in parents or siblings, marriage between relatives, and age of walking in siblings.
Social setting: who cooks and feeds the child, family income band, and distance to the nearest health centre.

teach.heading: Deficiency has an address
teach.body: Ask feeding and sunlight as one story: length of exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin supplements, age and content of weaning, daily milk and cereal intake, and hours the child spends outdoors. Indoors rearing with covered clothing can starve a child of vitamin D even where the sun is strong.

teach.heading: The mother is part of the history
teach.body: Ask about the pregnancy behind the child: the mother's own diet, time outdoors, and whether she took calcium or vitamin tablets. A deficient mother gives the infant poor stores at birth, so the illness can appear early even with fair later feeding.

teach.heading: Background that reframes the case
points: Preterm or low birth weight infants miss the late pregnancy mineral build-up and carry higher risk.
Long fits medicines and chronic gut, liver or kidney illness disturb vitamin handling and point away from diet alone.
Short bow-legged parents, affected siblings or related parents raise an inherited bone disorder that needs its own workup.

pitfalls: Asking diet without asking sunlight, so the indoor-kept child gets treated as a feeding problem only.
Skipping the mother's pregnancy diet and tablets, missing the depleted stores behind early disease.
Missing long fits medicines, which explain rickets that diet advice alone will not fix.

probes.q: Name three feeding or sunlight questions that belong in every suspected rickets history.
probes.a: Duration of exclusive breastfeeding without supplements, current daily milk and calcium food intake, and daily hours outdoors with clothing cover.

probes.q: Why does prematurity raise rickets risk?
probes.a: The preterm infant misses the late pregnancy transfer of calcium and phosphate, starting life with low mineral stores and faster postnatal demand.

probes.q: Which background findings push you toward an inherited rather than nutritional cause?
probes.a: Short bow-legged parents or siblings, related parents, and rickets that persists despite adequate vitamin and calcium replacement.

skill.present.rickets.case.title: Presenting the rachitic child
skill.present.rickets.case.oneLine: Two minutes from bending to plan, ending with healing markers
skill.present.rickets.case.why: The consultant judges the case on tempo and completeness: bending with its birthday, the body survey in order, the two blood results that decide the family of rickets, and a plan that names healing markers. A list of bone names without this shape is a viva failed.

teach.heading: The fixed order
teach.body: Open with age, feeding and sunlight in one line, then the bending with its birthday and the milestones beside it. Follow with the body survey from head to legs, the relevant negatives, the key blood and film results, and close with the plan and its healing markers.

teach.heading: Positives and negatives that decide
points: Positives in order: head size and softness, wrist width, rib beading, leg bowing measured between the knees, teeth and height gain.
Negatives that reframe: no fits or spasms, no fracture, no hair loss, no chronic drug or renal history.
Results that classify: low calcium and phosphate with high alkaline phosphatase and low vitamin D for nutritional disease, and the opposite vitamin D pattern for receptor resistance.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
This 2-year-old girl, breastfed for a year without supplements and kept indoors, has bilateral bow legs noticed since first steps at fourteen months, with wide wrists, a rachitic rosary and frontal bossing.

She never had fits, takes no long medicines, and her blood shows low calcium and phosphate with raised alkaline phosphatase. In summary this is nutritional rickets, for which I propose vitamin D with calcium, diet and sunlight counselling, and review of blood markers with a healing wrist film.

pitfalls: Presenting in examination order rather than age, tempo, syndrome, classifiers, plan.
Omitting feeding and sunlight, leaving the cause unstated and prevention unplanned.
Closing without healing markers, so nobody can tell response from failure at review.

probes.q: What five elements does a rickets case presentation carry in order?
probes.a: Feeding and sunlight clue, tempo of bending with milestones, head-to-leg survey with negatives, classifying blood and film results, and the plan with healing markers.

sources.locator: nutritional_rickets: clinicalPearls

asks.text: Fever in days: when the child first felt hot, whether fever returns each evening, how it is measured at home, and how it answers paracetamol syrup.
Cough from the start: the day it began, dry or wet, bursts or steady through the day, vomit after long bouts, and any gasp or whoop at the end.
Breathing as seen at home: the day fast breathing began, chest movement during sleep, whether it is faster than the usual, and whether breathing looks noisy or difficult.
Effort and sound: grunt with each breath out, whistle in the chest, flaring of the nostrils, and pulling in of the ribs or lower chest as the mother describes it.

Feeds and behaviour in this illness: breast takes and food quantity against the usual, drinking and swallowing, play and alertness, and whether the child recognises the mother and cries when disturbed.
The five danger signs, each asked outright: able to drink or breastfeed, vomit of everything given, fits in this illness, abnormal sleepiness or unconsciousness, and noisy breathing while calm.
Course and care so far: how each day differed from the last, syrups or antibiotics already given with doses where known, and visits to a clinic or health worker with what was advised.
Prolonged course screen: cough beyond two weeks, loss of weight over weeks, evening fever with night sweats, and any person at home with a long cough or on tuberculosis treatment.

keyPoints: Fix the tempo first: days of fever with new fast breathing is acute pneumonia, while weeks of cough with weight loss belongs to tuberculosis and recurrent bouts with colds belong to wheeze.
Take the story in order: which came first, how each day differed, and what the child can still do. Order carries the diagnosis.
Record home breathing in the mother's own words: fast, noisy or difficult, with grunt or flaring where seen. Home breathing is the classification before the count.
Ask every danger sign even when the child looks bright: inability to drink, vomit of everything, fits, abnormal sleepiness and calm stridor each raise urgency on their own.
Quantify feeds against the usual: half feeds with drinking kept down differs wholly from refusal of all fluids with vomit of everything.
Close the illness with drugs already given and the prolonged screen, so antibiotics taken and tuberculosis contacts are known before examination.
skill.hx.childhood.pneumonia_illness.oneLine: Days of fever and cough with home breathing, danger signs and tempo
pitfalls: Recording cough without days, so a three week tubercular cough hides inside an acute story.
Skipping the danger signs because the child smiles in clinic, missing the vomit of everything or the fit at home that decides referral.
Writing pneumonia as the complaint instead of fever, cough and fast breathing in the mother's own words with durations.
Forgetting what syrups were already given, so an antibiotic taken for days is mistaken for an untreated illness.
skill.hx.childhood.pneumonia_illness.practice: Take this illness history from the mother of a child with fever and cough, fix the days and the order of fever, cough and fast breathing, ask all five danger signs, and close with one line on tempo.

probes.a: The total days of fever, the day the cough began, and the day fast breathing appeared, taken in order.
probes.q: What three elements fix the tempo of a pneumonia history?

probes.a: Whether the child can drink or breastfeed, whether vomiting brings out everything given, any fits, abnormal sleepiness or unconsciousness, and stridor heard while calm.
probes.q: Which five danger signs must be asked in every child with cough and fast breathing?

probes.a: Weeks of cough with loss of weight and a household contact on treatment favour tuberculosis over acute pneumonia, so test for tuberculosis rather than repeat antibiotics.
probes.q: Cough for four weeks with loss of weight and a grandfather on tuberculosis treatment. What road does this favour?

rubric.text: Fixes days and order of fever, cough and fast breathing
Records home breathing with grunt, whistle or flaring where seen
Asks all five danger signs and acts on any one
Screens for prolonged cough, weight loss and household contact

sources.locator: pneumonia_long_case: clinicalPearls

teach.body: Days of fever with cough and fast breathing that began yesterday is acute pneumonia. Weeks of cough with loss of weight is tuberculosis until proved otherwise. Recurrent bouts that ease between colds is wheeze. Fix which road first, because each road owns a different drug and a different urgency.
teach.heading: Tempo is the diagnosis before the chest

teach.body: The mother saw the illness before you did, so her report of fast, noisy or difficult breathing opens the history. Then ask each danger sign outright: drinking, vomit of everything, fits, sleepiness and calm stridor. Any one of them outranks the chest signs and sends the child for urgent care.
teach.heading: Home breathing and danger signs

teach.body: Quantify what the child still takes against the usual, and list every syrup already given, since an antibiotic taken for days changes the reading of the fever. Close with the prolonged screen of weeks, weight and contacts, so tuberculosis never hides behind an acute label.
teach.heading: Feeds, drugs and the prolonged screen

skill.hx.childhood.pneumonia_illness.title: History of the pneumonia illness in a child
skill.hx.childhood.pneumonia_illness.why: The pneumonia story must sort three roads at once: days of fever with new fast breathing that needs antibiotics, weeks of cough with weight loss that needs tuberculosis testing, and recurrent wheeze that needs a bronchodilator and not antibiotics. Tempo plus danger signs does the sorting before the chest is touched.

asks.text: Age in months, birth weight, born early or at full term, cry at birth and any early hospital stay.
Feeds in a day: breast exclusivity, bottle quantity and dilution, age at weaning, and meat, egg and green intake, with growth faltering where seen.
Immunisation card: BCG scar, pentavalent and pneumococcal doses, measles dose with vitamin A, and the next dose due.
Past chest illness: admissions for breathing trouble, wheeze with every cold, inhaler or nebuliser use, and ear discharge that keeps returning.
Recent rash illness with fever that could be measles, loss of weight over weeks, and any household contact with a long cough or on tuberculosis treatment.
Home air and rooms: chulha or gas for cooking, where the child sits during cooking, beedi or tobacco smoke inside, and persons sleeping in one room.
Drugs already given for this illness: antibiotics, cough syrups and traditional remedies, with who advised each and for how many days.

keyPoints: Record age in months and birth weight together: every breathing cutoff and much of the risk turns on these two numbers.
Quantify milk and weaning: prolonged bottle feeds of over diluted milk with little else is the classic remediable setup for repeated infection.
Read the card, not the memory: BCG scar, pentavalent, pneumococcal, measles and vitamin A each close a preventable door.
Ask past chest episodes and rash illness directly: repeated wheeze points away from pneumonia and recent measles reframes the whole case.
Map smoke and crowding without judgement: chulha place, indoor beedi smoke and persons per room each carry advice for discharge.
List drugs already given: antibiotics taken change the differential, and remedies given can mask fever and delay the visit, so record each with days taken.
skill.hx.childhood.pneumonia_risk.oneLine: Birth, feeds, immunisation, smoke and contacts that explain this child
pitfalls: Skipping birth weight and feeds, so the remediable causes of repeated illness stay hidden.
Accepting immunised for age without seeing the card, missing the absent measles or pneumococcal dose.
Never asking where the child sits during cooking, so chulha smoke exposure goes unadvised.
Forgetting drugs already given, including antibiotics that change the differential and the culture result.
skill.hx.childhood.pneumonia_risk.practice: Take the risk history for a child with fast breathing, organise birth, feeds, immunisation, smoke and contacts in order, and end with one line of advice on each gap found.

probes.a: Low birth weight with prematurity, incomplete immunisation, malnutrition with faulty feeding, and indoor smoke with overcrowding.
probes.q: Name four background facts that raise pneumonia risk in a young child.

probes.a: Record the missing measles and pneumococcal doses as open preventable causes, arrange catch up under the national programme, and counsel that measles with a recent rash reframes the chest illness.
probes.q: The card shows three infant doses but no measles dose and no pneumococcal dose. What do you record and advise?

probes.a: Keep the child in clean air away from chulha smoke during cooking, keep beedi smoke fully outside the rooms, and ease night crowding with cross ventilation where the family can manage it.
probes.q: The child sits beside the mother at a chulha while the grandfather smokes beedis on the veranda. What advice on each source?

rubric.text: Records age in months, birth weight and daily feeds with dilution
Reads the card for BCG, pentavalent, pneumococcal, measles and vitamin A
Maps cooking smoke, indoor tobacco smoke and crowding
Lists drugs already given and past chest episodes

teach.body: A low birth weight infant fed on over diluted bottle milk with late weaning carries more risk than the same cough in a well grown child. Quantify each feed and plot growth faltering where seen, since faulty feeding is both cause and discharge plan.
teach.heading: Birth, feeds and growth set the risk

teach.body: Read the immunisation card dose by dose and name each gap with its catch up date. Ask past admissions, wheeze with every cold, recent rash illness and household cough or treatment, since measles and tuberculosis contacts reframe the case.
teach.heading: The card and the contacts

teach.body: Ask where the child sits while food cooks and who smokes inside, then advise clean air with outside smoking and cross ventilation. List antibiotics, syrups and remedies already given, since they change the differential and must never be repeated blindly.
teach.heading: Smoke, rooms and drugs

skill.hx.childhood.pneumonia_risk.title: Background and risk history in childhood pneumonia
skill.hx.childhood.pneumonia_risk.why: Two children with the same cough carry different risks: a low birth weight infant with gaps in immunisation who sits in chulha smoke is a different illness from the same cough in a well grown fully immunised child. The background also names what to fix at home, so this admission is not repeated next month.

skill.present.childhood.pneumonia.body: Present in a fixed order and keep it near two minutes for a focused case. The listener should reach the classification before you name it.
keyPoints: Open with the child in one sentence: age in months, informant, and days of fever with cough and fast breathing.
Give risks next in brief: birth weight, feeds, immunisation gaps and smoke, since they explain this child and shape advice.
Give breathing facts as classified evidence: counted rate with cutoff, indrawing, danger signs, then the local patch.

A worked example: This 2 year old boy, reported by his mother, has three days of fever with wet cough and fast breathing since yesterday, with half feeds but drinking kept down. Rate 54 with lower chest indrawing, no danger signs, and a dull bronchial patch at the right base. In summary this is severe pneumonia by indrawing, right lower lobe, for referral with oxygen and feeds with review in two days.
Close with plan and prevention: site of care, oxygen, feeds, follow up date, red flags told, and the gap fixed at home.
skill.present.childhood.pneumonia.oneLine: Age in months, tempo, breathing findings, classification and plan in two minutes
pitfalls: Presenting signs in the order collected rather than child, tempo, risks, breathing, classification, plan.
Quoting a rate without its age cutoff, so the number carries no meaning.
Closing without site of care, follow up date and red flags, leaving the mother unprepared.
Omitting relevant negatives such as absent danger signs, which do real work in grading.
skill.present.childhood.pneumonia.practice: Present the pneumonia case in under two minutes to your consultant, ending with classification, site of care and follow up before any question is asked.

probes.a: Age in months with the informant and reliability, then the tempo in days from fever to cough to fast breathing.
probes.q: What opens the presentation of a child with pneumonia?

probes.a: The counted rate against the age cutoff, indrawing present or absent, danger signs present or absent, and the local dull bronchial patch, each in abstract terms.
probes.q: What breathing facts must the middle carry, and in what form?

probes.a: With the ARI classification stated as the diagnosis, the site of care it decides, oxygen need from saturation, and the follow up date with red flags explained to the mother.
probes.q: How do you close the presentation, and what must never be missing?

rubric.text: Opens with age in months, informant and tempo in days
States counted rate with cutoff, indrawing and danger signs
States the classification with the feature that earned it
Closes with site of care, follow up and red flags

steps.text: Open with age in months, residence, the informant with reliability, and the tempo in days from fever to cough to fast breathing.
State the risks that matter: birth weight, feeds and growth, immunisation gaps, past episodes, and smoke with contacts.
Give the breathing findings in abstract terms: the counted rate against the age cutoff, indrawing present or absent, and danger signs present or absent.
Give the local chest in one line: the dull bronchial patch with side and lobe, or its absence where the chest wheezes without a patch.
State the classification as the diagnosis with the exact feature that earned it, and name what was excluded with one reason each.
Close with site of care, oxygen need from saturation, feeds, the follow up date, and red flags explained to the mother.

teach.body: One sentence carries age in months, informant and days from fever to cough to fast breathing. Add birth weight, feeds, immunisation gaps and smoke in brief, since they explain why this child fell ill and what advice follows.
teach.heading: Open with child, tempo and risks

teach.body: List the counted rate with its age cutoff, indrawing present or absent, danger signs present or absent, then the local dull bronchial patch. Never state severe pneumonia or pneumonia without the exact feature that put the child there.
teach.heading: Grade with the signs that earned it

teach.body: State home or hospital with oxygen need from saturation in the same breath as the classification. Then feeds, the follow up date, red flags told to the mother, and the gap fixed at home, so the case never returns unchanged.
teach.heading: Close with care, oxygen and return

skill.present.childhood.pneumonia.title: Presenting the child with pneumonia
skill.present.childhood.pneumonia.why: The consultant judges this case on whether classification and plan arrive together: the counted rate with its cutoff, indrawing and danger signs, then severe pneumonia or pneumonia with home or hospital in the same breath. A presentation that lists signs without classifying describes the child but leaves the listener unable to act.

skill.approach.paed.immunisation_counsel.title: Paediatric immunisation counselling and addressing vaccine hesitancy
skill.approach.paed.immunisation_counsel.oneLine: Structured parental counselling on vaccine schedules, benefits, minor adverse events, and addressing safety concerns
skill.approach.paed.immunisation_counsel.why: Vaccine hesitancy often stems from fear of adverse events or conflicting misinformation. Empathetic, structured communication establishing vaccine benefits, expected minor reactions, and contraindication facts preserves immunisation coverage and protects children from vaccine-preventable diseases.

steps.text: Greet the parents respectfully, introduce yourself, and create an unhurried, supportive environment.
Elicit specific parental concerns, doubts, or previous adverse experiences with vaccination using open-ended questions.
Acknowledge and validate parental emotions empathetically without adopting an argumentative or dismissive tone.
Inspect the child's Mother and Child Protection card to verify age, previous doses, and currently due vaccines.
Explain the protective benefits of the scheduled vaccines in simple, accessible, non-technical language.
Discuss common expected minor adverse events such as low-grade fever, irritability, and local tenderness, advising on paracetamol use.
Clarify false contraindications including mild colds, low-grade fever, diarrhoea, and malnutrition to prevent missed opportunities.
Explain urgent danger signs requiring immediate return, such as high fever, persistent crying for over three hours, or lethargy.
Confirm parental understanding, obtain consent, record the next due date on the card, and thank the family warmly.

skill.approach.paed.immunisation_counsel.practice: Practise a five-minute counselling session with a hesitant parent worried about post-vaccine fever following pentavalent vaccine, using the presumptive communication approach.
pitfalls: Dismissing parental concerns as unscientific, which damages rapport and drives parents toward complete vaccine refusal.
Failing to warn parents about expected mild fever or pain, leading to anxiety and loss of confidence in the healthcare system.
Cancelling vaccination for minor illnesses like common colds or teething, resulting in missed immunisation opportunities.
Omitting clear written and verbal return instructions for the next scheduled dose on the immunisation card.

probes.q: What common mild adverse events should parents be warned about after routine pentavalent vaccination?
probes.a: Mild fever, irritability, and transient pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site lasting one to two days.

probes.q: Name two common false contraindications to childhood vaccination that frequently cause missed opportunities.
probes.a: Minor respiratory infections with low fever, mild diarrhoea, malnutrition, and a stable neurological history.

probes.q: What constitutes an absolute contraindication to administering a subsequent dose of a vaccine?
probes.a: An immediate severe anaphylactic reaction or acute encephalopathy within seven days following a previous dose.

probes.q: How should a clinician address a parent who refuses vaccination due to false rumours regarding autism?
probes.a: Validate the parent's protective intent, explain that comprehensive international research has thoroughly disproved any link between MMR and autism, and outline the severe risks of measles outbreaks.

rubric.text: Greets parents respectfully, introduces self, and establishes a supportive dialogue
Elicits specific doubts, fears, and previous experiences regarding vaccination through open questions
Validates parental concerns empathetically without arguing or showing frustration
Inspects the immunisation record or Mother and Child Protection card to verify due vaccines
Explains the protection and disease-preventing benefits offered by the due vaccines in clear language
Counsels on expected mild adverse events including low fever, local tenderness, and paracetamol use
Dispels false contraindications such as minor cough, low fever, or teething
Outlines emergency danger signs requiring immediate medical contact (high fever, persistent crying, lethargy)
Records the date and vaccines for the next visit clearly on the card and confirms understanding

teach.heading: Communication strategy for vaccine hesitancy
teach.body:
Vaccine hesitancy represents a continuum between complete acceptance and outright refusal. Parents often delay vaccines because of alarming reports seen online or heard from peers.

Clinicians must adopt an open, empathetic approach. Validating the parent's protective intent before providing factual information builds trust. Dismissive communication increases resistance and drives parents toward total refusal.

teach.heading: Differentiating true contraindications from harmless myths
teach.body:
The majority of conditions cited by hesitant parents or misinformed health workers are not valid contraindications. Mild upper respiratory infections, low-grade fever under 38.5 C, mild diarrhoea, malnutrition, and stable neurological conditions are false contraindications.

True contraindications are few: severe anaphylaxis to a prior dose or constituent, and severe immunosuppression for live attenuated vaccines.

skill.approach.paed.ors_counsel_prep.title: Oral rehydration solution preparation, counselling, and fluid management
skill.approach.paed.ors_counsel_prep.oneLine: Correct reconstitution of low-osmolarity ORS, dosage explanation, feeding advice, and home fluid education
skill.approach.paed.ors_counsel_prep.why: Incorrect reconstitution of ORS powder with inappropriate water volumes produces hypernatraemic dehydration or ineffective rehydration. Clear maternal counselling on preparation, administration rate, and zinc supplementation prevents hospitalisation and reduces mortality from acute gastroenteritis.

steps.text: Greet the mother, explain the essential role of oral rehydration solution in replacing fluid lost through watery diarrhoea, and reassure her.
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and clean water before demonstrating solution preparation.
Show the standard packet of WHO low-osmolarity ORS and check the packet integrity and expiry date.
Measure exactly one litre of clean drinking water (boiled and cooled water if safety is uncertain) into a clean vessel.
Empty the entire packet of ORS powder into the measured litre of water; do not mix partial packets in smaller amounts of water.
Stir the solution with a clean spoon until all powder dissolves completely and the liquid becomes clear.
Instruct the mother to give the solution with a clean cup and spoon in small, frequent sips, rather than using a feeding bottle.
Explain management if the child vomits: wait ten minutes, then resume offering ORS slowly, one teaspoonful every one to two minutes.
Advise the mother to continue frequent breastfeeding and age-appropriate feeding throughout the diarrhoeal episode without dilution.
Counsel on zinc supplementation (20 mg daily for infants older than 6 months for 14 days) and explain that prepared ORS must be discarded after 24 hours.

skill.approach.paed.ors_counsel_prep.practice: Demonstrate the step-by-step reconstitution of a one-litre ORS sachet and counsel a simulated mother on volume requirements and feeding continuation during diarrhoea.
pitfalls: Mixing only part of an ORS sachet into an unmeasured cup of water, causing dangerous hypernatraemic dehydration.
Boiling the reconstituted ORS solution, which alters electrolyte stability and precipitates mineral salts.
Administering ORS with a feeding bottle and teat instead of a cup and spoon, increasing aerophagia and bacterial contamination.
Withholding food or breast milk during the diarrhoeal episode, which worsens intestinal mucosal atrophy and precipitates malnutrition.
Storing reconstituted ORS at room temperature for more than 24 hours, permitting significant bacterial proliferation.

probes.q: What volume of clean water must be used to dissolve a standard full packet of WHO low-osmolarity ORS?
probes.a: Exactly one litre of clean drinking water.

probes.q: How long can reconstituted ORS solution be safely kept before it must be discarded?
probes.a: It must be discarded after 24 hours because of the risk of bacterial contamination.

probes.q: Why is oral zinc supplementation recommended for 14 days in acute childhood diarrhoea?
probes.a: Zinc reduces the duration and severity of the diarrhoeal episode, repairs mucosal integrity, and prevents recurrences over the following two to three months.

probes.q: What dangerous metabolic complication occurs if a mother adds an entire packet of ORS powder to only one cup of water?
probes.a: Hypernatraemic dehydration, which can lead to intracranial haemorrhage, brain oedema, convulsions, and permanent neurological injury.

rubric.text: Washes hands thoroughly with soap and clean water before handling equipment
Inspects the WHO low-osmolarity ORS packet for integrity, expiry date, and instructions
Measures exactly one litre of clean drinking water into a clean container
Pours the entire sachet of ORS into the full litre and stirs until completely dissolved
Demonstrates feeding with a clean cup and spoon rather than a bottle or teat
Explains that if the child vomits, wait 10 minutes and then resume ORS slowly by spoonfuls
Emphasises continuous breastfeeding and uninterrupted feeding during the diarrhoeal episode
Prescribes zinc for 14 days and instructs the mother to discard leftover prepared ORS after 24 hours

teach.heading: Principles of low-osmolarity oral rehydration
teach.body:
The World Health Organization low-osmolarity ORS formulation has an osmolarity of 245 mOsm/L, containing 75 mEq/L sodium and 75 mmol/L glucose.

Coupled sodium-glucose transport across the intestinal brush border remains intact during secretory diarrhoea. Glucose facilitates sodium absorption, which draws water along an osmotic gradient. Low-osmolarity solution reduces stool output, shortens vomiting, and eliminates unscheduled intravenous therapy.

teach.heading: Practical counselling points for mothers
teach.body:
Measurement accuracy is vital. Adding powder to insufficient water causes severe hypernatraemia, while excess water dilutes electrolytes. The entire packet must be mixed in exactly one litre of water.

Feeding must continue during rehydration. Fasting compromises enterocyte repair and precipitates malnutrition. Frequent breastfeeding should continue on demand, and zinc must be given daily for 14 days.

skill.exam.paed.imnci_danger_signs.title: IMNCI general danger signs assessment and emergency triage
skill.exam.paed.imnci_danger_signs.oneLine: Rapid systematic evaluation for inability to drink, vomiting everything, convulsions, and lethargy or unconsciousness
skill.exam.paed.imnci_danger_signs.why: The presence of any single general danger sign categorises the child as severely ill under IMNCI guidelines, mandating urgent pre-referral treatment, stabilisation, and immediate referral to a hospital facility.

steps.text: Observe the child without touching to evaluate spontaneous responsiveness, resting posture, and eye contact.
Ask the mother: Is the child able to drink or breastfeed?
Offer the child clean water or breast milk directly to observe whether the child is able to suckle or swallow.
Ask the mother: Does the child vomit everything that is eaten or drunk?
Check if the child vomits immediately following fluid intake or exhibits persistent effortless emesis.
Ask the mother: Has the child had convulsions or fits during this current illness?
Assess the child's level of consciousness: determine whether the child is abnormally sleepy, difficult to wake, or completely unarousable.
If not awake, check if the child opens eyes or responds to voice or gentle tactile stimulation.
Check for emergency signs: obstructed breathing, severe respiratory distress, central cyanosis, cold extremities, or capillary refill over 3 seconds.
Categorise the child immediately and initiate emergency pre-referral measures including airway clearance, warming, and urgent transport.

skill.exam.paed.imnci_danger_signs.normal: Alert, attentive child who makes eye contact, drinks eagerly or suckles well, retains feeds without vomiting, with no history of convulsions, and arouses normally.
skill.exam.paed.imnci_danger_signs.abnormal: Inability to drink or suckle, vomiting everything, convulsions during current illness, lethargy, or unconsciousness.
skill.exam.paed.imnci_danger_signs.significance: Any one general danger sign indicates high risk of rapid mortality from sepsis, severe pneumonia, meningitis, or decompensated shock, requiring urgent pre-referral treatment and emergency referral.
skill.exam.paed.imnci_danger_signs.practice: Rapidly screen a paediatric patient in the casualty triage area for the four IMNCI general danger signs within two minutes.
pitfalls: Relying solely on maternal assertion that the child cannot drink without personally offering fluids or breast milk to observe swallowing.
Mistaking a sleeping healthy child for a lethargic child without attempting gentle awakening.
Failing to ask specifically about seizures that occurred at home before arrival at the clinic.
Delaying urgent pre-referral treatment and hospital transfer while waiting for non-essential investigations.

probes.q: What are the four IMNCI general danger signs in a child aged 2 months to 5 years?
probes.a: Inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions during this illness, and lethargy or unconsciousness.

probes.q: How should a healthcare worker verify if a child is unable to drink or breastfeed?
probes.a: Offer the child clean water in a cup or ask the mother to breastfeed, and observe if the child is too weak to suck or swallow.

probes.q: What distinguishes lethargy from normal sleepiness in an acutely ill child?
probes.a: A normally sleeping child wakes with voice or gentle touch and becomes interactive, whereas a lethargic child does not look at the parent or clinician, appears drowsy, and shows no interest in surroundings.

probes.q: If an 8-month-old infant with high fever has had two convulsions at home and is now lethargic, what immediate pre-referral actions must be taken before transfer?
probes.a: Ensure airway patency, administer oxygen, give a first dose of intramuscular antibiotic, and treat hypoglycaemia or provide oral sugar water.

rubric.text: Observes the child's alert state and interaction before touching or disturbing the patient
Asks if the child can drink or suckle and directly offers water or breast milk to observe swallowing
Inquires specifically whether the child vomits everything ingested
Asks whether the child had convulsions or seizures during the present illness
Determines whether the child is lethargic or unconscious by attempting verbal and tactile arousal
Screens for immediate emergency signs including stridor, severe retractions, and prolonged capillary refill
Correctly identifies any danger sign and classifies the child as severely ill
Initiates urgent pre-referral stabilisation (warming, airway, oxygen, first antibiotic dose) and arranges transport

teach.heading: The IMNCI triage framework
teach.body:
The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMNCI) protocol uses a colour-coded syndromic approach to triage sick children aged 2 months to 5 years.

The initial assessment always checks for the four general danger signs. A child with any danger sign has a high probability of severe infection, septicaemic shock, meningitis, or cerebral malaria, and is classified in the red row, requiring urgent hospital admission.

teach.heading: Immediate pre-referral stabilization
teach.body:
When a general danger sign is identified, transfer must not be delayed. However, essential pre-referral treatments significantly improve survival during transport.

Key interventions include clearing secretions, providing supplemental oxygen if cyanosed, administering a first dose of recommended parenteral antibiotic, preventing hypothermia by wrapping, and preventing hypoglycaemia with breast milk or sugar solution.

skill.exam.paed.development_screening.title: Developmental screening and milestone examination across four domains
skill.exam.paed.development_screening.oneLine: Objective clinical elicitation of gross motor, fine motor, language, and personal-social milestones using standard screening tools
skill.exam.paed.development_screening.why: Parental reporting can understate or overstate developmental progress. Direct observational screening with age-appropriate test items (such as red ring, wooden cubes, and small pellets) objectively verifies milestone acquisition and pinpoints domain-specific deficits.

steps.text: Establish rapport with the child and mother in a quiet, non-threatening room with adequate illumination.
Calculate the child's exact chronological age and adjust for gestational prematurity if born before 37 weeks.
Observe spontaneous behaviour: posture, mobility, eye contact, curiosity, vocalisation, and interaction with the caregiver.
Test gross motor milestones: evaluate head control, sitting balance, crawling, pulling to stand, standing unsupported, and walking according to age.
Test fine motor and adaptive skills: present a red ring or rattle, offer 2.5 cm wooden cubes, and test for transfer, tower building, and neat pincer grasp using a raisin or small pellet.
Assess personal and social skills: check for social smile, recognition of mother, response to mirror, waving bye-bye, and cooperative play.
Assess language and communication: evaluate response to voice, sound localisation, babbling, receptive vocabulary, and expressive words or sentences.
Screen for red-flag developmental signs: absent neck holding at 5 months, unable to sit without support at 9 months, not walking at 18 months, or absent words at 18 months.
Note any hand dominance before 18 months (suggesting contralateral hemiparesis) and verify that previously acquired milestones have not been lost.
Explain findings clearly to the parents, provide positive reinforcement, and outline developmental stimulation guidance or referral if delay is identified.

skill.exam.paed.development_screening.normal: Milestones achieved within the normal age windows across all four domains, with symmetric limb use and steady developmental progress.
skill.exam.paed.development_screening.abnormal: Failure to achieve key milestones by age limits, delay across two or more domains (global developmental delay), loss of previously attained skills, or early hand preference before 18 months.
skill.exam.paed.development_screening.significance: Early identification of developmental delay enables timely intervention, specialist referral, and neurodevelopmental therapy when neuroplasticity is maximal.
skill.exam.paed.development_screening.practice: Perform a structured developmental screen on a 12-month-old infant, testing gross motor stability, neat pincer grasp, and response to name.
pitfalls: Failing to calculate corrected gestational age in infants born preterm, falsely diagnosing developmental delay.
Conducting the examination when the child is hungry, fatigued, or distressed, leading to uncooperative refusal and false negative testing.
Ignoring early hand preference before 18 months, missing early spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy.
Overlooking milestone regression, which points to neurodegenerative or metabolic storage disease rather than static encephalopathy.

probes.q: By what age should an infant sit unsupported without falling, and what is the red-flag cut-off?
probes.a: Normal sitting without support occurs at 8 months; failure to sit unsupported by 9 to 10 months is a developmental red flag.

probes.q: What does the development of an apparent hand preference in an infant under one year of age suggest?
probes.a: It suggests pathological weakness or spasticity of the contralateral hand, such as in hemiplegic cerebral palsy, because handedness normally develops after 18 to 24 months.

probes.q: Explain the difference between a crude pincer grasp and a neat pincer grasp, and give the typical ages of attainment.
probes.a: Crude or inferior pincer grasp uses the pad of the thumb against the pad of the index finger at 9 months, whereas neat or fine pincer grasp uses the tip of the thumb against the tip of the index finger at 12 months.

probes.q: A 2-year-old child who previously spoke twenty words and ran steadily now stumbles, has stopped speaking, and does not respond to his name. How does this presentation differ prognostically from static developmental delay?
probes.a: This represents neurodevelopmental regression, indicating a progressive neurodegenerative condition, inborn error of metabolism, or subacute panencephalitis, which carries a guarded prognosis and requires urgent metabolic and neurological investigation rather than simple rehabilitation.

rubric.text: Calculates exact chronological age and adjusts for gestational prematurity if applicable
Directly observes and tests age-appropriate gross motor milestones including posture, sitting, and walking
Tests fine motor-adaptive skills using cubes, ring, or pellets to evaluate grasp, transfer, and pincer grasp
Observes personal-social interaction including eye contact, smiling, waving bye-bye, or interactive play
Tests receptive and expressive language milestones from babbling to vocabulary and phrase speech
Actively checks for domain-specific red flags such as absent sitting at 9 months or absent walking at 18 months
Examines for limb movement asymmetry, early hand preference, and verifies absence of regression
Communicates findings empathetically to the parent and outlines home stimulation or referral plan

teach.heading: Principles of objective developmental screening
teach.body:
Development progresses in an orderly cephalocaudal and proximodistal sequence. While parent questionnaires provide helpful screening, direct observation is essential to verify skill quality.

Testing must be conducted when the child is calm, fed, and rested, seated comfortably on the parent's lap. The examiner begins with less threatening observation before introducing test objects like rattles, cubes, and pellets.

teach.heading: Developmental red flags requiring prompt intervention
teach.body:
Red flags represent the outer limits of normal milestone attainment beyond which pathological delay is highly probable.

Major red flags include: absent neck holding by 5 months, inability to sit without support by 10 months, inability to stand with support by 12 months, not walking independently by 18 months, lack of single words by 18 months, and persistent primitive reflexes beyond 6 months.
